Preface This book returns, at greater length and by a different method, to a question first posed in Chapter XVIII of Early Christianity: what historical relationship can be established between the Avesta, Zoroastrianism and Yahwism of the Persian period, and which elements of that relationship reached early Christianity by way of Second Temple Judaism? The answer advanced here is a thesis, and is offered as such. The influence of Achaemenid Iranian religion and culture upon the communities of the Near East was real, and was concentrated decisively during the reign of Darius I (522–486 BCE). The imperial organization established under that king brought the Yahwist communities of Yehud, Mesopotamia and Egypt into sustained contact with the language, institutions and religious culture of Iran. This contact may be assessed on four mutually reinforcing planes: language and administration, where borrowing is demonstrable; royal ideology, where correspondence is probable; cult and material culture, where correspondence is probable in its general outlines; and the conceptual sphere (dualism, angelology, judgement, renewal of the world and the figure of the saviour), where Iranian influence is proposed as an explanation for affinities found in later Judaism and Christianity—although typological resemblance alone does not establish dependence. The thesis rests not on a repeated commonplace but on a graduated examination of each feature, distinguishing what the documents establish from what they merely suggest. An argument for influence can be sustained with rigour only if every link is identified as securely attested, probable or conjectural. Three decisions govern the work. The first is linguistic: words are compared before ideas. The book therefore opens with Hebrew, Imperial Aramaic, Greek and Iranian. Aramaic, already used in extensive administrative networks throughout the Near East before Darius and consolidated as a language of empire under the Achaemenids, was one of the documented vehicles through which legal terms, formulae and practices circulated. The second decision is documentary: each claim concerning the Iranian world is dated by reference to its source, since much of the Avesta in its transmitted form and almost the entire corpus of Pahlavi literature postdate the period under investigation. The third is philological: Aramaic texts from Iranian contexts and key Avestan passages are presented in parallel columns with study translations, allowing readers to examine the textual basis of each arguxv

xvi PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM ment. The degree of direct textual verification is specified separately where necessary. The author is neither a professional Iranian philologist nor a Hebraist, but an architect and writer. His particular contribution lies in the examination of material culture (temples, altars, places of worship, fire architecture) alongside the reading of texts. This condition explains the method and its limitations, which are declared without reservation in the section on verification. Prologue Those who approach the religious history of the Persian period encounter two corpora that are seldom studied together. The first is the Avesta, a collection of liturgical and poetic texts in two varieties of Avestan, preserved in a late written tradition and including the Gāthās, its oldest stratum, traditionally attributed to Zoroaster. The second comprises evidence for Yahwism between the Persian conquest of Babylon (539 BCE) and Alexander’s defeat of the empire (332 BCE): Hebrew and Aramaic biblical texts, composed at different times both within and beyond that period and therefore requiring book-by-book examination; the documents of the Judeo-Aramaic community at Elephantine; and evidence from Yehud, Samaria, and Idumea. Between these bodies of evidence stand two centuries of rule by a dynasty that proclaimed its allegiance to Ahura Mazdā while also supporting the worship of YHW on an imperial frontier. The book takes this chronological coincidence as the starting point for a thesis tested against an explicit method. Its rule is to separate three things that the bibliography often confuses: typological similarity, which exists between two ideas or practices due to their form; probable mediation, which requires a plausible historical channel (the imperial administration, Aramaic as the language of chancery, the diaspora communities); and demonstrable dependence, which can only be affirmed when a text or practice is better explained by its source than without it. The book’s thesis is singular and is formulated on several levels: the influence of Persian imperial culture under Darius I is documentable on the linguistic and administrative levels (imperial Aramaic, loans, chancery, cultic policy); it is probable in royal ideology and in general features of the cult; and for doctrinal transformation (dualism, angelology, judgement, resurrection, saviour), it is argued that there are distinct hy potheses, of varying degrees, which the critical matrix of Appendix D grades case by case. Many parallels remain at the first level, and several reach the second; the demonstrable dependence is found primarily in the lexicon and in the administration. In the major doctrinal themes, the strength of the argument does not stem from an isolated borrowing, but from the convergence of the four levels within the same imperial sphere. This does not weaken the thesis; it delimits it. The reader will find here a thesis of influence with its cartography of evidence, and not a general as sertion that the sources do not authorize. xvii

xviii PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM The work proceeds in layers. Part I establishes the lexical groundwork — Hebrew, Imperial Aramaic, Greek, and Iranian — because ideas travel in words and can only be properly compared when one understands what each term meant in its original language. Parts II through IV present separately the Avesta, the Achaemenid imperial framework, and the Yahwism of the Persian period, with Elephantine as the central case study. Part V compares the major themes (saviour, end times, resurrection, good and evil, temptation, angels, and paradise), with three positions presented for each, and Part VI traces the reception of these themes in Second Temple Judaism, at Qumran, apocalyptic literature, and early Christianity. Parts VII to X broaden the horizon with the history of Zoroastrianism, cosmology, the space of worship, the dialogue with Greece and the guiding thread of four chronological periods (Achaemenid, Seleucid-Parthian, the time of Jesus and Sasanian), with attention to fire, the word, the calendar and water. Parts XI–XVI contain the most technically detailed material: parallel-text editions of Aramaic documents from Iranian contexts and passages from the Avesta, together with critical apparatus and translations; studies of funerary material culture and comparative philology; the hierarchy of forces in Mazdaism; sacred architecture, Pahlavi texts, and Iranian poetry; comparative repertories of terminology, buildings, and classical sources; and supplementary studies of Gad Barnea’s hypothesis concerning the burning bush and fire, the Elephantine documents relating to the temple of YHW (Cowley 30–33), the religious buildings of Dura-Europos, Mani, and Parsi liturgical manuals. The indexes—of passages, Hebrew and Aramaic terms, Greek and Iranian terms, personal names, places, and subjects—together with the general conclusion, are designed to make the volume usable as a ref erence work as well as a continuous study. Three precautions guide the reading. The first is chronological: much of the Pahlavi literature and the transmitted Avesta survive in forms later than the Achaemenid period; for each argument, the composition, manuscript medium, and era to which the phenomenon is attributed are distinguished. The second is philological: the translations of the Gāthās are scholarly interpretations grounded in identified lemmas and editions; variants and reading difficulties are part of the apparatus. The third concerns the hierarchy of documents: a reference known through secondary bibliography is not equated with a direct reading of the material evidence, and historical hypotheses are given an explicit probative rating.

PROLOGUE xix If the book fulfils its purpose, the reader will emerge with fewer easy certainties and a conviction grounded in documents: that the Yahwism of the Persian period was formed in actual contact with Achaemenid Iran. Furthermore, the reader will gain a precise description of where these two worlds intersect, what vocabulary they share, what institutions unite them, and what, with the sources we have today, still cannot be proven. Buenos Aires, October 2026.

How to Read This Book The book is organized into sixteen parts that progress from language to text, from text to historical context, from context to major themes and parallel-text editions; from there it moves on to funerary material culture and comparative philology, to Mazdaism and the hierarchy of forces, to the architecture of worship, the Pahlavi texts (Dēnkard V and IX) and Iranian poetry, to comparative repertories in the form of tables, and, in the last part, to extensions on fire, Elephantine, Dura-Europos, Mani, and the Parsi liturgical manuals. A reader seeking the main argument can read Parts I to VI, Chapter XXII on the history of Zoroastrianism, and the con clusion; readers with philological interests can begin with Part XI, where each edition includes the text, apparatus, and commentary, and then return to the chapters that contextualize it. HOW THIS BOOK SHOULD BE READ Part lenistic Jewish witness sharing a distinctive, multi-part Iranian formulation and accompanied by a credible linguistic or social transmission route would strengthen a dependence claim. Editorial Note Content and organization of the documentary apparatus The monograph consists of sixty chapters arranged in sixteen parts, together with repertories of original-language texts, English translations, epigraphic sources, Aramaic documents, lexicons, and concordances. The documentary apparatus distinguishes the ancient text, the editorial reading adopted, the translation, and hypotheses concerning religious transmission. Incomplete texts are identified as such; conjecture is never presented as though it were preserved evidence. Typographic, pagination and indexing criteria The volume is typeset in EB Garamond, with Noto Serif Hebrew used for Semitic scripts. Ancient sources are cited by book, chapter, paragraph, verse, or line, provid ing stable references independently of pagination. Indexes of terms, authors, and places serve as finding aids rather than substitutes for philological analysis in context. The general table of contents uses cross-references and document markers; the specialist indexes provide concordances keyed to the pagination of the volume. The designation Ahura Mazdā is used for the deity in Avestan texts, while Achaemenid inscriptions also employ the Old Persian form Auramazdā. Transliterations and variants follow the conventions set out below. Images, maps and reproduction rights The three maps in this volume are original sketches by the author, drawn based on Natural Earth country maps (public domain); they do not reproduce third-party maps or their labels. Borders, satrapies, and provinces that the sources do not allow to be established have been deliberately omitted (Table M2). Sources and licences are identified in the figure apparatus. Ancient texts are cited by loci, and modern texts in brief extracts with attribution. The texts of Uesugi and Catt (2024) are reproduced with typographic adaptation under CC BY 4.0. The texts of Panthaky and the Textbook of Aramaic Documents collection by Porten and Yardeni are not reproduced; only their content and structure are described. xxix

Uncertainties are retained where the available evidence does not permit their resolution. Summary This book examines relations between Yahwist communities and Achaemenid Iranian culture from Cyrus II’s conquest of Babylon in 539 BCE to the end of Persian rule in the Levant in 332 BCE. It distinguishes that regional endpoint from the fall of the Achaemenid monarchy in 330 BCE. The book argues that Iranian influence on Jewish and Aramaic-speaking communities in the Near East was real and became particularly consequential under Darius I through four channels: language (Imperial Aramaic as a medium of imperial communication through which Iranian vocabulary and formulae circulated into Hebrew and Aramaic); administration and royal ideology (chancery practices, calendars, law, cultic policy, and the formula ‘God of Heaven’); cult and material culture (altars and fire vessels, purity prac tices, and ritual gestures); and religious concepts (truth and falsehood, angelology, judgement, and the renewal of the world). These channels bear different evidentiary weights: linguistic and administrative contacts are demonstrable; parallels in royal ideology and the general features of cult support probable mediation; and doctrinal influence remains an interpretative hypothesis to be assessed case by case. The investigation combines linguistic evidence, textual study, and material culture, distinguishing contemporary documentation from Avestan and Pahlavi tradi tions preserved in later forms. Its comparisons encompass salvation, dualism, eschatology, sacred speech, fire, architecture, calendars, and purification. The dossiers and appendices identify original-language texts, indirect translations, and material evidence described rather than directly examined. The overall argument finds its strongest support in linguistic and administrative evidence, identifies prob able connections in royal ideology, and advances doctrinal influence as a possible explanation where the chronological and documentary evidence permits; no isolated resemblance is treated as proof of borrowing. xlix

Abstract Abstract prepared for indexing in L’Année philologique and the ATLA Religion Database. It describes the contents of the full volume; see Volume 0 for the conceptual map and the ten central theses developed in the book. Persia and Ancient Judaism: Religious Traditions, Texts, and Transformations in the Persian Period. This book examines contact between Iranian religious traditions and Yahwism under Achaemenid rule (539–332 BCE), together with its later reception. It distinguishes documented borrowings, probable mediation, and typo logical similarities, while cautioning against the uncritical retrojection of later Pahlavi or Parsi sources onto the fifth century BCE. Part I examines the Hebrew, Imperial Aramaic, and Iranian lexicons and the mediation of Greek texts (the Septuagint, Theodotion, and the New Testament). Part II considers the formation and transmission of the Avesta (the Old Avestan Gāthās, the Young Avestan Yašts, and the Vendīdād), asking which forms of the religious traditions later associated with Zoroastrianism may be traced to the Achaemenid period. Part III establishes the Persian imperial setting through royal inscriptions and the Persepolis tablets. Part IV examines Persian-period Yahwism: the Elephantine community and temple (including its destruction in 410 BCE and the petitions of 407 BCE under Darius II); the ‘God of Heaven’ formula and ʾtrwdn; and Yehud, Samaria, and Idumea. Part V compares major themes: saviour and messiah (Saošyant, Cyrus, and Jewish expecta tion); the end of time and cosmic renewal (frašō.kərəti); resurrection; good and evil (aša and druj); temptation and the forty days (Vendīdād 19 and the Gospels); and angels, demons, and paradise. Part VI considers reception in Second Temple Judaism, at Qumran, and in early Christianity. Parts VII–X address cosmology, time and logos, cultic architecture (temples, fire altars, and mithraea), comparisons between Greece and Iran, fire, mantra, calendars, and water. Part XI presents textual editions and dossiers: the Aramaic version of Behistun (TAD C2.1), the Passover Letter (TAD A4.1), the Bagohi petition (TAD A4.7–9), the letters of Arsames, Biblical Aramaic passages from Ezra and Daniel, Avestan passages from Yasna 27 and 30, Vendīdād 19 and Yašt 19, Achaemenid inscriptions, and Plutarch’s De Iside et Osiride 46–49. Parts XII–XIV examine funerary practices (including dakhmas), comparative philology, Mazdaism and Zoroastrianism, the hierl

ABSTRACT li archy of forces from Ahura Mazdā to Aŋra Mainyu, Zoroastrian architecture, Dēnkard V and IX, and the Iranian epic Šāhnāme. Part XV provides comparative vocabularies. Part XVI extends the inquiry to the burning bush and fire, Elephantine documents, the synagogue, mithraeum, and church at Dura-Europos, Mani and Manichaeism, and Parsi liturgical manuals containing nīrangs. The appendices provide a synchronized chronology for 539–332 BCE, bilingual loci, a documentary dossier, a critical matrix of hypotheses, a study translation of the Vendīdād, Hebrew and Aramaic texts, and the Yasna Haptaŋhāiti. The book argues that Iranian influence in the region was real and became especially consequential under Darius I. It evaluates that influence across four distinct levels: language and administration (documented), royal ideology (probable), cult and material culture (probable in their general characteristics), and religious concepts (an interpretative hypothesis requiring independent assessment). Throughout, the inquiry distinguishes Achaemenid Mazdaism from later Sasanian Zoroastrianism, recognizes the Old Avestan Dictionary of Uesugi and Catt (2024) as a lexical point of reference for the Gāthās, and insists that historical contacts must be dated by their documentary contexts rather than inferred from etymology alone. Modern Parsi manuals are not treated as direct evidence for first-century CE practice.

Methodological summary The method adopted is historical-critical comparison. Each proposed parallel undergoes three tests: typological similarity (whether the phenomena are comparable), plausible mediation (historically situated circulation of people, texts, institutions, or vocabulary), and demonstrable dependence (specific evidence sufficient to establish transmission rather than mere resemblance). Rule of control by causal chain. A religious parallel is treated as a hypothesis of transmission only when the following have been identified: (1) the earliest evidence of each formulation, (2) the chronological interval between them, (3) a plausible social or textual channel, (4) shared non-trivial features, and (5) alternatives of independent development, Mesopotamian-Levantine antecedent, or Hellenistic and Romano-Parthian reception. The presence of a similar object, image, or word does not replace any of these five checks. This protocol also applies to anguiped-type gems, syncretic representations, cosmic cycles, and soteriological figures; their late documentation is not direct evidence of the Achaemenid court religion. lii

Conceptual map and central theses of the book This section precedes the General Introduction and outlines the structure of the book for different groups of readers. General Introduction See the Conceptual Map (p. liii) for the conceptual map of the sixteen Parts, Table 0 of critical nomenclature, and the ten central theses of the book. Between 539 and 332 BCE, with regional variations and interruptions of Persian rule in Egypt, communities in Judea, Samaria, Babylon, and Egypt maintained relations with the Achaemenid administration. Aramaic was an important language of this communication; royal inscriptions expressed the sovereign’s legitimation by Auramazda. The documents are diverse: inscriptions, administrative records, papyri and ostraca, biblical compositions, and later-transmitted Avestan texts. This diversity defines the limits of comparison. Darius I (522–486 BCE) provides a relevant core of documents: royal inscriptions, imperial administration, and the framework for the completion of the Temple in Jerusalem, dated by Ezra 6:15 to the sixth year of his reign. The Aramaic copy from Behistun attests to the circulation of royal propaganda. These facts make his reign the centre of gravity of the contact: the Aramaic chancery, royal theology, and the restoration of the Temple all converged during his reign. It is not argued that all religious transformation began then; subsequent reigns and Hellenistic mediations are evaluated with equal rigour. The book proceeds in four steps. First, language: without a controlled lexicon, no parallel is reliable, and Imperial Aramaic is the demonstrable medium. Second, the texts from each side, considered within their own stratum. Third, the themes for which the bibliography has proposed parallels (dualism, eschatology, angelology, creation, time, logos, fire, Mithras), each with a table of features and a three-tiered assessment. Fourth, the parallel-text editions. A thread runs through the work: the question of the relationship between the Greek-Hebrew world and Iran, posed in four chronological sections (Chapter XXXI), with a rule of terminological hygiene: the term “Sasanian” is only used from the year 224 CE onward. Hermeneutical control of textual strata. The Bundahišn and the Dēnkard, preserved in medieval and later compilations and manuscript traditions (including important ninth- and tenth-century CE redactions), are not direct sources for the Achaemenid period. They may be used for controlled typological comparison only, with explicit attention to date, recension, translation and mediation; their existence does not by itself establish doctrinal transmission from Darius I to Judaism or 1

2 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM Christianity. Each parallel must distinguish contemporary evidence from retrospective interpretation (cf. Boyce, A History of Zoroastrianism, I, 1975; Cereti, La letteratura pahlavi, 2001). Method and documentary corpus Language, vocabulary and text The philological method is comparative and stratigraphic. For each term, the attested forms (Avestan, Old Persian, Aramaic, Hebrew, Greek), the source location and date, and the direction of borrowing, when possible, are recorded. A distinction is made between lexical borrowing, which proves contact, and conceptual coincidence, which must be proven separately. The language of imperial communica tion was Aramaic: this is shown by the Aramaic version of Behistun, the correspondence of Arsames, and the documents from Elephantine. Hebrew remained the language of Judean literary production, and the coexistence of both languages within the same community is the context in which calques and borrowings become possible. Material culture and epigraphy Material culture provides what the texts omit. Considered are the royal inscriptions (DB, DNa, DNb, XPh), the fire altars carved in the tombs of Naqš-e Rostam and Pasargadae, the reliefs of Persepolis, the seals and coins of Yehud, Samaria, and Idumea, and the remains of the temple at Elephantine. The architectural analysis, which is the author’s area of expertise, is applied to the form of the altars and the cultic precincts, as well as the relationship between the fire vessel and its support. History of Scholarship This review of scholarship distinguishes historical reconstructions, comparative methodologies, and philological approaches. The following characterizations of individual scholars are introductory rather than exhaustive; specific claims must be assessed in relation to the works, editions, and passages cited. A reference encountered in secondary scholarship permits discussion of the position attributed to an author, but does not by itself establish direct consultation of the cited source.

GENERAL INTRODUCTION 3 The question of the relationship between the Iranian world and Judaism has its own history, and this history shapes how it is formulated today. It is useful to recon struct it in five stages: the origin of the problem in European scholarship; the major hypothesis of Iranian influence on late Judaism; the critical reaction; the shift in the discussion toward documents from the Persian period; and the current situation, in which philological criticism of the Avesta and the study of the Achaemenid and Elephantine archives have changed the premises of the debate. 1. The origins of the problem (17th – 19th centuries) The tradition of comparing “the Persians” to the Hebrews predates Avestan philology. Thomas Hyde, in his Historia religionis veterum Persarum (from Theatro Sheldoniano, 1700), worked with classical sources and late Persian texts, and proposed an interpretation that presented Zoroastrianism as a monotheism akin to the biblical one. Direct knowledge of the Avesta began with Abraham Hyacinthe Anquetil-Duperron’s translation (Zend-Avesta, N.M. Tilliard, 1771), based on manuscripts from the Parsis of Surat; its reliability was immediately questioned (William Jones rejected it), and the debate over the text’s authenticity continued into the following century. Nineteenth-century comparative philology (Burnouf, Haug, Spiegel, Geldner, Darmesteter, Mills) established that the language of the Avesta was an ancient stage of Iranian related to Vedic Sanskrit; with this, the Avesta became a linguistic source of the first order and, at the same time, was exposed to the temptation of dating its content by the antiquity of its language. Early comparisons combined biblical passages, Greek testimonies, and Iranian sources transmitted in different strata. The problem is not that all Iranian eschatology is medieval: Yt 19 already expresses renewal and the raising of the dead. The problem is distinguishing the Avestan strata, their uncertain date, and the more extensive development of the Pahlavi texts, whose final compilation is much later. 2. The hypothesis of Iranian influence (1900–1970) The classic formulation is found in Wilhelm Bousset, Die Religion des Judentums im neutestamentlichen Zeitalter (Reuther & Reichard, 1903), which attributed the angelology, dualism, eschatology, and resurrection of late Judaism to Iranian influence. Richard Reitzenstein (Das iranische Erlösungsmysterium, A. Marcus und E. Weber, 1921) expanded on this thesis with the hypothesis of an Iranian myth of the

4 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM “primordial redeeming man” that would have shaped Christology and Gnosticism. This construction was soon dismantled, among other reasons because it relied on much later Manichean and Mandaean texts. Geo Widengren, Jacques DuchesneGuillemin and Robert C. Zaehner maintained the comparatist line from different perspectives: Duchesne-Guillemin (La religion de l ‘ Iran ancien, Presses Universitaires de France, 1962) with a balanced vision of the whole, Zaehner (The Dawn and Twilight of Zoroastrianism, Weidenfeld & Nicolson, 1961) with a theoretical reconstruction logic of Zurvanism that was later considered excessive. 3. Mary Boyce and the Continuity Hypothesis Mary Boyce (1920–2006) gave the influence thesis its most complete version in A History of Zoroastrianism (Brill; vol. I, 1975; vol. II, 1982; vol. III, with Frantz Grenet, 1991) and in Zoroastrians: Their Religious Beliefs and Practices (Routledge & Kegan Paul, 1979). Its main features are three: a very high date for Zoroaster (in the 2nd millennium BCE; between 1700 and 1200 according to the work); essential continuity between the Gāthās, the Late Avesta, Achaemenid religion, and Sasanian Zoroastrianism, so that Pahlavi sources can be used to reconstruct ancient beliefs; and the conviction that the Achaemenid kings were Zoroastrians and that their contact with the Jews had an impact on the latter’s theo logy (moral dualism, angelology, final judgement, resurrection). Her contribution to the documentation is enormous (the three volumes remain the most extensive collection of sources), but each of her three premises has been disputed: the date, for linguistic and archaeological reasons; continuity, because it presupposes that later texts preserve the ancient without demonstrating it in each case; and the Zoroastrianism of the kings, because the Achaemenid inscriptions do not mention Zoroaster nor do they use the calendar or the terms of the Avesta in a way that proves it unambiguously. The proposed dates for Zoroaster do not coincide among researchers who favour acknowledging Iranian contacts. The high chronology defended by Boyce must be distinguished from Gnoli’s lower proposals. Nor does a date for the prophet alone determine when a motif was incorporated into a text or transmitted to another community: composition, dissemination, and reception are different issues.

GENERAL INTRODUCTION 5 4. The Philological Critique: Kellens, Skjærvø, and Stausberg Since the 1980s, French and German Avestan philology introduced a shift. Jean Kellens and Éric Pirart (Les textes vieil-avestiques, 3 vols., Reichert, 1988–1991) edited and translated the Gāthās using a strictly philological method; Kellens (Le panthéon de l’ Avesta ancien, Reichert, 1994; later titles cited in secondary bibliography) argued that the texts of Yasna 28–53 are liturgical compositions embedded in a ritual and not the direct testimony of a reforming prophet; that the supposed Gathic “dualism” is not systematic; and that the religion of the Old Avesta must be reconstructed with caution, without projecting Pahlavi theology onto it. Prods Ok tor Skjærvø, on the other hand, maintains that the Gāthās are personal poetry of a historical author (The Spirit of Zoroastrianism, Yale University Press, 2011), but rejects the projection of later categories. Michael Stausberg (Die Religion Zarathushtras, 3 vols., Kohlhammer, 2002–2004; with Yuhan Vevaina, The Wiley Blackwell Companion to Zoroastrianism, 2015) offered a critical synthesis of the history of scholarship and the state of sources. For our problem, the consequence is twofold. First, the date of the Avesta as transmitted (the written version probably dates from the Sasanian period, 5th–6th centuries CE, with a long prior oral transmission) requires us to distinguish between layers of language and content in each text. Second, the discussion about what constitutes “Achaemenid” Zoroastrianism remains open: Kellens has questioned whether the Achaemenids were Zoroastrians in the sense given by Boyce; others (Gnoli, Skjærvø) maintain this with different nuances; and studies such as Wouter Henkelman’s (The Other Gods Who Are, Nederlands Instituut voor het Nabije Oosten, 2008) on the Persepolis tablets show a plural state cult system, with Elamite, Babylonian, and Iranian gods, without clear indications in the Avesta. 5. Shaked, de Jong and contact studies Shaul Shaked is probably the author who has most rigorously discussed the conditions for Iranian influence on Judaism. In “Qumran and Iran: Further Considerations” (Israel Oriental Studies 2, 1972:433–446) and in “Iranian Influence on Judaism: First Century BCE to Second Century CE” (The Cambridge History of Judaism, vol. 1, 1984:308–325), he acknowledges notable parallels (the doctrine of the two spirits in 1QS III–IV, the calendar, certain angelic figures) but insists that the comparison is only legitimate when datable sources are available on both sides and a

6 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM plausible channel of communication exists. In Dualism in Transformation: Varieties of Religion in Sasanian Iran (School of Oriental and African Studies, 1994), he showed how much Iranian dualism changed between the ancient and Sasanian periods, thus invalidating the indiscriminate use of later texts. His criteria (datable sources, channel, internal alternative) form the basis of the three-pronged examination in this book. Albert de Jong (Traditions of the Magi: Zoroastrianism in Greek and Latin Literature, Brill, 1997) methodically studied the classical testimonies about the Magi and showed that many Greek “facts” are literary or polemical, so that passages about the resurrection (Theopompus, in Diogenes Laertius) or about dualism (Plutarch, De Is. et Os. 46–47) should be read as Greek tradition about the Persians and not as neutral reports. De Jong has also addressed contact with Judaism in shorter studies (among them his contribution on Iran and the Dead Sea Scrolls in the Oxford Handbook of the Dead Sea Scrolls, 2010). Antonio Panaino has worked on cosmology, astronomy, and the figure of the Magi (for example, his study on the Magi in the Gospel of Matthew) and has insisted that the Zoroastrian tradition is complex enough to prevent a schematic comparison. Anders Hultgård (for example, “Persian Apocalypticism,” in J.J. Collins, ed., The Encyclopedia of Apocalypticism, vol. 1, 1998) and Philip Kreyenbroek hold intermediate positions: they recognize the plausibility of contacts and demand that the textual stratum be specified. 6. The documentary turn: Persia, Yehud and Elephantine The most significant development of recent decades has been documentary rather than doctrinal. Pierre Briant (Histoire de l’Empire perse, Fayard, 1996; English translation From Cyrus to Alexander, Eisenbrauns, 2002) assembled the evidence for Achaemenid administration and presented an empire whose relations with local communities must be investigated through institutions, archives, and material evidence, rather than assumed from broad religious parallels. In Elephantine, Bezalel Porten (Archives from Elephantine, University of California Press, 1968; with Ada Yardeni, Textbook of Aramaic Documents from Ancient Egypt [TAD], Hebrew University, 1986–1999) offered the reference edition of the papyri. Gard Granerød (Dimensions of Yahwism in the Persian Period, De Gruyter, 2016) analysed colonial Yahwism as a distinct religion and not as a deviation; Gad Barnea, in a series of works from 2024–2026, has proposed reading

Position of this book This book defends a thesis of influence: the religion and culture of Achaemenid Iran, under Darius I, had a real impact on the Yahwist communities of the Near East, and this influence explains some of the parallels between Zoroastrianism, Judaism, and Christianity. On the question of influence, it is therefore closer to the tradition that runs from Bousset to Boyce than to Kellens’s position, although it ad opts from Kellens the terminological distinction between Achaemenid Mazdaism and Zoroastrianism. It also adopts the method of critical positions: from Shaked, the criterion of conditions (datable source, plausible channel, considered alternative); from Kellens and Skjærvø, philological prudence. De Jong’s work incorporates the critique of classical sources; Henkelman and Briant’s, the realism regarding Achaemenid administration; and Porten, Granerød, and Kratz’s, the attention to the specific Yahwism of each community. Unlike Boyce, he does not project Pahlavi texts onto the Achaemenid period without proof in each case, and he does not accept the decrees of Ezra 1, 6, and 7 as authentic without reservation. His own con tribution is twofold: shifting the centre of gravity to the reign of Darius I, where the Aramaic chancery, royal theology, and the restoration of the Temple coincide; and incorporating the examination of the material culture of the cult (altars, fire vessels, enclosures) as his own line of evidence, whose independence from the textual is established piece by piece.

GENERAL INTRODUCTION 9 Transmission model: agents, networks, and channels A practice or idea can be transmitted through people, languages, institutions, and networks. The Achaemenid period offers a documented framework for contact; it was not the only period in which Iranian and Jewish communities coexisted. The Seleucid, Parthian, and Sasanian periods provide additional scenarios that must be distinguished by their sources and dates. 1. Agents The documented agents are, first and foremost, scribes and officials: the correspondence of Arsames, satrap of Egypt, with his administrators reveals a chancery that wrote in Aramaic using Persian formulae and employed scribes from various origins; the letters from Elephantine (TAD A4.7–A4.8) are addressed to Bagohi, governor of Yehud, a name of Iranian origin (Bagavahya or similar), and to other Persian officials. Secondly, soldiers and colonists: the Judeo-Aramaic garrison of Elephantine coexisted with other units (degalin) under Persian command. Thirdly, merchants and artisans. Fourth, priests: Magi appear in Greek accounts as ritual specialists, although such descriptions require chronological contextualization and do not in themselves demonstrate their involvement in Yahwist communities. The Persepolis tablets record rations for priests (shatin) and offerings to various gods. Finally, communities of deportees and their descendants: the Babylonian Jews, documented in the Al-Yahudu archives and the Murashu archive of Nippur (5th century), where Jewish and Iranian names appear in the same transactions. 2. Networks and places of contact The strongest documentary evidence for such networks comes from Mesopotamia and Egypt, rather than Yehud. The Murašû archive (Nippur, c. 455–403 BCE) records land tenure, leases, taxation, and other transactions involving people with Akkadian, Aramaic, Judean, and Iranian names. Names provide evidence of social contact, not, in themselves, proof of religious borrowing. Additional linguistic criterion. An Iranian loanword attested in Imperial Aramaic or Hebrew demonstrates lexical transmission only if its etymology, chronology, and route of borrowing can be established. It does not, by itself, demonstrate the adoption of a religious doctrine. Each lemma must therefore be evaluated separ ately.

GENERAL INTRODUCTION 11 Thesis and research question Question: To what extent did the religion and culture of Achaemenid Iran, under the reign of Darius I, influence Yahwism and the Jewish and Aramaic communities of the Near East, and which of the parallels between Zoroastrianism, Judaism, and Christianity can be attributed to this contact? Thesis. Iranian influence on the region was real and was decisively concentrated during the reign of Darius I. This is evidenced by four mutually reinforcing levels of evidence: (1) the linguistic-administrative level, where imperial Aramaic as the language of communication and Persian loanwords in Hebrew and Aramaic prove sustained contact; (2) the ideological level, where Darius’s royal title and theology (Auramazdā, creator of heaven and earth, truth against falsehood, the king as the agent of the god) reappear in the Yahwist texts of the period as “God of heaven” and in the policy towards the temple; (3) the cultic and material plane, where the forms of fire worship (stepped altar, fire vessel on its stand, ritual attention to purity, gesture of reverence with bare feet) have correlates in the worship of the altar and the perpetual fire of the Temple; and (4) the conceptual plane, where moral dualism, angelology, judgement, renewal of the world and resurrection appear in later Judaism and in Christianity with an affinity that the contact hypothesis explains better than that of an isolated internal development. Independence and the Weight of Converging Evidence Converging evidence must be assessed for dependence between its components. A loanword, a chancery formula and an administrative title may be three expressions of the same bureaucratic network; counting them as three independent proofs of religious transfer would exaggerate their combined force. Imperial contact establishes a condition of possibility. Moving from that condition to a doctrinal explana tion requires a diagnostic feature, a defensible chronology and a specific intermediary, together with comparison against local traditions. This distinction strengthens the study of contact by specifying which question each document answers and which inference remains open. The thesis rests on convergence: no single isolated argument proves it, but the coincidence of four lines of evidence within the same imperial sphere and around the same reign makes it more economical than the opposing hypothesis. 14 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM Refutation criteria Hypotheses are reviewed on a case-by-case basis. A borrowing can be maintained as proven even if a doctrinal derivation fails; a shared formula can be explained by earlier regional uses; a functional attribution of an altar can be modified by archaeology. The general thesis must be adjusted to these results and not protected by the mere sum of coincidences. An incompatible dating, a better-documented alternative, or an absence of specific features reduces the level of comparison.

Research update and state of the question (1994–2026) The state of the question cannot be reconstructed as a linear progression from Shaked (1994) to the most recent digital tools. Shaked’s work on dualism remains central for analysing transformations in Iranian religious traditions, while subsequent research has refined the chronology of individual formulations, the social settings of ritual texts, and the distinction between Achaemenid testimony and later Zoroastrian exegesis. In particular, Uesugi and Catt’s Old Avestan Dictionary (2024) offers a lexical control instrument, not direct proof of Achaemenid reception; Hintze’s edition and commentary on Yasna 35–41 (2007) are indispensable for the liturgical dossier; and a digital text of Ezra or Daniel is not identical to a critical apparatus of manuscript variants. The period 2024–2026 is also significant methodologically for architectural and documentary history. Angelo and Silver (2024) re-examine the Dura-Europos Christian Building through architectural adaptation and spatial experience rather than a predetermined evolution from house-church to basilica. The Elephantine legal papyri remain central for the agency and property of women, whereas the Persepolis Fortification tablets document the organisation of commodities and rations in another administrative system. These corpora should be compared through legal forms and social functions, not through assumed religious identity. Comparative research must therefore retain three independent controls: (i) the date of the surviving witness and the probable date of the formulation; (ii) the specificity of the shared wording or practice; and (iii) the independently evidenced channel of contact. A lexical borrowing can document linguistic mediation without establishing doctrinal borrowing. A later Pahlavi interpretation cannot, without intermediate witnesses, establish what Jews under Darius I knew. An architectural resemblance cannot supply a missing transmission history. The following chapters preserve these distinctions even where the hypothesis remains intellectually productive. Chapter I. Hebrew, Aramaic and Iranian in the Imperial Space This chapter examines linguistic contact under Achaemenid rule, from the sixth to the fourth centuries BCE. Each proposed borrowing must be dated by its earliest attestation and by the literary stratum that preserves it. Historical control of linguistic contact The presence of Iranian vocabulary in a Hebrew or Aramaic corpus does not, in itself, constitute proof of doctrinal dependence. In a historically controlled reconstruction, four questions must be addressed: what is the documented linguistic form; what is the oldest surviving evidence; through what administrative, commercial, or literary means could it have been transmitted; and what semantic transformation did it undergo in its receiving language? An administrative borrowing can circulate for generations without carrying with it the religious worldview of the group from which it originates. In Imperial Aramaic, it is essential to distinguish between the date of the event in question, the date of composition of a document, and the dating of the surviving medium. The Elephantine papyri offer material evidence from the Persian period; however, the composition and successive transmissions of Ezra and Daniel present their own literary and textual challenges. Linguistic comparison will be more convincing when it indicates observable graphic and morphological parallels, and not merely similarities of meaning reconstructed from modern translations. 1. Imperial Aramaic as a contact language The chapter starts from identified archives and texts; linguistic contact and religious reception are evaluated separately. During the Achaemenid period (539–332 BCE), Aramaic served as the language of administrative communication between regions that did not share a common language. It is the language of much of the correspondence preserved in the archives of Elephantine, the Jewish military colony in southern Egypt, and it also appears, alongside Elamite, in the administrative documents of Persepolis. 17

Old and Middle Iranian: Avestan, Old Persian and Pahlavi Old Persian is the Iranian language of some royal inscriptions; Avestan is the liturgical language of a distinct corpus, preserved through its own tradition. They are related languages, but a Persian form cannot automatically replace an Avestan form, nor can it prove that an Avestan text circulated at court. 20 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM 5. Method of lexical comparison: loanwords, calques, and coincidences A loanword requires an explanation of form, meaning, and transmission: an isolated sound similarity is insufficient. A calque reproduces a semantic structure using materials from the receiving language and requires a plausible bilingual context. A cognate derives from a common linguistic heritage and does not constitute evidence of historical contact between the texts being compared. The procedure begins with the attested locus; it identifies the language and its stratum; it compares forms and meanings; it evaluates the chronology and possible routes; and it contrasts alternative explanations. Only then does it inquire about religious reception. This prevents a correct etymology from serving as proof of a doctrine that the word does not contain. 6. Comparative Onomastics: Personal Names, Theophoric Names, and Formulae in Hebrew and Aramaic Object and chronological scope The study of proper names provides evidence of contact that is not to be confused with doctrinal borrowings. The comparison is arranged in three sections: (a) Babylon and Judea under the early Achaemenids, with particular attention to Darius I (522–486 BCE); (b) Elephantine in the 5th century BCE, whose dated documents include later periods, especially that of Darius II (423–404 BCE); and (c) Judea and Galilee in the 1st century BCE – 1st century CE, when Hebrew, Aramaic varieties, Greek, and, in certain spheres, Latin overlap. The third section is comparative and receptive: it does not project back onto the reign of Darius I. A personal name record should include separate information on the language in which the name was formed, the language of the document that transmits it, the writing system, any inferred religious identity, and the chronology of the witness. The same individual may have different names, and the same name may belong to people from different communities. The coexistence of Northwest Semitic roots does not allow us to assume that two names are automatically interchangeable: some are cognates, others hypocoristics, others transcriptions from a different language, and still others are independent names with a similar sound.

HEBREW, ARAMAIC, AND IRANIAN IN THE IMPERIAL SPACE 21 6.1. Divine Elements and the Limits of Ethnic Identification A name containing a divine designation is called a theophoric name. In Israelite and Judean onomastics, the Yahwist element can be found at the beginning or end of the compound name, in spellings such as yhw-, yhw, -yh, or -yhw, depending on the era, region, orthography, and tradition of transmission. It is important to avoid treating each letter sequence as an automatic equivalent of the complete consonantal tetragrammaton, and even more so to avoid deducing the cultic pronunciation of YHWH from the abbreviated spelling of a name. There are also formations with ʾEl and non-theophoric religious names. In the Babylonian diaspora sources, a Yahwistic name remains a relatively strong indication of affiliation, but it is not an infallible linguistic marker. An anthroponym may combine a Judean religious element with broadly Semitic morphology; Jews bearing Akkadian or Iranian names, and people with Yahwistic names outside securely identified Judean contexts, complicate any automatic identification of language, ethnicity and cult. Elephantine offers unusually valuable evidence because, unlike many biblical texts, its contemporary administrative docu ments survive on papyrus and ostraca. Its onomastics therefore permit the study of concrete social practices without making an individual’s religious affiliation directly inferable from a name alone.456 6.2. Literary and epigraphic evidence requires distinctions among uses, regions and social groups: it establishes neither an exclusively liturgical role for Hebrew nor universal trilingualism. Names must be examined in individual documentary contexts; a name’s language is not proof of identity or linguistic competence. Mark 5:41 preserves an Aramaic expression, while John 19:20 represents a multilingual inscription; neither is a cens11us of spoken languages. The Hebrew ben (‫ )ֵּב ן‬and Aramaic bar (‫ )ַּב ר‬both serve as patronymics meaning “son of”, but they cannot be treated as universally interchangeable. Formulae and Expressions: Common Inheritance, Translation, and Functional Change Short formulae also allow for the comparison of languages, provided that a locus is cited for each expression and that translation is not confused with literal identity. In Ezra 1:2 (Hebrew), the expression ʾĕlōhê haššāmayim (“God of heaven”) belongs to an edict attributed to Cyrus; the Aramaic dossier of Ezra 5:11 uses ʾĕlāh šĕmayyāʾ wĕʾarʿāʾ (“God of heaven and earth”). The formulations share a semantic field and administrative context, but they are not identical phrases, nor do their similarity imply that the title was coined by the Persians. The coexistence of a Hebrew and an Aramaic formula proves literary mediation and different registers. More documentation is needed for historical derivation.13 The Hebrew bēn ʾādām (“son of man”; Ezekiel 2:1) and Aramaic kĕbar ʾĕnāš (“like a son of man”; Daniel 7:13) employ related Semitic vocabulary, but differ in syntax, language, and literary function. The figure in Daniel’s vision cannot be derived from lexical equivalence alone: the interpretation must account for the narrat ive setting and the reception of the passage. The New Testament tradition preserves glosses of Aramaic expressions in Greek: Mark 5:41 transmits ταλιθα κουμ and explains its narrative effect; John 1:42 interprets Κηφᾶς as Πέτρος; Acts 9:36 translates Ταβιθά as Δορκάς (“gazelle”). Mark 15:34 and Matthew 27:46 present Greek versions of an invocation linked to Psalm 22. This material reflects memory and translation of Semitic formulae, but the exact segmentation of each word transmitted by the Greek evangelists and their variants must be critically examined before establishing a definitive Aramaic reconstruction. Criteria of Evidence and Their Relevance to the Thesis The hierarchy of this dossier is expressed through four levels: A, verifiable form and context in contemporary material evidence and its edition; B, form present in biblical or New Testament texts whose transmission is known but whose date of composition does not necessarily coincide with the narrated scenario; C, reasonable ety mological or morphological correspondence supported by grammars and repertories; D, personal equivalence, reconstructed contact dating that still requires corroboration. The tables contain explanatory abbreviations and standardized spellings; the vocalizations are not attributed to the original Achaemenid consonants. The evidence contributes unevenly to the overall argument. In the sixth and fifth centuries BCE, administrative Aramaic, Yahwistic names, and kinship networks provide positive evidence of social contact within the Achaemenid imperial

They do not independently establish the transmission of Iranian religious doctrines; any such claim requires further, separately dated evidence. Chapter Conclusion Aramaic provides the strongest documentary evidence of contact between Yah wist communities and the Achaemenid administration. Hebrew, Avestan, and Old Persian belong to distinct traditions and serve different functions; their coexistence does not make them interchangeable languages. Research should begin with identified words and documents and move on to religious content only when additional evidence exists. Summary The languages of the empire, the archives that preserve them, and the mechanisms of borrowing are distinguished. The coincidence of a term allows for the investigation of a relationship; its demonstration requires phonetic history, context, and documentary distribution. Historical scope of the chapter. Persian loanwords transmitted through Imperial Aramaic between the sixth and fourth centuries BCE, and their preservation in biblical writings of differing dates of composition. A word of Achaemenid origin may persist in a Hellenistic text; linguistic origin and literary date must therefore be distinguished. Philological note: borrowings and their institutional channels. Imperial Aramaic was one of the principal written vehicles of Achaemenid administration, although it coexisted with other languages across different genres and documentary settings. Jonas C. Greenfield identifies Iranian loanwords in Old Aramaic, notably in the vocabulary of office, law and trade, and observes that some also circulated in Babylonian and Elamite documentation. Aramaic had, moreover, absorbed Akkadian vocabulary well before 539 BCE. The route from an Iranian word to its appearance in a biblical text must therefore be reconstructed rather than assumed. Neither its linguistic origin nor its institutional use, in itself, establishes religious de pendence. Controlled example. Aramaic gzbrʾ and Hebrew gizbār (“treasurer”; Ezra 1:8) have been compared with Iranian *ganza-bara-. This is an administrative term. Its occurrence does not establish that the biblical author adopted Iranian religious beliefs. The proposed etymology and route of transmission must be assessed against the attested forms. The lexicon offers one of the firmest bases for investigating Iranian contact with Hebrew and Aramaic, provided that each proposed loanword is assessed against its earliest attested form, phonetic correspondences, chronological setting, direction of transmission and mediating language. Borrowed terms normally adapt to the phonology and morphology of their recipient language; they do not invariably preserve their original form. The strongest examples belong to the spheres of administration, law and court life. Such correspondences attest to words and institutions; they do not, in themselves, demonstrate the adoption of religious doctrines. The following examples are arranged by semantic field and degree of certainty.

Doubtful cases and false etymologies Among the doubtful cases are ʾtrwdn (see chapter XII), rab-māg (Jer 39:3, 13), and the proposal that Ašmedai (Asmodeus, Tob 3:8) derives from the Avestan demon Aēšma-daēuua; the latter is plausible, but depends on the book of Tobit using an Iranian figure, and is discussed in chapter XIX. Etymologies of the type “Satan comes from Ahriman” must be discarded, as they have no linguistic basis: śāṭān is a Semitic term (“adversary”) that appears in Num 22:22 and Job 1–2 without Iranian intervention. Any list of loans that includes Hebrew religious terms must be justified with an etymology and a chronology. Assessment Typological similarity: not applicable to the lexicon. Probable mediation: certain for administrative and legal vocabulary, due to the language of chancery. Demonstrable dependence: only at the level of words, not ideas; lexical borrowing proves institutional contact, not religious borrowing. Chapter Conclusion Iranian loanwords demonstrate the circulation of vocabulary in the spheres of government, resources, communication, and courtly life. The reception of a word does not obligate one to accept the doctrine of the donor language. Rāz and pardēs precisely illustrate the capacity of receiving languages to expand or modify the meaning of the loanword. Summary The chapter distinguishes between secure borrowings, debated etymologies, and secondary religious uses. The direction of lexical transmission must be established for each word and not automatically transferred to associated concepts.

The Letter of Aristeas: date of composition, legitimizing narrative and Greek mediation The so-called Letter of Aristeas to Philocrates is not a contemporary diplomatic letter of Darius I. It narrates, from the court of Ptolemy II Philadelphus (third century BCE), the acquisition and Greek translation of the Jewish Law in Alex andria, but its composition is usually placed in the second century BCE. The date on which a narrative is said to have taken place and the date on which it was written belong to two distinct levels of evidence. Nor does the account of the Pentateuch constitute proof that the entire Hebrew Bible was translated at once by seventy-two experts under the described conditions. Linguistic and papyrological studies, for their part, place the language of the Greek Pentateuch in the first half of the third century BCE, so that the narrated event, the actual translation, and the writing of the Letter constitute three distinct levels.17 The distinction illuminates the thesis of this book: the text testifies to the self-definition of sectors of Hellenistic Judaism, the authority attributed to a translation of the Law, and the negotiation of knowledge between Judea and Alexandria; it does not constitute direct testimony of the Achaemenid religion nor does it serve, on its own, to reconstruct Yahwism in 522–486 BCE. At the level of mediations, however, it provides a central piece for explaining how a Semitic corpus ended up circulating in Greek and how it could be received by later interpreters. I had great hope that God would grant my request, since I was pleading for human deliverance: when people seek justice and honourable deeds in piety, the God who rules all things directs their actions and purposes. §19. The king raised his head and looked at me cheerfully. “How many tens of thousands do you think there will be?” he asked. Andreas, standing nearby, answered, “A little more than one hundred thousand.” “A small request Aristeas makes of us!” said the king. Sosibius and some of those present added, “It is worthy of your generosity to offer their release in thanksgiving to the supreme God. I consider it useful to transcribe the decree, for in this way the liberality of the king will be more clearly manifested, to whom God would have given strength to procure the salvation of such a numerous multitude.

50 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM § 22. The decree stated the following: “Those who, in participating in our father’s campaigns in Syria and Phoenicia and entering the territory of the Jews, acquired Jewish captives and took them to Alexandria or other parts of Egypt, or sold them, must release them immediately. The same provision will apply to those who were already in our territory before those campaigns and to those who were brought in afterward. For each person released, the possessor will receive twenty drachmas: soldiers will receive them along with their pay; others, from the royal bank (basilikē trapeza).” §23. “We judge that the capture of these people was contrary to the will of our father and due order, for the devastation of their lands and their transfer to Egypt were due to the uncontrolled nature of the war. The booty obtained by the soldiers in combat already constituted their share; to further enslave these people was an injustice.” §24. “Since it is our duty to administer justice, especially to those who suffer unjust servitude, and to treat all fairly out of justice and compassion, we decree that any Jew held in slavery in our domain shall be set free once the specified sum has been paid to his possessor. No one may delay the execution of this decree. Within three days of the publication of this decree, the lists of captives shall be delivered to the officials, and the persons included therein shall present themselves.” §25. “We consider it beneficial for the kingdom that the measure be fulfilled. Anyone may denounce whoever disobeys it; if the infraction is proven, the accuser will receive power over the guilty party, while the latter’s goods will pass to the royal treasury.” § 26. When the decree was presented to the king for reading, it contained all the clauses except the one concerning captives who had arrived before the campaign or were brought in afterward. The monarch himself added this clause, thus demonstrating his generosity, and ordered that the sums for ransom be distributed to the army paymasters and the royal bankers. §27. The decision was thus ratified within seven days. Expenditure amounted to more than six hundred and sixty talents, for many infants at the breast were also freed with their mothers. When the question arose whether the twenty-drachma payment should also be made for them, the king ordered that it be paid, carrying out his decision in full.

Egyptian monarchs were accustomed to handling matters through decrees and precise provisions, leaving nothing to chance. GREEK MEDIATION 67 Philological and architectural apparatus of §§ 66–100 1. Three documentary layers. The Letter narrates a royal donation, fictionalized and placed during the reign of Ptolemy II; the date of its literary composition is later and remains debated; the transmitting manuscripts are later than both periods. None of these three levels can replace the others. Comparisons with Persian or biblical documentation must be dated from each piece of evidence, not from the date attributed to the narrative scene. 2. The vocabulary of construction. In §§83–91 appear perimeter walls, jambs, lintels, curtains, altar, stone pavement, slopes, reservoirs, and conduits. The Greek words do not prove that the temple builders spoke Greek or that a Persian borrowing exists. They identify the lexicon of Hellenistic literary description. For the thesis of this work, their usefulness is twofold: a technical vocabulary that can be compared with Ezra and Ezekiel, and a history of the architectural imagination of the temple. 3. Ritual waste and water. The passage attributes to the pavement a system of slopes for channeling cleansing water, and to underground installations for the drainage of sacrificial fluids. It must be analysed in conjunction with Levitical legislation, the descriptions of Josephus, and the hydraulic archaeology of Jerusalem; neither the exact existence of all the elements described nor the material preservation of that system can be inferred without further analysis. Artistic descriptions and figures. Both the precision of the measurements and the profusion of gems, the extraordinary strength of the priests, and the silence of hundreds of servants contribute to the aesthetic and religious persuasion of the nar rative. In §§116–117, three types of data are distinguished: an internally consistent agrarian figure in arurae, a comparison of the Jordan River’s flow regime with that of the Nile, and Ptolemais’s assertion of a Mediterranean mouth. Only the arithmetic operation is directly consistent within the passage itself; the hydrography presents a substantial inaccuracy. The text is therefore used here as evidence of geo graphical representation, not as a precise topographical description of Palestine. The same applies to § 115: the list of ports (Ashkelon, Joppa, Gaza, and Ptolemais) does not claim that they were under Jewish control, but presenting Joppa and Gaza as the region’s outlets to the sea fits better with the situation after the Hasmonean conquests than with the third century BCE. Simon took Joppa and made it the port of Judea around 142 BCE (1 Maccabees 13:11; 14:5); Gaza only fell to Alexander Jannaeus around 96 BCE (Josephus, Jewish Antiquities XIII 356–364); Ashkelon and Ptolemais were never Jewish cities. The passage describes commercial access, not sovereignty, and its value as an indication of the date of composition of the Let ter (2nd century BCE) is cumulative, not decisive. The historical maps in this monograph do not adopt this literary hydrography or the commercial access described in §115 as Achaemenid political boundaries; naming a port does not establish Jewish sovereignty over it. The allusion to mines under Persian rule in §§ 119–120 is a particularly pertinent locus for the book’s central question. The phrase χαλκοῦ καὶ σιδήρου designates copper and iron; it should not be modernized as gold and iron, nor should the trans lation of a contemporary article be cited as if it were a Greek variant. The episode amounts to a retrospective accusation of false administrative information. Without corroboration from Persian documents, identified mining operations, and dating of mineral strata, it does not demonstrate an extractive policy of Darius I. Table III.A7. Genre and date. This is the Hellenistic exegesis that the narrator attributes to the high priest Eleazar, situated literarily in the reign of Ptolemy II. It does not constitute a contemporary Persian testimony nor does it allow us to attribute to Zoroastrianism every concept of purity or every image of divinity. B. Fence and architecture as metaphor (§§139 and 142). The phrases χάραξι καὶ σιδηροῖς τείχεσιν (“palisades and iron walls”) and περιέφραξεν (“fenced”) form here an allegory of ritual and moral separation. They do not describe a built work nor are they archaeological evidence of Jewish or Iranian fortifications. C. Dietary observance and ethics (§§145–151). Tame and raptorial birds, cloven hooves, and rumination are interpreted as emblems of justice, discernment, and memory. The shift from zoology to morality is a rhetorical strategy of the Charter itself; it should not be presented as an empirical description of all species nor as an Iranian doctrinal transfer. D. Monotheism (§§131–139). The assertion that God is unique, omniscient, and omnipresent expresses a Jewish apologetic formulated in Greek. The passage offers material for studying relations between Mosaic Law and Hellenistic moral philosophy, but its mere thematic similarity to the discourse of Ahura Mazdā does not demonstrate a borrowing. Textual and historical apparatus of the seventh unit (§§161–182) 1. Two levels of testimony. The composition of the Letter belongs to Hellenistic Judaism and situates the episode, in literary terms, under Ptolemy II. The edited Greek is the source of the translation; the digital copies are transmissions of a printed edition, not independent codices. No abbreviation or manuscript folio should be assigned to the words translated here without inspection of the material source. 2. Animal, impurity, and allegory (§§161–170). The weasel that conceives through its ears and gives birth through its mouth (§ 165) is an ancient representation that is zoologically false. Its historical interest lies in the moral explanation of the transmission of rumors and denunciation, associated with dietary precepts. The narrator transforms a ritual classification into civic ethics, without thereby demonstrating doctrinal dependence on an Iranian text. 3. Written and Ceremonial Supports (§§ 176–179). διφθέραι denotes prepared skins used as writing supports (here, parchment), while χρυσογραφίᾳ specifies letter ing executed in gold. The scene extols the value of the Torah and the reverence of the king. The almost invisible seams of the skins express a sumptuous quality described in the narrative: they do not prove the preservation or location of a specific copy. “Jewish Letters” translates “Ἰουδαϊκοῖς γράμμασι” without imposing on this phrase a paleographic identification of ductus that the passage does not demonstrate. 4. The victory over Antigonus (§ 180). The king mentions a naval victory over Antigonus as a cause for celebration. This account does not allow us to definitively assign the date of the translators’ arrival to a specific historical battle. Reconstructions that automatically equate it with Andros are controversial. This inaccuracy is a factor in evaluating the historical credibility of the courtly dramatization, not a reason to alter the ancient text. 5. Court and Reception Culture (§§172–182). Immediate reception, audience protocol, veneration of scrolls, and respect for guests’ dietary customs present a literary model of tolerance and royal authority. Contrasts with Ptolemaic archives, where possible, should be based on document type, language, date, and medium, not on general similarity.

GREEK MEDIATION 91 benefits the whole world, so too will you, by imitating Him, remain free from reproach.72” Critical apparatus and commentary of §§183–210 1. Narrative Sequence and Structure of the Symposium. The banquet is described over two days: ten responses during the first (§§187–199) and further interventions from the eleventh interlocutor (§§203–210). The structure organizes the philosophical exposition through a royal questioning. The literary form should not be used as direct evidence of a stenographic transcription from the court of Ptolemy II. 2. Eleazar and Elisseo (§184). Thackeray’s text, printed in Swete (1900), p. 551, reads Ἐλεάζαρον for the priest who pronounces the prayer, with no variant recorded in the apparatus of that line, and Andrews’ English version follows it; Josephus’ paraphrase (Ant. 12.97–98), by contrast, gives Ἐλισσαῖον. The Eleazar of §184 is not the high priest at the beginning of the work, but the oldest of the priests who ar rived with the embassy. The English translation adopts Ἐλεάζαρον, the reading of the base text, and gives Josephus’ form in brackets; it is not treated as a manuscript variant of the Letter. 3. Language of royalty, authority, and justice. Royal virtue is formulated around ἐπιείκεια (moderation, benevolence), δικαιοσύνη (justice), μακροθυμία (patience), and ἀδωροδόκητος (incorruptibility). The constant mention of God shapes a moral theory of government. Analyzing possible analogies with Achaemenid royal ideology requires proving the chronology and the channel of transmission: a functional parallel does not constitute a semantic or doctrinal borrowing. 4. God as a universal model (§§185, 190, 195, 201, 210). The title παντοκράτωρ in §185 and the vocabulary of providence in §201 are Greek elements preserved in the text. Their historical interpretation requires consideration of Hellenistic Judaism, its scriptural translations, and the philosophical genres of the period. Their for mulation cannot be dated to the reign of Darius I solely based on similarity to discourses on imperial sovereignty. 5. Dating the source and the narrated event. The Letter is set during the reign of Ptolemy II; modern scholarship, for the most part, dates its composition to the 2nd 72Pseudo-Aristeas §§ 205–210 uses “ἀδωροδόκητον” (free from bribes), “δικαιοσύνη”, “φιλαλήθης” and “φιλοδίκαιος”. They are useful political -moral terms for contrast, but they are not linguistic loanwords from Avestan or Old Persian.

Part II. The Avesta and Zoroastrianism Part II — research argument, principal evidence and limit. The Avesta must be read by textual stratum and witness. The limit is the distance between surviving recensions and the Achaemenid era. Formation, structure, and transmission of the Avesta, and the question of Zoroastrianism in the Achaemenid period. It provides the Iranian side of the contact and establishes the strata that allow each comparison to be dated.

Chapter IV. Formation and Transmission of the Avesta Historical scope of this chapter. The composition of Old and Younger Avestan texts is subject to chronological debate; the organization and transmission of the corpus under the Sasanians and its medieval manuscript copies belong to later periods. The Avesta as a whole cannot be dated to the reign of Darius I. Limits of Avestan textual reconstruction The linguistic evidence of Old Avestan is of enormous value, but the relative antiquity of a language variety does not allow us to automatically date each stanza or attribute it directly to the period of Darius I. The Avestan text has undergone oral transmission and later written transcriptions. Therefore, “old” in linguistic classification is not synonymous with “Achaemenid manuscript.” For the Gāthās and associated formulae, the Old Avestan Dictionary (Heindio Uesugi, ed.; Adam Alvah Catt, editorial supervision; ILCAA, 2024) is now available, the second part of which prints the text and translation of Y. 27.13–15; 28–34; 43–46; 47–50; 51; 53; and 54,1. This set serves as a lexical and segmentation control against Geldner’s historical transcriptions, but it does not automatically convert all the decisions of a modern dictionary into manuscript readings. Each variant should be referred to its edition and, where appropriate, to the manuscript. 1. Structure of the corpus: Yasna, Yašts, Vendīdād, Visperad and Khorda Avesta The discussion reconstructs the principal problems in the transmission of the Avesta. The Avesta that has come down to us is, for the most part, a liturgical corpus, and can be described in two complementary ways: by its ritual use and by its genre. For their ritual use, tradition distinguishes three major collections. The Yasna (“sacrifice”) brings together the texts of the basic Zoroastrian ceremony. The Khorda Avesta or Xwardag Avesta (“little Avesta”) contains short prayers and minor celebrations. The Vendīdād is the “law against the daēvas”: a set of purity prescriptions aimed at keeping away malevolent powers whose names are cognate with the devas of India. In addition, there is the Visperad, a supplement of invocations inserted into the Yasna liturgy. 119

120 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM By genre, however, the corpus is ordered differently: the Gāthās, the seventeen oldest hymns, form part of the Yasna; the Yašts are hymns to deities (yazatas) and di vine concepts; and the Vendīdād is a code of purification. The two classifications overlap, and therefore it is always advisable to indicate, for each passage, to which ritual collection and genre it belongs. To establish the nomenclature, it is necessary to provide an inventory of the preserved corpus and clarify four points that are often obscured by the usual summaries. First, “Zand-Avesta” is an improper name, inherited from Anquetil-Duperron: in Pahlavi, zand is the commentary or interpretive translation of the abestāg (the base text), so “Avesta and Zand” designates a text plus gloss, not a work. Second, the traditional figure of twenty-one nasks (volumes) comes from Pahlavi literature (Dēnkard VIII– IX) and describes the Sasanian canon, of which only a fraction survives; the Vendīdād is the only nask that has been preserved almost complete. Third, the text was not fixed in writing during the Achaemenid period: the oral tradition was transcribed using an Avestan alphabet created during the Sasanian period (fixation of the canon during the Sasanian period; Hoffmann proposes the 4th century CE), and the oldest surviving Avestan witnesses date back to the 13th century CE. Fourth, the Khorda Avesta as a book is a late compilation of prayers; it should not be used as evidence of the Persian period. Table 1 bis. Old and Younger Avestan Old Avestan comprises the Gāthās (Y. 28–34, 43–51, and 53), the core of the Yasna Haptaŋhāiti (Y. 35–41), and some prayers, such as Y. 27.13–14. The formula Yeŋhē Hātąm (Y. 27.15), on the other hand, belongs to Younger Avestan. Younger Avestan brings together materials of diverse composition and function. The classification is linguistic: it does not, by itself, assign a year of composition nor demonstrate that all texts within the same stratum are contemporaneous. Liturgical collections contain texts from different linguistic strata. The Yasna, for example, includes both Gathic and Younger Avestan chapters. The Yasna Haptaŋhāiti should not be classified as Younger Avestan merely because of its position within the Yasna: its core comprises Y. 35–41, whereas Y 42 is identified separately as an addition in archaizing Younger Avestan.

122 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM 3. Oral transmission and Sasanian written codification Priestly transmission preserved the corpus through recitation and, later, through specialized writing. The written record linked to the Sasanian world does not equate to the composition of all texts during that period. Nor does it allow us to simply reconstruct an Achaemenid Avestan library with the structure we know from later evidence. The surviving manuscripts date from the medieval period or later. Between composition and copying came liturgical organization, variations in recitation and scribal decisions. A critical edition must specify which stage of transmission it represents; it should not describe a modern transcription lacking a textual apparatus as the “original text”. 4. The twenty-one nasks and the lost corpus The Pahlavi tradition describes an Avesta organized into twenty-one nasks. This retrospective inventory preserves a much broader memory of knowledge and genres than the surviving liturgical corpus. The comparison between the described nasks and current books is incomplete and does not authorize filling in the missing texts with doctrinal conjecture. Textual-critical clarification: inventory and loss. The traditional number of twenty-one nasks does not mean that Dēnkard VIII provides a complete account of all twenty-one: it preserves summaries of nineteen, while the remaining two were subject to loss and uneven preservation. Book IX offers an exegesis of three Gathic nasks; this Pahlavi reconstruction does not recover the complete Avestan texts of the lost nasks. The Dēnkard preserves summaries useful for studying this organization and priestly reception. Its information comes from the Pahlavi testimony that trans mits it; the age of each summarized material requires its own demonstration. The work uses these summaries in chapters L and LI without presenting them as direct copies of an Achaemenid canon.

Editions, translations and the state of the textual evidence Geldner offers a reference edition of the manuscript transmission; Darmesteter provides a historical translation heavily reliant on the Zand; Uesugi and Catt offer a reference tool for Old Avestan. These works serve different functions, and none automatically replaces the others. The Spanish rendering of the Vendīdād in the source edition is identified as a translation mediated through Darmesteter’s English version; it should not be presented in this English edition as a fresh translation from Avestan. The Gathic hymns are discussed with reference to the glosses of Uesugi and Catt. Readers must distinguish the transmitted text, intermediary translations, commentary and readings that remain open to interpretation. Conclusion to Chapter IV The surviving Avesta is the result of a prolonged transmission, with composition, liturgical organization, writing, and manuscript copying occurring at different times. The linguistic antiquity of a passage alone does not date all of its re ligious content. This distinction limits any comparison with Achaemenid inscriptions and archives. Summary Old and Younger Avestan are distinguished by linguistic criteria. The division into liturgical books does not simply coincide with this stratification, nor with the twenty-one nasks of the Pahlavi tradition.
