Chapter V. The Gāthās: Moral Choice and Cosmic Order Historical scope of this chapter. The Gāthās belong linguistically to Old Avestan, but their absolute date remains disputed. Their subsequent liturgical transmission and modern editorial history must be distinguished from their composition. Biblical comparison requires independently established dates for the biblical texts. Critical supplement: Gathic vocabulary and the limits of theological equivalence Lexical analysis of the Gāthās requires four separate operations: identifying a form in its syntactic context, establishing its possible semantic values, choosing an appro priate English equivalent and only then arguing for a historical relationship with another religious corpus. The Old Avestan Dictionary, edited by Heindio Uesugi under the editorial supervision of Adam Alvah Catt (Tokyo University of Foreign Studies, ILCAA, 2024), offers an important point of comparison. Such lexical evid ence cannot by itself establish religious dependence. In discussing aša and druj, the levels of analysis must remain distinct. In particular Gathic contexts, aša belongs to the semantic field of rightness, truth and order; one English gloss cannot capture every occurrence. Druj can denote falsehood and its antagonistic force, but this does not automatically make it equivalent to a fully personified demonic being. Neither semantic comparison nor typological resemblance alone establishes historical borrowing. A full apparatus for a Gathic locus should identify the Yasna chapter and stanza, the Avestan form and segmentation, relevant lemmas, an English rendering, significant interpretative alternatives, comparison translations and the reasons for the chosen reading. Joseph H. Peterson’s online transcription of the Yasna (avesta.org), based on Karl F. Geldner’s edition, provides a reference transcription rather than independent manuscript collation. Lexicographical control of Old Avestan (Uesugi–Catt, 2024) The Old Avestan Dictionary, coordinated by Heindio Uesugi with editorial supervision by Adam Alvah Catt (Tokyo University of Foreign Studies, ILCAA, Asian and African Lexicon 67, 2024), constitutes an additional tool for the translation of the Gāthās. Its first part is a lexical repertory; its second part offers the text and trans lation of Yasna 27,13–15, 28–34, 43–46, 47–50, 51, 53, and 54,1. Its delimitation 125

126 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM is significant: the edition studies Old Avestan and cannot indiscriminately replace a dictionary of Younger Avestan for the Yašts or the Vendīdād. The transmitted form, compound segmentation, morphology, proposed sense and English equivalent should be assessed separately. Words such as aša and druj have semantic ranges that cannot consistently be reduced to the modern oppositions “truth” versus “lie” or “good” versus “evil”. Contextual readings, internal par allels and translation alternatives should be recorded without treating a single gloss as definitive. From the standpoint of textual criticism, an English translation should be linked to a specific stanza, an explicitly stated transcription convention and the edition used; significant interpretative disagreements should be documented in notes. The relative antiquity of Gathic as a language must be distinguished from the date of composition of the hymns and the considerably later dates of the surviving manuscripts. The Gāthās are the oldest texts of the Avesta and those that tradition attributes to Zoroaster (on the debate over authorship, see Chapter IV). They are written in Old Avestan, a language closely related to Vedic Sanskrit, and are preserved within the Yasna, the liturgical text. This chapter describes their organization, explains the central concepts with their loci, and distinguishes what the Gāthās actually say from what later tradition has attributed to them. 1. Aša and druj Aša designates the true order, and druj (“the Lie”) its opposite. This opposition orders all of Gathic theology: he who follows aša is the ašauuan, and he who follows druj is the drəguuant. It is a cosmic and moral opposition, which translates into the choice of the faithful. Achaemenid inscriptions use related terms (arta and drauga), but with their own political meaning (chapter VIII). 3. Its meaning depends on the construction in which it occurs; the distribution of divine names does not by itself establish a fixed hierarchy. Chapter VI. Younger Avesta: Yašts and Vendīdād Historical scope of this chapter. The Yašts and Vendīdād are written in Younger Avestan, but their strata and liturgical formation are difficult to date. Their surviving written witnesses are later and cannot simply be equated with fifth-century BCE religious practice. Note on textual criticism regarding Fargard 12. The summary of Dēnkard VIII.44 and part of the Pahlavi transmission omit chapter 12 and skip from 11 to 13. Malandra, following West, characterizes the redaction present in K2 and its derivatives as an 18th-century composition. This description needs clarification: Cantera identifies in K2 the creation of a new Pahlavi translation of Vd 12 within the revisions of the Surat school. The date of this translation does not automatically date the entire Avestan text of the Fargard. Therefore, the coverage of twenty-two Fargards requires distinguishing between the Avestan text, the Pahlavi translation, and the families of transmission. Contrast sources: Malandra, “Vendīdā di” (2000), and Cantera, “Vendīdād ii” (2015), https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/Vendīdād-02-transmission-india/. “Younger Avesta” here denotes works transmitted in Younger Avestan: much of the Yasna (excluding the Gāthās and Yasna Haptaŋhāiti), the Yašts, the Vendīdād, the Visperad and shorter Khorda Avesta texts. Their composition and transmission span distinct periods; the earliest surviving manuscripts belong to the medieval period (thirteenth and fourteenth centuries CE). The historical implications must therefore be assessed passage by passage. 1. Yazatas and hymns The Yašts are twenty -one hymns dedicated to yazatas, deities “worthy of worship.” Of particular interest among them are Yt 5 (to Anāhitā), Yt 10 (to Mithra), Yt 13 (to the fravashis), and Yt 19 (to Zamyād, the earth or mountain, and the “glory” of kingship, xᵛarənah-). The Yašts preserve ancient material that partly refers to IndoIranian mythology, but they were compiled and assembled in their current form in later periods. Yt 10 is the hymn to Mithra (see Text 14 and Chapter XXIV), and Yt 5 and 10 are related to the mentions of Anāhitā and Mithra in the inscriptions of Artaxerxes II (Chapter VII). 131

Yašt 19 and the final renewal Text 19 contains the description of the renewal of the world (frašō.kərəti) in verses 89 and 92–96: the saošyants bring about existence “without old age and without death, without corruption or decay,” and the dead rise (Text 19.89–96; see Text 15 for the study translation). It is a key testimony to the eschatology of the later Avesta; its composition and transmission do not have a single established date. The presence of the motif in this stratum does not prove that the complete narrative formu lation was known to the Yahwists of Darius I’s time. 3. Vendīdād: purification and law The Vendīdād (“law against the daēuuas”) has twenty-two chapters (fargards) and is primarily a treatise on purity: creation of the lands (Vd 1), Yima (Vd 2), rules con cerning corpses and defilement (Vd 5–12), dogs (Vd 13–14), expiations, and healing (Vd 20–22). It is not a code of general application but a ritual manual for specialists. Its value for comparison lies in the fact that it presents a system of purity that has been compared to Leviticus; the comparison is made in chapter 36. 4. Vendīdād 19 and the temptation of Zarathustra Vendīdād 19 recounts the attack of the evil spirit (Aŋra Mainyu) on Zoroaster: the demon wants to kill him, and Zoroaster repels him with the Ahuna Vairya prayer and ritual weapons. The spirit proposes that he renounce the good religion (daēnā mazdaiiasni) in exchange for dominion, as a king would, and Zoroaster refuses. The comparison with the temptation of Jesus is studied in Chapter XVIII and requires an examination of specific motives; here it suffices to point out that the passage is recent Avestan and cannot be precisely dated. 5. Chapter VII. What Form of Zoroastrianism Was Known in the Achaemenid Period? The historical setting is the Achaemenid Empire (c. 550–330 BCE), with particular attention to Darius I (522–486 BCE) and the rulers who succeeded him. Royal inscriptions and the transmitted Avesta represent distinct bodies of evidence and must be assessed separately. See Table 0 (Conceptual Map, p. liii) for the distinction between Mazdeanism and Zoroastrianism that guides this chapter. Achaemenid Religious Evidence The royal inscriptions constitute verifiable evidence of the vocabulary of power and the invocation of Ahura Mazdā, but they are neither theological manuals nor inventories of all the cultic practices of the empire. Inference must be restricted to what these texts actually say. The retrospective identification between Darius’s imperial religion, the received Avestan corpus, and Sasanian systematizations would only be legitimate if the steps of transmission were reconstructed and justified. A chronological distinction is particularly instructive: the religious formulae of Darius I should not be read as equivalent to the invocations of Mithra and Anahita in certain texts of Artaxerxes II. The difference between these two documentary ho rizons does not preclude continuities; rather, it prevents us from assuming them without proof. The monograph can defend intense cultural contact and interaction while simultaneously acknowledging that the concrete transfer of an eschatological doctrine remains open. The question posed in the title has three possible answers. The first maintains that the Achaemenid kings were Zoroastrians, that is, that their religion continued the Zoroastrian tradition preserved in the Avesta; this is the classical position, defended with nuances by Mary Boyce (A History of Zoroastrianism II, 1982). The second maintains that the Achaemenid sources document an Iranian religion of Ahura Mazdā that cannot be identified with Avestan Zoroastrianism because it lacks the features that define the latter (Zarathustra, the Aməša Spəṇtas, the Yasna liturgy); this critical position is represented, with different arguments, by Jean Kellens and, along different lines, by Wouter Henkelman. The third is intermediate and speaks of a common “Mazdaism,” of which the Avesta and the inscriptions would be independent testimonies. This chapter does not resolve the question: it 135

Greek sources: Herodotus and the Magi Herodotus (I 131–132) describes the religion of the Persians as a religion without statues, temples, or altars, with sacrifices in high places to Zeus, whom he identifies with the entirety of the sky, and also to the sun, the moon, the earth, fire, water, and the winds; the sacrifice is accompanied by a chant of the magus, a “theogony.” He does not mention Ahura Mazdā or Zoroaster and does not say that fire is lit in the sacrifices. Regarding the Magi, Herodotus presents them as a Median tribe (I 101), as interpreters of dreams (I 107, 120), and as those who practice exposing corpses to birds and dogs and killing ants, snakes, and other vermin (I 140). In III 61-79, he narrates the usurpation of the magus and the “magophony” in which the Persians kill him. Xenophon (Cyropaedia VIII 1,23) portrays the Magi as those who sing hymns to the gods at dawn, and Strabo (XV 3,13-15) describes sacrifices without al tar or fire on a clean surface and temples of Anaitis in Cappadocia. The comparison of these sources with the inscriptions and with the Avesta is not automatic: they are external descriptions, from different dates and territories, and several of those most frequently invoked (Plato, Alcibiades I 121e –122a; Diogenes Laertius, prologue 6–9; Pausanias V 27,5–6) require differentiated controls: the transmitting text of Diogenes is located and compared with an available edition; the other places here are only identified by reference.100 3. Archaeological evidence At Pasargadae, the so-called “sacred precinct” preserves two stone platforms that Stronach interpreted as altars, one of them stepped. In the reliefs of the royal tombs at Naqš-e Rostam, the king appears before an altar with a fire beneath the winged disk. This figure, commonly associated with Ahura Mazdā, is also identified with the royal xᵛarənah or with a representation of the king; its identification is debated. There are no definitively established Achaemenid fire temples: the building at Nush-i Jan in Media is earlier (8th – 7th centuries BCE), and its interpretation as a temple is also debated (Stronach and Roaf, Nush-i Jan I, 2007). Part III. The Empire as a Framework Part III — research argument, principal evidence and limit. Royal inscriptions and administrative archives reconstruct the imperial framework. Their genres cannot be combined into a single doctrinal manifesto. Inscriptions, tablets, and material culture of the Achaemenid imperial religion. Chapter VIII. The Royal Inscriptions and the Religion of the Great King Chronological context. Achaemenid inscriptions from the 6th–4th centuries BCE, with special attention to Darius I (522–486 BCE) and Xerxes I (486–465 BCE). Each inscription should be placed within its reign and on its specific support, without apply ing a single formula to all the kings. The inscriptions of Darius I and Xerxes are the central dossier for understanding what religion can be documented under Persian rule. Behistun presents a monumental trilingual version in Old Persian, Elamite, and Akkadian, and also has an Aramaic transmission; other inscriptions in the dossier require independent identification of their languages and supports. This chapter examines three: the Behistun inscription (DB), the Naqš-e Rostam inscriptions (DNa, DNb), and the “Daivas” inscription of Xerxes (XPh), and asks what theology of power they contain and what relationship they may have with the Avesta. 1. Behistun (DB) and the Theology of Royal Power According to the royal version recorded in Behistun, Darius states that, after the death of Cambyses, he eliminated Gaumata, presented as “the magus” who impersonated Bardiya, and defeated his adversaries in a series of campaigns. The identific ation of Gaumata as an imposter is part of Darius’s dynastic legitimation and remains a subject of debate. Its significance for the book lies in the religious language with which he justifies the kingdom. Darius declares that he reigns “by the favour of Ahura Mazdā” (DBI 11–12) and that Ahura Mazdā gave him the kingdom (DBI 12–13). He attributes each rebellion to Lie (drauga), and victory to the fact that he was not a “follower of Lie” (DB IV 33–36). The same inscription declares that Darius restored the sanctuaries (ayadanā) that the magus Gaumāta had destroyed (DB I 63–65). Finally, he invokes future readers: if they see the inscription and make it known, may Ahura Mazdā be their friend (DB IV 66–69, approximately). HISTORIOGRAPHICAL NOTE (DB, accession of Darius I). The inscription preserves the court-authorized version concerning Gaumata and Bardiya; Babylonian tablets confirm the political use of the name Bardiya, but do not in themselves resolve the ruler’s identity. Versions and Translations: Elamite, Akkadian, and Aramaic The trilingual inscriptions are not literal translations: the Elamite and Akkadian versions adapt the vocabulary to their audience. The Aramaic version of Behistun is known from a papyrus from Elephantine (TAD C2.1: Aramaic copy of Behistun, P. Demonstrable dependence: no, neither with the Avesta nor with the biblical texts; the inscriptions are an independent testimony that serves as a control for all subsequent comparisons. Conclusion to Chapter VIII The royal inscriptions express a political theology that legitimizes the sovereign and condemns rebellion as a lie. This discourse demonstrates the association between power and divinity at court, but not that every population in the empire adopted that theology.

Numismatic Dossier: The Daric, Biblical Memory, and Fire Altars Monetary evidence requires distinguishing between denomination, iconography, the sovereign depicted, and the date of minting. The Achaemenid gold daric, in its classic types, features a royal or heroic figure armed—with a bow and spear— and an incuse punch on the reverse: it is not a fire-altar coin. The coin from the Oxus hoard, recorded by the British Museum as 1897,1231.177 (museum no. 124080; 5th–4th century BCE; 8.50 g), serves as concrete material evidence of this type. It is an ancient piece identified in a collection, not a modern engraving or a ritual reconstruction. The episode is set, literarily, in the reign of David, well before the development of Persian coinage; therefore, its monetary terminology is an indication of linguistic updating by the narrator or the redactional tradition, not proof that darics were minted under David. Ezra 2:69; 8:27 and Nehemiah 7:70–72 should also be compared, as they contain related monetary forms and raise their own question of lexical transmission. The biblical figure also does not confirm that the offered coins have been physically found. The depiction of sanctuaries and altars associated with fire is attested on other Iranian issues, but the most expressive belong to different periods. For ex ample, the British Museum holds a silver drachma from Persis (1855,0928.1; circa 2nd century BCE; Parthian period) whose reverse shows a cult building, an altar, and a royal figure. The catalogue attributes the piece to “Darius I

Chapter IX. Persepolis: Tablets, Cult, and Administration This chapter considers the administration of Persepolis under Darius I and Xerxes I. The Fortification and Treasury tablets belong to separate archival groups and chronolo gical horizons; their records of cultic payments cannot be treated as a comprehensive de scription of later Zoroastrianism. The administrative archives of Persepolis are the closest source to the religion actually practiced and administered in Darius’s Persia, in contrast to the rhetoric of royal inscriptions. They are divided into the Fortification Archive (PFA), dated between the 13th and 28th years of Darius (509–494 BCE), and the Treasury Texts (PTT), documented approximately between 492 and 458 BCE. The classic edition of the Elamite Fortification Texts is that of Richard Hallock (1969); that of the Treasury Texts, that of George Cameron (1948). 1. The Fortification Tablets The archive comprises thousands of Elamite texts and several hundred Aramaic texts on clay tablets; the Aramaic texts may be incised or written in ink. A set of let ters on leather should not be attributed to this find: that material belongs, for example, to the correspondence of Arsames studied in Chapter XLI. The tablets record rations, movements, livestock, and flour, and preserve impressions of cylinder seals and stamps. Religion appears in the allocations for offerings: Hallock recognized a category designated by the Elamite term lan, related to officials who perform the rites. Source for verification of the material and the collection: University of Chicago, OCHRE, “Persepolis Fortification Archive,” https://voices.uchicago.edu/ochre/project/pfa/ Richard T. Hallock, Persepolis Fortification Tablets (University of Chicago Press, 1969). 2. The Treasury Texts The Treasury texts document silver payments to workers on the construction of Persepolis and are not a direct religious source. Their interest for the book is twofold: they confirm that the administration used Elamite and Aramaic in parallel, 151

152 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM and they reveal a population of artisans from very diverse backgrounds, illustrating the environment in which languages and practices circulated. The Treasury also yielded green-chert trays, plates, mortars and pestles in the 1930s: 269 objects, 203 bearing brief Aramaic ink formulae, dated to Xerxes and Artaxerxes I. R. A. Bowman published them in Aramaic Ritual Texts from Persepolis (1970), interpreting them as equipment for a “proto-Mithraic” haoma cult conducted by treasurers, an interpretation subsequently challenged. Gad Barnea (2025) proposes “regulated gifts” from Arachosia, a form of informal tribute designated ʾškr, and relates the mortars to the yasna more broadly. Seal PTS 20, with mortar, pestle and fire-holder, is interpreted as depicting a lay ritual patron. These are interpretative proposals; no residue analysis is cited. This assemblage is distinct from the Fortification Archive and Treasury payment tablets. Its dates and proposed Arachosian setting preclude mechanical transfer to Jerusalem’s provisioning under Darius I or to Elephantine. The comparison is typological, not a demonstrated ritual genealogy. 3. Offerings, Priests, and the Calendar A major finding of recent studies (Henkelman 2008, among others) is that the recipients of the offerings are primarily Elamite deities, including Humban, and that Ahura Mazdā appears, but does not dominate the scene. Among the officiants are priests with Elamite names and also the term that has been read as “magus” (makuš), suggesting an Iranian priesthood alongside an Elamite one.102 The emerging image of the religion is pluralistic: neither a uniform Zoroastrianism nor a monolatric religion of Ahura Mazdā. The designations šatin and makuš should not be treated as mutually exclusive ethnic categories: the personal names, institutional roles and cultic contexts of those so designated require assessment case by case. Chapter X. Religious Policy and Material Culture Chronological context. Achaemenid imperial policy, 6th–4th centuries BCE; local Egyptian, Mesopotamian, and Levantine evidence. The policy of one sovereign does not become a general decree of tolerance for the entire empire. The term “religious policy” refers to a set of interventions that the sources attribute to the Persian kings regarding temples and local cults. This chapter brings together the main evidence, distinguishes its type and reliability, and proposes a cautious conclusion: there was selective patronage, often at the initiative of local communities, and not a uniform doctrine of tolerance. 1. Fire altars and worship spaces Achaemenid cult spaces are an open question: the two platforms of the sacred precinct at Pasargadae, the rock altars at Naqš-e Rostam and Persepolis, and the altars in the royal tombs all demonstrate a fire cult within the royal sphere, but they do not establish the form of a temple. Boyce posited the existence of fire temples as early as this period, while the definitive evidence is later (see Chapters XXVIII and XLIX). The book concludes that fire was an element of the royal cult, though a spe cific building cannot be definitively identified. 3. Seals, reliefs and iconography Seal impressions from Persepolis depict banquet scenes, heroic figures, and cult rituals, some with fire altars; palace reliefs show delegations from subject peoples. The fact that imperial iconography incorporated traditions from various cultures does not in itself indicate religious adoption, and the identification of the winged disc with Ahura Mazdā is disputed. In the provinces, seals from Yehud (bearing the inscription yhd) and Samaria show that the local administration used Persian forms mixed with local iconography (Lipschits and Vanderhooft).

RELIGIOUS POLICY AND MATERIAL CULTURE 157 4. The Cyrus Cylinder and Imperial Propaganda The Cyrus Cylinder was written in Akkadian and presents Cyrus as chosen by Marduk, who returns the divine images to his cities. It is a text written for Babylon in the Babylonian language, not a testimony of Persian religion; its relationship to the edicts of Ezra 1 and 6 lies in the model of government it reveals, not in an identity of content. Isaiah 44:28–45:7 calls Cyrus “anointed” (māšîaḥ), but the prophetic text interprets this from the perspective of YHWH, not from Ahura Mazdā (see chapter XIV). Assessment Typological similarity: temple patronage is a practice of Near Eastern kings, not a specifically Persian trait. Probable mediation: yes, through the administration and local intermediaries such as Udjahorresnet or Nehemiah. Demonstrable dependence: no; in no case is it shown that Persian policy transformed the theology of the beneficiary communities. Conclusion to Chapter X Persian interventions in local sanctuaries are better understood as decisions of governance, funding, and negotiation than as a modern policy of religious freedom. Restoring a temple could foster imperial stability without requiring doctrinal assimilation from its users. The comparison must also consider coercion, conflicts, and regional differences. Summary Imperial politics, biblical memory, and archaeology are separated. The decrees of Ezra are studied in their preserved literary form and their possible relationship with documented practices, without considering their textual authenticity resolved.

Darius I, Imperial Religion, and Yahwist Communities: Texts, Practices, and Limits of Evidence Object, chronology and hierarchy of sources The reign of Darius I (522–486 BCE) offers the best contemporary framework for studying the contact between Achaemenid institutions and the communities of Judah. Its historical interest lies not in attributing the creation of Jewish doctrines to the Persian court, but in identifying demonstrable circumstances of contact: provincial government, administrative communication, the movement of officials and scribes, the subsidizing or regulation of sanctuaries, the mobility of resources, and the reworking of legitimacies. At least four sets should be distinguished: (A) contemporary royal inscriptions, (B) contemporary administrative archives, (C) biblical writings that depict events from Darius’s time, composed or reworked through complex literary processes, and (D) later testimonies that allow us to study reception but do not automatically describe practices of the 6th century BCE. 1. The royal inscriptions: Ahura Mazdā, truth and legitimation of power The Bisotun /Behistun Inscription (DB), created under Darius I and preserved in Old Persian, Elamite, and Akkadian, is a proclamation of dynastic legitimacy and the defeat of adversaries. The monarch attributes his success to the favour of Auramazda, and the contrast between true legitimation and falsehood (with drauga- expressly attested, but without an autonomous arta- in DB) articulates the discourse on rebellion and the order of the kingdom. It is a testament to royal ideology, not a systematic exposition of the Avesta. DB makes no explicit mention of YHWH, Jerusalem, or Yehud. Therefore, Darius’s invocation of Auramazda does not demonstrate the practice of all the later features of Zoroastrianism, nor a direct doctrinal transfer to the Yahwist religion. Their nomenclature distinguishes place, king, and text: DB (Darius, Bisotún), DNa/DNb (Darius, Naqš-e Rostam), DPd/DPe (Darius, Persepolis). In a critical edition, each proposition will be linked to the relevant inscription identifier and lines; a single abbreviation is insufficient to document a disputed reading. 2. Persepolis: material records of a plural administration The Persepolis Fortification Tablets (PFT), written mainly in Elamite with Aramaic inscriptions, record operations dated roughly between 509 and 494 BCE; the Persepolis Treasury Tablets (PTT) cover part of the end of Darius’s reign and later reigns. Their information on rations, movements, animals, workers, skilled personnel, and seals is valuable for reconstructing imperial networks. Many individuals bore names of Iranian and other origins. However, the existence of movements to the imperial centre does not necessarily prove regular travel by Judeans from Yehud to Persepolis: such a hypothesis requires positive nominal or geographical identific ations, not an extrapolation from the general records. Yehud and Jerusalem in the literature of the Persian era Haggai provides explicit chronological markers in the second year of Darius I, conventionally 520 BCE (Hag 1:1; 1:15; 2:1; 2:10; 2:20). Zechariah 1–8 places oracles in the second and fourth years of the king (Zech 1:1, 7; 7:1). These dates are especially relevant for reconstructing the discourses on the restoration of the sanctuary. The narrative of Ezra 5–6 represents an archival search, the mediation of Tattenai, and royal authorization concerning the work in Jerusalem; Ezra 6:15 dates its completion to the sixth year of Darius (conventionally 515 BCE). The date of the narrative and the date of composition —or redaction —of its preserved literary form are distinct problems. Consequently, it is not appropriate to present the entire book of Ezra, Nehemiah, Esther, or Daniel as if it had been written during the lifetime of Darius I. Testimonies to be presented in opposition within the framework: Haggai 1:1 and Zechariah 1:1, Masoretic Hebrew text and English translation with BHS identification (ed. K. Elliger and W. Rudolph; fifth edition revised by A. Schenker, 1997); Ezra 5:6–17 and 6:1–15, Masoretic Aramaic text and English translation, with a record of ketiv/qere; for the Greek tradition, the correspondences of 1 Esdras/Greek Ezra must be treated as distinct textual testimonies, not as translations without divergences. The representation of Darius as patron of the temple must also be analysed as a Judean discourse on the relationship between imperial power and the sovereignty of YHWH. 4. Names, writings and transmission of cultural habits The name Zerubbabel (Hebrew Zərubbāḇel) has a connection to the Babylonian onomastic sphere; it is not in itself evidence of a Zoroastrian religious borrowing. Mordecai is generally associated with a Mesopotamian nominal environment linked to Marduk; his inclusion in a Persian-style narrative does not transform it into an Iranian name. The etymology of Esther is disputed, and the proposed connection with an Iranian word for “star” should not be taken as a paleolinguistic certainty. The adoption of specific Iranian words must be tested word by word using historical phonetics, the chronology of attestations, and plausible transmission routes. The similarity of religious themes without a recognizable linguistic borrowing admits of multiple explanations.

162 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM 5. Religion, worship and politics: what can be inferred Achaemenid texts reveal an ideology of divine legitimation and the existence of an administration capable of intervening in local resources and sanctuaries. The accounts of Ezra present funding and authorizations related to the Temple in Jerusalem; the Elephantine documents (especially TAD A4.7–A4.10) demonstrate cultic negotiations under Darius II, approximately eight decades after the death of Darius I. These are two distinct chronological contexts: the Elephantine papyri should not be cited as acts of Darius I. It is also necessary to distinguish early Zoroastrianism from Parthian, Sasanian, and Pahlavi systematizations on topics such as the Last Judgement, resurrection, the eschatological saviour, and hierarchies of spiritual beings. A plausible historical hypothesis is that the Achaemenid government provided vehicles for the circulation of administrative formulae, languages, and representations of sovereignty among religious groups. The additional hypothesis of a specific doctrinal transfer requires, for each concept, a date of the transmitting source, a receiving source, comparable vocabulary, a historical channel, and verification against Mesopotamian precedents and earlier Israelite traditions. Analogies such as Ahura Mazdā /YHWH, Asha / justice, or Iranian celestial entities/ Judean angels are not sufficient in themselves to demonstrate dependence. 6. The Lachish ostracon revealed in 2023: documentary rectification The ceramic fragment announced in March 2023 as an Aramaic inscription from “the 24th year of Darius” cannot be used as contemporary evidence. The Israel Antiquities Authority withdrew the attribution after a specialist explained that she had engraved the text during a modern demonstration. The ancient fragment and the modern inscription do not constitute an authentic Achaemenid inscription. This episode illustrates the value of recording the authentication history of each ob ject before adding it to a corpus of evidentiary sources. See Associated Press, March 2023, and the Israel Antiquities Authority’s statement of correction referenced by the archaeological press.

Chapter XI. Elephantine: The Community, the Temple and the Papyri Women, contracts and administrative agency: three non-equivalent archives Women, documentary agency and property at Elephantine The dossier of Mibtahiah (also transcribed Mipṭaḥiah) adds a perspective on Persian-period Judean experience that priestly correspondence alone cannot provide. Aramaic property and marriage instruments register a woman as a legal participant, her assets and dowry, and clauses regulating divorce and the disposition of property. These agreements are documentary acts: their formulae reveal negotiated rights and household strategies, not a comprehensive code enforced identically across the empire. A contract involving Mibtahiah and the Egyptian royal builder Eshor / Ashor specifies the bride’s property and protections; other instruments concern house property and conditions of inheritance. They also require differentiating documents of this woman from those of Yehoyishmaʿ and Ananiah, another Elephantine family, whose similar clauses must not be conflated. Even when both parties can initiate divorce, the pecuniary consequences are not necessarily symmetrical. Original document, translation, restoration and modern legal interpretation must remain separate. A comparison with Persepolis is instructive only at the level of administrative visibility: the Fortification Archive records commodities, staff, estates and rations, including women and royal households; it is not a collection of Elephantine-style marriage contracts. Neither documentary group proves that women in Yehud possessed identical rights or that one legal regime derives directly from Zoroastrian doctrine. Names such as Shelomith require a separately identified Judean inscription or seal before being added to a cross-regional prosopography. 168 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM The legal dossiers of Elephantine offer an essential corrective to an exclusively priestly or male reconstruction of Persian-period Judaism. The contracts associated with Mibtahiah (for example TAD B2.6) document marital property, dowry and contractual provisions in a specific Aramaic legal milieu. They are not transparent accounts of every woman’s social standing, nor direct evidence for an Iranian religious borrowing. The text, legal act, archaeological archive and date of each instrument must remain distinguishable (Porten and Yardeni, Textbook of Aramaic Documents from Ancient Egypt; Azzoni, The Private Lives of Women in Persian Egypt, 2013). Evidence from the Persepolis Fortification archive belongs to another administrative environment and another language. Its ration records include women and mothers among the recipients, but their interpretation requires attention to institutional position, commodity, status, date and preserved context (Hallock 1969; Persepolis Fortification Archive, Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures, University of Chicago). Yehud seals and the prosopography of names such as Shelomith should form a third dossier only after readings, provenance, identification and chronological setting have been independently verified. No identity between named individuals should be inferred from identical names. Comparison is defensible at the level of document genre and institutional practice: property rights, contractual formulae, family relationships, rations and the visibility of women in official records. It does not establish identical rights across Elephantine, Persepolis and Yehud, still less a direct line of theological dependency. The book’s matrix of certainty should classify attested legal formulas separately from reconstructions of social institutions. The chapter examines the Yahwist community of Elephantine in the fifth century BCE, particularly the destruction of its temple in 410 BCE and the petitions of 407 BCE. These events occurred under Darius II (423–404 BCE), not Darius I. Critical Note — The Documentary Status of the Elephantine Letters

ELEPHANTINE: THE COMMUNITY AND THE TEMPLE 169 The distinctive value of Elephantine for the study of Judah under Achaemenid rule lies in the relative contemporaneity of its administrative and epistolary records, not in any assumption that the community shared a theological system with Iranian religion. The papyri reveal cultic practice, institutional relationships and appeals for authorization within an imperial framework. Because these documents address par ticular disputes and administrative needs, their silence on other doctrines must not be mistaken for evidence of what the community did—or did not—believe. Cowley’s edition, Aramaic Papyri of the Fifth Century BCE (Clarendon Press, 1923), is a testament to the philological history of these materials: it brings together Aramaic texts, translations and notes, but the editor himself indicates that he was unable to complete the planned checks on all the originals in the repositories of Cairo and Berlin. An argument for Iranian influence cannot rest solely on the fact that JudeoAramaic and Persian documents belong to the same political chronology. For each alleged parallel, it is necessary to formulate separately the presence of the feature in the papyri, the presence of the same feature in a datable Iranian source, and the pos sibility of institutional, linguistic, or ritual mediation. In the absence of all three elements, one should speak of imperial coexistence or comparative similarity, not of proven borrowing. This precaution strengthens, rather than weakens, the overall historical argument. The Elephantine Papyri: Degrees of Documentary Certainty The collection of A. The Community and Its Archives: Papyri and Ostraca Elephantine, the Nile island opposite Aswan (Syene), was home to a Persian army garrison where Judeo-Aramaic soldiers and their families served alongside Egyptians and other contingents. The documentation is of two kinds. The papyri, containing contracts, letters, and lists, make up series A, B, and C of the Porten and Yardeni edition, while the ostraca, fragments of pottery used as writing surfaces, comprise series D. The ostraca are short, everyday texts: messages, accounts of grain and wine, lists of names, receipts, and exercises; the papyri, more carefully formatted, preserve the major legal matters and official petitions. Both supports complement each other: the papyri frame the events, and the ostraca show the everyday life of a community in which theo- foros names (Yĕdanyāh, Mĕšullām, ʿAnanyāh) coexist with Egyptian and Persian names. The temple of YHW Petition TAD A4.7 describes the temple as a stone building with stone pillars, carved stone portals, bronze-hinged doors, and a cedar wood roof, as well as gold and silver trays. The petitioners claim that their parents built it during the time of the Egyptian kings and that Cambyses, upon entering Egypt (525 BCE), found it standing and did not touch it. This last statement carries political weight: the community invokes a precedent of Persian imperial respect, thereby establishing the sanctuary’s antiquity, predating Cambyses’ conquest. The urban area of Elephantine also included the cult of Khnum. The proximity of both religious spheres is relevant, but without precise archaeological identification, it does not authorize the assertion that they shared the exact same precinct. 3. The destruction of the temple by the priests of Khnum (410 BCE) According to the petition, in the month of Tammuz in the 14th year of Darius (410 BCE), the priests of the god Khnum (Ḥnûb) of Elephantine, in agreement with Vidranga, a local chief with an Iranian name, urged the removal of the temple of YHWH. Vidranga wrote to his son Nafayna, commander of the garrison at Syene, who, with Egyptian troops, stormed the temple, demolished the stone pillars, destroyed the gateways, burned the doors and the cedar roof, and carried off the gold

ELEPHANTINE: THE COMMUNITY AND THE TEMPLE 173 and silver vessels. The text does not explain the motive. Theories have included a clash between the cult of Khnum, a ram-headed god, and the sacrifices of the Yahwists, and a desire to expand the precinct of the Egyptian god. The bribery alluded to in the document itself, and the absence of the satrap Arsames, whom the petitioners claim to have no knowledge of what happened, further suggest a political explanation. These explanations are hypotheses; what is certain is that local priests, a Persian official, and Egyptian troops intervened in the destruction, meaning that the Yahwist community depended on a balance of power between imperial authority and the local Egyptian elites. For the book, the episode is important for two reas ons: it reveals a Yahwist religion with a temple and sacrifices on the periphery of the empire, and an administrative environment with Persian names (Vidranga, Arsames, Bagohi, Ostanes) that influenced its reception. 4. Petitions to Jerusalem and Samaria The petitioners state that they had previously written to Bagohi (Bagavahya), governor of Yehud, to the high priest Johanan of Jerusalem, and to a man named Ostanes, of Iranian origin, without receiving a reply. They also state that they fasted and mourned from the 14th to the 17th year without offerings of grain, incense, or burnt offerings. They ask Bagohi to intercede for the rebuilding of the temple and the restoration of offerings in the name of YHWH, and they send a copy to Delaiah and Shelemiah, sons of Sanballat, governor of Samaria. The fact that they address both Jerusalem and Samaria simultaneously suggests that the sanctuary at Elephantine was not considered a rival to Jerusalem, but rather a community appealing to the Yahwist authorities of the region. Memorandum A4.9 contains the response, which is read over the text: the reconstruction is authorized, and the offerings to be restored are listed with a restriction on burnt offerings that the edition must confirm. 5. Divine Names, Worship, and Religious Culture The Elephantine documents give YHW the epithet “God of Heaven” (ʾĕlāh šĕmayyāʾ), common in the Persian chancery and in Ezra, and associate him with other deities in contribution lists, leading to talk of a syncretic or polytheistic Yahwism. This assessment depends on how the lists are read (contributions to YHW

174 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM alongside Eshem-Bethel and Anat-Bethel) and the weight given to domestic religiosity versus the official cult. Barnea has also proposed traces of Iranian practice, such as the term ʾtrwdn, which is discussed again in Chapter XII. 6. The Later History of the Community and the Limits of the Evidence Aramaic documentation from Elephantine continues beyond the first Persian rule in Egypt. The letter TAD A3.9 (Brooklyn Museum 47.218.151), concerning the replacement of Amyrtaeus by Nepherites I, is dated to approximately 399–398 BCE. Its presence demonstrates documentary continuity at the beginning of the 4th century; however, it does not, by itself, prove how long the garrison remained or when its temple disappeared. To understand Yahwism in the 4th century, other centres must also be considered (Wadi Daliyeh, Idumea, Yehud, and Gerizim: Chapter XIII). Nor should one speak of a “synagogue” at Elephantine: the term designates a later institution; the building of YHWH is a temple with an altar and sacrifices. Chapter Conclusion The papyri and ostraca from Elephantine document a Yahwist community with a temple, priesthood, and relations with Jerusalem and Samaria, embedded within a Persian administrative framework and neighboring a temple of Khnum. The destruction of 410 is the best-documented episode, and its cause remains unresolved. Summary The chapter reconstructs the Jewish colony of Elephantine from its papyri and ostraca: the Temple of YHWH, its destruction in 410 BCE at the instigation of the priests of Khnum with the support of Vidranga, and the petition addressed to Bagohi and the authorities of Samaria. It concludes with the pantheon revealed in the documents and with the limits of what this source allows us to assert about Yahwism in the Persian period.

Chapter XII. “God of Heaven” and the Problem of ʾtrwdn Chronological context. Aramaic chancery formulae and documents from Elephantine of the 5th century BCE; ʾtrwdn belongs to the dossier of Darius II. Modern interpretations of the term must be distinguished from its ancient attestation. “God of Heaven” as a documentary formula: a contextual concordance The Aramaic expression ʾĕlāh šĕmayyāʾ must be indexed by grammatical form, speaking voice and documentary genre before comparing it with Old Persian Auramazdā. Ezra 5:11–12 belongs to the temple-building inquiry; Ezra 6:9–10 to royal provision and intercession; Ezra 7:12 and 7:21 to the royal decree framework. Repetitions of a divine epithet in a compiled biblical narrative are not equivalent to independent contemporary Achaemenid archival attestations. The formula can express political and administrative accommodation without attesting Mazdean doctrinal dependence. Its presence in biblical Aramaic is a datum about the received text; the dating and authenticity of an embedded decree, and the relation between epithets in different languages, must be argued separately. A direct equation between “God of Heaven” and Auramazdā is not established by the fact that both divine designations appear in Persianperiod contexts. Names of Witnesses and Traces of Iranian Influence The Elephantine papyri contain Iranian names of officials (Arsames, Vidranga, Bagohi) and community members, indicating an Iranian administrative environment, not a conversion of the Jews. The names of the Jews themselves are Hebrew or Aramaic, often theophoric (YHW) names (Jedanias, Meshullam, Hosha’yah), with some Egyptian and Babylonian. The collection suggests linguistic and occupa tional contact with the Persians, not an adoption of their religion. 4. Barnea and His Critics: The State of the Debate Barnea’s hypothesis concerning fire (burning bush, Ex 3, and ʾtrwdn) is discussed in Chapter LVI. Three objections can be expected from critics: the paleographic reading is uncertain; an Iranian term for fire in the vocabulary of a military community does not prove a cult; and the dating of Ex 3 (traditions J and E, of composition prior to the Persian period according to conventional criticism) cannot be based on a fifth-century document. The discussion is not closed, and this book presents it without taking sides with either reading.

Chapter XIII. Yehud, Samaria, and Idumea Chronological context. Yehud, Samaria, and Idumea during the Achaemenid period and their subsequent transitions. The documentation of each territory requires its own dating; a Hellenistic situation cannot be retroactively projected to the 5th century BCE. Temple economy and imperial administration: separating three documentary scales Elephantine temple correspondence, the Murašû business archive of Nippur, and the Fortification / Treasury archives of Persepolis illuminate different institutions. Elephantine TAD A4.7– A4.9 concerns the destruction, petition and negotiated restoration of the temple of YHW; these documents are evidence for a local religious institution addressing imperial officials, not a complete temple ledger. The Murašû contracts, dated broadly 454–404 BCE, record land leases, debts, taxes and obligations in Babylonia. They do not directly describe financing of the Jerusalem sanctuary under Darius I. The Persepolis Fortification Archive (especially ca. 509–494 BCE) is a record of royal administration and distribution, including travel provisions, rations and commodities for cultic activities. The Persepolis Treasury corpus includes payments for labour and other disbursements. Neither can be used to derive a fixed budgetary formula for every temple in Yehud or Egypt. The same office name, or a loan such as ganzabara, must be identified in its individual inscription or document before it becomes evidence of transfer. Ezra 4:13 and the fiscal triad conventionally rendered tribute, duty and toll must be analysed in the literary and political context of the letter; it is not an excavated tax return. By contrast, the material from Nippur often contains dated receipts and contracts. The methodologically defensible conclusion is a structured comparison of fiscal vocabularies and administrative practices, not an unproven equivalence of revenue mechanisms. The possibility of Judeans participating in the Nippur land economy is supported by personal names and dossiers; communal affiliation still requires onomastic caution. Mediating processes preceding the Persian conquest. The cultural history of the Jewish communities does not begin with Cyrus. The deportations and Neo-As syrian administrations, the Neo-Babylonian conquest, and the residence of Jews in Babylon shaped family networks, economic obligations, writing practices, and channels of circulation before 539 BCE. Their continuity under the new sovereignty necessitates comparing, for each supposed Iranian borrowing, an explanation of Achaemenid innovation with one of Mesopotamian and Levantine persist183

To attribute a trait to specifically Achaemenid influence, it is not enough to find it in a document from the 5th–4th centuries BCE: one must examine whether there are Neo-Assyrian, Neo-Babylonian, or Levantine antecedents and whether the change coincides with an innovation attested under the new sovereignty. The tablets of Ā lY āḫū du allow us to document Judaic networks in Babylon, but they do not in themselves equate to documentation of Mazdaean beliefs. The inference must be drawn through datable agents and practices, not by the general label “Persian influence.” Documentary evidence and limits of inference. The cuneiform tablets of Yehud and nearby populations document the economic life of Jewish people from the Neo-Babylonian period to the early Achaemenid period (Pearce and Wunsch corpus, CUSAS 28, 2014; Pearce synthesis, Religion Compass 10/9, 2016, 230–243). Their chronological continuity is relevant for identifying administrative and settlement networks, but an agrarian contract, a service obligation, or a theophoric name does not, by itself, demonstrate dualism, resurrection, or an Avesta reception. It must be compared with Yehud, Elephantine, and the biblical testimonies without treating them as copies of a single cultural process. Yahwism during the Persian period was not uniform. Elephantine is a case of military diaspora; Yehud, a territory with a rebuilt temple and a local elite; Samaria, a province with its own cultic centre; Idumea, a region where populations of Edom ite and other origins coexisted. This chapter brings together the kinds of evidence available for each and points out what is unknown, because the Jerusalem model as a universal pattern is the one least supported by the documentation. 1. Yehud under Persian Administration “Yehud” is the Aramaic name for the province (mĕdînat yĕhûd, Ezra 5:8), whose governor is called peḥâ (TAD A4.7 mentions Bagohi, “governor of Yehud”). Among the governors known from various sources are Zerubbabel (Hag 1:1), Nehemiah (Neh 5:14), and, from coins, a Hezekiah (4th century BCE). The temple was rebuilt according to Ezra 5–6 from 520 to 516/515 BCE, according to the reckoning convention of the sixth year of Darius I. The extent and population of the province are debated, and there is no documented border. The studies use seals

YEHUD, SAMARIA AND IDUMEA 185 with the inscription yhd and archaeological findings to delimit a small territory around Jerusalem (Lipschits and Carter). 2. Samaria and the Wadi Daliyeh Papyri The Wadi Daliyeh papyri are Aramaic documents from Samaria dating to the 4th century BCE (approximately 375–335 BCE), found in a cave in the Jordan Valley. They record slave sales and other transactions, including the names of governors from the Sanballat family (Gropp, DJD XXVIII, 2001). They demonstrate that Samaria had its own administration and that its population used theophoric names containing YHW. The sanctuary on Mount Gerizim has been excavated: Yitzhak Magen has proposed an earlier temple dating to the 5th century BCE, which others date later; the temple was destroyed by John Hyrcanus around 111–110 BCE (Josephus, Antiquities XIII 254–256; Magen 2008). Gerizim provides evidence of a Yahwism with its own centre, parallel to that of Jerusalem. 3. Idumea and the Ostraca The Idumean ostraca (4th century BCE; several hundred published by Eph’al and Naveh and others) are Aramaic texts from Maresha, Beersheba, and Arad that record transactions; the names of individuals show a mixed population, with worshippers of Qos (an Edomite deity), YHWH, and other gods. They are evidence that in southern Judea, cults other than that of Jerusalem coexisted, and that Persian “Idumea” was not a region of uniform population (the corpus exceeds two thousand ostraca: some 201 in Eph’al and Naveh 1996, 629 in Porten 2011, and nearly 1,500 in Vittmann 2003). 4. The Fourth Century BCE as a Historical Horizon The 4th century BCE contains most of the documentation of Judea, Samaria, and Idumea outside of the biblical books. It is also the century of the last reforms under Artaxerxes II and III and of the entry of Alexander the Great (332 BCE). The evidence allows us to rule out a uniform Yahwism: Jerusalem, Gerizim, Elephantine, and the cults of southern Judea coexisted, with relationships that the texts only hint at. Assessment. Typological similarity: not applicable to this chapter. Probable mediation: administrative, via Aramaic and the local bureaucracy. Demonstrable dependence: this is not a question of dependence, but of context; the main contribution is to show that any comparison with the Iranian world must indicate which Yahwism it refers to. Chapter Conclusion Yehud, Samaria, and Idumea do not constitute a single religious landscape. Comparing them requires distinguishing the institutions, populations, and documentation of each region. The existence of Yahwist sanctuaries outside Jerusalem modifies any model that assumes a fully realized centralization during the Persian period.

Documentary supplement to chapter XIII. Yehud and the Jewish communities: archeology, economics and limits of religious inference The archaeological record of Yehud should serve as an independent counterpoint to historiographical constructions based on Ezra, Nehemiah, Haggai, and Zechariah. The province is not limited to the Temple in Jerusalem: storehouses, transport containers, seal impressions, coins, dwellings, and settlements allow us to study its administration and economic life. These artifacts do not directly express a theology, but they help reconstruct the material circumstances in which religious traditions were preserved, discussed, and transmitted. 1. The YHWD Impressions: Material Evidence and Historical Scope The marks yhwd/ “Yehud” on the handles and bodies of ceramic vessels constitute material documentation of the province during the Persian and Early Hellenistic periods. The corpus of Lipschits and Vanderhooft (2011) identifies and contextualizes impressions by typology, paleography, site of discovery, and stratigraphy; the count subsequently published by the authors (2020) raises the number of identified examples to 647, based on the findings and studies recorded at that time. The concentration of seals in Ramat Rachel and their distribution throughout Jerusalem and other locations allows for discussion of the territorial organization of the administration. The exact function of each typological variant requires contextual analysis: a provincial imprint does not automatically demonstrate who owned the vessel, what the required tax was, or which religious authority was involved in its circulation.

188 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM It is important to distinguish three levels of evidence: (a) excavated and published material evidence, with identification of object, stratum, and photograph; (b) reconstruction of a provincial system of storage and redistribution, supported by the distribution of finds; (c) hypotheses regarding temple intervention or religious transmission, which require additional evidence. A YHWD legend is not a profession of faith nor does it demonstrate a reception of Zoroastrian ideas. 2. Provincial currency, iconography and chronology The silver issues of Yehud offer further evidence. Their provincial nomenclature, weight standards, and iconographic types must be studied with a precise chronology: not every coin bearing the name Yehud belongs to the reign of Darius I or the Achaemenid period. The catalogue by Gitler, Lorber, and Fontanille (2023) organizes the assemblage by types, dies, and minting relationships. A 2023 archaeometallurgical analysis examined fifty coins assigned to Persian and Hellenistic series; it distinguished, among others, Athena/owl types and Persian king/falcon representations and studied their alloys. Its historical interest lies in the contact between iconographic repertoires and Mediterranean monetary practices, without automatically equating the circulation of a visual motif with doctrinal adoption. 3. Land, tribute and daily life Imperial mechanisms manifested themselves in land management, production obligations, labor movement, storage, payments, and debt disputes. Nehemiah 5 depicts tensions between creditors and debtors and mentions houses, fields, vineyards, sons, and daughters; it is a literary source written and transmitted in a complex work, not a contemporary tax record preserved on a tablet. Its comparison with provincial impressions is heuristic, not a documentary identification. Rural constructions attributed to the Persian period have been interpreted as estates, fortified enclosures, or facilities associated with various forms of land tenure; archaeology alone does not allow us to reduce them to a single imperial institution. The sanctuary economy of Jerusalem requires a distinct analysis from the palatial and provincial economies. Direct temple control over all vessels marked YHWD should not be inferred. Nor should the existence of a uniform Achaemenid program of religious authorization be reconstructed as proven fact from the narrat ive of Ezra 7.

YEHUD, SAMARIA AND IDUMEA 189 4. The Jews of Babylonia: The Āl-Yāhūdu Archive The decisive extraterritorial contrast is provided by the cuneiform tablets relating to Jewish and other West Semitic deportees in Babylon. Pearce and Wunsch edited 103 texts from the David Sofer Collection (CUSAS 28) in 2014, with transliterations, translations, copies, photographs, and commentary. The documents contain personal names with Yahwist elements and accounts of everyday life, including eco nomic relationships and obligations within Babylonian institutions. The publication is a modern edition of ancient artifacts, not a transcription of biblical tradition its evidence comes from materially preserved tablets. The individual archaeological provenance of examples from the antiquities market may, however, be less precise than that of finds excavated in controlled contexts. The settlement called Ā lY āhū du (“City of Judah”), along with other sites identified through documentation, demonstrates the continuity of Jewish identities within the Mesopotamian diaspora. Yahwist onomastics is a relevant sign of belonging and cultural persistence, but the presence of a theophoric name alone does not indicate specific observance, individual doctrinal adherence, or the influence of Iranian religion. A comparison with Elephantine should clarify its differences in language and writing medium — Akkadian cuneiform on tablets versus Aramaic on papyrus and ostraca — as well as in administrative authority and social standing. 5. Wisdom, Gender, and Norms: A Controlled Comparative Approach The study of Iranian-Jewish reception should not be limited to eschatology. Proverbs, Job, Ecclesiastes, and Chronicles constitute corpora of different genres and chronologies; their use requires first establishing the literary strata and comparing them with non-Iranian traditions of the ancient Near East. The similarity between a Hebrew proverb and an Iranian moral maxim would be insufficient to assert borrowing without distinctive linguistic features, plausible intermediaries, and a defensible chronology. The conditions of women, minors, slaves, creditors, and non-priestly households must be included in the analysis of legal texts, contracts, and archival documents. In particular, a social history of the province must contrast biblical narratives of marriage, debt, and lineage with Babylonian documents and the Aramaic contracts from Elephantine, without equating literary norms with everyday prac-

190 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM tice. This distinction is also necessary when examining concepts of purity: prescriptions, ritual objects, and documented everyday practices must be separated. 6. From Persian to Hellenistic rule: continuity and rupture The transition in the fourth century BCE cannot be narrated as an immediate break from all provincial systems. The continuity of administrative names and some series of printed works and coins allows us to investigate continuities; changes in monetary and iconographic models reveal institutional transformations. Uniform chronologies of “Iranian influence” should be avoided: contact under Darius I and literary reception under Hellenistic rule involve distinct networks, genres, and agents. The subsequent persistence of a term or motif does not automatically prove its introduction in the sixth century BCE. 7. Historiographical Note: Meyer, Wellhausen, and Imperial Authority The thesis that Persian power played a constitutive role in the institutionalization of the Law of Ezra has a precise and debated historiographical history. Eduard Meyer defended a strong reading of the imperial sanction of the law, while nineteenth-century reconstructions associated with Julius Wellhausen integrated the formation of post-exilic Judaism into a model of historical -religious development. The modern discussion of “Persian imperial authorization” requires distinguishing between a permission narrated in Ezra, a historically plausible administrative practice, and a general imperial policy demonstrated by external documentation. None of these three levels should be automatically taken as proven from the others. 8. Methodological table of evidence and limits Yahwd seals: material and administrative evidence of marked vessels; not direct proof of a theological system. Yehud coins: provincial iconography and dating; not automatic evidence of worship or creed. Yahwd tablets: contracts and personal names of Jewish individuals; they do not replace liturgical sources. Ezra- Nehemiah: narrative and self-representation of institutions; not diplomatic documentation au thenticated by the mere fact of reproducing an edict. Elephantine: papyri and ostraca from Yahwist communities in Egypt; their chronological proximity does not authorize generalizing all practices to Jerusalem. A similarity between two exhortations on justice or reward does not in itself constitute dependence. Written wisdom, family teaching, and court literature were part of broader environments than Achaemenid Iran.

Torah, dāta, and Imperial Authorization: A Specific Controversy The ancient Persian word dāta- (“that which is established,” “law,” or “disposition,” depending on the context), disseminated through the administrative lan-

YEHUD, SAMARIA AND IDUMEA 193 guages of the empire, requires a distinction between etymology, legal function, and theology. The biblical Aramaic dāt may refer to actual norms; it does not automatically equate to the entire Hebrew Torah, nor does it demonstrate a direct conceptual translation from Mosaic revelation to Achaemenid law. Ezra 7:12–26, preserved in the biblical composition, presents a mandate attributed to Artaxerxes: it constitutes literary testimony regarding legal authority, not an excavated chancery original. The so-called “Persian imperial authorization” theory was influentially defended by Peter Frei and discussed by authors such as Joseph Blenkinsopp, Lester L. Grabbe, Gary N. Knoppers, and Jean-Louis Ska in the edited volume by James W. Watts (2001). This theory questions whether imperial validation of local norms contributed to the establishment and authority of the Pentateuch. The comparison by Meyer and Wellhausen is only valuable when its textual and historiographical postulates are clarified; neither the mere existence of an empire nor the narrative of Ezra proves a codification commissioned by the court. Konrad Schmid insists on distinguishing the Persian authorization as a historical fact from its use as a biblical literary construction. Mark G. Brett (2021) considers the indirect effects of imperial pressures and negotiations between priestly and non-priestly sectors and rival sanctuaries more convincing than a single, formal approval of the Torah. The edition must therefore confront three competing models: an effective decree of authorization; local adaptation of norms under imperial conditions; and a legitimizing narrative of a fundamentally internal textual formation. None should be taken as certainty without distinguishing evidence. The comparison with the Elephantine papyri is instructive precisely because of their differences: they allow us to observe the coexistence of legal formulae, provincial authorities, and cultic practices without projecting a uniform Pentateuchal observance onto all communities. The Bagohi case documents specific petitions within a provincial framework; it cannot be used as direct evidence of a general pro gram of Pentateuchal authorization. 11. However, the names in a contract do not, in themselves, reveal a family’s ritual practices; nor does the documentary silence regarding

194 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM women’s beliefs prove their absence. The gender of the document, the legal status of the individuals named, and the likelihood of archaeological preservation must all be considered. In Nehemiah 5:1–13, we hear a literary denunciation of indebtedness, mortgages, loss of fields, and the enslavement of sons and daughters. The passage is a fundamental source for understanding how the community remembered inequality, but it is not an independent tax table or a statistical sample of the province. To study it alongside cuneiform documents, one must distinguish between loans with interest, guarantees, forced labor, agrarian dependency, and the rhetoric of social reform. A comparative documentation program will record, for each contract: explicit date; place; language and medium; names of the parties; kinship and gender relationships when stated; good or service transferred; guarantees; witnesses; modern edition and material provenance. Without these fields, it will not be legitimate to automatically reconstruct the “typical” Yehud family from deported communities located outside the province. 12. Assessment of the Evidence and Questions Open to Reassessment Administrative convergence does not imply religious assimilation. YHWD seals demonstrate the operation and circulation of vessels within provincial structures; Babylonian tablets document agents, contracts, and the activities of descendants of deportees; biblical texts describe and evaluate practices for literary and theological purposes. Only when two or more independent categories converge in date, place, and practice can the strength of a hypothesis be increased. Iranian influence remains a historically testable possibility, not the default explanation for every shared feature. Rules of proof: (A) inscribed object or dated and located document; (B) early textual evidence transmitted by later witnesses with compositional criticism; (C) analogy of vocabulary or structure duly compared; (D) retrospective reconstruction from Sasanian or Pahlavi sources. The postulated date of composition and the date of the preserved copy must be presented separately. A central claim of cultural transmission will not be based exclusively on materials of type C or D. Cyrus as “Anointed” in Isaiah 44–45 Isaiah 44:28 calls Cyrus “my shepherd,” and Isaiah 45:1 calls him “his anointed” (mĕšîḥô), whom YHWH takes by the hand to subdue nations. This is the only instance in the Hebrew Bible where a foreign king receives this title. The text belongs to Isaiah 40–55, attributed to the Late Exile period (circa 540–539 BCE), and presents Cyrus as an instrument of YHWH, not as an eschatological saviour. The comparison with Ahura Mazdā as the one who “made” Darius king (DNa) is typological: both texts explain the monarchy by a god, but the form is different. 3. From the Davidic King to the Eschatological Messiah The “anointed one” in Israel is the Davidic king (2 Sam 7), also the priest (Lev 4:3), and in the Persian period a hope emerges linked to Zerubbabel (Hag 2:23; Zec 4) and, later, to a future figure (Dan 9:25–26, with discussion). Late messianism (11QMelchizedek, 4Q521, the Psalms of Solomon) belongs to the 2nd–1st centuries BCE; by that time the Hellenistic period and contact with the Iranian tradition had already occurred, so it cannot be projected onto the Persian era. 4. John 1 and Barnea’s proposal on the final Saošyant The comparison between the prologue of John and the Saosiyant traditions can be framed as a problem of the history of ideas, but it does not in itself constitute proof of transmission. Barnea (2026) argues that the Prologue reworks, within a Jewish framework, Mazdaean concepts — Mithra the creator, the incarnate Mąθra, and the final Saosiyant— (see chapter XXXIV). To assess a historical dependence, it is necessary to compare the Greek of John 1 with the Iranian texts in their respective strata and establish a chronologically plausible channel of transmission. 5. Hellenistic Jewish apocalyptic works and the later Pahlavi syntheses must therefore be assessed within their respective chronologies. Sheol and Post-mortem Destiny in Ancient Israel In the oldest Hebrew Bible, the dead descend to Sheol, a shadowy abode from which there is no return (Job 7:9; Psalm 88:11–13). Individual hope for life after death is scarce and comes late. The image of “resurrection” appears as a metaphor for the restoration of Israel (Ezekiel 37, the valley of bones; Hosea 6:2), and only later as an individual hope. 213

Isaiah 26:19 and Daniel 12:2 Isaiah 26:19 (“Your dead will live; their bodies will rise”) belongs to the “Apocalypse of Isaiah” (Isaiah 24–27), whose dating is disputed (Persian or Hellenistic period). Daniel 12:2 (“Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake, some to everlasting life, others to shame”) constitutes one of the most explicit state ments of individual resurrection in the Hebrew Bible, usually contextualized within the crisis of Antiochus IV (c. 167–164 BCE). The interpretation of Isaiah 26:19 as literal resurrection, collective restoration, or poetic language remains a subject of debate. The appearance of this clear formulation in the apocalyptic literature of the 2nd century requires analysing simultaneously its Israelite antecedents, the Hellenistic context and possible earlier Iranian contacts, without inferring a single genealogy from the similarity. The awakening leads to contrasting destinies and belongs to the literary horizon of Daniel 10–12. In Yt 19:89, Darmesteter’s historical version explicitly states that “the dead will rise” in the context of the renewal ef fected by the Saošyant. The comparison is pertinent, but the Avestan passage alone does not offer an Achaemenid date nor prove transmission to the author of Daniel. A similarity between a Danielic formulation and a doctrine expounded in a Pahlavi treatise constitutes a comparative fact: to transform it into a thesis of dependence, it is necessary to demonstrate the relevant priority of the motif in the Iranian tradition and a plausible historical channel. This gradation avoids two unjus tified conclusions: that the silence or obscurity of an ancient verse proves the absolute absence of the idea, and that a medieval Pahlavi redaction simply demonstrates its identical existence in the 6th century BCE. RESURRECTION OF THE DEAD 221 Expanded dossier: modalities of resurrection and universal renewal The comparison between Daniel 12:2 and the Bundahish tradition requires avoiding a hasty terminological equivalence. In Daniel, the awakening of those who sleep in the dust appears linked to opposing destinies; the phrase belongs to the horizon of Jewish apocalyptic literature and is examined within its own textual context. The Greater Bundahish, on the other hand, integrates the resurrection into a broader narrative of the transformation of creation, the defeat of evil, and the final stabiliza tion of the cosmos. Chapter XXXIV of the Iranian recension explicitly develops the “resurrection and final material life” and is read here alongside the corresponding chapter of the Indian recension, without erasing their divergences. A critical framework must establish, separately, the agents of restoration, the scope of the resurrected, the sequence of judgement and purification, the final con dition of the world, the time frame, and the terminology of each language. Similarity of outcome does not, in itself, reveal specific borrowings; to assess transmission, pre-Christian and later testimonies, the circulation of people and texts, translations, and genre differences must be considered. Correspondence A: both chapters associate the coming of Sōšyans/Saošyant with the corporeal reconstitution of the dead. The parallelism is internal to two recensions of a later Medio-Ir anian corpus, not an independent testimony from the Achaemenid period. Correspondence B: both translations use analogies about the original creation to defend the possibility of resurrection; they differ in word choice, glosses, and supplementary elements. The differences between two English translations do not become readings of codices without identify ing the corresponding Pahlavi original. Textual comparison on the Indian recension: the Middle Iranian edition accessible in TITUS (IBd XXVI.6, p. 65, lines 12–14, numbered by Behzādī) transmits “az ātaxš gyān,” literally “life [coming] from fire,” in the sequence “bones/earth, blood/water, hair/plants, life/fire.” This reading supports West’s English option in the Pahlavi text. The reading published by Behzādī establishes neither an Achaemenid doctrine nor an individual reading of K20, M51, TD1, TD2 or DH without collation. In the Gāthās the language of choice and truth has its own poetic setting; in the Community Rule op posed spirits operate within an explicitly governed creation. Their relationship can not be resolved by the shared word “dualism”. The opposition between good and evil is the most characteristic feature of Zoroastrianism and the one that has most prompted attempts to find its influence on Judaism. This chapter distinguishes between cosmic dualism, ethical dualism, and the dualism of spirits, and examines Jewish texts that might reflect it. 1. Cosmic and ethical dualism in Zoroastrianism Y. 30.3–5 presents a pair of spirits and contrasts their choices, the best and worst thoughts, vitality and its absence, aša in the face of the evil option. The syntax of Y. 30.4 and the imagery of Y. 30.5 should not be simplified into a fully systematized dualistic doctrine: the stanza implies choice and discernment; later cosmological de velopments belong to other strata. In the Gāthās, the conflict has a decisive ethical 225

226 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM dimension: humans are challenged to discern. The proper names Spəṇta Mainiiu and Aŋra Mainiiu are fixed in the later Avesta, and the fully developed cosmic dualism, with Ahriman as the coeternal principle of evil, is of the Pahlavi tradition. 2. Isaiah 45:7 and strict monotheism Isaiah 45:7 states: “I form the light and create darkness, I bring prosperity and create disaster; I, the Lord, do all these things.” Many read this as a rebuttal to Persian dualism, because it places the origin of both poles in the Lord. This reading is possible, but it does not prove that the author was familiar with Avestan dualism: the text could also be interpreted in opposition to Babylonian conceptions. What it does show is that the monotheism of Second Isaiah is aware of the issue of evil. Chronology control: Isaiah 45:7, Y. 30.3 and the heavenly adversary The passage in Isaiah 45:7 is not a contrast predating Iranian contact. It belongs to the framework of Isaiah 40–55, whose chapter 45 identifies Cyrus as YHWH’s anointed (45:1). The contrast between light and darkness and between peace and raʿ does not, in itself, lead to the conclusion that the prophet is refuting the Persian Magi: it can function as an affirmation of divine sovereignty against other theologies and imperial pretensions. The semantic field of raʿ includes harm, misfortune, and adversity; the translation “evil” should not be equated without nuance with the moral evil produced by a rival entity. In Y. 30.3, the pair of spirits offers a relevant point of comparison, but it remains a subject of philological debate. Interpretations of ethical dualism have been put forward, as well as interpretations linked to ritual thought or behavior. Neither the absolute ontological autonomy of a malevolent principle nor an opposition between two equivalent gods can be unequivocally deduced from a single stanza. Consequently, the comparison must remain on the level of documented conceptual opposition, reserving the developed cosmological dualism for its own specific evidence. Control of the argument in Y. 30.3–5. The documented diversity of philological translations of Y. 30.3 makes it impossible to treat “two spirits,” “two states of mind,” and “two impulses” as ontological equivalents. Chapter Conclusion The contrast between Asha and Druj does not simply coincide with the biblical role of Satan.
