In the reference Avestan transcription published on Avesta.org (fargard 19), the scene names Aŋra Mainyu and the daēva Būiti; Zarathustra’s reaction includes the clause “zarathushtrô ahunem vairîm frasrâvayat” (19,2), which makes explicit the recitation of the Ahuna Vairya. Darmesteter’s English translation will be used as a testament to interpretive history, not as a substitute for the Avestan. Chapter XVIII of Early Christianity raised the comparison between Vendīdād 19 and the Gospel accounts of the temptation. Here it is taken up again with a more rigorous method: specific motifs are compared, independent Jewish traditions are considered, and a compatible chronology is required before speaking of transmission. 1. The accounts of the temptation of Jesus Mark 1:12–13 summarizes the temptation in two verses: the Spirit leads Jesus into the desert, where he remains for forty days tempted by Satan, among wild beasts, and ministered to by angels. Matthew 4:1–11 and Luke 4:1–13 offer three elaborate tests and responses taken from Deuteronomy (8:3; 6:16; 6:13). In the TwoSource Hypothesis, this shared material is attributed to the reconstructed source Q; other solutions to the Synoptic Problem explain the literary relationship without postulating this document. The coincidence of Torah quotations is a textual fact; the existence and reconstruction of Q belong to the hypothetical analysis of the sources. 2. The biblical root of the number forty The forty days have clear Jewish antecedents: Moses on Mount Sinai (Exodus 24:18; 34:28), Elijah on the way to Horeb (1 Kgs 19:8), and the forty years of Israel in the desert, which Deuteronomy 8:2 interprets as a test (lĕnassōtĕkā, from the root nsh, “to test”). Jesus ‘ relationship with Israel in the desert is key to understanding Matthew and Luke: each of Jesus’ responses quotes the Deuteronomic text about Israel’s testing. An Iranian model is not needed to explain the number or the structure.

Vendīdād 19 and the Motif of the Tempted Prophet Vd 19:1–3 recounts that Aŋra Mainyu sent the demon Būiti to kill Zoroaster; the prophet sings the Ahuna Vairya and the demon flees. Transmission asymmetry: angels, hostile spirits and paradise The comparison has at least three independent propositions. (1) The language of an enclosed park and Greek paradeisos admits an Iranian lexical history: this is not equivalent to borrowing an entire eschatology. DOCUMENTED: Avestan and Jewish texts name divine or intermediary beings, but their earliest attested wording and functions belong to different historical contexts. COMPARABLE: aša/druj, the Aməša Spəṇtas and angelic or demonic hierarchies can be placed in structured comparative tables once their lexical and ritual functions have been stated. NOT DEMONSTRATED: an equivalence between a named Iranian entity and a Jewish angel, or derivation of a complete angelological system from Achaemenid Mazdaism, requires stronger evidence than analogous enumerations. The interpretative order should run from lexical morphology and textual layer to institutional setting, not in reverse. Terms rendered “demon”, “angel”, “spirit” or “immortal” are not automatically interchangeable. An editorial apparatus must retain alternative translations at disputed loci and distinguish Hellenistic, Arsacid and Sasanian receptions from Persian-period data. The chapter examines celestial beings, hostile spirits and images of paradise across early and later Avestan traditions, Second Temple Jewish literature and Christian reception. These strata must remain distinct: evidence from the first century CE cannot be treated as direct testimony to religious practice under the Achaemenids. Neither the number of celestial beings nor the presence of hostile spirits establishes descent from one pantheon to another. The comparison becomes historical only when structure, terminology, date and channels of circulation can be assessed together. This chapter examines three fields: celestial beings (Aməša Spəṇtas and angels), hostile beings (daēvas and demons), and the paradisiacal garden. Each requires its own chronology. 1. Demons: Daēvas and Evil Spirits The daēvas are condemned false gods in the Gāthās (Y. 32.3–5) and demons in the later Avesta; among them, Aēšma, “the fury,” stands out. Asmodeus (ʾAšmĕdāy, Tob 3:8) has been compared to Aēšma-daēuua; the etymology is plausible, but the Book of Tobit is of disputed date (3rd – 2nd centuries BCE), and the identification should be treated as a hypothesis. Jewish demonology also has Babylonian antecedents, so an Iranian origin is not necessary for its development. Lexical verification: Asmodeus, Tobias and the beneficent beings The association of Asmodeus (Tobit 3:8) with the Iranian Aēšma is more specific than an analogy between demonologies. The usual etymology derives from a reconstructed Iranian form * aēšmō.daēva- (“demon of fury”), although this exact com-

238 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM position has not been found as such in the extant Avestan texts. The lexical continuity seems plausible; it does not, however, prove the specific route of borrowing nor the dependence of the entire narrative of Tobit. The demon belongs to a Jewish work of Eastern origin whose text is preserved in both Aramaic and Hebrew fragments from Qumran and in Greek recensions. The number seven also does not constitute a sufficient identity: in the Zoroastrian heptad, six Ameša Spəṇtas are normally counted along with Ahura Mazdā (or his Benevolent Spirit), while Tobit 12:15 identifies Raphael as one of seven angels who stand before God. The functions, ontological status, and textual traditions of both sets must be compared separately. 3. Pairidaēza and Paradeisos The Garden of Eden (Gen 2–3; Ezek 28:13; 31:8–9) is a divine garden with a tree of life; in the Septuagint it is called paradeisos (chapter III). It is possible that the model of the king’s garden, pairidaēza-, influenced the biblical image of Eden, but the Eden of Genesis has Mesopotamian and Canaanite antecedents of the divine garden; the form paradeisos is a Greek translation, not an influence on the original narrative. In the New Testament (Luke 23:43; Rev 2:7), paradise is the place of future blessedness. The Destiny of the soul, the Činwad bridge and the lexical origin of “paradise” The oldest Israelite traditions frequently present Sheol as the realm of the dead and emphasize the cessation of the deceased’s activity (e.g., Ecclesiastes 9:5); this does not authorize the categorical denial of all ancient diversity regarding survival, nor the identification of the dead person’s fate with an already developed system of rewards and punishments. The Hadohext Nask 2 is a fundamental Iranian testimony concerning the three days after death and the soul’s meeting with its daen; the tradi tion of the bridge is also preserved in Vod 19:29–30 and other sources. The exact se quence of Hādōxt Nask 2,24–25 must be read in an edition of the fragment, not summarized as if those two paragraphs alone contained the entire account of judge ment and passage. For the Hādōxt Nask, manuscripts of late medieval transmission have been documented, including H6, with a colophon of 1397, and K20, whose materials in

ANGELS, DEMONS AND PARADISE 239 clude a copy dated 1350. The dates of these witnesses are material history data of the text, not datings of the doctrine in the time of Darius I. The same principle applies to the Middle Iranian expositions that order the particular judgement, the otherworldly destinies, and the universal renewal. The lexical family of “paradise” does provide a documentable line of linguistic contact: an ancient Iranian base related to an enclosed space was transmitted to forms such as the Greek παράδεισος and the Hebrew pardēs. However, the young Avestan pairi.daēza- designates an enclosure, not necessarily the eschatological abode of the blessed; the theological identification between garden, Eden, and postmortem reward represents a semantic evolution that must be explained by Jewish and Greek sources, not by automatic derivation from an Iranian doctrine. 4. Evaluation Typological similarity: moderate (seven beings; garden). Probable mediation: possible, but the Jewish texts with multiple angels (Tobit, 1 Enoch) are Hellenistic, not Persian. Demonstrable dependence: no. Jewish angelology grows upon the biblical “heavenly court” (1 Kings 22; Job 1) and upon the Babylonian world. Chapter Conclusion Comparing celestial beings requires distinguishing between functions and hierarchies. Aməša Spəṇtas, yazatas, angels, and demons do not belong to the same taxonomy. Paradise offers an identifiable lexical borrowing, but the images of the garden and the destiny of the righteous have a receptive history that is not explained by that etymology. Summary The chapter distinguishes between the history of words, religious systems, and functions of protection or judgement. The grouping of seven figures requires confronting Mesopotamian alternatives and internal developments.

Chapter XX. The Second Temple, Qumran, and Apocalyptic Literature Chronological context. Second Temple, conventionally 515 BCE – 70 CE; Qumran in the centuries before 70 CE; Daniel’s final visions in the 2nd century BCE. Not all of this development is concentrated in the Persian period. Comparison of apocalyptic texts without automatic genealogy In the study of the Second Temple period, resurrection, judgement, angelic revelation, and the periodization of history must be distinguished as analytically separable motifs. Their combination varies among Daniel, the Qumran texts, and other Jewish compositions; nor do all the Judean Desert documents share a single eschatology. The category “apocalyptic” describes formal and thematic affinities, not a monolithic tradition. To measure the possibility of Iranian mediation, it will be necessary to record for each parallel a specific Iranian text, its linguistic stratum, the available manuscript evidence, and a proposed chronology that does not depend circularly on the Jewish parallel itself. Where the most explicit Iranian source is Pahlavi and medieval, the relationship should be formulated as a problem of comparative history, not as an already demonstrated Achaemenid antecedent. The Second Temple period (516/515 BCE – 70 CE) encompasses the Persian, Hellenistic, and Roman periods. This chapter focuses on the texts in which contact with the Iranian world has been most actively sought: Qumran, apocalyptic literature, and the traditions of Hellenistic Judaism. It proposes a criterion for their use: a Persian influence cannot be inferred from a text without demonstrating that its date and context make it possible. 1. The Second Temple under the Persians Under the Persians, the Temple in Jerusalem and its personnel (high priest and Levites) lived under the jurisdiction of the province of Judea. The main sources (Ezra, Nehemiah, Haggai, Zechariah 1–8, Malachi) are heterogeneous texts of disputed composition; a distinction must be drawn between the period they describe and the period in which they were written. 243

Comparative documentary dossier: The Treatise of the Two Spirits (1QS III,13–IV,26) Identification of the testimony. The Community Rule is cited by the abbreviation 1QS (manuscript from cave 1 of Qumran) and its conventional division by columns and lines: 1QS III,13–IV,26. This nomenclature is a textual reference, not a folio reference. Historical Problem. The Treatise presents a moral anthropology articulated by two spirits and contrasts the realms of truth and perversity. Its value for a history of Iranian-Jewish relations does not depend solely on the similarity between dualisms. It is essential to distinguish: (a) the chronology and material state of the Qumran testimony; (b) the stratification and hypothetical date of composition of the writing; (c) the biblical antecedents of its oppositions; (d) Iranian parallels documented in independently dated sources; and (e) specific channels, where they exist, of trans mission between the traditions. Comparative Reading A: The Iranian Hypothesis. An Iranian religious influence can be formulated as a historical hypothesis due to the long circulation of people and vocabularies within and after the Achaemenid domains. However, the opposition between aša and druj in Iranian texts is not identical, either linguistically or doctrinally, to the two spirits of 1QS. To defend a specific dependence, it would be necessary to explain the semantic transformations and document the mediations; the mere existence of moral pairs does not prove a borrowing. Comparative Reading B: Intra-Jewish Elaboration. Ethan Schwartz has proposed studying 1QS III:13–IV:26 as an exegesis of the creation narratives in Genesis 1–3, with a reorganization of the question of evil within a divinely created order. This explanation may compete with a predominantly Iranian attribution or be partially integrated into a model of cultural contacts; therefore, it should be presen ted as a real alternative, not merely an ornamental objection. The reference is: Ethan Schwartz, “The Exegetical Character of 1QS 3:13–4:26,” Dead Sea Discoveries 27, no. 1 (2020), pp. 31–65.

Chapter XXI. From Persian-Period Judaism to Early Christianity Transmission and independent alternatives An account of religious transmission from Persian-period Yehud to early Christianity needs more than a narrative of successive empires. Each proposition should identify a datable witness, a plausible social carrier (scribal circles, bilingual administration, diaspora or translation), a non-trivial feature, and competing explanations. The alternatives include older Mesopotamian and Levantine traditions, inner-Jewish exegesis, Greek philosophical language and independent development. Contact in one period does not automatically entail theological dependence several centuries later. Classification for the chapter: documented contact is not equivalent to documented adoption; a plausible network without textual anchors remains an hypothesis; parallel apocalyptic or eschatological motifs alone are typological. These grades are not numerical probabilities. They are transparent statements of the source status and of what would falsify or strengthen a proposed connection. Chronological context. From Achaemenid antecedents to Hellenistic Judaism and Christianity of the 1st century CE; Arsacid Iran contemporary with the latter. Successive mediations must be documented at each stage. This chapter closes the comparative section with a reception question: what part of the similarities found could have reached early Christianity through Second Temple Judaism? The book’s answer is that the direct link with the Persian period is very weak, and that what remains is a shared comparative horizon. 1. The Magi and Early Christianity Matthew 2:1–12 presents the Magi who come from the east following a star. The Greek term designates priests and also astrologers and sorcerers; in Acts it appears with a negative connotation (Acts 8:9–11; 13:6–8). The Matthean figure has been linked to Iranian Magi, but the exact identity of the characters is debated, and the text does not call them Persians. 251

Model of Transmission: Agents, Networks, and Limits Testing the Historical Chain. Any claim of Iranian origin for a Christian motif requires verifying four separate steps: (1) the existence and date of the relevant Iranian formulation; (2) documentable contact with a Jewish group or milieu; (3) the trans formation and appearance of the motif in identifiable Jewish attestations; (4) its reuse in a datable Christian text. The identification of a lexical borrowing or an institution from the Achaemenid period strengthens the possibility of general cultural contact, but does not automatically prove the transfer of eschatology, angelology, or soteriology. A gap in the chain must be shown as such, not filled by later analogies. For a religious idea to pass from one tradition to another, agents (translators, scribes, officials, soldiers, merchants), channels (common languages, archives, temples), and time are necessary. In the Persian period, the channels existed (Aramaic, the court, the garrisons); what is lacking is a document showing an Iranian-re ligious idea being transferred to a Jewish text. This absence does not prove that there was no contact, but it does preclude asserting it as fact.

FROM PERSIAN JUDAISM TO EARLY CHRISTIANITY 253 4. Conclusion to This Section Yahwist communities of the Persian period lived within an empire with an official Aramaic language, surrounded by Iranian names, with royal inscriptions that mention Ahura Mazdā and the Lie, and with an administration that selectively supported local cults. It follows, then, that the similarities in administrative vocabulary and the use of the title “God of Heaven” have a likely historical explanation. However, the origin of the major theological themes (resurrection, dualism, angels, saviour) cannot be established from the available sources. The remainder of the book examines more sources, but this is the result of the comparative analysis. Chapter Conclusion Early Christianity received Jewish traditions already transformed during centuries of regional contact. Attributing a Christian idea to Iran requires reconstructing that mediation and not jumping from an Avestan passage to a New Testament text. Comparisons must respect the Jewish, Greek, and Roman con texts of each author. Summary The reception is studied in stages: documented institutional contact (Imperial Aramaic, the Elephantine papyri, Ezra-Nehemiah), attested lexical borrowings, and finally, the eschatological and dualistic similarities that the book does not consider proven without a verifiable chain of transmission. The chapter concludes the comparative section by warning against making a direct leap from the Achaemenid period to early Christianity. Zarathustra and the Gāthās The core of the tradition consists of seventeen hymns in Old Avestan, the Gāthās, incorporated into the Yasna and traditionally attributed to Zoroaster. The language is archaic, comparable in age to the Ṛgveda, and its date, according to the recent consensus compiled in the Encyclopaedia Iranica, is placed around the turn of the second to the first millennium BCE. Zoroaster’s homeland, probably in eastern Iran or Central Asia, is debated on geographical and linguistic grounds. Beyond the date, the fundamental debate is hermeneutical. According to the traditional interpretation, represented by Helmut Humbach, the Gāthās are the preaching of a historical reformer. For Jean Kellens, they are ritual poetry, composed within the

HISTORY OF ZOROASTRIANISM AND THE WORSHIP OF YHWH 259 framework of sacrifice, from which one cannot simply extract a biography or a doc trinal system.114115 With this caution, the features relevant to comparative analysis can be stated. Ahura Mazdā, “the Wise Lord,” is the supreme and creator god. Alongside him act abstract powers, the Aməša Spəṇtas (“benevolent immortals”), among them Vohu Manah (“good thought”) and Asha (“true order”). Opposing order stands druj, falsehood, of which Aŋra Mainyu will be the personification in the later Avestan. The Hymn of the Two Minds (Y 30) presents two twin spirits, one benevolent and the other destructive, between which humans and the gods themselves must choose. From this framework emerges the idea that has most influenced subsequent comparisons: a cosmic and moral conflict in which each human being is responsible for their choice and will be judged. 3. The Younger Avesta and the Religion of Eastern Iran The Younger Avestan corpus is that of the Yašts, the Vendīdād, and a good part of the Yasna. Their religion is broader and more ritualistic than that of the Gāthās. A pantheon of yazatas (“worthy of veneration”) reappears: Mithra (Yt 10), Anāhitā (Yt 5), Tištrya, the rain star (Yt 8), Vərəθraγna, victory (Yt 14), and the fravashis of the deceased (Yt 13). The cult revolves around the sacrifice of the Yasna, the prepar ation of the haoma, and the fire, ātar, which receives daily offerings. The Vendīdād, the purity code, devotes long sections to contamination by the corpse, the expulsion of the daēvas, and the preeminence of the dog, and contains in its chapter 19 the episode of Zarathustra’s temptation by Aŋra Mainyu, studied in chapter XVIII. The Yašts also preserve the expectation of a final renewal of the world (Yt. 19.88– 96), which is discussed in chapter XV. 114See, in the Companion cited, Frantz Grenet, “Zarathustra’s Time and Homeland: Geographical Perspectives,” and Almut Hintze, “Zarathustra’s Time and Homeland: Linguistic Perspectives.” On the date, see Jean Kellens, “Avesta,” Encyclopædia Iranica III / 1 (1987): 35–44, and the following chapter of this book. 115Helmut Humbach, “The Gāthās,” and Jean Kellens, “The Gāthās, Said to Be of Zarathustra,” both in the Companion; also Prods Oktor Skjærvø, “The Gāthās as Myth and Ritual,” in the same volume. 260 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM Two methodological caveats are necessary. First, none of these texts were written before the Sasanian period; what we have is a long-transmitted oral version, codified relatively late, so its chronological stratification is a result of philology and not an external fact. Second: the internal geography of the texts points to eastern Iran and Central Asia, not to Persia (Fars) or Media. Whether the Achaemenid kings of Fars shared this religion is precisely the open question. 4. The Achaemenid Period Achaemenid documentation is the first that allows for dating. Darius I (522–486 BCE) proclaims in Behistun (DB) that Ahura Mazdā bestowed kingship upon him and that the rebels lied, using the term drauga, cognate with the Avestan drukha. Xerxes, in the Daiva Inscription (XPh), states that he destroyed a Daiva sanctuary and established the cult of Ahura Mazdā “with Arta” (the Avestan asha) in an order he presents as correct. The documents from the Fortification of Persepolis (circa 509–493 BCE), on the other hand, record rations for ceremonies dedicated to a multitude of Iranian and Elamite gods, with Ahura Mazdā in a relatively minor pos ition. Herodotus describes the Persians as sky worshippers, without temples, statues, or altars, who offer sacrifices in high places and give the corpses to birds and dogs under the care of Magi. With Artaxerxes II (404–359 BCE), Mithra and Anahitā appear in inscriptions alongside Ahura Mazdā, and Berossus, cited by Clement of Alexandria, attributes the spread of images of Anahitā to this king.116 The data support three interpretations. For Mary Boyce, the Achaemenids were Zoroastrians from Cyrus onward, and the apparent polytheism of the court reflects a living religion with its yazatas. For those who follow Kellens, Achaemenid “Mazdaism” is an Iranian cult of Ahura Mazdā whose connection to Zoroaster’s re form remains unproven. An intermediate position (Albert de Jong, among others) accepts a genetic affinity with the Avestan without identifying the actual religion with a later orthodoxy. The book maintains this last interpretation as a working hy pothesis: it was a religion that shared basic vocabulary (Ahura Mazdā, arta / asha, drauga / druj, Magi, fire) with the Avesta, without any guarantee that it shared its 116Herodotus, I 131–140; the exposure of corpses, I 140. On the material level, royal iconography shows the king before an altar with fire (reliefs from the tombs of Naqš-e Rostam), but there is no consensus on whether Pasargadae or Persepolis had fire temples in the strict sense; the subject is discussed in Chapter X.117 5. From Macedonian Rule to the Parthian Empire The conquest of Alexander (331–330 BCE) and the burning of Persepolis cut short Achaemenid history; later Zoroastrian tradition would remember Alexander as a calamity, although that memory is late and Pahlavi. Under the Seleucids and Parthians, Iranian religion is poorly understood. Two types of sources help. The first is epigraphic and archaeological: the sanctuary of Antiochus I of Commagene at the Nemrud Dağ (circa 62 BCE), which assimilates Zeus to Oromasdes and Apollo to Mithra-Helios-Hermes, and the ostraca from Nisa, with theophoric names of Mithra and an Iranian calendar from the Parthian period. The second source is literary: a collection of Greek writings attributed to Zoroaster, Ostanes, or Hystaspes, which Roger Beck has shown contain little genuine Iranian content. Hystaspes is the author of an apocalypse cited by Justin (1 Apology 20 and 44) and Lactantius (Divine Institutes VII); its character is Hellenistic and probably Judeo-Iranian, and therefore it is a mediating source rather than an Avestan testimony.118 6. Kerdir boasted of having fought against Jews, Buddhists, Brahmins, Christians of various denominations, and Manicheans. It is during this period that, according to Karl Hoffmann, the Avesta was committed to writing, with an alphabet created specifically for this purpose, probably in the 4th century, and the surviving manuscripts descend from a single base manuscript of the 9th– 10th centuries. The Zand, the Pahlavi commentary, and later the great books such as the Bundahishn, the Denkard, and the Zandi Wahman Yasn, with their developed eschatology—three Saoshyants, general resurrection, judgement by fire— were also composed. This literature is no longer Achaemenid. The Babylonian Talmud, compiled in Sasanian Iran, is the Jewish testimony of this environment, and its relationship to Zoroastrianism is the subject of specific study. 7. Under Islamic Rule and in the Parsi Tradition The defeat of Yazdgerd III and the Arab conquest (642–651) ushered in the Islamic period. Zoroastrianism survived as a tolerated religion with the status of a dhimmi, gradually losing followers and becoming concentrated in Yazd and Kerman. Around the 8th – 10th centuries, according to tradition, a group migrated to Gujarat and formed the Parsi community, which preserved the manuscripts that would serve as the basis for European editions. The editions we use are the result of this process: the Westergaard edition (1852–1854) and the Geldner edition (1886– 1896) are based primarily on Indian manuscripts. European knowledge begins with Abraham-Hyacinthe Anquetil-Duperron, whose translation of the Zend-Avesta (N. M. Tilliard, 1771) was the first; the 19th century brought philological understanding, with the recognition of the relationship between Avestan and Vedic Sanskrit, and hence the reading of the Gāthās as the text of a single author. This chain of readings, from Anquetil to the Corpus Avesticum Berolinense, explains why the Avesta seemed to say different things 119in each era. 119Abraham Hyacinthe Anquetil-Duperron, Zend-Avesta, ouvrage of Zoroaster, 2 t. in 3 vols. Assessment The result can be formulated in four statements. One: there is a common horizon of language, administration, and representation of the supreme god between Persia and Judah / Egypt, documented and mediated by Imperial Aramaic. Two: some features of late Yahwism (angelology, attenuated ethical dualism, universal eschatology) have Iranian parallels that make the hypothesis of a mediated influence reasonable, but this hypothesis cannot be transformed into a demonstration with the sources available to us. Three: the parallels of fire and purity are typological and remain open; Barnea’s proposal discusses them (chapters XII and LVI). Four: Most of the points traditionally attributed to “Persian influence” (resurrection, Satan, paradise) have equally defensible internal explanations, so the strongest position is that of convergence between spheres of influence, not one-sided dependence. Chapter Conclusion The history of Zoroastrianism shows that the Avesta is not an Achaemenid document, but rather the result of a transmission process that culminated in the Sasanian period. This necessitates separating the question about Persia from the question about the Avesta. The parallels with Yahwism support the thesis of a shared horizon; they do not support that of a direct lineage. 120Morton Smith, “Bible ii. Chapter XXIII. Jesus and the Saošyant: An Assessment of a Hypothesis Jesus and Saošyant: asymmetrical source chronology The singular and plural forms associated with saošiiaṇt- must be kept distinct across the Gāthic, Younger Avestan and later Middle Persian strata. A fully developed individual eschatological saviour in a later exposition cannot be projected back into the reign of Darius I without intermediate evidence. For the Christian comparison, the date of the New Testament testimony and its Jewish exegetical ancestry must be made explicit before testing Iranian parallels. The strongest defensible conclusion may be that several traditions developed configurations of future renovation and salvation within overlapping imperial worlds. This is not the same claim as identification of Jesus with a particular Iranian saviour, nor proof that one textual formulation supplied the source for the other. The apparatus should list these propositions separately so that rejection of a strong dependency claim does not erase demonstrable contact in language or administration. Chronological context. Saošyant in Avestan sources from different strata and in later Pahlavi developments; Jesus and Christian reception from the 1st century CE. A late Pahlavi testimony does not establish priority over the gospels. The chapter’s thesis is a historical hypothesis graded according to the evidence; its formulation does not constitute a demonstration of doctrinal dependence. 1. The Saošyant in the Sources saošiiaṇt- is an active participle of future value (formed in -yant-) of a root meaning “to benefit”: “the one who will bring benefit.” In the Gāthās, it appears as a generic designation for one who works for good (e.g., Y. 46.3 and 48.9), and not as a singular eschatological figure. In Yašt 19 (Zamyād Yašt), the passage in Yt. 19.88–96 describes the Saošyant and his companions as those who “will make the world renewed” and overcome falsehood. The later Avesta already recognizes the singular saviour and his origin. Yt. 13.128–129 names the “victorious Saošyant”, Astvat̰ .ərəta, and explains the name because he will make all bodily existence prosper; Yt. 13.142 names his mother, Vīspa.taurvairī (“she who conquers all”), who will give birth to him; and Vd. 19.5, Yt. 19.92 and Yt. 13.62 make him arise from the waters of Kąsaoya, from the seed of Zarathustra guarded by 99,999 fravaši. Y. 26.10 and Yt. 13.145 place him at the end of the series of the righteous, from Gaya Marətan to the victorious Saošyant. The characteristic feature of Pahlavi literature (Bundahišn 33–34, Dēnkard, Zandī Wahman Yasn), compiled in the Islamic era, is systematization: the cycle of three successive saviours — Ušēdar, Ušēdarmāh, and Sōšāns —, with dates in

Jewish Messianic Traditions of the Second Temple Period Before seeking an Iranian origin, one must ask whether Jewish tradition already possesses the necessary elements. The texts reveal a plurality of figures: the Davidic king (Isaiah 11; Jeremiah 23:5–6; Zechariah 9:9), the anointed priest (Zechariah 4; Qumran texts), Cyrus as YHWH’s anointed (Isaiah 45:1), the Servant (Isaiah 52:13–53:12), the heavenly “son of man” of Daniel 7 and the Book of Parables of Enoch, and Melchizedek in 11Q13. Within this plurality, the figure of a universal judge and saviour at the end of time has internal antecedents. This does not preclude the possibility that contact with Iranian ideas may have influenced certain shifts, such as the universalization of eschatology and the concept of a final judgement. but it requires that Christology not be treated as the result of a single source. 4. The Magi in Matthew 2 and the Oracle of Hystaspes The episode of the Magi in Matthew 2:1–12 is the only place in the New Testament where a figure associated with the Iranian world appears. The Magi, in Herodotus’ Greek, are the priests of the Persians; in Matthew, it is not stated where they come from or what they believe, only that they are from the East and that they see a star. The theme of the star has a precedent in Numbers 24:17, and the narrative sense of the passage (the Gentiles recognize the King of the Jews before the leaders of Jerusalem) is explained without the need for a Zoroastrian background. There is also a historical context: in 66 CE the Armenian king Tiridates, accompanied by Magi, visited Rome and paid homage to Nero, according to Pliny the Elder (Natural History XXX 16–17) and Dio Cassius (LXIII 1–7), which shows that the figure of the Eastern Magi was known in the Empire around the time Matthew was 124On the relationships between Christianity and Sasanian Zoroastrianism, see Marco Frenschkowski, “Christianity,” in The Wiley Blackwell Companion to Zoroastrianism (2015). The direction of influence cannot be determined from an isolated resemblance between formulations; it requires dating their witnesses, identifying the polemical context, and examining channels of contact.

Later Christian traditions linked the Magi with Zoroaster; the Arabic Infancy Gospel (chapter 7) has them come “according to the prophecy of Zoroaster,” but it is a late text.125 Closer to the topic is the oracle of Hystaspes, a Hellenistic apocalypse with Iranian pretensions, cited by Justin (1 Apology 20.1 and 44.12) and by Lactantius (Divine Institutes VII 15 and 18) to announce an end of the world with a saviour king. Its character is already mediated by Hellenism and, according to Beck, the genuinely Iranian content of these writings is very small. Its interest is twofold: it confirms that in the Mediterranean, from the Hellenistic period onward, prophecies about a final saviour attributed to the Persians were being read, and that Christians of the 2nd century were already using them in apologetics.126 5. Paul, John, and the History-of-Religions School At the beginning of the 20th century, the “school of the history of religions” maintained that Pauline and Johannine Christology depended on an Iranian myth of the “redeemed redeemer.” Wilhelm Bousset (Die Religion des Judentums im neutestamentlichen Zeitalter, 1903; Kyrios Christos, 1913) and Richard Reitzenstein (Das iranische Erlösungsmysterium, 1921) are its main proponents. This thesis was refuted by Carsten Colpe, who showed that the myth of the redeemed redeemer is a reconstruction based on late Manichean and Mandaean texts and did not exist before Christianity. The prologue of John (John 1:1–18), with its pairing of light and darkness, has returned to the debate from another perspective: Gad Barnea has pro posed reading it as the fulfilment of the expectation of the final Saošyant. John’s duality of light and darkness, however, has a close parallel in the “sons of light” of Qumran (1QS III– IV), a contemporary and Jewish source. The Iranian hypothesis must therefore explain why a similar Jewish source is insufficient.127 125Pliny, Natural History XXX 16–17; Dio Cassius, LXIII 1–7. 272 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM 6. Later Reception: Mani, Persian Christians, and Religious Controversy Hypothesis H4 is indeed documented. Mani (216–274 CE), who wrote in Middle Persian, included Jesus in his pantheon in various roles (the “Jesus of splendor,” the “patient Jesus”) and presented Zoroaster, Buddha, and Jesus as apostles preceding him, so that Manichaeism is the first place where the figure of Jesus is expressed in Iranian categories. In Sasanian Iran, Syriac Christians were persecuted by Kerdir and later by Shabuhr II, and the literature of the Persian martyrs preserves the Christian view of the Magi’s religion. On the Zoroastrian side, the 9th-century Škand-gumānīg wizār contains a reasoned critique of Christianity, Judaism, and Manichaeism (chapters 13–16). These sources prove contact and polemics between communities, and thus are useful for studying how Zoroastrians and Christians understood each other; but they do not prove that the Gospels were written based on a Zoroastrian model. 7. Assessment of the Hypotheses Table 4 serves as a criterion. H1 lacks evidence in any first-century source and must be discarded. H2 is possible in general aspects of eschatology (renewal of the world, general resurrection, universal judgement), but there is no Iranian-Achaemenid source to support the specific figure of the saviour, and the Pahlavi sources that contain it are late. H3 is the most well-supported reading: Judaism and Iranism share a horizon in which an eschatological saviour was conceivable. H4 is documented and must be studied within its own period. This assessment allows for a cautious formulation of the book’s question: Jesus cannot be presented as an “interpretation” of the Saošyant in the sense of H1 or H2, but it can be said that the first Christians possessed a language of final salvation (judgement, resurrection, renewal of the world) that Second Temple Judaism had developed in contact with an environment in which Iranian thought was one of its interlocutors, and that it was this language that was applied to Jesus. Anyone who supports a stronger thesis must provide an Achaemenid or Hellenistic text, prior to the first century, that contains the specific feature from which they wish to derive it.

JESUS AND THE SAOŠYANT: EVALUATION OF A HYPOTHESIS 273 Chapter Conclusion Saošyant and Jesus share a function, that of agent of final renewal, and differ in how they exercise it. The available documentation allows us to speak of a common horizon and subsequent reception, but not of a direct identification or derivation. Summary Four hypotheses are distinguished (identification, transfer, convergence, reception). Only the last two have sufficient documentary support. Selective bibliography for the chapter W. W. Chapter XXIV. Mithra, Mithras and the Beginnings of the Church Chronological context. Iranian Mithra and Roman Mithras: Avestan and Achaemenid traditions versus Roman documentation from the first centuries CE; Early Church from the 1st century. Shared name, cultic organization and historical transmission are distinguished. 1. Defining the Comparison: Five Traditions of Mitra/Mithra(s) and an Emerging Church Under the name Mithras, at least five realities must be distinguished: Vedic Mitra, associated with agreements; the Avestan Mithras (Yt 10), lord of the given word; the Mithras of the Achaemenid kings, invoked alongside Ahura Mazdā from Artax erxes II onward; the Hellenistic Mithras, assimilated to Helios in Commagene; and the Mithras of the Roman mysteries. The first two share an Indo-Iranian root with a double meaning: the god and the noun mithra- (“contract, pact”). The relationship between the last and the previous ones is the most debated question in the history of ancient religions. The other half of the comparison also needs clarification. The expression “Catholic Church” cannot be applied to the beginnings of Christianity without anachronism. The adjective katholikḗ first appears applied to the Church in Ignatius of Antioch (Smyrnaeans 8.2, c. 110 CE) with the meaning of “universal,” and only in the fourth century does it become a designation for the orthodox Church as opposed to the dissenting ones; Theodosius’s edict Cunctos populos (380) uses the term in a normative sense. In this chapter, we speak of the Church of the origins or of early Christianity, and reserve “Catholic” for the sources that use it. 2. Mithra in the Avesta Yašt 10 (Mihr Yašt) is the longest hymn to a god in the later Avesta. Mithra is the guarantor of contracts and promises, the destroyer of those who break them (mithra-drug, “he who deceives Mithra”), lord of the vast plains, with a thousand ears and ten thousand eyes, who travels the earth on a luminous chariot and ensures the application of the law. He is a god of society and war, not of mysteries, and in 275

276 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM the Avesta he never appears killing a bull. This feature, which would become the iconographic centre of the Roman cult, is what most clearly separates the two Mithras.128 3. The Roman Mithras shares with the Vedic Mitra the name and little else.130 4. Mithra among the Persians and Greeks Under Artaxerxes II, Mithra appears in royal inscriptions alongside Ahura Mazdā and Anahita, indicating that his cult was part of the court religion in the 4th century BCE. The name Mithra spreads in the onomastics of Asia Minor and Armenia (the Mithridates) and is linked to Helios in the program of Antiochus I of Commagene, around 62 BCE. In 66 CE, the Armenian king Tiridates, according to Dio Cassius, addresses Nero, saying that he comes to worship him “as I worship Mithra,” showing that the god was still a figure of Eastern royalty in the time of the first Christian generation. At no point, however, does this series document a mystery religion with initiation. 5. The mysteries of Mithras in the Roman Empire Plutarch relates that the Cilician pirates defeated by Pompey (67 BCE) practiced “secret rites” of Mithras, which were preserved in his time (Pompey 24.5, Greek text consulted in the cited digital edition; the passage is discussed in chapter XXXIII). 130For Kushan coins with the Bactrian legend ΜΙΙΡΟ or ΜΙΟΡΟ (Mithra), see Robert Göbl, System und Chronologie der Münzprägung des Kušānreiches (Österreichische Akademie der Wissenschaften, 1984).

278 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM Statius alludes around 80-90 CE to Mithras bending the horns of a bull (Thebaid I 719-720), and the first sanctuaries (mithraea) date from the 2nd century. These were underground or semi-underground halls, with side benches for the ritual banquet, and a central relief or painting, the tauroctony: Mithras kills a bull while a dog, a snake, and a scorpion intervene, with the torchbearers Cautes and Cautopates on either side. The community was organized into seven ranks (Raven, Bride groom, Soldier, Lion, Persian, Heliodromus, Father), according to Jerome (Letter 107,2) and the paintings in the Mithraeum of Santa Prisca in Rome. The community was small (each Mithraeum housed a few dozen people), its members were recruited from among soldiers, officials, merchants, and freedmen, and the known epigraphic evidence mentions almost exclusively men; the absence of women is accepted with the caution due to the nature of the sources.131 Regarding the origin of this cult, there are, in short, four positions. Franz Cumont’s, who derived it from a Mazdean Iran transmitted by Hellenized Magi; Cumont was a classicist and did not read Iranian languages, and his reconstruction of the sacred narrative has been questioned, especially because Iranian sources do not depict Mithras killing a bull. Reinhold Merkelbach and Manfred Clauss’s, for whom the mysteries originated in Rome, or perhaps in Ostia, from Hellenistic and astrological motifs, without a clear continuity with Persian Mithras. Roger Beck’s, who interprets the symbolic body of the cult as an astronomical language (“startalk”) within a Mithraeum conceived as a model of the cosmos, in a Platonizing intellectual framework, and who admits that the Iranian element is a possible but sec ondary reference. And Richard Gordon’s, whose chapter “From Mithra to Roman Mithras” in the Companion examines the transition. Mithras and the Eucharist: Examination of the Texts From the Christian perspective, the sources are abundant and varied: the words of institution in Mark 14:22–25 and in 1 Corinthians 11:23–26 (the latter with the formula of transmission, “I received from the Lord what I also passed on to you”), Paul’s warning in 1 Corinthians 10:16–21, the Eucharistic prayer in the Didache 9–10, the “medicine of immortality” of Ignatius of Antioch (Ephesians 20:2), and Justin Martyr’s description (First Apology 65–67). From the Mithraic perspective, there is neither a liturgical text nor a preserved formula. What exists are banquet scenes of Mithras and Sol on the bull’s hide, eating benches inside the Mithraea, and remains of vessels and animal bones found in various sanctuaries.132 Everything said about the Mithraic rite comes from iconography, archaeology, and Christian controversy, and the latter is the only one that mentions bread and a cup. One methodological point should be emphasized: Paul, around 54-55, already contrasts “the Lord’s table” with “the table of demons” (1 Corinthians 10:21). He is referring to pagan sacrificial banquets in general, in which the Corinthians regularly participated, and not to a specific cult. Chronology and direction of the influence The chronology of the surviving testimonies strongly restricts hypotheses of ritual dependence, but it does not allow for a complete reconstruction of the formation phase of both cults. The tradition of the Last Supper that Paul “received from the Lord” (1 Corinthians 11:23) and handed down around 54–55 CE predates the first literary testimony of Mithras in Rome, Statius, around 80–90 CE, which refers to the earliest known Mithraeum. Therefore, there is no positive evidence that the first Christian Eucharistic tradition originated from the Roman Mithraic banquets; nor is the order of the earliest attestations sufficient, in itself, to demonstrate that no unknown earlier practice could have existed. The opposite view, that the Mithraists imitated the Christians, is proposed by Christian apologetics, which sees it as demonic imitation: Justin states that the demons imitated the bread and the cup of water in the mysteries of Mithras with certain words (1 Apol. 66,4), and Tertullian states that the devil, God’s rival, imitates in Mithras baptism, the mark on the soldiers’ foreheads, the offering of bread, and the image of the resurrection (De praescriptione haereticorum 40). A more robust historiographical explanation avoids seeking an origin in one of the two cults and resorts to a third term: the shared ritual grammar of Greco-Roman initiation cults and associations (common meals, purifications, hierarchies of initiates, secrecy). Dura-Europos: three cults in the same city The Syrian city of Dura-Europos, destroyed after the Sasanian siege around 256– 257 CE, preserved a Mithraeum (with phases from the mid-second century to approximately 256 CE), a synagogue (decorated around 244–245 CE), and a Christian house-church (adapted around 240–256 CE). It was studied by Cumont, who considered its Mithraeum representative of frontier cults. The case illustrates coexistence, not affiliation: the three cults occupied the same urban space and adopted the domestic gathering form offered by the city’s architecture. The dates are approximate; see Chapter LVIII. The Constantinian turn and the disappearance of Mithraism When Christianity became a protected religion, Mithraism, lacking a supralocal organization or its own texts, declined in the 4th century, and its mithraea were closed or destroyed, according to archaeological evidence; the decrees of Theodosius (391–392) prohibited pagan cults. Evaluation Four statements summarize the chapter. On the common root: Vedic and Avestan Mithras share a root of covenant and sovereignty that the Roman cult does not preserve. First: there is no evidence that the early Church derived from the mysteries of Mithras, and chronology discourages this hypothesis for the main rites. Second: the two cults share a period ritual grammar, which Christian apologetics perceived and reinterpreted as diabolical imitation. Third: the link with Zoroastrianism is weak, because the Roman Mithras has a disputed Iranian character and because the bridge between the Avestan Mithras and the Roman mysteries, if it exists, is what is under discussion. Therefore, a parallel between “the cult of Mithras” and the Church cannot be used as an argument in favour of a Zoroastrian influence on Christianity. Chapter Conclusion The cult of Mithras illuminates the religious environment in which Christianity de veloped, but not its origin. For the book, its value lies in defining the field of comparison: the Iranian Mithras belongs to the horizon of the Avesta and the Persian kings; the Roman Mithras, to the world of imperial associations. Summary The Roman Mithras is not the Mithras of the Avesta, nor are the mysteries the origin of the Church. There is a common ritual grammar and a subsequent Christian controversy.

Sources and strata of cosmogony The structure of creation in Zoroastrianism is known through four layers: the Gāthās, which pose questions about the origin of cosmic order; the Yasna Haptaŋhāiti, where creation appears in the form of a liturgical enumeration; the later Avesta, with the account of the lands created by Ahura Mazdā in Vd 1; and the Pahlavi books, especially the Bundahišn (“fundamental creation”), which organize everything into a system. Between the first two layers and the last lies more than a millennium, and the systematic exposition belongs to the Pahlavi books, from the Islamic period. This is why the Avestan and Pahlavi traditions are distinguished at each point. 2. The questions of Y 44 and creation in the Gāthās The interrogative form is rhetorical: the answer is Ahura Mazdā, “father” of order (asha). The Gāthās do not offer a continuous account of creation; they treat it as the basis of an ethical choice. Y. 30 adds that the two primordial spirits, beneficent and destructive, chose between life and non-life, but from that passage alone, neither the detailed chronology of creation nor the cosmogonic system transmitted by later Middle Iranian compilations can be derived. 3. The Pahlavi system: spiritual and material creation The Bundahišn presents a coherent system. Ohrmazd dwells in infinite light above; Ahriman, in darkness below; between them is emptiness. Ohrmazd knows of Ahriman’s existence, offers him a limited time for combat as a pact, and creates first in the spiritual state (mēnōg) and then in the material state (gētīg). The history of the world lasts 12,000 years, divided into four 3,000-year periods: spiritual creation, material creation without attack, mixing (Ahriman’s attack), and final separation and renewal. The seven material creations are, in the traditional order, sky, waters, earth, plants, cattle (the primordial bull, gāwīēwdād), man (Gayōmard), and fire, each entrusted to an Aməša Spəṇta. Ahriman’s attack pierces the sky, pollutes the waters, burns the plants, and kills the bull Gayōmard; from his remains spring plants and useful species, and from Gayōmard’s seed, the first human couple (Mašyā and Mašyānē). Adam, the primordial Man and the Eastern currents The creation of the first man is the point at which comparative analysis has been most ambitious. In the biblical account, there are two texts: Genesis 1:26–27, where God creates humankind (ʾādām) “in his image,” male and female, and Genesis 2:7, where YHWH forms ʾādām from the dust of the earth (ʾădāmâ) and breathes into him the breath of life. The first is duality: Zoroastrian cosmogony begins with two principles, while Genesis 1 and Isaiah 45:7 affirm a single creator; the discussion of a possible Yahwist response to this already known dualism is addressed in Chapter XVII. The second is the enumeration by works: the series of seven creations and the series of six days do not coincide in either content or order, so the numerical similarity (seven) is insufficient as proof. The third is Plutarch’s testimony, which confirms that in the first century CE the Greeks knew a Mazdaean cosmogony with benevolent and opposing gods, a cosmic egg, and a time appointed for the destruction of evil, and that they transposed these into Greek categories. That testimony is the oldest surviving documentary link of the story known today from Pahlavi sources, and for that reason it is published in chapter XLIV.

296 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM Chapter Conclusion Zoroastrian creation is an ethical order rather than a physical one: every good deed is met with resistance and defended through worship. The systematic structure of seven creations and 12,000 years is Pahlavi; the former is reduced to questions, enu merations, and the scheme of the 16 lands. Summary Zoroastrian cosmogony is presented in four layers: the questions of Y 44 and the two spirits of Y 30, the orderly creation of Y 37 and Vd 1, and the complete system of the Bundahišn. This material is then compared with Genesis 1 and with Plutarch’s exposition, distinguishing in each case the date of the text from the antiquity of the idea. Chapter XXVI. Aeon, Time and Zurvan Chronological context. Traditions concerning time and Zurvan attested by sources from diverse periods, including Late Antiquity and Pahlavi literature. Any priority over a Jewish or Christian text depends on an identifiable early testimony. Control against retrojection: the Bundahišn and Dēnkard. The date of a tradition, the redaction of a text, the formation of a recension, and the material antiquity of a codex are not equivalent. The Bundahišn survives in different Indian and Iranian recensions whose redactional history cannot be dated as a whole; MacKenzie, “Bundahišn”, Encyclopaedia Iranica, distinguishes manuscripts and points out the difficulty of dating its first compilation. The Dēnkard, for its part, articulates Mazdean knowledge from the 9th - 10th centuries and older traditions according to Gignoux, “Dēnkard”, Encyclopaedia Iranica VII/3 (1994), 284–289. Both corpora are fundamental to the historical development of Mazdaism, but they do not provide a direct snapshot of the palace doctrine under Cyrus or Darius I. Scale of evidence for comparative reading. Level I: contemporary Achaemenid document, with its own function and limitations (inscription, tablet, seal, or dated papyrus). Level II: work whose composition or linguistic stratum can be placed, with uncertainty, near the period under investigation. Level III: Hellenistic, Parthian, or Sasanian testimony useful for reception history, but not transferable without arguments to Cyrus and Darius. Level IV: medieval Pahlavi exegesis compilation, source for the history of its tradition and possible vestige of earlier materials; ancient continuity requires specific demonstration for each reason. The date of the manuscript is not to be confused with the composition of the text or with the proposed antiquity of its sources. Critical complement — Zurvan: negative control of chronological inferences The problem of Zurvan requires special caution in a work whose core is situated in the 6th – 4th centuries BCE. The language of time, the personification of Zurvan, and the construction of a theology in which Time occupies a genealogical role with respect to opposing principles are not equivalent expressions. The presence of a temporal vocabulary in an Iranian text does not demonstrate the existence of a Zurvanite school; nor is a late polemical reference sufficient to identify the beliefs of officials or priests under Darius I. 297

298 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM The extensive translation of the Bundahišn allows us to observe cosmological and chronological developments within a Middle Iranian tradition, especially in its initial chapters and the sections dedicated to the duration of the world. However, its value for the 5th century BCE is limited. It is advisable to construct the analysis from ordered documentary layers: verifiable Avestan lexicon; datable Achaemenid inscriptions; Greco-Roman allusions with identified author and temporal distance; Armenian and Syriac testimonies; and Pahlavi compilations. Within this sequence, negative testimonies or silences must be classified by genre and documentary extent before being considered as historical arguments. The parallel with Jewish or Christian concepts of the end times does not prove direct transmission as long as technical correspondences, a compatible chronology, and a vehicle of reception are lacking. Therefore, “eon,” “time,” “eternity,” and “Zurvan” will not be presented as interchangeable translations; each term must be examined in its language, context, and semantic history. This distinction leaves comparative research open but prevents a general analogy from being mistaken for a textual borrowing. Zurvan and the risk of retrospectively projecting a systematic theology The argumentative sequence must begin with a distinction between lexical testimony and theological narrative. The Iranian words that designate duration or time belong to a semantic field; the treatment of Time as a personal agent and the accounts of the generation of Ohrmazd and Ahriman belong to specific literary constructions. Neither the use of an ancient word nor the presence of a temporal scheme in a cosmology justifies, in isolation, attributing a fully developed Zurvanite theology to the Achaemenid kings. The reading of the Bundahišn relies on the Iranian recension (ed. B. T. Anklesaria, 1956), without obscuring the differences between this Iranian recension and the Indian tradition that forms the main basis of E. W. West’s version (which uses TD1 in other sections). Manuscripts TD1, TD2, DH, and K20 provide evidence of later transmission; their codicological age should not be confused with the date of composition of each stratum. When dealing with Greek, Syr iac, or Armenian accounts, it will be indicated to whom the doctrine is attributed, for what polemical purposes, and whether a direct quotation or only a paraphrase is known.

Aiōn: Semantics and Etymology The Greek noun aiṓn means first “vital force, duration of life” and then “epoch, age, eternity.” Its family includes the Latin aevum and aetas, the Avestan āyu- (“life, lifespan”), and the Sanskrit āyu-, and the connection is one of the best established in Indo-European etymology (though not directly verified in dictionaries). The existence of Iranian cognates does not imply that the Greek concept originated in Iran: it is a shared inheritance. The other relevant Iranian term, zruuan- (“time”), is not cognate with aiṓn and designates a different reality (time as potentiality). 2. The Greeks and the Age: From Heraclitus to Plutarch In this philosophical tradition, aiōn encompasses four values. Heraclitus (fr. 52 DK) refers to aiṓn as a playing child, an image of time governed by chance or divine play. In Plato, the Timaeus (37d) distinguishes the aeon, an eternal model that remains in unity, from time (chrónos), a moving image of the aeon that progresses according to number. Aristotle, in De caelo I 9 (279a), derives aiṓn from aei on (“always being”),

In the imperial era, Plutarch makes the aeon the mode of being of the god: in De E apud Delphos 20 he affirms that the god is not according to any time, but according to the immobile, timeless and inflexible aeon (393A).140 See the text and translation in the edition of chapter XLIV (section 5). The idea that the divine is one and simple, in contrast to the multiplicity of humans, links with the philosophical monotheism that Plutarch also applies to the dualism of Zoroaster in De Iside 45–49. 3. Pythagoras and the Aeons Pythagoras left no writings, and everything said about his doctrine comes from later accounts. From the pre-Platonic tradition, the most reliable information is the table of opposites that Aristotle attributes to the Pythagoreans (Metaphysics A 5, 986a): limited and unlimited, odd and even, one and many, right and left, male and female, rest and motion, straight and curved, light and darkness, good and evil, square and oblong. Plutarch reproduces a similar list in De Iside 48 and places it alongside the dualism of the Magi and of Heraclitus, Empedocles, Anaxagoras, Aristotle, and Plato (text in the edition of chapter XLIV). There is no mention of “aeons” in the full sense in ancient accounts of Pythagoras: his doctrine deals with number, harmony, transmigration, and purification. What does circulate is the tradition of his contact with the Magi: Porphyry (Life of Pythagoras 12) and Clement (Stromata I 15) make him a disciple of a “Zaratas” or “Zaratos” of Babylon, a name the Greeks adopted for Zoroaster, and these accounts are late and legendary.141142 4. Aeons in the Second Temple and in Christianity The Hebrew ʿôlām (“remote time, forever”) is translated in the Septuagint as aiṓn, and the New Testament uses aiṓn for “this age” and “the age to come” (Matt 12:32; Eph 1:21; Heb 6:5), for the “ages” of creation (Heb 1:2; 11:3), and for the powers “of this age” (1 Cor 2:6–8). The doctrine of the two ages, with its culmination in the final judgement, is present in 4 Ezra and 2 Baruch, and is a component of apocalyptic eschatology. The Valentinian Gnostics gave it their own twist: the “aeons” are divine emanations that form the Pleroma (Irenaeus, Adversus haereses I 1–8). Between Plutarch’s timeless and divine aeon and the Valentinian aeons, which are personifications, there is a shift in meaning that illustrates how Greek vocabulary was reused. There is no evidence that Judeo-Christian usage depended on Zurvanism; however, there is a shared horizon of thought regarding time and its ages. Table 12. Plutarch and the logos In De Iside 45, Plutarch discusses explanations for the origin of evil and rejects both the atomists, who place the principles in lifeless bodies, and the Stoics, who defend “a single logos and a single providence” that presides over all. In paragraph 49, he defines Osiris as the nous and logos that guides all that is best within the soul of the universe: “in the soul, the intellect, and the logos, guide and lord of all that is best, is Osiris.” For Plutarch, the logos is, therefore, an ordering reason that is insufficient to explain evil; evil requires a second principle, and for this reason he resorts to the du alism of the Magi, to that of Heraclitus, and to that of Plato (Laws X). 4. The Logos in John and Its Intellectual Context The prologue to the Gospel of John (John 1:1–18) brings together three traditions: the creative Word of Genesis 1 and Psalm 33, the pre-existent Wisdom of Proverbs 8 and Sirach 24, and the logos of Hellenistic philosophy, which had already acquired a mediating function in Philo. The distinctive Johannine claim is the incarn

312 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM ation (John 1:14). Iranian hypotheses, including Barnea’s proposal concerning the Saošyant and John 1, must explain why this Jewish-Hellenistic context is insufficient. The closest Iranian functional parallel concerns the efficacious sacred utterance, mąθra, and the Ahuna Vairya prayer; functional resemblance, however, does not establish textual dependence. Conclusion to Chapter XXVII Logos is a multivalent concept. Greek traditions deploy it in accounts of cosmic rationality (Heraclitus and the Stoics) and human reasoning (Aristotle), while Hellenistic Judaism develops its mediating function. The Iranian sacred utterance operates differently: it is an efficacious formula rather than reason as a philosophical principle. Chapter Summary Logos spans three semantic domains—speech, reckoning, and thought—which this chapter examines across fifteen ancient authors and traditions. Plutarch provides an important Greek witness to accounts of Persian religious thought; the Johannine prologue is considered within its Jewish and Hellenistic intellectual setting. Chapter XXVIII. Cultic Architecture: Temples, Fire Altars, Mithraea, and Synagogues Historical scope of the chapter. The archaeological data synthesized here are derived from the secondary bibliography mentioned; they are not presented as a result of direct examination of the original excavation records. 1. Method: Buildings, Cult, and Sources A religious building is examined through three kinds of evidence: its form (plan, materials, orientation), its use (the cultic practices it accommodated), and the sources that document it (excavations, inscriptions, or texts). Form and cult do not correspond automatically: similar structures can accommodate different practices, and cultic activity may occur without a dedicated building. This chapter arranges the evidence by period and cult, avoiding the projection of later architectural forms onto earlier contexts. 2. Temples of the Persian Period: Elephantine, Jerusalem, and Mount Gerizim The temple of YHW at Elephantine is documented by the Aramaic archive, and its destruction is reported for 410 BCE. The following architectural details come from petition TAD A4.7, not from an excavated plan: stone portals, stone pillars, doors with bronze hinges, a cedar roof, and gold and silver vessels. The urban context of Elephantine also included the cult of Khnum, an Egyptian god associated with the ram; the exact relationship between the sites requires archaeological caution. The Second Temple in Jerusalem, according to Ezra 6:15, was dedicated in 516/515 BCE under Darius and constitutes an authoritative cultic reference in the correspondence; however, the documents do not prove a physical journey of the petitioners to Jerusalem. On Mount Gerizim, excavations have documented a Samaritan 315

Diachronic Comparison of Cultic Architecture: Iran, Elephantine, Jerusalem, Mount Gerizim, and Synagogues (Fourth Century BCE–First Century CE) Architectural comparison requires distinguishing between the Achaemenid antecedent of the 5th century BCE, the period between the 4th and 1st centuries BCE, and the buildings existing around the time of the life of Jesus of Nazareth (late 1st century BCE and first half of the 1st century CE). Elephantine is not a contemporary building of Jesus: its documented destruction occurred in 410 BCE. Its inclusion is justified because it provides almost unique evidence of a peripheral Yahwist sanctuary, distinct from the precinct of Jerusalem and known through a contemporary diplomatic record. The criterion will not be to equate religions based on the appearance of their buildings, but rather to distinguish between archaeology, inscription, iconographic representation, and literary testimony. The Sanctuary of YHW at Elephantine: Textual Description, Not an Excavated Plan Aramaic petition of Jedaniah and his colleagues to Bagohi, governor of Yehud (TAD A4.7 = Cowley 30; P. Berlin 13495), dated to the 17th year of Darius II (407 BCE), attributes the destruction of the temple of YHW in 410 BCE to priests of Khnum, in agreement with Vidranga and with the intervention of his son Nafayna Stone pillars and portals, doors with bronze elements, a cedar roof, and gold and sil ver objects are mentioned. These are details relevant to the architectural materiality, but they stem from a self-serving petition: the document seeks political redress and authorization to rebuild. Its description should not be transformed into an excavation plan. The reconstruction proposed by Stephen G. Rosenberg is expressly hypothetical, not an archaeologically recovered building in elevation [1–2]. The proximity of the Yahwist community to a centre of the Khnum cult explains part of the urban context, without in itself proving that the conflict had a single theological cause. The response preserved in TAD A4.9 (= Cowley 32) provides for the reconstruction of the altar’s location and mentions vegetable offer 146 Magen, Mount Gerizim Excavations II.

These documents must be compared line by line, not combined into a single text. In particular, none of the references authorizes the automatic identification of the Yeb building with an Iranian fire temple [1]. Fourth–Third Centuries BCE: Jerusalem, Mount Gerizim, and Iran after Alexander In Jerusalem, the Second Temple represents the institutional continuity of the sanctuary restored in the Persian period, although the architectural form known from Herodian sources cannot be retrospectively projected to the 4th century BCE. Philological attention should be directed to the distinction between the sacrificial altar, the precinct, the building itself, and the outbuildings. Ezra 5–6 describes controversies and authorizations concerning the rebuilding but does not provide a plan of Hellenistic Jerusalem. The use of common terminology— house, altar, precinct, gate — does not prove Iranian architectural borrowing. The sanctuary at Gerizim offers a third Yahwist trajectory, distinct from Jerusalem and Elephantine. Its sacred precinct and epigraphic finds show Samaritan religious activity, but the dating of its first phase remains debated. Yitzhak Magen proposed a foundation in the 5th century BCE; Jodi Magness (2025), after reviewing the published stratigraphy, questions whether the findings necessitate such an early date. Eran Arie has also reviewed the construction phases and their Ionic tradition elements. Consequently, a single date should not be fixed in a table without indicating the debate [3–5]. For Seleucid and Parthian Iran, the evidence of altars, platforms, courtyards, and fire-related enclosures does not allow for the indiscriminate application of the Sasanian architectural type of the čahārṭāq. The forms of the altars are known from objects, representations, and sites of uneven dating. Kūh-e Ḵᵛāja, in Sistán, preserves architectural phases whose beginning has been debated between the Seleucid and Parthian periods, with later transformations. It is not appropriate to describe all these remains as unequivocal Zoroastrian temples or to present them as predating the period of Jesus without stratigraphic argument [6–8].

318 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM Second–First Centuries BCE: Hellenistic Transformations and Differences in Cultic Function The Gerizim precinct, enlarged in the Hellenistic period, was destroyed by John Hyrcanus around 111–110 BCE, according to the prevailing archaeological interpretation; its use as a direct model for a 1st-century CE synagogue would be chronologically inappropriate [4]. The Temple in Jerusalem, on the other hand, was transformed by the end of the 1st century BCE by Herod’s work: large platforms, retaining walls, porticoes, and courtyards arranged by levels of access. This comparison allows us to identify scales, circulation patterns, the sacredness of the centre, and sacrificial practices; it does not postulate a single floor plan for Jerusalem, Elephantine, and an Iranian fire precinct. In Iran, fire altars and ritual spaces reflect specific relationships between priestly agents, fire, purity, and recitation; in Jerusalem and Gerizim, the sacrificial sanctuary is linked to altars, offerings, ritual circulation, and a hierarchy of access. The possible analogies — delimitation of a sacred area, maintenance of cultic objects, and the relationship between political authority and the priesthood — are institutional and typological; they do not prove architectural identity or a transfer of floor plans. In the comparative edition, these should be discussed separately: source of reliable date, support, demonstrated function, and any possible channel of contact. In the Time of Jesus: Jerusalem and Synagogues Compared with Iranian Cultic Spaces Toward the turn of the era, the great Jewish sacrificial sanctuary was the Temple in Jerusalem in its Herodian configuration. The synagogue did not duplicate it: it con stituted a place of assembly, reading, teaching, and diverse community practices, with local architectural features. The buildings at Gamla, Magdala, and other sites attributed to the end of the Second Temple period must be evaluated according to their respective dates of excavation and publication; their perimeter benches and as sembly spaces are not equivalent to the sacrificial altar of the Temple. Therefore, they should not be automatically compared to an Iranian fire chamber as if they were all spaces for the same rite [9]. The testimonies of Strabo (Geography XV.3.13-15) and Pausanias (V.27.5-6) are useful ancient comparativists for rituals of Magi, enclosures, and fire, but they describe practices of specific locations and chronologies; their accounts do not offer plans of an Achaemenid sanctuary of the 5th century BCE. Even less should the

ARCHITECTURE OF WORSHIP 319 Sasanian temples of Taḵt-e Solaymān/Ādur Gušnasp or the fully developed type of čahārṭāq be introduced as contemporaries of Jesus. These are testimonies from later centuries whose comparison is legitimate for long-term history, but it constitutes an anachronism if they are used to reconstruct buildings of the 1st century CE [78]. Comparative Assessment in Relation to the Book’s Thesis This sequence reveals three distinct levels of evidence. First, Achaemenid administration and military communities document coexistence, negotiation, and conflict among religious groups, most clearly at Elephantine. Second, the excavated or reconstructable architecture of Jerusalem and Mount Gerizim shows that Yahwist cultic spaces followed distinct historical trajectories. Third, comparisons with Iranian fire-related ritual spaces must distinguish evidence of shared imperial settings from claims of architectural borrowing. Similarity of function or form alone does not establish a historical line of transmission. Gerizim — sacred precinct, with a de bated initial foundation. ARCHITECTURE OF WORSHIP 321 of fire in the Achaemenid period Herodotus (I 131) states that the Persians did not erect statues, temples, or altars, and that they sacrificed in elevated places. Material sources qualify this picture: in Pasargadae, two stone platforms are preserved that are interpreted as fire altars, next to the so-called Zendan -e Soleiman, a stone tower of disputed function, and in Naqš-e Rostam, the Kaʿba-ye Zardošt, a 5th-century BCE tower whose function as a fire sanctuary is a subject of debate; royal reliefs show the king before an altar with a flame. Two Greek authors describe later practices in Asia Minor: Strabo (XV 3,15) mentions “fire chambers” (pyraithoi) in Cappadocia, with an altar and ashes, where the Magi maintain the fire, and Pausanias (V 27,5–6) describes in Lydia a magus singing before an altar of ashes, where the fire is kindled without wood. These descriptions correspond to the late Persian and Hellenistic periods, and their connection to the cult of eternal fire instituted in Sasanian temples is indirect. It is also important to clarify the vocabulary: the Zoroastrians do not “worship” fire, but rather venerate it as an agent of worship, kept burning and fueled with purity rites. The expression “fire worshipers” is Greek and controversial. 4. Sasanian fire temples With the Sasanian dynasty appears the characteristic building, the chahārṭāq (four arches), a square chamber covered by a dome, with a hearth in its centre, and the great hearths of special status: Ādur Farnbāg, Ādur Gušnasp (associated with Takht-e Soleiman), and Ādur Burzēn-Mihr. These temples, with their hierarchical priesthood, are the culmination of a process, not its origin, and therefore do not ex tend into the 4th century BCE. 5. Mithraea, house churches and synagogues In the Roman Empire, the mithraeum was a small, subterranean or enclosed room with side benches and a relief of the god, depicting a cave (Porphyry, De antro 6). Christian communities met in adapted private houses (domus ecclesiae), and Jewish communities in synagogues, examples of which survive from the Hellenistic period. Dura-Europos preserves a mithraeum, a synagogue (244–245 CE), and a house-church (circa 240–256 CE), with the city’s destruction dated to around 256–257 CE.

Herzfeld defended a Parthian phase of the 1st century CE with Sasanian remodelings of the 3rd century CE; Gullini proposed six levels from the Achaemenid to the Islamic period, a thesis that Tucci rejected; Schippmann and Kawami maintain a Sasanian date; Faccenna considers a late Parthian dating doubtful; and the radiocarbon samples from Ghanimati give 80– 240 CE for a ceiling sample and 540–650 CE for tamarisk pegs (with margins of ± 50 years), suggesting successive phases. The paintings include figures of horsemen, a processional figure, a winged Eros on the gallery ceiling (which Herzfeld considered Hellenistic and Kawami of the 1st century or later), and a group that Herzfeld read as a royal couple. Therefore, to assert without reservation that Kuh-e Khwaja is a “Parthian fire temple” from the time of Jesus, or “the missing link between Achaemenid altars and Sasanian temples,” exceeds what the evidence allows: it is a Zoroastrian cult site with a fire cella and circumambulation, whose initial phase may be late Parthian, and whose final form appears Sasanian. The Iranica rejects Herzfeld’s label of “palace-temple” and prefers a pilgrimage site, noting that its plan does not correspond to any other known Iranian temple. The inventory suggests a cautious approach. By the 5th century BCE, there are formal structures (Pasargadae, Bard-e Nešānde, Dahan-e Gholaman) that can be linked to high and fire rituals, but their precise identification as “fire temples” is not established. By the 3rd century CE, coins of the Frataraka depict a building with a Persian religious symbol in Persis, under Seleucid rule or in its decline. For the time of Jesus, the dating of Kuh-e Khwaja and other eastern sites is uncertain, and there is no Parthian fire temple whose date is assured for that period.
