326 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM 7. The Magi and their precincts: what Strabo and Pausanias say Textual note. The passages from Strabo (Geography XV 3,13–15) and Pausanias (Description of Greece V 27,5–6) have been consulted through the digital edition of Perseus. Classical accounts of the fire precincts of the Magi outside Iran are from the early Roman period and describe Anatolia, not Parthian Iran. Strabo (around the turn of the era) writes of Cappadocia: “There is a large tribe of Magi, who are also called pýraithoi (those of the fire); there are many temples of Persian gods. There are also pyraitheîa (houses of fire), notable precincts (sēkoí), and in the middle of them an altar on which there is much ash and where the Magi keep an inextinguishable fire (pŷr ásbeston).” Each day they enter and chant incantations for almost an hour before the fire, with a bundle of sticks in their hands and with felt tiaras hanging down on both sides until they cover their lips with their cheeks” (XV 3.15; en d è tê i Kappadokíāi … tiáras perikeímenoi pilōtàs katheikuías hekatérōthen mékhri to û kalýptein t à kheílē tà s paragnathídas). Pausanias (second century CE) describes two “Persian” sanctuaries of the Lydians, at Hierocaesarea and at Hypaepa: in each one there is a chamber (oíkēma) and in the chamber, on an altar, ash; A magus enters, piles dry wood on the altar, puts the tiara on his head, invokes some god with a chant in a barbarian language, unintelligible to the Greeks, reading from a book, and the wood catches fire without fire (V 27.5–6).148149 Precise details can be gleaned from these texts. In both, the fire space is an enclosure or chamber with a central altar and abundant ash, tended by Magi who chant or recite with a bundle of sticks (the baresman of the Iranian-Vedic tradition) and wear a felt tiara with flaps covering the lips, corresponding to the padām, the mouth veil that prevents contaminating the fire with breath. Neither Strabo nor Pausanias mentions a circumambulatory corridor, dark chapels, or secret rituals of priests walking in a circle; these features are absent from the sources. Nor do they locate the sanctuaries at Nemrud Dağ: the sanctuary of Antiochus I of Commagene 148Pausanias, Description of Greece V 27.5–6 (Perseus, Greek text consulted online). The two Lydian cities are Hierocaesarea and Hypaepa; the identification of the place and the period of the cult is disputed. 149Strabo, Geography XV 3.15 (Perseus, Greek text consulted online; the paragraph numbering of this passage may vary between editions, XV 3.14–15). In the same context, Strabo adds that the Persians do not blow on the fire but fan it with a fan, and that they punish with death anyone who blows on it or throws a corpse into the fire.

ARCHITECTURE OF WORSHIP 327 (1st century BCE) is a royal monument with terraces, colossi, and a tumulus, without known fire chambers, and its inscriptions speak of a dynastic cult (chapter XXXI). What Pausanias does reveal is that, in Lydia, the cult was practiced with a book, in a language the Greeks did not understand, and with a miracle: wood that kindles itself, a fact comparable to fires that burn without being lit (chapter XXXIII). Three clarifications regarding the image of a “hereditary guild” that supposedly centralized the cult at the turn of the era. First: that the Magi were a tribe or priestly caste is an ancient Greek tradition (Herodotus, Hist. I.101, counts them among the six Median groups), and Strabo calls them phŷlon (“tribe”) in Cappadocia, so the hereditary trait is well attested; but there is no source that describes an “absolute monopoly” or a political centralization of the cult in Parthian times. Second: the pādyāb (ritual ablution of purification with water) does not designate a circumambulation; the word, which appears in the Pahlavi tradition, refers to washing, and should not be applied to the Kuh-e Khwaja passage. Third: Takht-e Soleymān, identified with the sanctuary of Ādur Gušnasp, is a first-rate Sasanian-period site (5th – 7th centuries CE), featuring a lake, a fire temple, and a monumental precinct. The presence of earlier occupation (Achaemenid and Parthian) and the existence of a fire cult during those phases is a matter of debate, preventing a definitive Parthian date for the sanctuary (Naumann, Huff, and Boucharlat). It is also uncertain whether the corridor plan, attested at Kuh-e Khwaja and in Sasanian temples, spread throughout the vassal states from a Parthian model. 8. Altars, degrees and sacred fires: a text subjected to control The altars and ritual degrees of fire require rigorous periodization: many descriptions rely on Sasanian or Parsi tradition and should not be projected onto the Achaemenid period without independent evidence. The terms are: Av. ātar- (fire), Pahl. ātazš and ātaš, from which the modern Persian ātaš derives; ātazšān or ātašdān (“receptacle of fire”), the support of the fire; ātazškada (“house of fire”); and padām, the veil covering the priest’s mouth, already mentioned in connection with Strabo (section 7). The idea that Zoroastrians are not “fire worshippers” is the tradition’s self-definition, and the qualification is found in Christian and Muslim sources; it is a case where the name of the accusation cannot be used as proof of what was done.

328 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM Three points require caution. First, the Avesta does not mention fire temples in the proper sense, which agrees with Herodotus I 131; Strabo XV 3.13 describes a sacrifice without an altar, but 3.15 mentions fire precincts and sanctuaries of Anaitis in Cappadocia; ritual fire does exist, but in the context of the hearth and the sacrificial enclosure. Second, the interpretation of Achaemenid fire altars is disputed: at Pasargadae there are two stepped stone platforms near the palaces, which are identified as either altars or bases (Stronach, Pasargadae, 1978), and at Naqš-e Rostam fire altars are carved into the rock, their date disputed, while it is certain that the king in the reliefs of the royal tombs appears before a fire altar. Third, the chahār-ṭā q (modern Persian čahārṭāq, “four arches”) is a form typical of the Sasanian period and is not reliably documented earlier. The consecration of the Ātaš Bahrām according to Modi. The Parsi ethnographer and priest Jivanji J. Modi (1854–1933) describes, in The Religious Ceremonies and Customs of the Parsees (2nd ed., J.B. Karani’s Sons, 1937; digital edition by J.H. Peterson, 2011, CC-BY-NC), the consecration of the first-degree fire. According to his account, the ritual developed from Vendīdād VIII 73–96, which lists the fires of various trades (the cremation fire, the potter’s fire, the blacksmith’s fire, the baker’s fire, the shepherd’s fire, the soldier’s fire) that can be moved to their own place (dādgāh, av. dāityō.gātu-). From that list, later ritualists deduced the practice of gathering sixteen fires of different origins (among them a corpse fire, a dyer’s fire, a king’s fire, a potter’s fire, a lightning fire, and the hearth fire of a Zoroastrian), purifying and consecrating each one, and combining them into a single fire. Each fire is consecrated with a fixed number of recitations from the Yasna and the Vendīdād, totaling 1,128. If a single pair of priests were to recite them all, it would take 1,128 days, or about thirty-seven months, and so several pairs are employed, and the ceremony lasts about a year or less. Modi notes that authorities differ on the details, and that the six Ātaš Bahrām of Bombay and elsewhere did not follow the same procedure. For the book, this fact is important in two ways. First, it shows that the system of degrees and consecration is an elaboration of the later priestly tradition, which derives its legitimacy from a passage in the Vendīdād; there are no sources of a similar ritual in the Achaemenid period, and the comparison with the fire on the altar of Jerusalem (Lev 6:5–6) remains at the typological level. Second, it provides a useful contrast with the idea of a single, permanent fire: what Second

ARCHITECTURE OF WORSHIP 331 Temple Judaism describes as a fire that “does not go out” (Lev 6:6) has a highly elaborate ritual counterpart in later Zoroastrianism, but one of medieval origin. 9. Evaluation Architecture confirms what the texts show: the Persian period did not have a single type of religious building. Yahwism had stone temples with sacrificial altars; Achae menid Zoroastrianism celebrated fire rituals at open altars and towers; the covered fire temple is Sasanian. From this follows a methodological consequence: any comparison between the “fire cult” and the altar of Leviticus 6 must be made with rituals and not with buildings. Chapter Conclusion Elephantine, Jerusalem and Gerizim document a Yahvism with temples; Pasargada and Naqš-e Rostam, an Achaemenid fire nest without a covered temple; the sasánidas, the canonical building. The mithraeums and church houses are from the Roman Empire. Summary After establishing the method (building form, cultic use, and the source that describes it), the chapter explores the Yahwist temples of the Persian period, the Achaemenid fire altars, and the Sasanian temples, and concludes with the Mithraea, house-churches, and synagogues. This is the architectural core of the third section of the thesis. Chapter XXIX. Greece and Iran: Wisdom, Mithra, Maitreya and the Saviour Chronological context. Greco-Iranian contacts from the Achaemenid period, Hellenistic developments, and Roman reception; Maitreya belongs to an independent Buddhist history. The comparison of the saviour requires specific paths and dates. Chronological note. The contacts of the 5th–4th centuries BCE correspond to the Achaemenid framework. The Sasanian horizon begins in the 3rd century CE and belongs to Late Antiquity. 1. Period correction The Sasanian Empire began in 224 CE, centuries after Greek philosophy had developed its vocabulary (6th – 4th centuries BCE). Therefore, the question of Iranian influence on Greek thought must be divided into two periods: the contact with the Achaemenid Empire, during which the Greeks encountered the Magi and Zoroaster; and Late Antiquity, when philosophical schools became associated with the Sasanian state. Only during this second period can one speak of the Sasanian civilization. 2. The Greeks and the Magi in the Achaemenid period Herodotus (I 131–140) provides the first extensive account of the customs of the Persians and the Magi. Plato mentions in Alcibiades I (122a) the “magic of Zoroaster, son of Oromazus” as part of the education of the Persian prince. Accord ing to Diogenes Laertius (proem 6–9), Aristotle, Eudoxus, Hermippus, and Theopompus discussed the antiquity of the Magi and the date of Zoroaster, which Hermippus placed five thousand years before the Trojan War, as Plutarch repeats. These authors do not transmit Avestan doctrine, but rather the Greek image of an Eastern wisdom. What spread throughout the Greek world was the figure of the magus as a wise man and the idea that philosophy had a barbaric origin, which Dio genes Laertius opposed at the beginning of his Lives.152153154 152Herodotus I 131–140; Plato, Alc. I 122a; Diogenes Laertius, proem 1–9; Plutarch, De Is. 46 (text verified on Bernardakis). 333

334 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM 3. “Love of wisdom” and “love of Mazda” The hypothesis that philosophia (“love of wisdom”) could derive from a “love of Mazda,” the name of the god whose epithet means “wise,” is not philologically sound. Philosophia is formed from Greek elements, philos (“friend, beloved”) and sophia (“skill, wisdom”), and Greek tradition attributes the word to Pythagoras (Heraclid Ponticus, quoted by Diogenes Laertius, Proem 12). The Avestan name Ahura Mazdā means “Wise Lord” (mazda-, “wise, he who puts into the mind”); no element of the Greek word corresponds to it, and there is no attested Greek form philo-Mazda-. What can be stated is a semantic parallel: both cultures conceived of the divine as wisdom, and Plutarch includes sophia among the six gods that Oromazes created (De Is. 47). The parallel is thematic, not etymological. GREECE AND IRAN: WISDOM, MITHRAS, MAITREYA AND THE SAVIOUR 335 4. Greece, Iran, and Late Antiquity One specific episode links Greek philosophy to the Sasanian state. According to Agathias, around 529, Emperor Justinian closed the Academy of Athens, and several philosophers, including Damascius, Simplicius, and Priscian of Lydia, sought refuge at the court of Khosrow I, drawn by his reputation as a philosopher-king. The philosophers returned shortly afterward, disappointed, according to Agathias’s account; their stay left no identifiable Iranian-Sasanian influence on their work. At the same time, Syriac Christians in Persia were translating Aristotle and Porphyry, a bridge by which Greek philosophy passed to the East, and not the other way around. The result is that the Sasanian influence on Greek thought is minimal, and that the important movement is from Greece to Iran: Khosrow I receives Greek texts, and from them a part of the later Islamic intellectual tradition is born. 5. Mithras and Maitreya: semantic parallels The Sanskrit word mitra- means “friend” and “covenant.” From this root are derived maitrī (“friendship, benevolence”) and Maitreya (“he who belongs to friendship”), the name of the future Buddha. In the language of the Avesta, miθra- means “contract,” and the god Mithra is the guarantor of covenants. The lexical relationship between Maitreya and mitra- within Sanskrit is certain; what is debated is whether the Buddhist Maitreya owes anything to the Iranian god. There is support ing evidence: the presence of Mithra on Kushan coins (Miiro) and the spread of the Maitreya cult in Gandhara, where Iranian, Greek, and Buddhist traditions coexisted. The opposing arguments point out that the Buddhist Maitreya is a figure from the same Indian tradition, whose name can be explained by maitrī, and that his role as a future Buddha does not require an Iranian model. The structural parallel with the Saošyant (a future saviour who will renew the world) is striking, but it does not prove dependence either. Table 16. Fragment B52 DK reads: “Aiṓn is a child playing pessoí (pieces of a board game, not dice); the kingdom belongs to a child” (aiṓn paîs esti paízōn, pesseúōn; paidòs hē basilēíē), preserved by Hippolytus, Refutation IX 9.4 (indirect testimony preserved from fragment B52 DK). Aiṓn here means “life, duration, age” and cannot be safely translated as “eternal time”; the game is a board game (pessoí), not a dice game. There is no connection in Heraclitus with Eros or Zurván. Etymology clarifies the term: aiṓn comes from an Indo-European root h₂eyu- (“vital force, duration”), with cognates in Avestan ayu- (“life”) and Sanskrit ā yu-, and Latin aevum; the Persian zruuan- (“time”, Pahl. zamān, zurwān), on the other hand, derives from another root, that of “old age” (ǵerh₂-; Gr. gérās, Ved. jarā-), and is a different term that applies to unlimited time (zruuan- akarana-; cf. Vd. 19.9.13.16, with its differences in textual function). Second, the Orphic Eros and Phanes. In Hesiod’s Theogony (116–122), Eros is among the first beings; in Aristophanes’ Birds (693–703; transmitted Greek text), Eros is born from an egg laid by Night; and in the Orphic tradition, we find Protogonus, also called Phanes (“the one who appears”), an androgynous, winged, and radiant god who is born from the cosmic egg, as attested by the Derveni Papyrus (4th century BCE) and the Orphic Rhapsodies (testimonies and fragments in Barnabas, Orphicorum fragmenta). In these sources, Eros is not a “child”: the childlike Eros is a Hellenistic image. And there is no ancient testimony that identifies, in the time of Heraclitus, the child Aion with Phanes; the identifications of Phanes with Khronus and with Aion are from Neoplatonic authors and from late Orphic texts (West, The Orphic Poems, 1983).156157158 156Hippolytus, Refutatio omnium haeresium 9.9.4, in the historical translation collected by ANF, “Refutation of All Heresies”, Book IX, Hippolytus, Refutatio omnium haeresium, trans. 338 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM Third, Zurvan. Here the text contains the strongest assertion, which must be corrected: there is no evidence of Zurvanism in the Achaemenid period. The first Greek testimony is from Eudemus of Rhodes (4th century BCE), preserved by Damascius, according to whom “the Magi and the entire Aryan lineage” call the intelligible, some “place” and others “time” (Khronos), and from it separate a good god and an evil daemon, or light and darkness. The myth of Zurvan, who sacrifices himself for a thousand years to have a son and conceives Ormazd and Ahriman within his womb, is known from Eznik of Kolb (5th century CE), Theodore bar Koni, and Elišē — that is, from Armenian and Syriac sources of the Sasanian period. The very name of unlimited time appears in the Avesta (zruuan- akarana-), but without a conception myth. Eznik does not claim that Zurvan is androgynous; he says that the twins are conceived within him, so “cosmic womb” is a modern inference. Whether there was a “Zurvanite heresy” is a matter of fundamental debate: Zaehner asserted its existence, while later scholars see them more as variants of a single myth. And, of course, Zurván does not “play” nor is he a “child”: he is the father who doubts and who, because of that doubt, engenders evil. Fourth, the lion- headed Aion and the “Modena Relief.” In the Mithraea, a figure appears with a lion’s head, a human body entwined by a serpent, with four wings and keys (Rome, Ostia, Mérida, York, among others), which has been called Aion, Zurvan, Khronus, Saturn, Ahriman, or Deus Arimanius; no identification is certain. It is important to distinguish two images that the text conflates. The Modena figure (Galleria Estense) is a winged, nude youth within an oval containing the zodiac, interpreted as either Phanes or Aion, and stands on a base depicting an egg; its connection to the Mithraic mysteries is uncertain. The lion-headed figure, on the other hand, is not on a broken egg, nor is it a youth: it is a leonine figure with a serpent. Finally, the Mithraea are not from “the 1st century BCE to the fourth century CE”: their earliest remains date from the end of the 1st century CE (chapter XXXVII, section 10). The assimilation of the lion-headed figure to Zurvan is a hy- disputed.

Jesus and the figure of the saviour in Zoroastrian culture Two questions must be distinguished: whether Jesus was conceived from the Saošyant (discussed in Chapter XXIII), and how he could have been interpreted by Zoroastrians. The second can be answered with data on reception. A Zoroastrian of the Sasanian period had few categories to integrate a crucified saviour: the Saošyant is, by definition, an agent of final renewal who does not die in expiation for anyone, and Christianity, persecuted by Kerdir and Šābuhr II, was perceived as a rival religion. The Manichean response is different: Mani incorporated Jesus into his pantheon as a messenger and revealer. From the Zoroastrian perspective, the Škandgumānīg wizār (9th century) criticizes Christology and does not incorporate it.

GREECE AND IRAN: WISDOM, MITHRAS, MAITREYA AND THE SAVIOUR 341 The conclusion is that “Jesus as saviour of the world for Zoroastrian culture” is a formulation that only makes sense as an exercise in cultural translation: a Zoroastrian reader might say that Jesus plays, on the Christian scale, a role analogous to that of a Saošyant, but neither the Christians nor the Zoroastrians of the time framed it that way. Chapter Conclusion The direct influence of Sasanian Iran on Greek thought is scarce; the Achaemenid influence is limited to the image of the magus; the parallel between “philosophy” and “Mazda” is thematic, not linguistic. Mithras and Maitreya share a lexical root that, within Sanskrit, is certain. Summary The chapter first corrects the chronology of the contacts and gathers what the Greek authors say about the Magi and the relationship between philosophy and Mazda. It continues with the philosophers who took refuge at the court of Khosrow I, the question of Mithras and Maitreya, and the reception of Jesus in the Zoroastrian world. These are three distinct historical contexts; the Indo-Iranian affinity does not equate to ritual identity with Roman imperial Mithraism. The places in the Ṛgveda and the Avesta are identified by textual references. Vedic or Avestan readings are not reproduced without explicit support in a textual source. 1. MITRA AND AGNI 345 3. Agni, Ātar and fire: common roots and differences In the Vedas, Agni is one of the most important gods: some two hundred hymns in the Rigveda are addressed to him, and the first hymn in the collection (RV 1.1) is for him. He is called the messenger (dūta) between the gods and men, the priest (hotṛ, purohita), and the mouth of the gods through whom offerings arrive. He is conceived as present in three places: the hearth, the lightning, and the sun. In Vedic ritual (śrauta), three fires are maintained (the house fire, the oblation fire, and the southern fire), and the agnihotra is the daily offering. Agni consumes the ghee, soma, and fats of the sacrifice, carries the dead in cremation (RV 10.16), and is the fire that burns. In Zoroastrianism, ātar- is the fire of worship. The Avestan tradition calls him “son of Ahura Mazdā”; he fights in Yašt 19 (Yt. 19.46-50) against the dragon Aži Dahāka for the xᵛarənah (“royal glory”); and he is attributed a role as guardian of order (aša) in the Gāthās (Y. 31.34, 43, 46). In the Pahlavid texts, five classes of fire are distinguished (Bundahishn 17), and the Sasanian period organized temple fires into three levels: Ādur Wahrām, the highest-ranking fire, Ādurī Ādurān, and Ādurōg. The fire was kept burning continuously with dry wood and sandalwood, under the care of priests who wore veils over their mouths to avoid contaminating it. A decisive feature separates it from Vedic Agni: the fire could not be contaminated with dead matter. According to the Vendīdād (chapter 8), dead matter contaminates the fire, and for this reason Zoroastrianism rejects cremation, which in India is a rite of Agni. This corresponds to the value of purity that Zoroastrianism gives to fire: it is a pure agent that must be protected from corpses, and not a universal devourer. Table 18. Comparative philology of Indo-Iranian fire The comparison between Agni and Ātar is based first on language. Indo-European has two roots for fire. The first is an animate noun, reconstructed as h₁n̥ gʷnis, which survives in Vedic Sanskrit agni-, Latin ignis, Lithuanian ugnis, and Old Slavic ogni; its animate character explains why fire is thought of as a being. The second is the one that Iranian retains as the name for fire: Av. ātar- (gen. āθrō), pahl. ātaxš, Persian ātaš, Ossetian art, to which the Sanskrit átharvan- (priest of fire) and the Avestan āθrauuan- (priest) are usually associated, although the ultimate etymology of ātar- is disputed (Mayrhofer, EWAia, sv átharvan-). Iranian does not have a clear reflection of agní- as a common name for fire, which suggests that the dialectal division had already chosen one of the two words. It does not follow from this that Agni is a borrowing or an invention: the name of the Vedic god and the Iranian name for fire do not coincide, but the functions do.161 161On the roots of fire in Indo-European: J. MITRA AND AGNI 349 Domestic fire, marriage and points of the text submitted for control Vedic ritual attributes a domestic and civil role to fire. In the Grhya, household rites (Grhya- sūtras, for example, Āśvalāyana) are performed before the fire of the householder; in marriage, the bride and groom take the seven steps (saptapadī) before the fire, and the bond is considered sealed with this act. For Iran, the domestic fire is attested by the Vendīdād and by classical sources, but the Zoroastrian marriage rite is not structured as a walk around the fire; the parallel with the saptapadī is one of function (fire as witness) and not of ritual. Vedic domestic fire also has a destiny that the Iranian rejects: in India, the corpse is given to Agni; in Iran, the dead matter contaminates the fire and the body is exposed. First, Zoroaster cannot be dated simply “to the second millennium BCE”: his dating remains a subject of debate, with proposals ranging from high to low, preventing a narrow consensus chronology (Chapter II, Table 2). Second, it is not accurate to say that Zoroastrianism rejected animal sacrifices: Herodotus I 132 and Strabo XV 3.13–14 describe animal sacrifices among the Persians, the Yasna includes meat offerings (myazda), and what the Gāthās criticize (Y. 32.12; 48.10) is a type of violent offering and its connection with the daewuas. Third, the figure of Ātar is more than an “abstract symbol”: the Yasna 62 and the Ātaš Niyāyišn address praises to him, he is a yazata, and a lineage and an action are attributed to him, so that the difference with Agni is one of degree and place in the pantheon, and not that which goes from an anthropomorphic god to a symbol. Fourth, that Agni has bodily features (“golden beard,” “teeth of fire”) is a poetic description of the Ṛgveda that varies by hymn (Macdonell, Vedic Mythology, 1897). Fifth, the inversion of the daēuuas is documented in the Avesta (Vd. 10.9, where Indra appears among the daēuuas, and Vd. 19.43, with Naoŋhaiθya and Saurva) and is interpreted as a religious choice; the Vedic parallel is the reverse inversion, in which the asuras (cf. ahura) become the opposing group, and both movements are readings of an an cient religious division, not projections of a later theology. Sixth, “Padam” and “Atashgah” are Pahlavi terms; the veil covering the lips and cheeks is described in Strabo XV 3.15 and the “house of fire” no earlier than the Sasanian period (chapter XXVIII).

350 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM The altar: Avedic geometry and Iranian platforms One aspect that affects the book due to its relationship with geometry and architecture is the form of the altar. Vedic ritual requires altars with a defined geometric shape: the Agnicayana is a brick altar in the shape of a bird, built in layers according to strict proportions, and the Śulbasūtras (altar-building manuals, circa the middle of the 1st millennium BCE) contain geometric rules, including relationships equivalent to the Pythagorean theorem. The Zoroastrian altar, on the other hand, is a fire stand: a platform or stepped pedestal on which the flame is held, as suggested by certain Iranian stands and, in a much later context, by Sasanian coinage depictions of fire altars; its function and religious significance must be evaluated by period. Thus, the geometry of the altar is a highly developed Vedic theme, and its Iranian equivalent is more austere: the value lies in the fire and not in the construction. The relationship with the geometry of the Greek terms (chapter XXIX, etymological lexicon) therefore remains in the realm of Indo-European cognates, not of the transmission of knowledge.163 7. Fire in comparative traditions The maintenance of sacred fire also appears in other ancient societies: the fire of Vesta in Rome, with the Vestal Virgins as its guardians; the hearth of Hestia in Greece, which Greek authors associate with the fire of the Magi; the perpetual fire of the altar of Israel (Leviticus 6:5–6), which must never be extinguished; and the Egyptian royal hearth. A similarity of function does not imply a genetic relationship: the vigil of the fire is a common ritual technique in societies with hearth cults. For this book, the conclusion is limited: Agni and Ātar both derive from an Indo-Iranian practice of sacrificial fire, and they diverge in theology (major god versus yazata and pure element), in death (cremation versus exposure), and in space (diversity of early supports versus institutions of guarded fire documented in later stages). 8. Soma and Haoma: the Indo-Iranian ritual drink The ritual drink is another fundamental Indo-Iranian parallel, besides fire, and has solid lexical support. The Vedic * soma- * and the Avestan * haoma-* both refer to 163For Iranian altars, see Chapter XXVIII of this book.

MITRA AND AGNI 351 an Indo-Iranian *sauma-*, derived from the root *su- / hu-* (“to squeeze, to extract”; Vedic * sunóti *, Avestan * haoma- * from *hu- *), so that the name means “that which is squeezed”; the change from *s-* to *h-* is a phonetic regularity of Ira nian (as in *sapta- */ *hapta- *). Both traditions recognize the substance on three levels: the plant, the drink, and the deity that is invoked. The Ṛgveda dedicates the entire Book IX to it, with about one hundred hymns, and the Avesta chapters Y. 9– 11 (the Hōm Yašt) and, in worship, the ritual of the Yasna revolves around its preparation.164 The ritual similarity is real and must be described with nuance. In both cases, the stems are crushed with stones on a board or mortar (see grāvan-, av. hāvana-), the juice is filtered through wool (see áviḥ, “sheep,” and pavítra-; for Iran, the hair filter in the Yasna) and mixed with water and milk. However, there is no evidence that in Iran the first drops were poured onto the fire: in the Vedic ritual, libations are offered to the gods in cups (graha-) and on the fire, but in the Yasna, the prepared haoma (parahaoma) is drunk by the priest, 165 so the textual claim must be treated as unconfirmed for Iran. The effects are described with the same vocabulary of immortality: RV 8.48.3, “we have drunk the soma, we have become immortal (amṛtā), we have attained the light, we have found the gods” (apāma sómam amṛtā abhūma, áganma jyótir ávidāma devān). Ṛ t á-ya š a-: the cosmic, ritual and moral order - Iranian parallel is the concept of order. Philology supports this: the Vedic ṛtá- and the Avestan aša- (Old Persian arta-) are cognates, derived from an Indo-European root reconstructed as h₂er-, “to adjust, to articulate”; from the same family come the Greek harmonía and arithmós, the Latin ars, ritus, and ordo, so that the idea of “adjustment” has an Indo-European basis and not only an Indo-Iranian one (Beekes 2010, sv ἀραρίσκω). Three dimensions can be distinguished — cosmic, ritual, and moral — according to the uses documented in each corpus. The cosmic level: In the Ṛgveda, ṛtá- is the regulated course of things, the “path” (pathāṛtásya) followed by the sun, the dawn, and the waters, and the “chariot” or “wheel” of ṛta (RV 1.164.11); the guardians of order are above all Mitra and Varuṇa, called ṛtāvṛdh- (“who make ṛta grow,” RV 1.2.7–9). That Varuṇa has a thousand eyes or “spies” (spáś-) and that these are the stars is an attribution of later tradition rather than an explicit statement of the hymns (Lüders, Varuṇa, 1951–1959). The ritual level: sacrifice is constructed as a replica of order (ṛtásya yóni-, “the womb of ṛta,” designates the place of sacrifice, RV 1.164.47 and other passages), and error in recitation is considered damage to order; in Iran, correct recitation of the mąθra- is a condition for the efficacy of the Yasna (chapter XXXIV). The moral level: ṛtá- is opposed to ánṛta- (“non-order,” deception) and nírṛti- (“dissolution”), and in the Avesta aša- is opposed to druj-, “the Lie.” The word druj- is cognate with the Vedic drúh- (“hostile being, deceitful demon”), so the opposition is not a Gathic invention but continues an Indo-Iranian pair: order and its adversary. The divergence lies in emphasis and location. In India, ṛta does not disappear as a word, but its functions are transferred to dharma- (“that which sustains,” from dhṛ-), satya- (“truth”), and karman- (“action”); to say that ṛta “evolves directly” 171Ignatius of Antioch, Epistula ad Ephesios 20.2, middle recension; text in “Epistle to the Ephesians”, ANF, A. MITRA AND AGNI 357 Chapter Conclusion Mitra and Agni are two cases of Indo-Iranian heritage with distinct trajectories: the Roman Mithras diverges from the Iranian in function and worship; the Iranian fire departs from the Vedic in its treatment of death and purity. Both cases reinforce the book’s methodological criterion: a common root does not authorize projecting the later onto the earlier. Summary The table of the three Mithras (Vedic, Iranian, and Roman) opens a comparison that separates Agni from Ātar and the Vedic altar from the Zoroastrian altar. The perpetual fire of other traditions serves as a contrast to measure what is proper to the Iranian cult. Part X. Guiding Thread, Fire, Word, Calendar and Water Part X — research argument, principal evidence and limit. Fire, speech, calendars and water are compared through identifiable rituals and chronological contexts. Ritual analogies alone are insufficient. Four chronological periods (Achaemenid, Seleucid-Parthian, the time of Jesus, Sasanian); Mazdaism and the evolution of concepts; the fire of Olympus in Lycia; the mantra and the logos; ancient calendars; baptism and purification by water. The thesis is traced over the long term, through the elements — fire, word, calendar, and water — in which the influence is most visible.

Chapter XXXI. A Guiding Thread: The GreekHebrew World and Iran in Four Periods Chronological context. Four comparative periods: Achaemenid, Hellenistic and Arsacid, Roman, and Sasanian. The 1st century CE is situated between Arsacid and Roman powers; the Sasanian phase begins in 224 CE This methodological synthesis chapter organizes the comparison between the Greek-Hebrew world and Iran through four chronological sections and distinguishes documented transmission routes from hypotheses of influence. 1. Terminological approach and correction The central theme of this work is a recurring question: what contact, direct or mediated, did Greek and Hebrew cultures have with the religious culture of Iran, and what does each source allow us to assert? The question changes form according to the period, because Iran at each moment is a different state. Between 550 and 330 BCE, Iran is the Achaemenid Empire; from 312 BCE, it is largely the Seleucid kingdom; from the mid-3rd century BCE (the traditional date for the beginning of the dynasty is 247 BCE), it is the Arsacid or Parthian kingdom, which expands and consolidates in the following centuries; and only from 224 CE is it the Sasanian Empire. A reader who uses the term “Sasanian culture” in reference to the fourth or third century BCE is committing an anachronism, because that state did not exist; the correct expression for those centuries is “Achaemenid Persian culture,” “Hellenistic Iranian culture,” or “Parthian culture.” This book retains the term “Sasanian” only for events after 224 CE, and uses it primarily to indicate which sources (the Pahlavi texts, the establishment of the Avestan canon, court theology) are too late to serve as evidence for earlier periods. Under the Seleucids, western Iran became part of a Greek-speaking administrative kingdom, and the Greek world had intermediaries with Eastern traditions. One example is Berossus, priest of Marduk in Babylon, who around 290 BCE wrote a history of Babylon (Babyloniaka) in Greek; this is evidence that Eastern traditions were translated into Greek by native hands. In the eastern part of the empire, the satrapy of Parthia broke away from Seleucid rule and founded the Arsacid kingdom. In Egypt, under the Ptolemies, the Jewish community of Alexandria translated the Torah into Greek (the Septuagint of the Pentateuch, which tradition dates from the 3rd century BCE), so that the Hebrew vocabulary was converted into Greek forms: there the language was formed in which Philo and the authors of the New Testament would later write. For the book, this break matters for one reason: it is the moment when Hebrew and Greek come into textual contact, and therefore when the Iranian concepts that had entered Hebrew and Aramaic under the Persians can begin to have a Greek translation (pardē sy parádeisos, as forms of a borrowed history; rā zy mystḗrion, as a translation correspondence that is examined separately against ancient Greek already Theodotion in Daniel, not as an etymological derivation of the Greek word). To that generation also belongs a circulation of names: in later Greek tradition, Zoroaster, Ostanes, and Hystaspes become authors of books that no one wrote in their original Greek form (the Zoroastrian pseudepigrapha). Outside the Mediterranean world, the edicts of the Indian king Ashoka, which include Greek and Aramaic versions (Kandahar, mid-3rd century BCE), show a contact zone where moral concepts were translated between languages; this material is discussed in Chapter XXXIV.

Method: three questions for each parallel The book applies three questions, in order, to each comparison. In what cross -section do we document each element of the parallel? Was there a possible means of transmission in that cross-section (language, institution, person)? Is there a nonshared feature that changes the reading? If the answer to the first question places one side of the comparison in a cross-section later than the other, the parallel is recorded as a typological similarity and not as an influence. This rule affects several of the most frequently cited cases: the Saošyant versus the Messiah, the Logos versus the Mantra, the Mithraic cult versus the Eucharist. Setting the cutoff point before comparing is the condition for the comparison to have value. Mazdaism and the Evolution of Zoroastrian Concepts Mazdaism and Zoroastrianism: criteria for periodisation The terms “Mazdaism” and “Zoroastrianism” overlap but must not be treated as dated institutional labels for every ancient source. Royal Achaemenid invocations of Auramazdā, Avestan priestly formulations and later Sasanian scholastic syntheses differ in documentary genre, language and political context. A sound history of concepts therefore follows each lemma through attestations rather than reconstructing a seamless system across many centuries. For each doctrine discussed in this chapter, distinguish (a) its earliest secure textual attestation, (b) the present manuscript or documentary support, (c) its ritual or polemical setting, (d) evidence of institutional adoption, and (e) later explanations that should not be used as direct witnesses for the Achaemenid period. Chronological context. Long-term religious history, from Avestan sources of disputed dating and the Achaemenid religion to Arsacid and Sasanian Iran. The evolution of a term or doctrine must be supported by its successive testimonies. 1. Mazdaism and Zoroastrianism: two names, a question of method “Zoroastrianism” designates the religion that refers to Zoroaster; “Mazdaism” (or Mazdaean religion), the religion of the worshippers of Mazda. The two terms overlap in common usage, but the latter has a methodological advantage: it is based on documented self-designation. In the Avesta, the faithful call themselves mazdayasna- (“those who sacrifice to Mazda”); the formula of profession of faith in Yasna 12 describes them as mazdayasnō zarathuštriš (“Mazdaean, Zoroastrian”). Achaemenid inscriptions, on the other hand, invoke Auramazda and say nothing about 367

Whether the religion of the Persian kings is “Zoroastrian” or only “Mazdaean” is an open question that conditions this entire work.175176 Here we adopt the following distinction. “Zoroastrianism” is reserved for the tradition linked with Zoroaster and the texts attributed to him (the Gāthās). “Mazdaism” designates the broader sphere of worship of Ahura Mazdā and his associates, without presupposing that its adherents have followed any teaching of Zoroaster. Mazdaism, Hellenism and syncretism Mazdaean culture also changed in contact with Greece. In Nemrud Dağ (chapter XXXI), the gods of the Mazdaean pantheon are presented with their parallel Greek names. In Cappadocia and other regions of Anatolia, the memory of the Persian Magi was preserved in communities that Strabo describes with their “houses of fire” (XV 3,15) and that Pausanias mentions in Lydia (V 27,5–6). These communities served as a conduit through which the Greek world learned, from afar, something of Mazdaean religion. The evidence is sparse, but points to one conclusion: what the Greeks observed was a Mazdaean cult of the Iranian-Anatolian diaspora, with fire and sacrifice in its own sanctuaries, distinct from the clerical Zoroastrianism of the Sasanian period. 4. Consequences for comparison with Yahwism Speaking of “Mazdaism” requires specifying what is being compared to what. If the comparison of Yahwism in the Persian period is made with the Mazdaism of the Achaemenid court, the relevant parallel is that of the state religion: a supreme god of heaven (ʾĕlāh šĕmayyāʾ and Auramazdā, Chapter XII), a state cult, and royal law in Aramaic. If the comparison is made with the Gāthās, the parallel is of a different kind: poetic texts of an individual master, where the natural comparison is with the prophets. Each of these comparisons has its own rules of evidence, and the book ad dresses them separately. Chapter Conclusion The term “Mazdaism” allows us to describe the evolution of Zoroastrian concepts without presupposing strict doctrinal continuity. Distinguishing the phases avoids attributing to the 5th century BCE what is found only in the Pahlavi texts.

Chapter XXXIII. The Fire of Olympos in Lycia, Plutarch and the Fire Cult Historical context of the chapter. Plutarch writes during the Roman imperial period, 1st–2nd centuries CE; the fires of Lycia and the news about Iran have their own local contexts. His testimony may preserve earlier traditions without becoming a contemporary source for Darius I. 1. The problem and the place On the southwestern coast of Turkey, in ancient Lycia, near the city of Olympus (distinct from Mount Olympus in Thessaly, the abode of the Greek gods), there are permanent emanations of natural gas that burn on the surface of the hillside. The place is known today as Yanartaş (“burning stone”), and classical tradition associated it with the Chimera, the monster that Bellerophon defeated in Lycia. A broader question is whether this fire, which burns without having been lit by anyone and which requires no visible fuel, was the object of worship as a divine fire. There are two distinct questions: what do ancient sources say about the fire at this site, and what does the archaeological record offer about the cult? And yet a third: whether this fire can be compared with the sacred fire of the Zoroastrians, or with the Vedic Agni. 2. Ancient sources on the fire of Lycia Classical accounts fall into three categories. Poetic accounts: Homer portrays the Chimera as a fire-breathing monster (Iliad 6.180–183; Homeric original consulted in the digital edition), and later tradition places it on Mount Lycia. Geographical and naturalist accounts: Strabo (XIV 3.5) describes the territory of Olympus and the Chimera’s flame; Pliny (Natural History II 236) speaks of perpetual fires in Lycia, Mount Hephaestus, and the Chimera’s flame, noting a peculiarity repeated in tradition: water does not extinguish the flame, but earth or hay does; Seneca (Epistles 79.3) mentions it among the phenomena of Lycia. And those of scholia, such as Servius to the Aeneid (VI 288), who rationalize the myth: the Chimera would be a mountain with a volcano. Added is the testimony of Ctesias of Cnidus, 373

Lenfant 2004).177178 Ctesias deserves special attention in a book about the Persian world. He is the only Greek author who, by virtue of living at the Achaemenid court, combines knowledge of Persia with the description of a natural phenomenon in Anatolia. If his account of the fire of Lycia is authentic, it presents us with a case in which a Greek from the Persian sphere describes a natural fire in a region (Lycia) that had been part of the Achaemenid Empire since the mid-6th century BCE. 3. Plutarch: The Olympus of Pirates and Other Fires The central passage is Pompey 24.5. Writing in the Roman imperial period, Plutarch describes the power of the Cilician pirates in the 80s and 70s BCE and lists the sanctuaries they plundered (Claro, Didyma, Samothrace, Hermione, Epidaurus, the Isthmus, Taenarum, Calauria, Actium, Leucas, the Heraion of Samos, that of Argos, and that of Lacinium) and adds: “They themselves offered foreign sacrifices (xenas thysias) on Olympus and celebrated certain secret rites (teletastinas aporrhḗtous), of which the one of Mithras is preserved to this day, instituted for the first time by them” (Pomp. 24.5: xénas dè thysías éthyon autoì tàs en Olýmpō, kaì teletás tinas aporrhḗtous eteloûn, hôn hē toû Míthrou kaì méchri deûro diasṓzetai katadeichtheîsa prôton hyp’ ekeínōn). Three observations are necessary. First: Plutarch speaks of sacrifices, not processions, and does not say to which god they were addressing; nor does he say that the Olympus is that of Lycia, although the context (pirates from southern Anatolia) makes it probable. Comparison with the Mazdaean and Vedic fire Three structural differences separate the fire of Lycia from the fire of the Avesta and the Veda. First: the Mazdaean fire is kindled, fed, and guarded by priests, with purity rites (Vendīdād, chapters on fire); it is not conceived as a “spontaneous” fire. Second: in the Veda, Agni is the sacrificer and the messenger, and his fire is kindled by the friction of two pieces of wood (araṇi); fire without apparent fuel is not the central figure. Third: natural fires (Babylon, Lycia, later Baku) are places of fascination, and in some cases of worship, but they do not appear in the Avestan texts as a type of fire. In the Pahlavi tradition, there is talk of large fires, Farnbag, Gušnasp and Burzēn-Mihr, venerated as primordial fires (Boyce, “Ādur Farnbāg”, “Ādur Gušnasp” and “Ādur Burzēn-Mihr”, EIr); their “natural” character is a matter of tradition, not of geological observation. The comparison is only valid on a typological level: all three cases show that an cient societies attributed divinity to fire independent of human intervention. How ever, the institutions differ greatly: in Lycia, there was a local cult in a specific place of manifestation; in the Zoroastrian world, a priestly cult in a constructed sanctuary; in Vedic India, a sacrifice with domestic and solemn fires (the three fires, śrauta, Chapter XXX). A possible link is the Persian presence in Anatolia from the 6th cen tury BCE: satraps, garrisons, and communities of Magi in Cappadocia and Lydia (Chapter XXXII). The hypothesis that the Zoroastrians revered the flames of Lycia thus remains open and without proof. Chapter Conclusion The fire of Olympus in Lycia is evidence of natural fire with probable Greek worship; there is no evidence of Mazdaean worship. Plutarch (Pompey 24.5) places foreign sacrifices and Mithraic rites on an Olympus, probably that of Lycia, without mentioning fire; in Mulierum virtutes 9 he explains the Chimera by solar reflections; he also offers the interpretative framework (prodigy, institution, philosophy) in Alexander 35, Numa 11 and De defectu 2.

THE FIRE OF OLYMPUS IN LYCIA 379 Summary The natural fire of Yanartaş, along with the myth of the Chimera, is studied through ancient sources (Homer, Strabo, Pliny, Seneca, Servius, and Ctesias) and five passages from Plutarch (Pompey 24.5; Mulierum virtutes 9; Alexander 35; Numa 11; De defectu 2). The local cult of Hephaestus is finally compared with the fires of Iran and India. Chapter XXXIV. Mantra, Vāc, Ahuna Vairya, and Logos Chronological context. Vedic and Avestan traditions, transmitted liturgical formulae and reception of the logos in Hellenistic and Roman times. The relative linguistic dating and that of the manuscript are recorded separately. 1. Approach: word, power and body The comparison between the Greek logos and the Indo-Iranian notions of the sacred word is based on a structural fact: in ancient traditions, the ritual word is not only a vehicle of meaning but a power that acts upon the world. In Sanskrit, mantra- designates an instrument (from the root man-, “to think,” and the suffix-tra, from instrument: “instrument of thought”); in the Avesta, matra- is the inspired and powerful word, from the same root. The question of this chapter is whether there exists, in the Veda and the Avesta, the idea of an “incarnate” word that is com parable to the incarnate logos of the Prologue of John, and what each tradition understands by the “body” of the word. 2. The expression “embodied mantra” and its verification The form “tanumatram,” proposed in an earlier phase of this work, is not Sanskrit, but it most likely corresponds to the Avestan epithet tanumąθra-, which the recent Avesta applies to Sraoša and which Sraoša shares with Mithra and with humankind. W.W. Malandra glosses it cautiously: “perhaps, he who embodies the sacred word” (“Sraoša,” Encyclopaedia Iranica). Gad Barnea (2026) locates it for Mithra in Yt 10:25 and relates it to the incarnate logos of the Prologue of John. The exact meaning of the compound (tanu-, “body, person,” ymąθra-, “sacred word”) is debated, and its use as a parallel to John 1:14 is a proposal, not an established fact. It should not be confused with the Sanskrit tanmātra (“subtle element” in Samkhya philosophy) nor with the Tantric notion of mantra- mūrti (“form of the mantra”). Alongside this Avestan epithet, the chapter works with two notions documented in India: Vāc, the personified Word, and the mantra as the sound body of the divinity. 381

382 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM 3. Vāc in the Rigveda In the Rigveda, Vāc (the Word, feminine) is both a goddess and the faculty of ritual speech. The hymn RV 10.125 (Vāc’s Hymn, in eight stanzas) presents Vāc in the first person: she proclaims that she upholds the gods, that she is sovereign and gath ers treasures, and that she makes the man she loves a priest, a seer, or a sage. The hymn RV 10.71 deals with the emergence of speech (Vāc) and how the sages formed and discovered it; and RV 1.164.45 teaches that Vāc has four “steps”: three remain hidden, and only the fourth is spoken by men. In Brahmanical literature, the identification between Vāc and sacrifice, or between the Brahman and the word, becomes common (in the Brāhmaṇa). In grammar and the philosophy of language, Bharathari (around the 5th century CE) formulated in the Vākyapadīya the principle of śabda-brahman, ultimate reality as Word. This line of thought becomes, in Indian thought, a monism of the word: it is not a figure that “is embodied” in a man, but the substratum from which the world proceeds.181 4. The mantra and divinity: the sound form There is a second, later line of thought in which the deity is identified with its mantra. In Tantric and devotional Hinduism (medieval centuries onward), each deity has its seminal mantra (bija), and the mantra is taught as the deity’s “subtle body” (mantra -sharira). In this tradition, the mantra is the means by which the deity makes itself present to the devotee: something close to the idea of sonic incarnation. But this line belongs to a religious context after the Persian period, and its comparison with Johannine logos should be treated as typological. The vocabulary of “incarnation” (avatara, “descent”) belongs to another register, that of Vishnu and his manifestations, and not to that of the mantra. 5. Mąθra Spəṇta and the Ahuna Vairya in the Avesta The Avesta offers the closest counterpoint. In the Gāthās, mąθra- is the word of the poet-priest, inspired by Mazdā (in Y 31 and Y 45). In the later Avesta, Mąθra 181Rigveda 10.125, Sanskrit text in Vedic Heritage Portal, Government of India, https://vedicheritage.gov.in/hi/samhitas/rigveda/shakala-samhita/rigveda-shakala-samhitamandal-10-sukta-125/; Ralph T.H. Griffith’s version (1896) reproduced by Vedic Samhita, https://www.vedicsamhita.in/vedas/rigveda/10/125. The original text declares the powers of the first-person voice.

MANTRA, VĀC, AHUNA VAIRYA AND LOGOS 383 Spəṇta, “the Holy Word,” appears as an almost personified reality, invoked in the liturgy (in Yasna 20 and Yasna 57). And, centrally, the prayer Yatha ahu vairyo (Yasna 27.13), called Ahuna Vairya, the most sacred prayer of Zoroastrianism, which tradition says Ahura Mazdā uttered before creation and with which he defeated evil. In Pahlavi, the prayer (Ahunwar) has twenty-one words, and the twenty-one sections (nasks) of the Sasanian Avesta correspond to them (in the Dēnkard). Here, the word is linked to the structure of creation and of the sacred book: the prayer is a compendium of the Avesta and a principle of the cosmos.182 Two observations. First: what the Avesta calls Mąθra Spəṇta is not a body in the sense of a human person, but rather a figure of the word that is worshipped, and which later theology places before creation. Second: the distance between Ahuna Vairya and the logos of John is great at the crucial point, which is the incarnation: in early Christianity, the logos “became flesh” (John 1:14) and is identified with a historical person (Jesus); in the Avesta, the sacred word is spoken by Ahura Mazdā and transmitted to Zoroaster, but is not identified with any person. 6. The Greek and Jewish logos in comparison From the Greek perspective, Heraclitus’s logos (fr. 1) is the reason of the world to which people remain deaf; for the Stoics, it is the immanent rational principle; for Plato, it is language and discourse; for Philo of Alexandria, logos is a “second god” (deuteros theos) and the instrument of creation (chapter XXVII). In Judaism, the Word of God (dābār) creates (Gen 1; Ps 33:6) and Wisdom (ḥokmāh) has personal characteristics (Prov 8). The Prologue of John brings these lines together and adds the Incarnation. From the comparison with the mantra and Vāc and with the Ahuna Vairya, a table of features emerges showing where they coincide and where they differ. 182On the Ahuna Vairya: Yasna 27.13 (text of the prayer) and Yasna 19 (commentary on its origin and power) according to Geldner’s numbering. The translation of the prayer is one of the most discussed in the Avesta; the prayer and its interpretative alternatives are discussed in chapter XLIII, without treating differences between translations as manuscript variants.

The background of the Prologue is explained, in most commentaries, by personified Wis-

MANTRA, VĀC, AHUNA VAIRYA AND LOGOS 385 dom (Prov 8:22–31; Sir 24; Wis 7–9), by the creative Word of Gen 1, and by the Torah, in addition to the philonic use of logos. This is the most solid level of explanation because it is supported by earlier Hebrew and Greek texts in the same language.183 On that basis, two questions arise regarding a possible Mazdaean influence. The first: does a figure in Mazdaean theology resemble the logos in function? The closest figure is Mithra, and four characteristics can be identified in him. Mithra is, by his name, the “covenant” (miθra-), guarantor of the word given and of contracts (Yt 10); he is a god of light, who appears before the sun and watches over the world (Yt. 10.13 ff.); he is a defender of truth against falsehood (aša/druj); and, in Plutarch’s Greek testimony, he is a mediator (mesítēs) between Oromazes and Areimanios (De Iside 46, chapter XLIV). These traits generally correspond to attributes of the Johannine logos: light that enlightens every man (John 1:4, 9), truth (John 1:14, 17; 14:6), mediation (“through him all things were made” and “no one comes to the Father except through me”: John 1:3; 14:6). A second Mazdaean figure, Sraoša, “the Listening” or “Obedience,” appears in the Avesta as guardian of the holy word and combatant of demons (Y 57), and offers another parallel of mediation and pro tection. Here, the method of chapter XXXI is decisive. The Gospel of John is dated towards the end of the first century; the mysteries of Mithras in the Roman Empire are attested from that same generation (Statius, Thebaid I 719–720, c. 90; chapter XXIV), but their monuments appear in number in the second century; the Avestan Mithras is much earlier, although its written form is not. There is, therefore, no direct and documented route from Mithras to the logos. There are three indirect routes: Second Temple Judaism, for which Iranian connections have been proposed in angelology and dualism (1QS III-IV, chapters XVII and XX), whose apocalyptic traditions should be compared with John without presupposing a direct channel from Qumran; Greek philosophy, exemplified by Plutarch, where the mediator is a philosophical concept; and the Syro-Anatolian context where the community may have lived, which was close to the Parthian world and the Mithraic cults of Commagene and Cappadocia (chapters XXXI and XXXV). All are possible, and none is proven.

MANTRA, VĀC, AHUNA VAIRYA AND LOGOS 387 Update to the proposal regarding Juan Barnea’s article, published in Religions on September 17, 2026, proposes reading the prologue of John within a religious context shared with Mazdaean tradi tions. His summary distinguishes this conceptual assimilation from a direct tex tual dependence or a general derivation from the Roman mysteries of Mithras. The proposal brings together geographical, archaeological, linguistic, and theological arguments concerning Mithras, Mithras, and the Saoshit. The article draws on the Mithraeum of Caesarea Maritima, which Barnea dates to around 80 CE alongside an early Christian community; on the epithet tanum athra- of Mithras (Yt 10:25), which he understands as “Mithras incarnate”; and on Numenius of Apamea, who presents Mithras as a demiurge. It presents this as a cu mulative case, not as a direct borrowing from Mithraism or a specific Mazdaean text. This chapter identifies the approach without assuming that convergence demonstrates transmission. Its evaluation requires dating the donor testimonies, verifying the channels, and comparing Jewish and Greco-Jewish explanations. The conclusion, therefore, is as follows. That the Johannine logos is an Iranianinfluenced figure is a hypothesis put forward by the school of the history of religions (Bousset, Reitzenstein) and not confirmed by subsequent criticism (Colpe, Brown, Schnackenburg); what can be affirmed is that the fourth gospel shares with Mazdaean theology a language of light, truth, and mediation, and that this language is sufficiently explained by wisdom and Qumranic Judaism. The comparative study retains its value: the figure of Mithra allows us to see how a different culture organized the mediation between the divine and the human without resorting to the incarnation, and thus clarifies the singularity of the Prologue. 8. Guiding thread: chronological cuts and contact routes Applying the method of Chapter XXXI, we obtain the following. In the 5th – 4th centuries BCE, the Rigveda and the Gāthās already existed in the oral tradition, but there is no documented transmission of the concept of the sacred word between Greece, Judea, and Iran; Heraclitus’s logos (circa 500 BCE) is explained within the Greek tradition. In the 3rd century BCE, the edicts of Ashoka (Kandahar, in Greek and Aramaic) show a space where Indian moral concepts were translated into

388 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM Greek (euse beia for dhamma); this is a case of contact, but not of the incarnate word. In Jesus ‘ time, trade and diplomacy between Rome, the Parthian Empire, and India intensified, but the vocabulary of John’s Prologue is well explained by Jewish and Greek sources (Prov 8, Wis 7–9, Philo). The approaches proposed in the literature for attributing a direct influence on John 1 to India or Iran lack conclusive proof. What comparative study offers is something else entirely: a typology of the sacred word, in which Greece, Israel, Iran, and India independently develop the idea of a word with creative power, and only early Christianity fixes it in a historical person. 9. Transmission and interpretation problems Limits of the comparison. The form “tanumatram” is not Sanskrit; its Avestan equivalent, tanumąθra-, is discussed in § 2, and its meaning of “incarnate word” is an interpretation, not a certain gloss, and is therefore not used as evidence of religious transmission. The Vedic passages RV 10,125, 10,71 and 1,164,45, Bharthṛhari’s Vākyapadīya I and the Tantric traditions relating to mantra-mūrti belong to contexts and periods that require separate study. For the Iranian sphere, the formula Ahuna Vairya (Y. 27.13), its liturgical commentary (Y 19), the Mihr Yašt (Yt 10), and the Srōš Yašt (Y 57) are distinguished; the Greco-Roman comparison is identified by Plutarch, De Iside et Osiride 46. Similarities with John 1 or with the figure of the Saošyant do not in themselves constitute a historical chain of transmission. Etymological equivalences and citations from these sources require a verifiable locus and, when a reading is discussed, the specific edition that transmits it. Chapter Conclusion Vac, Mąθra Spəṇta, and the Ahuna Vairya are figures of a sacred word with creative power, comparable in type to the logos. Incarnation in a person is the distinctive feature of the Prologue of John, and is not documented in the Rigveda or the Avesta. Summary The chapter compares the Vedic mantra and the Avestan mantra, the Vac of the Rigveda and the mantra as a sound body in Tantra, and contrasts them with the Mąθra Spəṇta and the Ahuna Vairya. The Greek, Philonic, and Johannine logos concludes the series with a comparative table, the question of the Johannine com-

Chapter XXXV. Ancient Calendars: Persian, Zoroastrian, Cappadocian, and Hebrew Chronological context. Achaemenid calendars and later evidence of Zoroastrian, Cappadocian, and Jewish systems. Correspondences of names or months must be dated be fore reconstructing a borrowing or a reform. 1. Why a calendar matters in a book about religion The calendar is the most consistent way in which a religion organizes social time: it establishes festivals, names for months and days, and with them a repertoire of deities invoked in turn. In the Zoroastrian world, moreover, the names in the calendar are names of deities and divine concepts; that is, the calendar is a summary of the pantheon. In the Jewish world of the Persian period, the calendar is a different kind of document: the months bear Babylonian names, and the dates are anchored to the reign year of a Persian king. Comparing the two calendars allows us to measure what entered Hebrew culture from Mesopotamia and what remained outside. 2. The ancient Persian calendar The oldest documentation comes from the Achaemenid Empire. The inscriptions of Darius I (Behistun) date events by months with ancient Persian names, of which about eight are known from the texts and four more from Elamite transcriptions,184 including, by way of example, Ādukanaiša, Θūravāhara, Garmapada, Bāgayādiš, and Viyaxna. The forms and etymologies are discussed by Kent and Schmitt; several interpretations remain disputed. An interesting detail is that at least one of these names, Bāgayādiš, is interpreted as a religious dedication (“veneration of the baga-, the gods”), which anticipates the principle of the later calendar: naming the month after the cult. The Old Persian calendar is classified as lunisolar, like the Babylonian calendar. Its lunar reckoning and intercalations must be distinguished from the regular scheme of twelve thirty-day months and epagomenal days in the later Zoroastrian calendar. It is accepted that it was in use at least until the middle of the 5th century BCE (the entry consulted gives 459 BCE). 184 Kent, 2nd ed; Tavernier, Iranica in the Achaemenid. 391

392 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM Aramaic sources provide a second layer. In the Elephantine papyri, the same day is sometimes dated using two calendars, the Egyptian and the Babylonian, along with the year of the Persian king’s reign (for example, the Passover letter TAD A4.1, which prescribes observances in the month of Nisan; chapter XI and edition of chapter XXXIX). This dual dating shows that the Persian chancery had to reconcile local calendars with an imperial order. The consulted entry also proposes that after Cambyses’ conquest of Egypt (around 525 BCE), a 365-day year was introduced with months that essentially coincide with the Egyptian ones, and places this introduction between 525 and 430 BCE (Stern). The discussion about whether there was a 360-day year before remains open.185 3. The Zoroastrian calendar: months and days as dedications The traditional Zoroastrian calendar has twelve thirty-day months and five final days (the days of the Gāthās, Gatha or Andargah, which do not belong to any week). Each month and each day is named after a deity or divine concept, in the form of a dedication: in Avestan, the name appears in the genitive case (e.g., “of Asha Vahisha,” “of the Fravashis”). The Cappadocian calendar Cappadocia was an Achaemenid satrapy, and a region where Strabo later describes communities of Magi with “houses of fire” (Strabo, Geography XV.3.15 (ed. and trans. H.L. Jones, Loeb; see chapter XXXII)). The Cappadocian calendar is evidence of a Zoroastrian calendar of twelve thirty-day months with five epagomenal

It is assumed to have been established when Cappadocia was a Persian satrapy; the consulted entry includes the proposal of Marquart (around 490 BCE) and that of Duchesne-Guillemin (between 490 and 480 BCE), and acknowledges that there is no consensus. Documentation of the calendar is late, as it is known primarily through Greek astronomers and calendars of Late Antiquity, and was still known in the fourth century CE. This gap necessitates caution: the evidence proves that, in Cappadocia, the Zoroastrian calendar was preserved for centuries outside of Iran, not that its form was that of the Achaemenids.186 Two features are important. Second, according to the consulted entry, the Cappadocian calendar was “Julianized,” perhaps in 44 BCE (Stern’s proposal), and an epagomenal day was added in leap years. According to the consulted entry, the Sasanian reform of 224 CE found Nawruz (New Year) around October 1 and corrected the calendar; in 226–272 it shifted again to September 19; and in 632 the New Year fell on June 16, so the calendar lost a day every four years (de Blois 1996). There are three modern variants: the Qadimi, the Shahanshahi (based on the Dēnkard, which describes methods of intercalation), and the Fasli, proposed in 1906 with a leap day. The Yazdegerdi era counts from June 16, 632. For this book, the lesson is that the structure of dedications is ancient, but the specific dates of the festivals depend on the variant. 7. The Hebrew calendar and Babylonian names The Jewish calendar of the Persian period and later uses Babylonian month names (Nisan, Iyar, Sivan, Tammuz, Av, Elul, Tishrei, Marcheshvan, Kislev, Tebet, Shebat, Adar). A rabbinic tradition recorded in the Jerusalem Talmud (Rosh haShanah 1,2,56d) states that “the names of the months came up with them from Babylon,” meaning with those who returned from exile. The oldest biblical months are identified by number (“the seventh month”) or by Canaanite names (Ḥō de šhā ʾĒtānîm, 1 Kgs 8:2), and Babylonian names appear in the books of the exile and the Persian period (Zechariah 1:7; Esther 3:7; Nehemiah 1:1). The contrast with Zoroastrianism is striking: in the Zoroastrian calendar, the name of the month is a divine dedication; in the Jewish calendar, the name of the month is of Mesopotamian origin and is stripped of its religious meaning, while the religious dimension is transferred to the festivals within the month (Passover in Nisan, Tabernacles in Tishrei). Zoroastrian calendar and Christian Christmas It has often been suggested that the Christian feast of Christmas, celebrated on December 25, has a connection to the Iranian and Zoroastrian worlds. The question is legitimate, and the answer requires distinguishing three things: the date, the reason for the feast, and the possible points of contact. The date of December 25 appears for the first time in a reliable Christian document in the Chronograph of 354, a Roman compilation that, in its list of bishops’ depositions, records “VIII kal. Ian. natus Christus in Betleem Iudeae,” that is, the birth of Christ on December 25; the same calendar records on that date the natalis Invicti, the birthday of Sol Invicti (the Unconquered Sun). A single piece of information already guides the discussion: the document places the feast within the context of the Roman calendar, and the cult associated with that date is that of the Sun, not Mithras by name.191 Modern explanations fall into two main hypotheses. The first, called the “history of religions” hypothesis, maintains that the Church established the date to replace a pagan winter solstice festival, Dies natalis Solis Invicti, which Emperor Aurelian is said to have instituted in 274.192 The second, called the “calculation” hypothesis (Duchesne, Talley), argues that the date resulted from an internal Christian calculation: if it was believed that Jesus died on March 25, it was assumed that he had been conceived on that same day, and nine months later he was born on December 25. This tradition of calculation is seen in authors before Aurelian or contemporary with him (Tertullian, Adversus Iudaeos 8; Hippolytus, Commentary on Daniel IV 23, of disputed authenticity). A third position, which the most cautious specialists consider the most solid, admits that the two lines influenced each other, without one excluding the other. 191On the Chronograph of 354 (the so-called “Philocalian calendar”): Michele Renee Salzman, On Roman Time: The Codex-Calendar of 354 and the Rhythms of Urban Life in Late Antiquity (University of California Press, 1990). In calendars without intercalation (Qadimi, Shahanshahi), the months shift with the seasons over the centuries (section 6), so the coincidence of the month of Day with the solstice cannot be simply projected onto Antiquity. The second observation is that Mithra has his own month (the seventh, Mihr) and his own day (the sixteenth, also called Mihr); when they coincide, Mihragan is celebrated, an autumn festival, not a winter one. The link between Mithra and December 25 is therefore based on the Roman tradition of the Unconquered Sun, not on the Zoroastrian calendar. The third is that the documented route of contact is that of the mysteries of Mithras in the Roman Empire (chapter XXIV), which are a Roman creation that uses an Iranian name, not an import from the Mazdaean calendar. There remains a geographical link of interest, though without proof of causality. Cappadocia, which preserved the Zoroastrian calendar with its month of Mithra (section 4), was also the homeland of the Cappadocian Fathers, and Gregory of Nazianzus is credited with introducing the December 25 feast in Constantinople around 379–380 (Gregory of Nazianzus, Or. 38; Talley 1986). The coincidence of region is not proof: the feast arrived in the East from the Roman calendar, and the Cappadocian calendar of that time was already Julianized (section 4). What can be said is that, in the eastern provinces, two calendars with festivals by month and by day, the Zoroastrian and the Christian, coexisted and that the ordering of the Christian liturgical year around the sun and the months of the Roman year is a phenomenon of integration into the imperial calendar, so that Christmas and the Zoroastrian calendar are comparable as cases of sanctification of the solar year, not as dependence of one on the other. According to the book’s central theme (chapter XXXI), Christmas belongs to the fourth period (4th century CE), three hundred years after the time of Jesus and two hundred years after the formation of the Roman cult of Mithras. A comparison with the Zoroastrian calendar, whose complete record is found in the Sasanian and Pahlavi texts, thus links two later phenomena. For this reason, it is recorded as a typological parallel in the ordering of sacred time, and not as an influence.

The twelve names of the months of the Zoroastrian calendar and their interpretations are examined according to the sources identified in the chapter. The theological principle of the calendar is the correspondence between time and creation. According to the Pahlavi cosmogony, Ahura Mazdā (Ohrmazd) created the material world in seven creations, each placed under the patronage of one of the seven supreme deities: the sky, water, earth, plants, animals, man, and fire (Greater Bundahišn 1 and 3; chapter XXV). Chapter XXXVI. Baptism, Initiation, and Purification by Water in the Mazdean and Parthian Worlds Chronological context. Iranian purifications transmitted in Avestan and later sources; Arsacid context and Jewish and Christian practices of the Roman period. Modern Parsis manuals are not direct descriptions from the 1st century CE 1. Approach: two different questions The relationship between Christian baptism and purification by water in the Zoroastrian world raises two questions that should be considered separately. The first is typological: what function does water fulfil in each tradition, and what features do the Christian rite of initiation and Zoroastrian purifications share? The second is historical: is there a point of contact that suggests influence? For the second question, the starting point is that Christian baptism has a well-documented Jewish antecedent: the ritual immersions of purification (ṭĕbîlâ) and the baptism of John. This explanation alone accounts for most of the rite’s features. The book’s central question is what, if anything, the comparison with the Zoroastrian and Parthian worlds adds. 2. Water in Zoroastrianism: sacredness and purity In Zoroastrianism, water is a sacred creation, sponsored by a deity (Āpō, the Waters; chapter XXXV), and is celebrated in worship with a libation (zaoθra-; in Pahlavi, ā bzōhr). The ethical consequence is the prohibition against polluting it. Herodotus (I 138) says that the Persians do not urinate or spit in the rivers, do not wash their hands in them, and do not allow anyone else to do so; Strabo (XV 3,16, Greek text consulted in the cited digital edition) adds that they do not bathe in the river, nor throw a corpse or anything considered impure into it: eis gà r potam ò no ú t’ ouroûsin oúte nípontai, oudè loúontai, oudè nekròn embállousin. The regime of purity is codified in the Vendīdād, whose first chapters of laws deal with the contamination of water, fire, and earth by dead matter (nasu-), and with the purifica407

408 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM tion of persons and things (Vendīdād 5–9, distribution of subjects compared with the Darmesteter digital edition). Two practices belong directly to the subject: the barašnūm, a nine-night purification rite described in Vendīdād 9 (arrangement of the rite compared with the Darmesteter edition), in which the one being purified washes himself with consecrated bull urine (gaomaēza-, pahl. gōmēz), with water, and with sand, under the direction of a priest; and the pādyāb, the daily ablution of hands and face before praying, which in Pahlavi means “receiving the water” (pādyāb).195 Zoroastrian initiation and the role of water Lay initiation (navjote or sedra-pūšī) of a Zoroastrian child, the sedra-pūšī (“wearing the sacred shirt”), consists of receiving the white shirt (sedre, from vastra-, “garment”) and the 72-strand cord (kustī), with the recitation of the profession of faith, the Fravarāne (Y 12; chapter XXXII). The ceremony is not a baptism: it is not done by immersion nor does it confer the rite of entry through water. It is preceded by a purification bath (nahn), and candidates for the priesthood also undergo the barašnūm and several other step-by-step initiation ceremonies (nāwar, martab). Thus, while Mazdaean initiation includes water, it is not the central rite. The sources are Pahlavi and late; there are no descriptions of Achaemenid or Parthian initiation, and this gap prevents projecting the rite to the time of Jesus. A ninth-century priestly controversy provides evidence for what water meant in the priestly practice of the 9th century. The Epistles of Manuščihr (Nāmagīhāī Manuščihr), dated by his translator E. W. West between March and July of 881 CE (years 249 and 250 of the Yazdegirdi era; SBE 18, Clarendon Press, 1882; digital edition by J. H. Peterson, 2004), reproach his brother Zādspram, then a priest in Sīrkān, for a teaching considered heretical about the purification of one who has touched a corpse. According to Vendīdād VIII, the defiled person must wash fifteen times with bull’s urine (gōmēz), run to a village, and request the ritual purification ceremony (barašnūm); Zādspram would have maintained that the fifteen washes were sufficient. Manuščihr responds that ordinary washing purifies the body, but 195Vendīdād 9, “The Nine Nights ‘ Barashnum”, in Darmesteter, The Zend-Avesta, Part I, SBE 4; transcription https://avesta.org/vendidad/vd9sbe.htm. The fargard describes the preparation of the place and the purification ritual; The dating of the rite is not automatically deduced from the nineteenth- century translation.

BAPTISM, INITIATION AND PURIFICATION BY WATER 409 only the ritual ceremony, performed with water and by a qualified purifier, cleanses the soul (West, note to Ep. I). This controversy is direct ninth-century evidence that, in Zoroastrianism, ritual purity was not equivalent to hygiene, and that water acted in conjunction with formulae and priestly authority. Its value for the book is twofold. On the one hand, it confirms the date of Zadspram (881 CE), so the legends of Zoroaster that he transmits (section 12 of chapter XXXVII) cannot be used as a source for the Persian period. On the other hand, it offers a conceptual parallel with the Jewish debate on immersion (ṭeḇîlāh) and its relation to inner purification, but the parallel is typological, since the two systems developed in different places and times, and nothing indicates contact between the two controversies. 4. Water, impurity and purification in Second Temple Judaism Second Temple Judaism has its own system of water purification, with biblical roots: washings and baths for each impurity in Leviticus 11–15 (rāḥaṣ, “to wash”; ṭāhar, “to be pure”), the water of purification with the ashes of the red heifer for one who has touched a corpse (Numbers 19), and the mikveh (“water reservoir,” Leviticus 11:36; Jeremiah 17:13), the immersion pool of which numerous examples have been found in Jerusalem and other cities of Judea from the first century. At Qumran, the Community Rule subordinates the efficacy of immersion to inner conversion: without repentance, “one shall not purify oneself in the waters of purification” (1QS III 4–9), and He describes the action of the spirit in terms of water: God will sprinkle the chosen one with the spirit of truth “like purifying water” (1QS IV 20-21). This passage links purification by water with the context of the two spirits (chapter XVII), which is the point of greatest contact with Mazdaean dualism. The baptism of John, the “immerser” (ho baptízōn), is known from the Gospels (Mark 1:4–11 and parallels; John 1:25–34) and from Flavius Josephus (Antiquities XVIII 116–119), who describes it as a purification of the body for those who had already been purified in soul by righteousness. It is a unique rite of conversion, administered by another, unlike the usual immersions, which each person performed and repeated on their own. This is the form that early Christianity adopted and reinterpreted (Matt 28:19; Acts 2:38; Rom 6:3–4; Didache 7:1–3, which prefers running, “living” water; Justin Martyr, First Apology 61).
