Possible contacts: Parthian Mesopotamia, Mandaeans and the mysteries of Mithras There are three routes mentioned in the literature. 412 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM Two Spirits (1QS III 13–IV 26) teaches that the God of knowledge created the children of men and assigned them two spirits to walk within them until the time of his visitation: the ruaḥʾĕmet (“spirit of truth”) and the ruaḥʿawlâ (“spirit of perversion”). The righteous are “children of light” (bĕnêʾôr), under the “Prince of Lights” (śarʾôrîm, 1QS III 20), and the unrighteous walk under the “Angel of Darkness” (malʾakḥōšek). Three features separate this dualism from the Avestan. First, both spirits are creatures of a single God: evil is neither coeternal nor independent. Secondly, predestination dominates, since each person receives “portions” of the two spirits (1QS IV 15–16), whereas in Y. 30.2–3 the debate centres on human choice between opposing orientations, not on the choice of the very existence of two spirits (an interpretation of the verses discussed in the bibliography). Thirdly, the struggle is waged within each person and not only in the cosmos. The opposition of two spirits constitutes a pertinent comparison with Y 30, without automatic equivalence between sectarian anthropology, Avestan cosmology, and the Frašō tradition. Comparison with Zurvanism requires chronological caution. That a higher principle precedes the two spirits (Zurvan) is attested in Christian and Armenian sources from the Sasanian period (Eznik of Kołb, Theodore bar Koni), so it cannot be used as a direct source for a text from the 2nd century BCE. If Qumran resembles Zurvanism, there are two explanations: an earlier West Iranian tradition that has left no text, or a convergence on a common problem— how a single, good God tolerates evil. The book does not resolve the alternative; it merely indicates that each is compatible with the level of “probable mediation” and not with that of “demonstrable dependence.” The War Scroll (1QM) adds a military organization of the celestial powers: the “sons of light” against the “sons of darkness,” with Belial (bĕlîyyaʿal) leading the opposing forces and Michael (Mîkāʾēl) and the “Prince of Light” as leaders of the forces of good (1QM XIII and XVII). The names and ranks are a novelty compared to the “messengers” of the Hebrew Bible. A comparison with the Aməša Spəṇta and the daēuuas is possible, but the catalogue is not the same: the Aməša Spəṇta are aspects of Ahura Mazdā with abstract functions (Aša, Vohu Manah), while the Qumran angels are named individuals who fight. Demonology and apocalyptic warfare are a terrain where one can speak of convergence, and debt is a matter of degree.

Thus, the parallel with the Frašō.kərəti- is reduced to the pattern of a final purification and a victory of good, without the detail of the metal river or the Saošyant, for which Qumran offers no equivalent (see Chapter XXXVII, Section 8). 7. John the Baptist: Qumran, the water and the desert The connection between John and the Qumran circles is geographical (the Judean Desert and the Jordan River), thematic (purity through water, imminent judgement, Isaiah 40:3 as a program), and chronological (first century). The Gospels apply Isaiah 40:3 to John (Mark 1:2–3; Matthew 3:3; Luke 3:4–6; John 1:23), and the Community Rule applies it to the community itself, which withdrew “to the desert to prepare the way” (1QS VIII 12–16 and IX 19–20). Luke (1:80) says that John lived “in the deserts” until his manifestation to Israel. The current consensus is that John may have had contact with Essene circles or with the community, but he was not a member of it. The differences matter as much as the parallels. John’s baptism is public and directed to “all Israel” (Mark 1:5), received only once, and administered by another, whereas the Qumran immersions are repeated and restricted to members of the community who have converted (1QS III 4–9 and V 13–14). Josephus (Ant. XVIII 117) emphasizes that John’s baptism was a purification of the body for those who had already been purified in soul by righteousness, which is close to 1QS III 6–9 in its emphasis on inner conversion. There is no evidence of a direct link between John and Iranian practices; the link, if it exists, would pass through the Jewish milieu of Qumran, which in turn may have received Iranian ideas in previous centuries. John, Qumran and the circle of Jesus: contacts, differences and transmission The hypothesis of a relationship between John and the Essenes or Qumran has been proposed since the 1950s and remains debated. There is no documentary evid ence that John was a member of the community. The consensus is that he was not a full member, although it is plausible that he was familiar with the movement and shared its atmosphere. There are six points of contact. Geography: the Judean Desert and the Jordan Valley (Luke 1:80; Mark 1:4). Lineage: his father Zechariah was a priest (Luke 1:5), and many members of Qumran came from priestly families opposed to the Hasmonean and Herodian priesthood. Diet: Mark 1:6 mentions lo custs and wild honey, and the Damascus Document regulates the consumption of locusts (CD XII 14–15). Isaiah 40:3: This is the program of John in the Gospels and that of the community in 1QS VIII 13-16. Water and repentance: both link im-

BAPTISM, INITIATION AND PURIFICATION BY WATER 415 mersion to conversion. Apocalyptic: imminent judgement, separation of the righteous and the wicked, “wrath to come” (Matt 3:7 = Luke 3:7).198 The differences are five and they outweigh the contacts. First, exclusivity: Qumran requires a novitiate of up to two years and gradual entry into the purity of the community (1QS VI 13-23), while John addresses “all Judea and Jerusalem” (Mark 1:5), tax collectors, and soldiers (Luke 3:10–14). Second, the rite: the immersions at Qumran are repeated and performed within the community, and John’s baptism, according to the Gospels and Josephus, is a public act of conversion. Third, the scope of the message: Qumran curses the “children of darkness” (1QS II 4-10) and considers itself to represent the rest of Israel; John invites everyone to bear “fruit worthy of repentance” (Matt 3:8). Fourth, the Torah and the calendar: Qumran is rigorous with the Law and with a 364-day solar calendar, and the Gospels attribute nothing comparable to John. Fifth, the organization: the community has a mebaqqer (“inspector”), council, and hierarchy, while John appears with disciples (John 1:35; Luke 11:1) without any known rule. One clarification regarding the last point of contact that is often added: that John and Qumran reject the Temple is true of Qumran, but the Gospels do not say that John rejected it; he only criticizes the elites (Matt 3:7). The most prudent thing is to think of a common apocalyptic environment of the Judean Desert, between the 1st centuries BCE and I CE, more than an affiliation. The transmission of this message to the circle of Jesus rests on a highly reliable historical fact: the baptism of Jesus by John, which the Christian community could hardly have fabricated due to its awkward nature (Mark 1:9–11; Matthew 3:14–15, where John resists). From John, Jesus is said to have received the call to conversion, the urgency of judgement, and the language of the two paths and of light and darkness. It differs from John in three aspects: inclusiveness (he eats with tax collectors and sinners, Mark 2:15–17), the relativization of certain purities (Mark 7:1–23), and eschatology, because in John the coming judgement prevails (“the ax is laid to the root,” Matthew 3:10 = Luke 3:9), while in Jesus the kingdom “has come” (Mark 1:15; Luke 11:20). Three-level evaluation Typological similarity: high. Water as a means of ritual purity, the distinction between purity and impurity, the preference for running water, and the link between water and a rite of passage appear in Zoroastrianism, Judaism, and Christianity. Probable mediation: limited. Contact between Jews and Zoroastrians is verifiable in the Persian Empire (Chapter XI) and in Parthian Mesopotamia; but the closest environment to Christian baptism, Second Temple Judaism and the baptism of John, has its own purification system, with texts and archaeology that explain the main features of the rite. Demonstrable dependence: none. There is no

BAPTISM, INITIATION AND PURIFICATION BY WATER 417 text that shows early Christianity adopting the rite from Zoroastrianism. And the differences are significant: Christian baptism is unique, administered by another, initiates one into a community, and is linked to the death and resurrection of Christ (Rom 6), whereas Mazdaean purification is repeated, is done through contact with death, and does not initiate one into a community of salvation. The most interesting parallel is the affinity between the water of purification in 1QS IV 20–21, linked to the spirit of truth, and Iranian dualistic logic; but the evidence of an Iranian mediation at Qumran is not conclusive. Chapter Conclusion Baptism is explained primarily from a Jewish perspective, and the comparison with Zoroastrian purification helps to see what ancient religions share with a system of purity (water and death as opposing forces) and what makes the Christian rite unique (uniqueness, agent, beginning of community). The Parthian route provides context, not proof. Summary The water of Mazdaism (Āpō, Vd 5–9, bara šnū mypā dyā b) and Zoroastrian initiation are compared with Jewish and Qumran purifications, with the baptism of John, and with Christian baptism. Parthian Mesopotamia, the Mandaeans, and the mysteries of Mithras complete the picture before the final evaluation. Christmas, baptism, and resurrection require independent chronologies; no single etymology demonstrates a doctrinal borrowing. 1. The hypothesis and how it is tested The hypothesis, in its best formulation, is as follows: six motifs from early Christianity and the later Church (the birth of the Saviour at the solstice, the victorious sun, baptism, the Saviour, temptation, and resurrection of the dead) have parallels in Zoroastrian texts, and these Zoroastrian parallels are either earlier or contemporary; therefore, Mazdaean culture would be a source, either directly or through Jewish mediation. This is the line of the history of religions school (Bousset, Reitzenstein) and part of the later tradition (Boyce). We test this with three tests, applied to each motif. First, dating: what is the earliest attestation of the motif in an IranianMazdaean source that we can date, and what is it in a Jewish or Christian source? Second, philology: do the terms of each tradition correspond in form, origin, or only in translation? Third, the route: was there documented mediation? Saviour: Saošyant, sōtḗr, mōšîaʿ and christós The Avestan term saošyant- is an active participle of future value (formation in yant-) of the root sū- /sav- (“to be useful, to take advantage, to give strength”), so that it literally means “the one who is to benefit” or “the one who will bring benefit”; the root is the same as the Sanskrit śavas- (“strength”) and is related, through the reconstructed Indo-European root ḱewh₁- (“to swell, to be strong”), to the Greek kýō, “to be pregnant”. The participle can also refer to contemporary people in the Gathic stratum. In Yt 19 and in later tradition, the Saošyant acquires an indi vidualized eschatological profile that culminates in the renewal of the world (frašō.kərəti-), defeats the Lie and resurrects the dead (Yt. 19.88–96; chapter XXIII). The languages of Christianity offer three terms that do not correspond in form or root: the Greek sōtḗr, “saviour”, derived from sōzō, “to save”, from sôs, “safe and sound” (of disputed etymology), the Hebrew môšîaʿ, “the one who saves” (root y-š-ʿ, “to be broad, to help”; with which Yēšûaʿ is formed, “YHWH saves”), and mašîaḥ, “anointed” (m-š-ḥ, “to smear”), which gives the Greek christós. A fundamental philological point: saošyant- and mašîaḥ or sōtḗr are not cognates or loan words; the kinship is of function, not of language. 4. Būiti, and, defeated by the recitation of the Ahuna Vairya (chapter XXXIV), addresses Zarathustra in person and tells him to renounce the religion of the Mazdaeans (mazdaiiasni- daēnā-) and he will obtain the reward that Vadaγna, lord of the nations, obtained (Vd. 19.6). The parallel with the Gospel accounts of the temptation (Mark 1:12–13; Matt 4:1–11; Luke 4:1–13), where the devil offers Jesus “all the kingdoms of the world” (Matt 4:8–9), is structural (the envoy is tested, and the test includes an offer of dominion). The vocabulary does not correspond: the Greek peirasmos derives from peira, “proof, attempt” (Indo-European root per-, “to pierce”), diabolos (from diaballos, “to throw through, to slander”) is “the slanderer,” and the Hebrew haśśāṭān is “the adversary” (śāṭan, “to accuse, to oppose”); while the Avestan aŋra- is “hostile” and druj- is “lie.” The terms of each tradition are independent, and the similarity lies in the scene, not in the lexicon. Christmas, sun and triumph of the sun The Spanish word Navidad comes from the Latin nativitas, from nascor (“to be born”), and is a Christian term formed on the category of “birth” (gennēsis in Greek; molad in later Hebrew); the name Natal has the same root, and Epiphany comes from the Greek epipháneia, “manifestation”, from epiphaínō. In the Iranian world, the Persian name for the solstice festival, Yaldā, is a loanword from the Syriac yaldā (“birth”), from the Semitic root yld, so that the name of the Persian festival it self is of Aramaic-Christian origin and not Avestan. This etymology is relevant because it reverses the direction of borrowing that is sometimes assumed: the name for the winter “nativity” in Persian comes from the Syriac-speaking Christian world. For the sun, Avestan distinguishes hvarəxšaētəm (“shining sun,” the subject of Yt 6) from Mithra; Old Persian does not name a solar god of its own; the Greek hḗlios and the Latin insōl (from the same Indo-European family, from a reconstructed root seh₂ul- / sh₂uen-) designate the sun, and the Avestan hvarə is related to the Sanskrit svàr- (“sky, sunlight”). Herodotus (I 131) refers to Persian sacrifices to the sun, and Strabo (XV 3.13) says that the Persians “also honor the sun, which they call Mithres” (timôsi d è ka ì hḗlion, h ò n kaloûsi Míthrēn; text by Perseus consulted in the edition cited digital code). Invictus is the Latin in -uictus (“unconquered”, from uincō), and is applied to Sol, Hercules, Jupiter and Mithras; The Greek equivalent is aníkētos, and the Avestan vərəθraγna- (from vərəθra-, “obstacle, resistance,” and γna-, “striking”) names the personified “victory” (Yt 14), which in Commagene is

Mithras: name, forms and epithets The name Mitra is one of the oldest documented in the Indo-Iranian world: it appears as mi-it-ra- in the treaty between the Hittite and Hurrian kings of Mitanni (circa 1380 BCE), among the guarantor gods (CTH 51; Thieme 1960). In Vedic Sanskrit, mitra- is a god (along with Varuna) and, as a neuter, means “friend, alliance”; in Avestan, mitra- means “pact, contract” and designates the god of the pact; in Old Persian, the name appears as Mitra- and in theophoric names as Mitraradata- (Greek Mithridata, “given by Mithra”; Middle Persian Mihrdad); in Middle Persian, mihr means “love, sun, friendship”; In Armenian, Mihr; in Sogdian, Bactrian, and Kushan, Miiro (coins from Kanishka, 2nd century CE); in Greek, Mithras; in Latin, Mithras. The most widely accepted etymology (Meillet) explains mitra- as derived from the root mei- (“to change, exchange”), with the instrument suffix -tra-: “that which serves for exchange,” that is, “contract, pact.” Thieme proposed that the primary meaning is “agreement, friendship” and that the god is its personification. In both cases, the sense of “pact” precedes the god, so that Mitra is “the Pact” personified. The most frequent Avestan epithet is vouru.gaoiiaoitiš (“of wide pastures”, Yt 10), and Yašt 10 describes him as the god who watches over those who break the covenants (miθrō.druj-, “the one who lies to the covenant”).201 Table 33. The Saošyant, the virgin birth and renewal: a note subject to control Note on comparative method. The relationship between Christian representations of Jesus as eschatological saviour and resurrection motifs in Zoroastrian traditions requires distinguishing the dating of each testimony and its possible routes of transmission. The comparison draws a structural parallel between Jesus, the eschatological saviour, and the Sao’yant. The elements it comprises are real, but it is advisable to order them according to the source that preserves them. In the recent Avesta, Yašt 13 (the Farvardīn Yašt) relates that the seed of Zarathustra is preserved in Lake Kąsaoiia (Yt. 13.62; Yt. 19.66; the Kansava of the Pahlavi texts), guarded by the fravaši of the righteous, and that from it will be born three posthumous sons: Uxšiiat̰ .ərəta (“the one who makes aša grow”), Uxšiiat̰ .nəmah- (“the one who makes reverence grow”) and Astuuat̰.ərəta (“the one who embodies aša”), the latter identified with the Saošyant (Yt. 13.128; Yt. 19.92). The name Astuuat̰.ərəta- is composed of astuuat̰ - (“having bones, corporeal”, from ast-, “bone”) and ərəta(variant of aša-, “truth, order”): “the one who gives body to truth” or “the corporeal truth”, and is a feature that chapter XXXIV can relate to the question of the word “incarnate” (astuuat̰ - is opposed to manahiia-, “spiritual”). The detail of the virginal conception is later. The Pahlavi texts (Bundahišn, Dēnkard VII, Zādspram, Wizīdagīhā ī Zādspram) tell that each of the three Saošyants is born of a young virgin who bathes in the lake where the seed of Zarathustra is preserved; The name of the mother of the latter, Ērēdat-fedri (Avesti ərəδat̰ .fəδrī-, “she who advances the lineage”), appears in the Bundahišn and in the Yašt 13. This tradition is attested in written form in the 9th–10th centuries CE, although it is assumed to be based on older Avesti and Sasanian materials. The virgin

Greek and Latin sources on the Magi: Pythagoras and the tradition of travel When the primary source is lacking or late, the correct methodological question is what Greek and Latin antiquity said about Magi and their supposed disciples. The corpus is extensive. Pliny the Elder, in Book XXX of his Natural History, states that magic originated in Persia with Zoroaster, and that Eudoxus places it six thousand years before Plato’s death, adding that Aristotle confirms this; Hermippus supposedly commented on two million verses of Zoroaster himself; and he cites Apusorus, Zaratus, and other names. He adds that “Pythagoras, Empedocles, Democritus, and Plato sailed to learn this science” in what he calls more “exiles than journeys,” and that upon their return they proclaimed it and preserved it among their secrets (Nat. XXX). Pliny is critical: he considers magic to be an imposture with “shadows of truth” and does not attribute to Zoroaster a doctrine that coincides with that of the Avestan fragments. Regarding Nero and Tiridates, Pliny recounts that the king of Armenia, a magus, went to Rome and, because of his religion, refused to sail, since magi do not believe it permissible to pollute the sea with spittle or human waste; that he initiated Nero into “magical banquets” (magicis cenis), and that Nero could not learn the art from him (Nat. XXX 16-17). The episode is contemporary with the Christian preaching of the first century and presents an Armenian Arsacid king with recognizable Zoroastrian taboos at a banquet with the emperor. It is explicit Latin testimony to the purity of water and to the figure of the magus in Rome during Paul’s lifetime204. 204Pliny, Naturalis historia XXX 16–17, Latin text of the Mayhoff edition available in Perseus; compare Strabo XV 3.14–16 on the protection of rivers and waters (chapter XXXII). Tiridates’s visit to Rome took place in 66 CE. Pliny associates his overland journey with the Magi’s concern about polluting the sea; this explanation belongs to the Roman account of the episode.

COMPARATIVE PHILOLOGY AND ETYMOLOGY 433 Critical reading distinguishes two things. The earliest ancient mentions (Heraclitus, Plato, Aristotle, Theopompus) show that from the 5th century BCE the Greek world was familiar with the Magi and associated Zoroaster with archaic wisdom, and that from this a philosophical topos is constructed: the Greek sage as traveler. In contrast, the texts that make Pythagoras a direct disciple of Zaratas (Hippolytus, Clement, Porphyry) are later and repeat the idea that Greek philosophy is an Eastern borrowing, a thesis that Jewish and Christian authors use in their apologetics (Philo, Josephus, Clement). The existence of the topos does not imply that Pythagoras learned from the Magi; It only follows that Antiquity held that the Magi were a source of wisdom and that nascent Christianity inherited this in the form of “wise men from the East” (Matt 2:1–12, mágoi ap ò anatolôn), a passage that deserves separate study. The Iranian sources proper (Y 30, Yt 13, Yt 19) remain the criterion for deciding whether a concept is Zoroastrian. 10. Logos, saviour, resurrection, Sol Invictus and Roman Mithraism: an assessment of the hypothesis The hypothesis examined in this chapter has four components: that logos and the “incarnate word” could originate from the Zoroastrian world; that the saviour of the end times and the resurrection also do; that Christ was represented as Sol Invictus, just like Mithras; and that the Church and Roman Mithraism have parallels, including the Eucharist as the distribution of the “bread of the sun” in a cave-like chamber. Each component is examined according to the book’s rule: typological similarity, probable mediation, and demonstrable dependence. Regarding the logos, it has already been stated in Chapter XXXIV that the comparison with mąθra-, Vāc, and the Ahuna Vairya is typological. John’s prologue can be explained without the need for an Iranian source: the personified Wisdom of Proverbs 8, Sirach 24, and Wisdom 7, the creative dābār of Genesis 1 and Psalm 33:6, the memra of the Targums,205 the logos of Philo of Alexandria, and Stoic reason. What makes John 1:14 something new, “the Logos became flesh” (ho ōgōgos sārx egéneto), is the incarnation in a historical person, and this step has no documented equivalent in the Avesta. The saviour and the resurrection belong to a better situation: the Saošyant and the Frašō.kərəti- are Iranian, and the resurrection is 205 Boyarin, “Gospel of the Memra”.

434 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM attested in the 4th century BCE by Theopompus (in Plutarch and Diogenes Laertius), which is the closest thing to external proof. The Jewish mediation of Daniel 12:2 and of the Pharisees is plausible, and for this reason these two concepts are the strongest candidates for “probable mediation.” Regarding Sol Invictus, the data are clear and from well-separated dates. The official cult of Sol Invictus was instituted by Aurelian in 274 CE. The Chronograph of 354 records the Christian feast of the birth of Christ on December 25, alongside the natalis Invicti. The image of Christ as Helios on a solar chariot appears in the mosaic of Mausoleum M in the necropolis beneath St. Peter’s, dating from around the 3rd or 4th century,206 and Clement of Alexandria (Protrepticus XI 114) already refers to Christ as the “sun of righteousness” based on Malachi 4:2. That is, Christ is depicted with solar features, but Mithras is not the sole model: the vocabulary comes from the Hebrew Bible (Mal 4:2; Ps 84:12; Luke 1:78, anatolḗ ex hýpsous) and from the Roman solar cult of Helios and Sol. Mithras and Sol appear as companions in Mithraic iconography and not as the same figure. Mithraism requires a prior distinction. The “mysteries of Mithras,” documented in Mithraea and Latin, Greek, and Dacian inscriptions, as well as those from Germania and Rome, constitute a cult of Imperial Rome with initiation in seven degrees (Corax, Nymphus, Miles, Leo, Perses, Heliodromus, Pater; Jerome, Ep. 107,2). The central figure, the tauroctonus with his Phrygian cap, has no clear Iranian parallel, and the cult lacks its own texts, so its theology is reconstructed from iconography and external authors, such as Porphyry (De antro nympharum 6). It is a Roman phenomenon that borrows its name and some features from Iran. Furthermore, the earliest Mithraeums date from the late 1st century CE at the earli est (first literary mention: Statius, Thebaid I 719–720, around 90 CE; Plutarch, Pompey 24.5, consulted in the cited digital edition, already associates it with the Ci lician pirates in the 1st century BCE). Consequently, Roman Mithraism could not have influenced the emergence of Christianity in the 1st century, although a parallel or competition between the two is possible in the 2nd –4th centuries CE. Regarding the Eucharist, the most important ancient testimony comes from Justin Martyr. In his First Apology (66.4), he compares the bread and the cup of water to certain formulae that “evil demons” imitated in the Mithraic mysteries; Tertullian (De praescriptione haereticorum 40) says that the devil also mimics the of206 Toynbee and Ward-Perkins, Shrine of St.

COMPARATIVE PHILOLOGY AND ETYMOLOGY 435 fering of bread. The ritual meals of the Mithraists are real: the banquet reliefs of Mithras and Sol, the tables (triclinia) of the Mithraea, and the remains of animals and tableware. But the origin of the Christian Eucharist is explained by Jesus’s Last Supper, with its Passover context, and by the Jewish blessings over the bread and wine (1 Cor 11:23–26; Mark 14:22–25; Didache 9–10), and the communal meal at Qumran (1QSa II 11–22) is a closer Jewish parallel. The “bread of the sun” is not attested: Mithraism does not offer solar bread, and the formula does not belong to any source. In Zoroastrianism there is a ritual bread, the drōn (av. draonah-, “portion”), consecrated at the Yasna along with the haoma drink, but its relationship to the Eucharist is one of typological similarity without any direct transmission.207 The “cave-room” has a basis. The Mithraea imitate a cave (spelaeum) with a star-studded vault, and Porphyry (De antro 6) recounts that Zoroaster consecrated a flowery cave with springs in the mountains near Persia in honor of Mithras, “creator and father of all things,” and that the cave was an image of the cosmos. This tra dition, of which Porphyry is the only source, is late (3rd century) and has a Platonic philosophical meaning. The Christian communities of the 1st century met in houses (oikoi, Acts 2:46; Rom 16:5), and the first identified churches date from the 3rd century (Dura Europos). There is no Christian parallel with the cave except for the tradition of Christ’s birth in a grotto, which appears in the Protoevangelium of James and in Justin (Dialogue with Trypho 78), a detail that some relate to Mithras born from the rock and that others explain by Isaiah 33:16 in the Septuagint. Plutarch, in Isis and Osiris 46, calls him mesítes, “mediator” between Oromazes and Areimanios, and derives from this a rite of offerings (De Iside et Osiride 46, μεσίτης; distinct from the chronological development of 47). The Roman Mithras kills the bull, eats with the sun, and governs the ascent of souls. And Christianity calls Christ mesítes of a new covenant (Heb 8:6; 9:15; 1 Tm 2:5), judge of the living and the dead (Acts 10:42), and “light of the world” (John 8:12). The Bundahišn, the root í zb ʰ ewd ʰ - and the name of Buddha Reading the Bundahišn in E.W. West’s translation (Sacred Books of the East 5, Clarendon Press, 1880, reprinted 1897; digital edition by J.H. Peterson, CC-BY 4.0) naturally raises the question: is the title Bundahišn or any word in the text related to Buddha? The answer requires separating two distinct roots that are confused by their graphic similarity. This is a matter of comparative Indo-European philology,

COMPARATIVE PHILOLOGY AND ETYMOLOGY 439 which does not imply any religious dependence between Zoroastrianism and Buddhism. First root: bun-, “ground, base.” The Pahlavi title Bundahišn is analysed as bundahišn (“creation of the ground” or “primordial creation”), and is also called Zandāgāhīh, “knowledge of the Zand” (Boyce, in the Handbuch der Orientalistik, cited in the prologue of the digital edition). The Pahlavi bun (“ground, root, origin”) continues an ancient Iranian related to the Avestan buna- (“ground”). Its cognates are Vedic Sanskrit budhná- (“bottom, base”), Greek pythmḗn (“bottom, stock”), Latin fundus, and English bottom (from bʰudʰ-mé n-; Mayrhofer, EWA and KEWA; Beekes, Etymological Dictionary of Greek). This root has no relation to Buddha. Second root: bʰewdʰ -, “to be awake, to perceive”. Buddha- is the past passive participle of the Sanskrit budh- (“to awaken, to understand”), and means “the awakened one, the one who has understood”; the noun bodhi- (“to awaken”) comes from the same root. The Indo-European bʰewdʰ- has continuators in the Avestan baod- (“to perceive”, from which baodah-, “perception, awareness” and baoiδi-, “smell, aroma”), in the Greek peúthomai (“to inform”), in the Lithuanian budė́ ti (“to watch”) and in the Old Slavic bъděti (“to be awake”); the Germanic form biudan (English bid, German bieten) belongs to the same group with an evolved sense (“to offer, to announce”). In Middle Iranian, this root gives the Pahlavi bōd (“consciousness”) and bōy (“smell, perfume”), and the modern Persian bū. The Bundahišn itself contains both forms. In chapter 1, West translates “Ohrmazd consulted with the conscience (bod) and guardian spirits (fravahr) of men” (chapter 1, section 10, West’s version), and in the chapter on plants, he classifies as “aroma” (bod, from bōy) any fragrant root, gum, or wood (frankincense, sandalwood, camphor, among others). What is certain is that the Pahlavi bōd (“consciousness”) and the Sanskrit buddha- (“awake”) are cognates, that is, they share the Indo-European origin, and the Bundahišn uses bōd in a cosmogonic context: the “consciousness” of human souls is consulted by Ohrmazd before the creation of the material world. (1) Achaemenid court (late 6th–4th centuries BCE): Gandhara and the Indus were part of the Persian Empire, and Darius’s inscriptions list Gadhara and Hidu among the provinces (DB I 17; DPe); the Kharoṣṭhī alphabet was formed from Imperial Aramaic. This is a context of contact, not evidence of religious transmission. (2) Seleucid and Mauryan court (3rd century BCE): Ashoka’s edicts in Kandhara were written in Greek and Aramaic, and are direct evidence of cultural bilingualism between eastern Iran, Greece, and India. (3) Parthian-Roman court (1st–2nd century CE): The Parthian monk An Shigao operated in China around 148 CE; Buddhism spread along the Silk Road with Iranian mediation (Sogdian and Bactrian). (4) Sasanian court (from 224 CE): Mani (3rd century) counts Buddha, along with Zoroaster and Jesus, among the messengers of truth; the Arabic source is al-Biruni (Athar al-Bakiya), which quotes Mani’s own Shabuhragan (trans. Sachau 1879). For the period of the book (539–332 BCE), there is no source showing transmission of Buddhist ideas to Persian Yahwism (the dates of Zoroaster and the historical Buddha are also highly debated). Classical sources. Clement of Alexandria mentions the Indians who “obey the precepts of Buta” (Strom. I 15,71); Jerome and Cyril of Jerusalem know the Manichean “Buddha” or “Scythianus” (Adv. Iovin. I 42; Cyril, Cat. VI 22). These 209 Göbl, System und Chronologie.

COMPARATIVE PHILOLOGY AND ETYMOLOGY 441 texts prove that the name reached Christian literature through the Manichean and Alexandrian channel, not through the world of the Avesta. Conclusion. The relationship between Bundahišn and Buddha should be formulated as follows: the title Bundahišn does not contain the root of Buddha (it contains bun-, “ground”); however, the Pahlavi word bōd, “consciousness,” is cognate with buddha- through the Indo-European root bʰewdʰ-, and the Iranian word also possesses a later loanword (but). There is no indication of religious dependence of one on the other. A hypothesis circulating in popular culture, that the name Buddha is “Iranian” or that “Buddha” derives from Bundahišn, lacks philological support. One legitimate question remains: whether the Śākya were a people in contact with Saka groups (eastern Iranians). It is a minority and debated hypothesis (F. W. Thomas; H. W. Bailey), which does not change the etymological conclusion. 12. The legends of Zarathustra in the Wizīdagīhā ī Zādspram The Wizīdagīhā ī Zādspram (“Selections from Zādspram”) is a 9th-century Pahlavi anthology attributed to Zādspram, a priest and brother of the high priest Manuščihr (circa 881 CE: the Epistles of his brother Manuščihr, translated by West in SBE 18, are dated March and July of that year and refer to Zādspram as a living priest; cf. Gignoux, Encyclopaedia Iranica, sv “Zādspram”). It brings together extracts from the Zand (the Pahlavi translation-commentary on the Avesta) on creation, the life of Zarathustra, and the final restoration (frašegird). Its chapters 12 to 23 contain the so-called “legend of Zarathustra”, parallel to books V and VII of the Dēnkard; the reference study is that of Molé, La légende de Zoroastre selon les textes pehlevis (Klincksieck, 1967). It is cited according to the translation by E. W. West (Pahlavi Texts, SBE 5, 37 and 47), in the digital edition by J. H. Peterson (CC-BY 4.0), and refers to the edition with French translation by Gignoux and Tafazzoli (Anthologie de Zādspram, Association pour l’avancement des études iraniennes, 1993). The historical use of these legends requires a clear chronological distinction: the material belongs to a post-Sasanian Pahlavi textual tradition, and its date of composition (9th century CE) is more than a millennium after the Achaemenid period examined in this book. It serves to document what the Mazdaean community recounted about its prophet, not to reconstruct what was believed in the time of Cyrus or Darius. Each motif is examined separately, contrasted with Greek

442 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM and Latin sources, and compared with biblical and Gospel accounts only at the typological level. Main motifs. (1) Conception and glory. Chapter 13 says that Zarathustra’s xᵛarənah- (“glory”) descended “from infinite light, in the form of fire,” and mingled with the fire and then with the mother, Dogdō (Dukdaub); for three nights passersby saw a radiance above the house. (2) Laughter at birth. In Chapter 14, Zarathustra “laughed aloud” at birth, unlike other children, who cry; the magicians explain that those who cry have seen their mortality and those who laugh have seen their own righteousness. Pliny the Elder records the same trait: Zoroaster was supposedly the only man who laughed on the day of his birth (NH VII 72: “He laughed on the day of his birth… Zoroaster; his brain throbbed, so that his hand would be re pelled, foretelling the future knowledge”). This is the clearest ancient confirmation that an Iranian legend circulated in the Latin world, although it does not prove that the Pahlavi version is the same as Pliny’s. (3) Attacks by demons and the Karb. In chapter 14, the demons of fever, pain, and wind come to kill the child, and Ahriman sends Akōman (the “evil thought”), whom Wahman (Vohu Manah) deceives. In chapter 16 An enemy priest (“Karb,” karapan-, cf. Y. 44.20) tries to kill the child five times: he twists his head, throws him under the feet of oxen and horses, places him on a fire, and leaves him in a wolf’s den, where Wahman and Sraoša give him sheep’s milk. (4) Prophecy of the signs. In chapter 17, one of the Karbs looks upward, downward, and to the sides and proclaims that the child will take souls to heaven, cast down demons, and spread his law throughout the earth. (5) Ascent and conference. In chapter 21, at the age of thirty, Zarathustra crosses the river Dāityā, which has four channels: the water reaches his ankle, his knee, his groin, and his neck, indicating that his religion will achieve supremacy four times, through him, through Ušēdar, through Ušēdarmā, and through Sōšāns; afterwards he finds Wahman, who leads him to the assembly of the seven Aməša Spəṇta, where he no longer casts a shadow because of the radiance. (6) Time. In chapter 15 Zarathustra occupies the “middle” place, with three millennia before and three after. Table 41. The first is the universal motif of the hero threatened in the cradle, which unites Sargon of Akkad, Moses, Cyrus (in Herodotus’s version), Romulus, and Jesus, and which is explained by narrative logic and not by borrowing. The coincidence of the Zadspram with Pliny (laughter at birth) is enough to assert that the legend predates the ninth century and circulated in the Hellenistic and Roman world; it is not enough to date the other episodes. Also of interest is the list of ancestors in chapter 13, which passes through Yima and Gayōmard and places Zarathustra in a mythical genealogy, and the tradition of the four ages, which links with the frašegird already discussed. It is a historiographical source of primary interest, but not a primary source: its chapters XXXI and XXXII on the birth of Christianity and Mithraism reproduce the state of the discussion at the beginning of the 20th century (Cumont’s thesis, December 25 as the birth of the Sun, the Mithraic resurrection), which subsequent criticism revised (Gordon, Beck, Clauss; see section 10). It is therefore cited as a testament to the learned memory of the Parsi community and not as proof of the facts it asserts. Since the work is protected by copyright in most jurisdictions, no passages are reproduced in block form. 13. Evaluation An evaluation by motif, according to the three pieces of evidence (to which is added the analysis of section 8: the Saošyant, the virgin conception, and the metal river are features of late Pahlavi sources, so the comparison with the New Testament is typological). Resurrection: the dating favours an earlier Mazdaean attestation (Theopompus, 4th century BCE), but philology shows no borrowings and the route is not documented; the hypothesis is plausible but not proven. Saviour and tempta-

COMPARATIVE PHILOLOGY AND ETYMOLOGY 445 tion: there are parallel scenes in the later Avesta (whose written form is Sasanian and whose oral date is uncertain); the terms are independent; Jewish mediation (Isaiah 45, Qumran) is possible. Sun worship and Mithra: these are documented in Persia in the 5th century BCE, but Christianity did not adopt a Persian sun cult; the Unconquered Sun of the Chronograph of 354 is Roman. Christmas: the date and name are Christian and Roman, and the Persian name for the Persian festival is a Syriac borrowing. Baptism: the Jewish antecedent is sufficient, and Zoroastrian purifications are another matter. The general thesis, therefore, holds only in a weakened version: the Mazdaean and Jewish worlds shared a horizon of eschatological and purity ideas in the 5th – 2nd centuries BCE, and this convergence, along with Hellenism, formed the environment in which Christianity was born; but Zoroastrian culture is not the source of the six motifs. The arguments of those who defend the strong thesis (Bousset, Boyce) and those of its critics (Colpe, Stausberg) are presented in the previous sections so that the reader can decide with the sources. Chapter Conclusion Only the resurrection and, with reservations, the figure of the saviour and the temptation scene have attested Mazdaean parallels of comparable date with Jewish sources; Christmas and baptism are explained in Roman and Jewish contexts. Philology confirms that the terms of each tradition are independent. Summary The chapter tests the hypothesis of six common motifs with comparative dating: resurrection (Theopompus, frašō.kərəti-, anástasis), the saošyant-, Vd 19, baptism, Christmas with Yaldā and Sol Invictus, and the name, forms, and epithets of Mithras. It adds the Bundahišn, the root bʰewdʰ- and the name of Buddha, and the legends of Zarathustra in the Zādspram, before evaluating each motif separately. Chapter XXXVIII. Edition 1. The Aramaic Version of Behistun Chronological context. Royal inscription of Darius I at Behistun, c. 520 BCE, and Ara maic transmission preserved on a later support from Elephantine. The date of the original inscription and that of the Aramaic copy do not coincide. Transmission of Behistú and Scope of Aramaic Translation The Aramaic fragments from Behistun are especially relevant because they document the circulation of royal narratives in a language used by the imperial administration. However, the distance between a translated version and the monumental relief requires comparing equivalent units, paying attention to omissions, adaptations of proper names, and formulae of legitimation. The general equivalence of a narrative does not allow for the automatic reconstruction of missing words from an Aramaic fragment. The apparatus must distinguish between: visible stroke, Cowley reading, restitution by comparison with Old Persian or other versions, and English translation. Only the first class constitutes direct observation on the reproduction of the physical object; the others are successive editorial acts. 1. Introduction to the document Among the Elephantine papyri are fragments of an Aramaic version of the Behistun inscription (TAD C2.1; Cowley edition, 1923, pp. 248–271; numbered by Cowley). Cowley describes them as remnants of at least two copies of an official translation that Darius would have sent to the provinces around 510 BCE; the surviving copies would be a later transcription, around 420 BCE, made by the Jews of Elephantine, who left gaps where the original was illegible. The Aramaic version closely follows the Babylonian text, not the Old Persian: it gives, for example, the figures for dead and prisoners, which appear only in the Babylonian version. The Aramaic copy is not limited to the rock text: its final part reproduces a pas sage from Darius’s funerary inscription at Naqsh -e Rostam (DNb § 9), suggesting a later commemorative edition and not simply a translation from Behistun. Gad Barnea (2025) studies the epilogue of DB (DB IV 36–92), in which Darius addresses the future king and the reader in the second person, and reads it as a program 449

450 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM of imitatio dei — the king aligned with Auramazda against the Lie — which extends into an imitatio Darii demanded of the reader; according to Barnea, the Qumran text 4Q550 would preserve a legendary reworking of that epilogue in an Achaemenid -style narrative. Both proposals confirm the circulation of the actual text among Aramaic-speaking subjects; its religious scope is an interpretation. 2. Documentary comparison of the versions The Aramaic text of the fragments is so damaged that the Cowley facsimile, in the available copy, does not allow for a reliable transcription, and is not reproduced here. This section offers, instead, the documentary comparison that serves for the book: the beginning is edited from the Old Persian version (DB I 1–3; see Text 5), and the following table summarizes how the versions relate. These pieces of evidence do not authorize a literal equivalence of all the columns. 4. Philological commentary Darius’s official account, with its theology of power and falsehood (chapter VIII), circulated in Aramaic among the inhabitants of Elephantine. Second, it testifies to the practice of translating an official text into the language of the administration and having it copied by the subjects themselves. Third, it illustrates that the Jews’ contact with the Persian royal theology could have occurred through a text written in their everyday language, which is an argument for probable mediation, not demonstrable dependence. Chapter Conclusion The Aramaic version of Behistun demonstrates the circulation of a royal Persian discourse through translation. Its preservation at Elephantine attests to access to the imperial narrative; it does not demonstrate the religious affiliation of each copyist or reader. The fragments require their own edition and should not be presented as a recovered, complete text. Chapter XXXIX. Edition 2. The Passover Letter (TAD A4.1) Historical context of the chapter. The so-called “Passover letter” from Elephantine (TAD A4.1 = Cowley 21 = P. Berlin 13464) is placed in the fifth year of Darius II, usually 419 BCE (or 419/418 depending on the reckoning). The date corresponds to the document, not to the reign of Darius I. The references to royal authority and Arsames do not allow us to reconstruct the entire content of an order from the court without further analysis. Critical complement — Documentary control of the Passover letter The so-called “Passover letter” must be identified before being interpreted: TAD A4.1 = Cowley 21, P. Berlin 13464, held in the Egyptian Museum and Papyrus Collection of the Staatliche Museen zu Berlin. The ERC Elephantine project catalogue records six lines recto and four verso, fragmentary text and correspondence from Ḥananyāh to Yedanyā and his colleagues. The modern title of the piece does not equate to a complete and certain reading of the Passover celebration: the object contains substantial gaps, and the reconstruction of formulae concerning the festival requires recognizing the surviving letters, editorial supplements, and interpretive conjectures. Catalogue used to identify the physical object: https://elephantine.smb.museum/objects/object.php?o=100463. The analysis distinguishes a calendrical or ritual prescription attested in official correspondence from a doctrine concerning the origin of that prescription. The ad ministrative integration of a Jewish community into the Achaemenid world does not allow us to deduce, without further evidence, that every element of its calendar originated from an Iranian religion. Historical analysis gains strength by comparing the document with other known Jewish practices, recognizing its local particularities, and formulating only the inferences that the text itself allows. The Passover letter in the Elephantine archive: genre and scope The so-called Passover Letter, TAD A4.1, must be situated among the Aramaic documents of Achaemenid Egypt and discussed according to its status as a written document, not as a page extracted from biblical legislation. For any correspondence with Exodus 12, Deuteronomy 16, or the calendrical practices of Judah, it is essential to distinguish the explicit indications on the papyrus, the restorations of obscure passages, and the interpretive developments of the editors. 453

454 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM A. Cowley’s edition, Aramaic Papyri of the Fifth Century BCE (1923), serves as the primary reference for this document. However, its preface explicitly states the reliance on facsimiles for many readings and the impossibility of directly comparing some originals. The critical notes record the document number, support, provenance, lines, and bibliography, as well as distinguishing between the document date and the date of the material evidence. The main value of this thesis lies in the plurality of Yahwist practices under Persian rule, as well as in the administrative channels through which communications circulated between authorities and communities. Nothing in the document justifies making the Passover practice a necessary derivative of the Zoroastrian religion. The dossier may be expanded with Porten-Yardeni, Textbook of Aramaic Documents from Ancient Egypt I, once access to its relevant readings becomes available. 1. Philological commentary The dating by reign, the communal recipient, and the reference to an authority make the letter evidence of institutional communication. These elements alone do not allow us to determine whether the instructions originated at court, from a Jewish authority, or from Ananias’s own initiative. The calendar and dietary prohibitions must be studied in their preserved form before associating them with a general reform of worship. Chapter Conclusion The so-called Passover letter documents the circulation of communications regarding the calendar and festive practices within a Yahwist community in Achaemenid Egypt. Its precise interpretation remains subject to gaps and reconstructions: the mention of a year of reign and a communication from the court does not prove that the monarch drafted the instructions, nor does it allow us to derive the origin of the festival from Iranian religion. The distinction between the preserved text, the reconstruction, and the historical scope preserves the unique value of the document without unduly expanding its probative force. Summary An indirect translation and commentary on its problems are provided. The document is identified as TAD A4.1 = Cowley 21; its content should not be re constructed by automatic harmonization with biblical law.

THE LETTERS OF ARSAMES 467 4. Philological commentary The control value of Arsames’ correspondence is institutional and linguistic: it allows for a comparison of formulae, titles, recipients, and vocabulary of the Achaemenid administration with Yahwist testimonies from Elephantine. When a word appears in both sets, it establishes a shared usage within that documentary context; to demonstrate its Iranian origin and specific meaning, independent etymology, first attestation, syntactic context, and communicative function are required. It cannot be inferred that every Iranian word has an exclusively administrative meaning, nor that the letters thereby transmit Mazdaean beliefs. Chapter Conclusion The letters of Arsames serve as a point of comparison for administrative, supply, and mobility practices. Their language allows us to assess whether a formula from Elephantine belongs to the use of the chancery. The examined docu mentation attests to administrative channels of contact; to propose the transmission of a religious teaching, it would be necessary to identify the content, date, agent, and recipient through independent evidence. Summary This chapter compiles a contextual dossier of Arsames’ correspondence (TAD A6) and does not constitute a complete translation. Its value is institutional and linguistic: formulae, titles, and Iranian vocabulary from the chancery allow us to situate the Yahwist documents from Elephantine, even though the letters do not convey Mazdaean beliefs. The three material concordances in § 3 serve for verification of shelfmarks; they are not considered translated letters. BIBLICAL ARAMAIC OF EZRA AND DANIEL: PASSAGES 471 The texts edited here require a distinction between the dates they describe, the dates at which they acquired their surviving literary forms, and the age of the manuscripts that transmit them. Ezra places much of its narrative in the Persian period, yet its embedded documents require independent historical and textual assessment. Daniel sets its court stories in earlier imperial settings, whereas its final visions belong to the historical horizon of the second century BCE. The Masoretic text used in this volume is preserved in a medieval manuscript tradition. Critical complement — Protocol for the parallel-text translation of Ezra and Daniel The edition therefore follows five controls: (1) identification of book, chapter and verse; (2) distinction between Hebrew and Aramaic in the Masoretic text; (3) separ ate treatment of the consonantal text, Masoretic vocalization and marginal notes; (4) explicit identification of ketiv (‫כתיב‬, written form) and qere (‫קרי‬, reading form) wherever applicable; and (5) comparison with relevant Greek witnesses without conflating them. Ezra 4:8–6:18 and 7:12–26 are Aramaic; Daniel 2:4b– 7:28 is the principal Aramaic section of that book. The remaining passages must not be described indiscriminately as Aramaic. Examples of the two Masoretic forms are documented in Appendix F. A facing-text edition requires consistent verse numbering and equivalent segmentation of the ancient text and the English study translation, which was prepared with reference to the Spanish study translation. Each unit should allow the reader to return to the wording on which its rendering rests. Where restitution or syntax is disputed, the preferred translation and its alternatives must be distinguished. In Daniel, the Old Greek and the version associated with Theodotion remain separate textual witnesses; in Ezra, the Hebrew–Aramaic Ezra–Nehemiah tra dition must not be conflated with the distinct Greek witness of 1 Esdras. Narrative overlap does not remove that textual distinction. An electronic database makes passages easier to locate and compare; it does not replace critical editions or examination of manuscript witnesses. Where a transcrip tion is mediated by digital conversion or an earlier printed edition, the intervening source is identified. Facing-page typography, however clear, does not itself create a new critical edition. The collation of ketiv/qere and other significant variants remains open wherever the relevant edition or witness has not been independently checked.

472 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM Philological expansion: from textual testimony to English study translation Working with Ezra and Daniel requires separating four operations that a paralleltext presentation could confuse: (1) transcription of a source text; (2) recording of variants, including ketiv and qere; (3) translation of a given reading; and (4) historical interpretation of the passage. When the electronic source text includes two readings on the same line, the translation cannot choose one without a note stating the chosen reading. It is preferable to preserve the mark of doubt rather than create the appearance of a single manuscript reading. Ezra 4:8–6:18 and 7:12–26 belong to the major Aramaic sections of the book; Daniel 2:4b – 7:28 constitutes the main Aramaic section of Daniel. This linguistic delimitation does not equate to a dating of composition. The presence of Iranian loanwords, authorization formulae, lists of officials, and epistolary headings is consistent with an imperial administrative environment, but their presence in a work transmitted through literature does not transform each cited decree into an original document from the Persian archive. For each letter, it is proposed to record the sender, recipient, literary unit, administrative vocabulary, documentary parallels, and the degree of debated authenticity. Equivalence criteria in Ezra and Daniel The edition of Ezra and Daniel will be organized by the units that have actually been preserved: Hebrew text, Aramaic text, and Greek versions. Language transitions should not be obscured by the continuity of the English translation. In Ezra, 4:8–6:18 and 7:12–26 constitute the major Aramaic sections; in Daniel, 2:4b – 7:28. An academic apparatus should identify, for each passage, the differences between the textual form and the reconstruction of historical events. In particular, the presence of chancery language in Ezra can be analysed in light of material Aramaic papyri, but this linguistic affinity alone does not resolve the authenticity of each decree or letter included in the biblical narrative. For Daniel, it is necessary to separate the narrative setting of the Persian court, the literary composi tion of its units, and the Hebrew-Aramaic and Greek transmission. This distinction avoids converting a setting into a date of authorship. Textual protocol for the bilingual edition. Ezra 4:8–6:18 and 7:12–26, as well as Daniel 2:4b – 7:28, are transmitted in Aramaic within the Masoretic text; the adjacent passages belong to Hebrew units. Daniel requires distinguishing between the ancient Greek text and the Theodotion tradition, as well as the Greek additions. Scope of the textual dossier. The title “passages” identifies the comparative dossier of this chapter and not the entire biblical corpus reproduced in the volume. The general concordance indicates the presence of original texts and English renderings for the 280 Masoretic verses of Ezra and the 357 verses of Daniel, including their Hebrew sections. For Daniel, the inventory records its Aramaic section 2:4b – 7:28 and the remaining Hebrew sections, including 2:1–3. The Masoretic text of both books is listed in full (Ezra, 280 verses; Daniel, 357), which does not equate to certifying each reading, the ketiv/ qere, or the Greek recensions.

Textual commentary and reading problems The passages in Ezra present critical problems: the authenticity of the cited documents (Ezra 4–7) is debated, with some scholars considering them the author’s own compositions based on official models, while others believe them to be copies or paraphrases of actual documents.213 The passages in Daniel are literary compositions from the second century BCE and cannot be used as documents from the Per sian period. 4. Philological commentary In both corpora, Iranian vocabulary appears (chapter II): ʾăḥašdarpĕnayyāʾ, dāt, gizbār, pitgām, rāz, and ʾazdāʾ. This is to be expected in Aramaic of the Persian court. In Ezra, the vocabulary appears in letters attributed to Persian kings; in Daniel, it is used to situate the narrative at court, although its presence does not prove composition during the Persian period. Lexical control — function of borrowing. The criteria to be applied are: attested form, etymology and proposed intermediary language, documented chronology, syntactic function in the passage, and comparison with contemporary administrative usage. A theophoric anthroponym of Iranian origin documents the circulation of names; however, it does not in itself determine the personal beliefs of its bearer. Imperial Aramaic was the medium of administration and correspondence under the Achaemen ids, but this did not make it an automatic translation of the Great King’s religious program. Ezra’s letters should be evaluated both as documents attributed to kings and within a literary composition. The formula functions as a linguistic hinge. History The Babylonian setting under Nebuchadnezzar II belongs to the narrative timeframe, while the dating of the book’s composition and the circulation of its stories require separate analysis. The mention of court specialists does not authorize a direct transfer of Mazdean vocabulary or a date of composition under Darius I. The courtly lexicon of this scene should not be automatically identified with the documented administrative practice of Darius I. Dan 2:18–23. “God of heaven” is a designation shared by different corpora of the Persian period and later; the terminological coincidence alone does not establish doctrinal borrowing from Mazdaism. Daniel 2:20–21. The attribution to God of deposing and establishing kings must first be read in its biblical and literary context. Comparisons with Achaemenid royal legitimation require argumentation based on contexts and chronologies. Dan 2:28–30. “Mystery” translates the Aramaic rāz, a term whose linguistic and interpretative history requires specific commentary; its etymology must be separated from its possible influence on the apocalyptic conception.

Textual and hermeneutical notes on Daniel 3 1. Dan 3:2–3: the administrative titles form a literary enumeration. The appearance of words of possible Iranian origin is evaluated term by term (chapter II); it does not prove that the narrative was composed under Darius I. 2. Dan 3:5–7 and 3:10–15: the enumeration of instruments presents terms of complex origin and transmission, some associated with Greek. Dating by isolated linguistic borrowings is insufficient.

Dan 3:17–18: the faithfulness of the three officials does not depend on the success of the liberation; “and if not” prevents reducing the story to a contract of divine reward. Aramaic expression bar ʾĕlāhîn is translated according to the voice of the foreign king “son of the gods”; it cannot be converted into a Christological designation without argument. 5. Dan 3:28: the term for messenger/angel must be studied in its Semitic context before proposing a derivation from Iranian angelology. 6. Greek testimonies: The Prayer of Azariah and the Song of the Three Young Men appear in the Greek traditions of Daniel, but they are not part of the Masoretic Aramaic chapter 3. They are treated as distinct Greek texts and are not interpolated in the translation from the Aramaic. 7. For consonantal forms and the ketiv/qere distinction, the reader should refer to the textual basis stated by each table.215 Note 3. The Watchers (ʿîrîn). Daniel 4:10, 14, 20: ʿîr, “watcher,” is used with “holy” for the heavenly messenger. Its connection with angelology and with later Iranian materials does not in itself equate to a Zoroastrian dependence. Compare Daniel 7; 1 Enoch 6–16, considering their independent dating. Note 4. Decree and sovereignty. The “decree of the watchers” (Dan 4:14) and the command of the “Most High” (4:21–22) present a literary articulation between celestial agents and divine sovereignty. Compare with imperial titles only after distinguishing the centuries of composition and the channels of transmission. Note 5. Seven times. The Aramaic term ʿiddānîn (“times”) does not require a translation of “years” in the main text. The chronological interpretation should be set forth in a separate commentary. Note 6. Justice and mercy. Dan 4:24: ṣidqā and ḥănān ʿănāyîn admit nuances of justice/almsgiving and mercy towards the needy. “Break with your sins” reflects the moral exhortation without making it a test of transmitted Iranian ethics. Note 7. Parallels and Historical Criticism. The account must be compared with the Nabonidus traditions, especially 4Q242 (Prayer of Nabonidus), whose edition, fragmentary nature, and dating require independent study. Daniel’s narrative about Nebuchadnezzar should not be read as a contemporary administrative record of the historical king. Note 8. Control Editions. The transcription follows the Leningrad text; divergences with BHS, with the ancient Greek of Daniel, with Theodotion, and with the Qumran fragments are recorded when they affect the meaning. Only one reading is assigned to a papyrus or manuscript that preserves the corresponding locus. II sexies. Dan 5:1–4. The sacred vessels refer to the plundering of the sanctuary in Jerusalem; compare 2 Kings 24–25, 2 Chronicles 36 and Ezra 1:7–11. The chapter contrasts the courtly use of ritual vessels with the exaltation of the God of heaven; it does not demonstrate a doctrinal transfer from Zoroastrianism.

518 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM 2. Dan 5:2. “Father” (ʾab) can designate an ancestor in dynastic discourse, not necessarily immediate biological filiation. Distinguish the narrative relationship from the genealogy reconstructed from Neo-Babylonian sources: Belshazzar was the son of Nabonidus. 3. Daniel 5:5–9. The mysterious inscription belongs to a courtly narrative. The failure of the wise men and the intervention of Daniel create a literary contrast; the description does not allow for the historical identification of all the officials with Zoroastrian priests. 4. Dan 5:7. “Third in the kingdom” (taltāʾ) is translated functionally. Its possible connection with Belshazzar’s historical position as second ruler during Nabonidus is a historiographical explanation, not a textual variant. 5. Daniel 5:10–12. The queen recalls Daniel’s gifts. The “spirit of the holy gods,” uttered by Babylonian interlocutors, reflects their literary viewpoint; it should not be transformed by harmonization into an explicit Yahwist confession. 6. Dan 5:17. Daniel refuses gifts as a condition of interpretation. See the structure of courtly wisdom stories in Daniel 2 and Genesis 41; similarity of genre does not mean specific borrowing. 7. Daniel 5:18–23. The sovereignty of the Most High God over the kingdoms is echoed in Daniel 4; compare Ezra 1, Isaiah 44–45, and the inscriptions of Darius, keeping language, date, and gender separate. Divine titles do not in themselves equate to identity between Ahura Mazdā and YHWH. 8. Dan 5:25–28. The Aramaic sequence mnʾmnʾtql wprsyn plays with nominal values linked to weights and with verbal roots “to count,” “to weigh,” “to divide.” The final form of v. 25 is PARSÍN, while the interpretation of v. 28 uses PERÉS; the play on “Persia” should not obscure the morphological difference. Retain both forms and explain them. 9. Daniel 5:29–30. The outcome of the banquet foreshadows the dynastic change. Compare the Babylonian accounts of the end of the Neo-Babylonian Empire before reconstructing a historical chronology from the isolated narrative. 10. Condition of the device. Selective Comparative Critical Apparatus — Daniel 6 1. Dan 6:1. “Dari the Mede” belongs to the narrative framework of the book. His historical identification is problematic and should not be equated without demonstration with Darius I Hystaspes. The transition from Belshazzar is also examined in Dan 5:30–6:1. 2. Dan 6:2–4. “Satraps” translates the Aramaic ʾăḥašdarpənayyā, an administrative term of Iranian origin; it is a lexical borrowing relevant to imperial contact. The number one hundred and twenty is a narrative statement, not an independent census of Achaemenid satrapies. 3. Dan 6:5–10. “Prohibition” and “decree” represent distinct legal categories within the narrative; the topic of the irrevocability of Medo-Persian law is contras-

BIBLICAL ARAMAIC OF EZRA AND DANIEL: PASSAGES 525 ted with Esth 1:19 and 8,8, avoiding automatically turning it into a documented description of Persian law. 4. Dan 6:11. The windows towards Jerusalem and the prayer three times a day constitute the literary framework of cultic fidelity in the diaspora. Compare 1 Kgs 8:44–48 and Ps 55:18; this prayer does not prove Zoroastrian influence. 5. Daniel 6:17–18. “Ditch” translates gubbā; the sealing by royal rings expresses legal and narrative control of the confinement. These images have biblical parallels, including Ezekiel 1 and prophetic texts, so the mere presence of heavenly judgement is not enough to attribute a Zoroastrian origin. Daniel 7:13–14 — The figure “like a son of man” must retain its comparative form: the expression describes the visionary appearance, it does not in itself establish a pre -formed Christological title. Daniel 7:15–28 — The angelic interpretation distinguishes vision, royal symbols, and the destiny of the holy people. The usual dating of the final form of Daniel within the context of the crises of the second century BCE requires separating the narrative period of the imperial courts from the period in which eschatological hope is articulated. 532 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM 4. Daniel 7:10. “The books were opened” corresponds to a heavenly judgement scenario. Compare Exodus 32:32–33; Psalm 69:29; Malachi 3:16 and later traditions. For an Iranian hypothesis, the parallels must be dated separately. 5. Daniel 7:13. “Someone like a son of man” maintains the Aramaic comparison kəbar ʾĕnāš: it describes a figure of human appearance and does not decide on its own whether the figure is collective, angelic, or individual. Later Christian reception requires independent analysis. Comparative apparatus — Dan 7:13 (Aramaic / Ancient Greek / Theodotion). The Aramaic form kəbar ʾĕnāš designates a figure comparable to a human being who reaches the Ancient of Days. The Greek tradition attributed to Theodotion preserves the approximation “to the Ancient” (ἕως τοῦ παλαιοῦ τῶν ἡμερῶν); the ancient Greek version transmits, in the decisive sequence, “as an Ancient of Days” (ὡς παλαιὸς ἡμερῶν). The second formulation may approximate the human figure to the enthroned character, but it does not compel us to declare them identical. Neither this textual difference nor the subsequent iconography establishes, in and of themselves, a derivation from the Iranian Saošyant. Maintain three separate levels: textual reading, historical exegesis, and Christian reception. Source and verification: Benjamin E. Reynolds, “The ‘ One Like a Son of Man’ According to the Old Greek of Daniel 7:13–14,” Biblica 89 (2008): 70–80; B.G. Bucur, “The Son of Man and the Ancient of Days,” Phronema 32/1 (2017): 1–27. 967. Note on Aramaic Semantics — Daniel 7:13–14. The comparison kəbar ʾĕnāš (“like a son of man / like a human figure”) remains distinct from its reception as a title. The verb yipleḥûn, from pəlaḥ, appears in Daniel in other instances linked to religious service (Daniel 3 and 6), so translating it as “they will serve him” requires commenting on the possible cultic resonance, not automatically imposing or discarding “they will worship.” The vision should be read in conjunction with Daniel 7:18 and 7:27, which assign the kingdom to the saints. The difference between an individual, angelic, or collective referent is exegetical; it does not authorize a direct genealogy from Iranian salvific figures. Orientation bibliography: J. J. Collins, Daniel (Hermeneia, 1993); C. A. Newsom, Daniel (OTL, 2014). 6. Daniel 7:14. “To serve” translates a form of pəlaḥ, an Aramaic verb associated in Daniel with religious or cultic service. The interpretation of its intended recipient and its political-religious meaning must be made explicit without altering the original. 7. Dan 7:18. “Saints of the Most High”: the Aramaic allows us to discuss the reference to a collective and its relationship with the human figure of 7,13. Compare Dan 7:22.27 and the context of the chapter. 8. Daniel 7:25. “A time, two times, and half a time” maintains the temporal formulation without immediately replacing it with an absolute historical chronology.

BIBLICAL ARAMAIC OF EZRA AND DANIEL: PASSAGES 537 Textual Criticism Note — Ezra 5:4. The Masoretic text presents ‫ֲא ַמ ְר ָנא‬ (ʾamarnā, “we said”), which the preserved English translation reproduces literally. The alternative ‫( ֲא ַמ רּו‬ʾamarû, “they said”) is found in the critical note of NET Bible, based on a medieval Hebrew manuscript and supported by the Septuagint and the Peshitta; hence the contextual reading “they asked them their names.” The original should not be amended without informing the reader, nor should the third-person version be presented as an exact translation of the preserved Masoretic form. The context is an inspection of the temple works: the administrative designa tions and the word ṭeʿēm (“order/decree”) do not prove Zoroastrian doctrinal adoption. Ezra 6:1–18. Original Aramaic and English study translation (via Spanish) Ezra 5:1–2 — The account attributes the resumption of the works to the actions of Haggai and Zechariah and the initiative of Zerubbabel and Joshua. Ezra 5:3–5 — The inspection by Tattenay, governor of the province Beyond the River, constitutes the administrative framework of the narrative. The territorial expression is comparable to imperial Aramaic language, but the general lexical parallels do not demonstrate the literal authenticity of the document reproduced by Ezra. Ezra 5:6–17 — The letter combines a heading, identification of senders, a report of the investigation, and a request for archival consultation. A distinction must be made between the literary epistolary formula embedded in Ezra and contemporary administrative papyri. In 5:11–16, the elders justify their rights by means of a memory of the previous temple and the decree attributed to Cyrus; the passage conveys a historical claim, not an archaeologically verified record. Ezra 6:1–5 — The search ordered by Darius and the discovery of a memorandum in Ecbatana (Achmetha, Aram. ‫ ;ַא ְח ְמ ָת א‬Ezra 6:2) raises a problem of archival geography: a text found in a Median residence cannot automatically be transformed into proof of a single central Persian archive. It is important to retain the distinction between a “memorial” or record of an order and the administrative event itself whose memory the narrative preserves. Ezra 6:6–12 — The second communication instructs transfluvial officials not to obstruct the work and to order services using tax revenues. For the analysis of Persian influence, the main interest lies in political language, taxation, and the

Historical-critical note: Ezra 6:2–3:11, 14. The memorial attributed to Cyrus is narratively located in Ecbatana (Achmetha, Ezra 6:2), although the search is directed to Babylon. The architectural magnitudes of the decree and the sanction in 6:11 must be treated as narrative formulations whose precise historicity requires documentary comparison. In 6:14, the preserved text mentions Cyrus, Darius, and Artaxerxes in connection with the completion of the works; since the narrative itself places this completion under Darius (6:15), the third name introduces a retrospective perspective, not a new year of completion. BIBLICAL ARAMAIC OF EZRA AND DANIEL: PASSAGES 545 Philological Criticism Note — Ezra 7:12. The existing translation “perfect peace; and now” is a plausible interpretive expansion of ‫( ְּג ִמ יר ּוְכ ֶע ֶנת‬gəmîr ûkəʿenet), but the noun “peace” does not appear explicitly in those two Aramaic words. Documented alternatives: applying “perfect/complete” to the scribe’s qualification, understanding it as an abbreviated formula of greeting, or reading “and now” as a transition to the body of the letter. The main translation should be retained with this clarification, not presented as an unequivocal calque of the original. See NET Bible, translation note on Ezra 7:12, and Cambridge Bible for Schools and Colleges, commentary on that verse. In 7.14 the seven advisors are part of the literary representation of the chancery, and the taxation of 7.24 and the sanctions of 7.26 provide data on legal language, not immediate proof of Iranian-Yahwist religious transmission.

Textual criticism of Ezra and Daniel: verse integrity, languages, witnesses and scope of translations Subject. The text of Ezra and Daniel is offered in its entirety: 637 verses with Hebrew or Aramaic and English (Ezra, 280; Daniel, 357), with the standardized division by chapter and verse. A. Nature of the Languages. The expression “ancient Hebrew” requires precision. The books preserve both Biblical Hebrew and Biblical Aramaic, represented here in square Hebrew script, sometimes with Tiberian Masoretic vocalizations. This medieval notation is not a reproduction in Paleo-Hebrew script of an Achaemenid-era autograph. In Ezra, the main Aramaic blocks are 4:8–6:18 and 7:12–26; in Daniel, Aramaic begins within 2:4 and ends in 7:28. The linguistic strata should not be attributed to a single date of composition, nor should the language of the narrative be equated with a contemporary administrative document.

556 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM The nine documentary controls employed for Ezra and Daniel should be adapted to the Avestan passages without treating editions as interchangeable: (1) locus and textual stratum; (2) witness and edition; (3) transcription convention; (4) morphology and disputed segmentation; (5) alternative translations; (6) translation printed here; (7) comparative apparatus; (8) transmission and chronological limits; and (9) direct or indirect verification status. Geldner, Mills and Uesugi–Catt serve different scholarly purposes and cannot all be cited as equivalent autoptic controls. Priority loci: Y. 30.3–5, Y. 44.20, Vendīdād 19.1–2, and the Y. 35–41 sequence. A direct comparison requires recording the actual reading and its editorial provenance before assigning a translation. Until this is done, the study translation may be useful for orientation but is not to be presented as a new critical recension. This chapter brings together Gathic and Younger Avestan texts of disputed date with Achaemenid inscriptions datable by reign. Their presence in the same documentary dossier is not evidence of contemporaneity. The dating of Y. 27 and Vd. 19 must be argued independently of the royal inscriptions, with due regard for liturgical reuse and the later manuscript history of the Avesta. 1. Their loci are Y. 28–34, 43–51 and 53; the full in ventory appears in Appendix B. Selections from the Ahuna Vairya, Yašt 19, Vendīdād 19 and the Achaemenid inscriptions retain the source indicated for each entry. The English renderings and glosses are offered for study, and uncertainties of reading remain explicit. Reproducing a transliteration does not constitute either a new critical edition or an independent philological collation of every verse. The Avesta is composed in Avestan, an ancient Iranian language conventionally classified among the eastern Iranian languages, although its precise historical affiliation remains debated. Its linguistic strata include Old Avestan (the Gāthās and the Yasna Haptaŋhāiti) and Younger Avestan. Neither should be confused with Old Persian, the language of the Achaemenid royal inscriptions, or with Ara-

Yasna 28: initial supplication of the poet; text by Uesugi and Catt (2024) and English translation of its gloss Yasna 28–34: Lexical distinction — In this section, aša should not be automatically equated with “law” or with an abstract principle identical in all stanzas: depending on the syntactic construction, it can approximate truth, righteousness, or just order. The Spanish interpretation must respect number, case, and context of each occurrence. Similarly, vohu manah is an inflected phrase and not an invariable doctrinal term in every instance. Yasna 30.3–5: Semantic difficulty— The pair of spirits and the verbs of choosing must be studied in relation to the Old Avestan of each stanza. The dualistic Pahlavi ontology of Late Antiquity should not be projected unmediated onto the entire hymn. The modern English gloss and historical versions serve as interpretive controls, not as independent manuscript witnesses. In the pair hudā̊ ŋhō / duždā̊ ŋhō, the glosses “munificent” and “misers” of Uesugi– Catt correspond to “generous” and “miserly” (or “of generous disposition” / “stingy”).
