In the Avestan segment aṣ̌ ā vīspə̄ṇg š́iiaoθanā, vīspə̄ṇg agrees with š́iiaoθanā (“all actions”): the gloss “for all beings” is not adopted, because it introduces a referent that that sequence does not express. The syntactic function of š́iiaoθanā and the segmentation of the sentence continue to admit alternatives in modern translations; For this reason, the entire stanza is not transformed into a supposedly definitive version. Reference translation: C. Bartholomae, Die Gatha’s des Awesta (1905), Y. 28.1; base edition of the book: H. Uesugi and A. A. Catt, Old Avestan Dictionary (2024), part II. Y 28, the first hymn of the Gāthā Ahunauuaitī, is a prayer by the poet to Ahura Mazdā and the Aməša Spəṇta, and contains two passages of interest to the book. The first is Y. 28.5, where the mąθra- (“sacred word,” “incantation”) appears as a means of approaching the god. The second is Y. 28.11, which relates the voice and mouth of Mazda to the origin of the first existence (ahu- paouruiia-), an obscure passage that does not authorize speaking of a “creative word” in the strict sense, although it is mentioned in the bibliography on the logos (chapter XXXIV). Y. 28.7 names Vištāspa, the protector of Zarathustra, and Y. 28.8 Frašaoštra, his disciple. Readings. The readings of the basic edition are followed in these texts. The forms that deviate from the commonly used transcription are: paouruuīm and paouruiiē (Y. 28.1; 30.3; 30.4; 30.7) instead of pouruuīm and pouruiiē, that is, the spelling with -ao-; mainiiə̄ uš (Y. 28.1), with +, that is, amended; srəuuīmā (Y. 28.7); aγžōnuuamnəm (Y. 28.3); pərəsamnə̄ ṇg (Y. 30.6); The separation of enclitics (hiiat̰ cīt̰ , aṣ̌ āat̰ cā) and preverbs (ādəbaomā) and the compound gə̄ uš.āiš (Y. 30.2). Furthermore, the spelling ṣ̌ of the previous transcription is replaced by š where the Uesugi and Catt edition does so. Readings that the dictionary itself classifies as disputed are marked in the text.

COMPARISON GUIDE — Y. 31.8. The stanza calls Mazdā “father of Good Thought” (ptarə̄m manaŋhō) and “creator of aša” (aṣ̌ ahiiā dąmīm). The English translation retains the Avestan form, but this Gathic predication should not be presented on its own as an exposition of a fixed hierarchy of seven divine entities: such a systematization requires later evidence and its own dating. Y 31 is the second hymn of the Gāθā Ahunauuaitī and contains three passages relevant to the book. First, Y. 31.3 and 31,19: fire (ātar-) figures as an instrument of judgement (“the satisfaction that you grant through the spirit and the fire”, “by your reddish fire, O Wise One, in the distribution of the balance”); it is the clearest ancient Avestan attestation of fire as an agent of judgement, which is linked with the metal ordeal evoked in Y. 32.7 and, with a distinct adjective supporting “molten metal”, in Y. 51.9 and with the judicial fire of later Jewish texts (e.g., Isa 66:15–16; Dan 7:10). Second, Y. 31.8: Mazdā is “father of good thought” (ptarə̄m manaŋhō), the formula of divine paternity discussed in connection with Vohu Manah as “son” of Ahura Mazdā. Third, Y. 31.20 and 31,17: the retribution for “spiritual vision” (daēnā-) and the aša-/druj- opposition, discussed in chapter XXX. Text 11. The translation is based on the gloss by Uesugi and Catt, supported by the gloss in the Old Avestan Dictionary, and marks verses where the proposals diverge with “uncertain reading.” In 32:8, the reading of Uesugi and Catt (“swearing by God”) is followed, which differs from the traditional reading (Yima as the giver of beef). The phrase xᵛaēnā aiiaŋhā is constructed with an instrumental element (“with incandescent metal / by means of glowing metal”). The locus does not contain a form that alone necessitates translating it as “molten metal”: that description belongs to other formulations and traditions of the ordeal. The Old Avestan Dictionary (Uesugi–Catt 2024, Y. 32.7) glosses “glowing metal”; this should not be equated with the vocabulary of Y. 51.9 without verifying its distinct adjective. This distinction is important for the chapter on fire, but it does not document an identical ritual at the court of Darius I. Text 12. Textual criticism —Y. 29.1–2. The translation “soul -breath of the cow” for gə̄uš uruuan- and the voice of denunciation in Y. 29.1 are retained. “Cow” should not be quietly equated with “world,” nor should the shepherd’s language be taken as evidence of an Achaemenid administrative institution. The hymn personifies suffering and the search for protection; its ritual, pastoral, and allegorical scope is debated from different interpretations. The English column is a scholarly translation based on Uesugi–Catt (2024), not a new reading of a codex. See William W. Malandra, “Gōšurun,” Encyclopaedia Iran ica XI/2 (2002): 176–177; Helmut Humbach, “Gāthās i. Texts”, Encyclopaedia Iranica X/3 (2000). Exegetical Control — Y. 29.8–9. The recognition of Zarathustra in Y. 29.8 as the recipient of the teaching should not be confused with the unequivocal acceptance of his sufficiency as protector: the complaint continues in Y. 29.9. This sequence is crucial for not reading the hymn as a complete presentation of the cosmic saviour of later Iranian traditions. The translation of the verse is not altered: the explanation of the dramatic movement conveyed by the hymn is added. Cf. Malandra, “Gōšurun” (2002), and Uesugi– Catt, Old Avestan Dictionary (2024), Part II, Y 29. Separation of strata—Y 29 and the Pahlavi reception. The Gōšurun of the Bundahišn, associated with the primordial bull and Middle Iranian cosmogony, belongs to a literary tradition of much later transmission and redaction. The correspondences with gə̄uš uruuan- show reception and reworking of motifs, but do not authorize transferring the complete medieval narrative to the period of Darius I. The levels are compared separately: Gathic hymn; Pahlavi reworking; historical reconstruction. See Malandra, “Gōšurun,” especially its references to Bundahišn 22 and 46. Ah, I ask about this: those who carve pleasures for these, for whom the karapan and the usij deliver the cow to fury, and what the kauui howls to the wind. They do not lead it to encourage the pasture with the aša. Yasna 44 is a series of questions to Ahura Mazdā about the origin of asha, the course of the sun and stars, the support of the earth, light and darkness, sleep and waking, and about the punishment of the deceiver (44:1–20). Verse 20 mentions the karapans, the usij, and the kauui. Study translation; several verses are of uncertain reading. I know the One who conceived it, the father of invigorating good thought. Ah, His daughter is Righteousness of thought, which brings about good deeds. Hermeneutical notes and historical comparison 1. Y. 44.3–5 and cosmic causality. The poem successively inquires about the asha, the movements of the sun, stars, and moon, the support of the earth, atmospheric agents, and the alternation of light, darkness, sleep, and wakefulness. The interrogative structure authorizes the study of a theology of cosmic order; it does not establish, without in termediate evidence, either a doctrine of creation ex nihilo or an Iranian-biblical genealogy of Genesis 1. The questions in 44:3–4 must be compared with the specific dating of each Hebrew passage, not with the historical context chosen as the argument of the monograph. 2. Y. 47.6 and judgement by fire. The reading “balance” is based on the lexical solution adopted by Uesugi–Catt for rānōibiiā, but the gloss recognizes an alternative semantic field. The image combines fire, distribution, weight, ārmaiti and aša; it does not, by itself, contain the narrative apparatus of the Pahlavi eschatological ordeal. In the comparison with Daniel 12 and with Christian texts, the following are distinguished: (a) what is expressed in the verse; (b) the later Iranian development; (c) the contact hypothesis, which requires separate transmission routes and datings.

ANCIENT AVESTAN AND PERSIAN PASSAGES 621 3. Y. 51.18, Jāmāspa and xvarənah. The nominal mention of Jāmāspa Hvōguuā informs about the networks represented in the Gathic composition, but does not in itself equate to a contemporary historical inscription of Darius I. Nor is there an automatic semantic continuity between xᵛarənah, the titles of the Achaemenid king and the later formulations of royal glory: each step requires datable evidence and a linguistic compar ison, not just modern translation equivalents such as “glory” or “power”. 4. Y. 53.2–4, persons and verb forms. The reading of 53.2 distinguishes the name of the kavi Vištāspa, the disputed relationship expressed by zaraθuštriš and Frašaoštra; these references belong to the universe of the hymn, not to an independently corroborated Achaemenid prosopography. In 53.3 the second singular imperatives are addressed to Pouručistā; translating them in the plural would erase this change of addressee. Grammatical correctness does not decide, without analysis of 53.4–7, whether the whole is a marriage liturgy, a wisdom instruction, or a composition with different rhetorical layers. 5. Degrees of certainty: A = presence and location of the verse in the tables of chapter XLIII; B = grammar / form according to the published edition of Uesugi–Catt; C = interpretive English translation with alternatives; D = hypothesis of interreligious transmission that still requires external data. The change to singular in Y. 53.3 is classified B; the “balance” of 47:6 remains C; the direct derivation of the Jewish final judgement from that verse would be D, not an established result. In Y. 30.3, the adjectives hudāŋhō and duždāŋhō are read as “of good/bad action” or “of good/ bad gift.” For Y 30 (text 7), Kanga’s Parsi gloss reads humązdrā (30,1), translates avaēnatā as “meditate” and takes aiiaŋhā (30,7) as the verbal form of i-, “to go, to come,” while other readings see in it the instrumental of ayah-, “metal,” and an allusion to the test of molten metal; that test appears more clearly in Y. 32.7 and 51,9, where metal is mentioned. ANCIENT AVESTAN AND PERSIAN PASSAGES 623 5. Philological commentary The philological commentary on the Ahuna Vairya addresses three issues. The first is the meaning of ahu- and ratu-, which the Pahlavi tradition interprets as the two “lords,” the spiritual and the temporal, and which modern criticism reads in other ways (Y 19 contains the Avestan commentary on the prayer; chapter XXXIV). The second is the relationship between mąθra- and the prayer as a “primordial word” (Mąθra Spəṇta), which serves as a point of comparison for the discussion of logos and the Vedic Vāc. The third is the position of Mazdā and Ahura in the formula, which precedes the joining of both names. In Y. 30.3, the central issue is that of the “twins” (yəmā, cf. ved. yamá- and the name of Yima/Yama) and their relation to ethical dualism: the verse does not say that the spirits were created by Ahura Mazdā, nor that they were his children, as later sources and the Zurvanite discussion will say (chapter XXIX, section 6). The two inscriptions of Darius (texts 4 and 5) are the historical counterpoint to the Avestan texts. Auramazda appears as “great god” and creator of earth, heaven, man, and happiness (shiyati-), with no further mention of Zoroaster or the Gāthās; the formula DNa is one of the oldest securely dated declarations of a creator god in the Iranian world. Two consequences for the book. First, the phraseology is compatible with the monotheism of Isaiah 45:7 and with the “God of heaven” of Ezra (chapter 17), although the comparison is one of type (typological similarity) and not of dependence. Second, the king is the mediator: Darius is king by the will of Auramazda, and in Behistun his legitimacy is opposed to the drauga- (chapter XXX, section 9). The Ašəm Vohū (text 3) allows us to see, in Avestan, the term ašawhich Old Persian gives as arta-. 6. Scope of these texts for the hypothesis of influence on Judaism and Christianity The liturgy provides a concrete object of comparison, not merely similarities formulated by the interpreter. In Y XVI.7, the better existence of the righteous appears linked to the souls of the dead; in Y XVIII.1–7, the reuse of LI.7 and XLVII.1–6 preserves the vocabulary of integrity, immortality, spirit, right disposition, action, and word. Their repetition in a liturgical context shows that these terms operate within a tradition of recitation, veneration, and religious memory. The contrasting translations of the dossier

624 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM for XI and XVI–XVIII allow for a comparison of the cited units. The comparative use of these passages depends, however, on distinguishing the Gathic stratum from the liturgical framework that reuses them and on not attributing the same date to both. For Judaism, the vocabulary of judgement, restoration, and the life of the righteous offers a field of comparison with prophetic and apocalyptic texts; for Christianity, it allows for contrasting developments received through Jewish traditions with formulations of salvation and immortality. Therefore, its positive contribution lies in documenting the Iranian repertoire that a contact hypothesis must explain, and in defining which of its components can be compared. The transition to a historical influence also requires compatible dating, a context of circulation, and features whose combination is not better explained by their own traditions or by the shared cultural background. And XVI.7 does not in itself amount to a declaration of bodily resurrection; and XVIII.7, read by Uesugi- Catt in terms of fire, distribution, and scales, does not demonstrate that an image of Jewish judgement derives from that verse. The divergence of interpretation of rānōibiiā prevents constructing proof of transmission based on the word “scales” alone. The prayer concerning the rule of Ahura Mazdā in XI.12–13 belongs to an Iranian ritual context, and its comparison with the kingdom of God requires working the biblical expressions within their own contexts. Thus, these testimonies strengthen the textual basis for a possible, layered influence; the causal degree of each re lationship remains open to further testing. Chapter Conclusion The repertory brings together ancient Avestan and Persian texts that must be cited by their locus, as well as by their internal number. A translation based on a modern gloss, a translation from an English version, and an interpretation of a transliteration do not have the same scope. Maintaining this traceability is necessary so that the reader can evaluate each argument. Summary The chapter contains the seventeen Gathic hymns and selections of prayers, Yašts, Vendīdād, and inscriptions. Chapter XLIV. Edition 7. Plutarch, De Iside et Osiride 46–49 and De E apud Delphos 20 Chronological context. Plutarch, 1st–2nd centuries CE, and earlier sources that he cites or reworks. His account of Magi and dualism belongs to a Roman-era Greek reception, not to an Achaemenid inscription. Greek text: Bernardakis (Teubner, 1889), as reproduced in Perseus (CC BY-SA 4.0). The English text is a study translation. 1. Introduction to the text On Isis and Osiris (Moralia 351C– 384C) is a treatise by Plutarch (c. 100–120 CE) addressed to Clea, a priestess of Delphi, on the myth of Isis and Osiris. Chapters 45–49 contain the most extensive exposition in Greek of a dualism attributed to Zoroaster and the Magi, specifically the Oromazes, Areimanius, and Mithras, and compare it with the dualisms of Heraclitus, Empedocles, the Pythagoreans, Anaxagoras, Aristotle, and Plato, concluding that Egyptian theology conforms to this philosophy. Plutarch relies on an intermediate source: he cites Theopompus (4th century BCE) for successive three-thousand-year dominions and a further interval of struggle (De Iside 47), which cannot be collapsed into the later Pahlavi twelve-millennium scheme. The text, which is the most detailed Greek source of the myth of the battle between two principles, should not be read as a faithful trans mission of the Avesta, but as a Greek interpretation of Iranian material.220 2. Expanded philological commentary The commentary on the Greek passages must distinguish between the names used by Plutarch, the source he attributes to another author, and the philosoph ical interpretation with which he organizes his exposition. Oromazes, Areimanius, and Mitres belong to a Greek account of Persian religion; the equi valence of names with Iranian entities does not guarantee a complete equivalence of functions. References to Theopompus attest to a Greek tradition concerning the Magi. This testimony does not constitute a channel of transmission to Judaism. For the historical argument, both the date of the cited author and the distance between Plutarch’s testimony and the Achaemenid events must be considered. Θεόπομπος and the 3000 years Theopompus of Chios (fourth century BCE; fragments discussed under FGrHist 115 F 64b–65) is cited indirectly in Plutarch, De Iside et Osiride 47. The transmitted account speaks of one divine power prevailing for three thousand years, then the other for three thousand years, followed by a further three thousand years of mutual struggle and the final disappearance of Hades. The sequence as narrated therefore comprises three successive three-thousand-year stages, not merely a total of six thousand years. The later Pahlavi scheme of twelve thousand years in four three-thousand-year periods belongs to a distinct textual and doctrinal setting. With this passage, Plutarch defines the aeon as a present without before or after, proper to the divine. The contrast with the dualism of De Iside is instructive: there, time is the stage for a struggle between two principles (two alternating three-thousand-year dominions and a further three-thousand-year struggle attributed to Theopompus (De Iside 47)), and here the aeon is the mode of being of the one god, without mixture. Chapter Conclusion Plutarch offers the most complete Greek exposition of the dualism attributed to Zoroaster and the Magi: Oromazes and Areimanius, Mithras as mediator, propitiat ory and apotropaic sacrifices, and a succession of three thousand years’ worth of periods taken from Theopompus. It is a testament to the reception of Greek thought in the Roman era, mediated by sources from the fourth century BCE and by the author’s own philosophy; it does not describe the religion of the Achaemenid court. De E apud Delphos 20, with its timeless aeon, and the passages from Pompey and Alexander concerning Olympus and natural fires complete the dossier without altering its status. Summary The chapter edits and translates De Iside et Osiride 46–49 and De E apud Delphos 20, with Pompey 24.5 and Alexander 35.1–2 as a supplement. It separates Theopompus’s account from Plutarch’s elaboration and establishes the value of the text as a Greek reception, not as an Achaemenid source.

Later customs must not silently be assigned to the Persian period. The Mazdean funerary ritual and the towers of silence, and the etymological and ecdotic comparison of key terms in Iranian, Indian, Greek, Hebrew, and Aramaic. Chapter XLV. Towers of Silence (Dakhma): Funerary Ritual, Classical Sources, and Architecture The evidence considered here ranges from classical accounts of Iranian funerary practice to late Zoroastrian and Parsi documentation. Surviving dakhmas and modern ritual manuals cannot by themselves establish the architecture or precise observances of Achaemenid funerary rites. 1. Approach and vocabulary This chapter examines the Zoroastrians ‘ disposal of their dead, specifically the display of the corpse in an elevated structure called a dakhma (in English, “Tower of Silence”), and brings together three types of sources: Avestan and Pahlavi texts that establish the norm, Greek and Latin authors who describe the practice from an external perspective, and ethnographic descriptions of towers in Iran and India. The topic belongs to material culture rather than doctrine, but it is relevant to the book for two reasons. First, the funerary ritual is the point at which the idea of purity (aša-, nasu-) becomes architecture and gesture, and allows us to compare Mazdaism with the Yahwism of the Persian period, which treats the corpse as the ultimate source of impurity (Num 19) but buries it. Second, it is one of the few Mazdaean features described by an author of the Achaemenid period (Herodotus), thus offering an ancient and independent attestation. The vocabulary needs precision. The Avestan daxma- designates a place for the dead, and its etymology is disputed (Bartholomae, AirWb); in the Parsi tradition, dakhma is the general word for “receptacle of the dead” (Modi, The Religious Ceremonies and Customs of the Parsees, J.B. Karani’s Sons, 1937, p. 56 n. 1). The English expression Tower of Silence is modern: Modi, following Sir George Birdwood, attributes it to the Oriental translator for the Bombay government, Robert X. Murphy (circa 1832), who would have combined the round shape of the structure with the Persian khāmūsh (“silent”) applied to the dead. A distinct term is the Pahlavi astōdān (“receptacle of bones,” from ast-, “bone”), the ossuary where the defleshed and dried bones are deposited; it should not be confused with the tower, which is the place of display. The central Avestan passage is Vendīdād 6,44–51, and 643

The Aves Standard The Vendīdād (“law against the daēuuas”) contains the most extensive part of the regulations concerning the dead. Within this normative framework, the contact of the corpse with earth, fire, or water presents problems of ritual contamination; the textual prescriptions must be distinguished from the historical diversity of funerary practices. According to the law, the corpse should be exposed to birds and dogs in a high place so that the sun dries it and the animals “devour” the flesh, and the bones are then collected in an ossuary. The first is the recitation of the Gāθā Ahunauuaitī with the corpse present: these are the same hymns that appear in Chapter XLIII (Y. 28.30, and 31), so that the oldest text in the Avestan corpus accompanies, in Parsi practice, the most domestic moment of life. The second is the omnipresence of the number two (bearers, priests, attendants in pairs), which Modi explains as a sign of solidarity. The third is the fire that is kept burning for three days at the site of the body, which reinforces the function of fire as a purifying element (Chapters XXVIII and XXX). 5. The architecture of the towers Modi reproduces a description of a Bombay tower by Nusserwanji Byramji, secretary of the Parsi Panchayat, which serves as the basis for the following summary. The tower is a massive, round stone structure built on a hilltop or in an isolated location. It is accessed by steps and an iron gate, secured with a metal padlock, to a circular platform of large cemented stone slabs, about 300 feet (90 m) in circumference, divided into three concentric rows of shallow receptacles (pāwi). The outer row receives the bodies of men, the middle row those of women, and the inner row those of children; the three rows are symbolically associated with the three precepts of good thought, good speech, and good deed (humata, hūxta, huuarəšta). In the centre is a circular pit (bandār) about 150 feet in circumference, where the bones are thrown once dried and where, according to the description, they “crumble into powder.” Rainwater that passes through the pit is channeled through four underground drains to four wells and filtered through layers of sand, charcoal, and sandstone, so that the infiltrating water does not contaminate the ground. Outside the tower,

650 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM within the enclosure, is a small structure called a sagri where a sacred fire, or at least a lamp, burns day and night. The construction is accompanied by religious ceremonies (excavation, laying of the foundations, consecration), and the tower is only opened to the public after the consecration. Modi insists that the entire design serves a hygienic and egalitarian purpose: bodies are unclothed, rich and poor are exposed in the same way, and con tamination of the land, water, and fire is avoided. This sanitary interpretation is that of a Parsi priest and scholar from the late 19th and early 20th centuries; historical criticism prefers to read the practice from the perspective of ritual purity (nasu-) rather than hygiene. The towers in Iran In Iran, the dakhma of Yazd, Kerman, and other locations (Tehran, near Rey) have been described in ethnographic and travel literature since the 19th century (Boyce, A Persian Stronghold of Zoroastrianism, Clarendon Press, 1977, and in Stausberg, 2004). They have a different form from the towers of Bombay. They are not tall towers with an interior platform, but rather circular enclosures with low stone or mudbrick walls, built on the summits of arid hills outside the city, with an interior stone floor and a central hollow for bones; the distance from the town and the eleva tion of the site correspond to the norm in Vd 6:44–45. They are recognizable from afar by their position on the hill and by the ritual path leading up to them. The dakhma of Yazd are now ruins visited as heritage sites. For the ancient periods, information is indirect. Rock-hewn ossuaries (astōdān) are known from Fars (near Naqš-e Rostam and Persepolis) and other sites in Iran, dating to the Sasanian period, as well as decorated terracotta ossuaries from Khwarezm and Sogdiana (Samarkand, Panjikent, 6th – 8th centuries CE). These ossuaries show that, at least during the Sasanian period, defleshed bones were preserved in special containers, in accordance with the Avestan rule against contaminating the land and water. No definitively identified Achaemenid dakhma has been found (Stausberg 2002–2004). 6. Biblical and Jewish parallels and contrasts The comparison with the Yahwism of the Persian period must be made with caution. In both systems, the corpse is a major source of impurity: in Numbers 19:11–

THE TOWERS OF SILENCE (DAKHMA) 651 22, the person who touches a dead body becomes impure for seven days and must be sprinkled with the “water of purification” (ashes of the red heifer) on the third and seventh days; the Vendīdād prescribes washings with gomēz and water and the barašnūm ceremony (chapter XXXVI, sec. 3). It is a remarkable typological parallel, but the two systems differ in essence: Israel buries its dead in the ground and on the same day when possible (Deut 21:22–23; Tob 1:17–19 and 2:3–7, where burying the dead is an act of piety), whereas Zoroastrianism sees burial as a profanation of the land. Ezek 39:11–16 contains a similar image in vocabulary, though not in practice: after the defeat of Gog, the men search for the scattered bones, mark them so that no one will touch them, and bury them to “purify the land” (Ezek 39:12, 16). There is no indication of contact: Ezekiel is an exile, and the interest in bones and in the purity of the land is explained by the internal logic of priestly law. A second contrast concerns the fate of the soul during the first three days. The Parsi tradition states that the soul remains with the body for three nights (Hādōxt Nask 2; Dhalla notes that the Jews believed the same, and refers to a rabbinic tradition according to which the soul hovers around the body for three days, and on the fourth departs; the rabbinic source, preserved in the Midrash Rabbah (Gn Rab. 100,7; Lv Rab. 18,1), is much later than the Persian period). The Gospel of John, in the story of Lazarus, emphasizes that he had already been dead for four days (John 11:39), a detail that has been linked to this belief. The connection is typological and based on later sources, and therefore does not warrant any conclusion of dependence. It should be added that there is no evidence that the Jews of the Persian period (Yehud, Samaria, Elephantine) exposed their dead; the archaeology of tombs in Yehud in the 5th and 4th centuries BCE shows burials in caves and pits, and the Aramaic papyri from Elephantine make no mention of exposure. The Qumran writings (Temple Scroll, 11QT 48,11–14) regulate cemeteries outside the holy city, in line with the priestly conception of impurity, not the Zoroastrian one. 7. A contemporary problem: vultures The practice of displaying carcasses poses an ecological problem today. In India, the vulture population (Gyps spp.) declined by more than 95% starting in the 1990s, and the cause was identified as diclofenac, a veterinary anti-inflammatory drug that contaminates livestock carcasses (Oaks et al., Nature 427 (2004): 630–633,

652 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM https://doi.org/10.1038/nature02317). The towers of Mumbai were left without birds capable of quickly consuming the bodies; the Parsi community experimented with concentrating solar panels to accelerate desiccation and created aviaries for breeding vultures, and the debate continues as to whether cremation or burial should be adopted. This problem, which is not from the period studied, clearly shows the link between ritual norm and ecological infrastructure, and serves to remind us that the “tower” only works with the element described by Herodotus and Strabo: the birds.223 8. Three-level evaluation Typological similarity. Zoroastrianism and Judaism share the idea that the corpse is the ultimate impurity and requires purification with water, a period of seven days or three to four days, and strict vigilance; this similarity is real but is explained by the logic of priestly purity, which exists in many cultures. Probable mediation. There is no probable mediation in the Persian period: there is no evidence that the Jews adopted the exposure of the body or that the Persians adopted Jewish burial; what does exist are contacts in the vocabulary of purity (chapter XXXVI), the extent of which must be measured separately. Demonstrable dependence. There are none: the sources that describe the exposition (Herodotus, Strabo) are Greek and establish no connection with Judaism, and those that describe the modern tower (Modi) are from the 20th century. What the texts do allow us to do is date the practice of the Magi to at least the 5th century BCE, attribute it in principle to the Magi and not to all Persians, and recognize that its generalization and its architecture are from a later period. Chapter Conclusion The display of the dead is, among the features of Zoroastrianism, one of the best attested from outside (Herodotus I 140) and one of the latest in its architectural form (the towers and ossuaries). Vocabulary of various languages and stages: Old and Young Avestan, Old and Middle Persian, Biblical Hebrew and Aramaic, and Greek. Each cognate, loanword, or semantic comparison should be situated by its earliest attestation. Control of anachronistic objects — magical gems. An iconographic parallel only acquires historical value after establishing dating, provenance, archaeological context, function, and interpretive tradition. Anguiped- type gems, with names like Abrasax and Iao, predominantly belong to magical environments of the Roman imperial period and may be part of Greco-Egyptian, Jewish, and other repertoires. They do not, in themselves, authorize a direct genealogy from Achaemenid Iran nor an automatic identification of their figures with Zurvan, Mithra, or a Yahwist god. Árpád M. Nagy studies the anguiped in the Journal of Roman Archaeology (2015). The Fitzwilliam Museum dates gem CG 510 with Abrasax and Iao to the 3rd–4th centuries CE. The comparison will be of late antique reception, unless independent evidence of an earlier sequence is found. 1. Approach and method The chapter compares, in six languages and using criteria of textual criticism and historical philology, eight terms that the book uses constantly: architecture and architect, geometry, saviour, logos, purity, end of the world, and resurrection of the dead. The languages are Avestan (with Old Persian where attested), Old Indian (Vedic and Sanskrit) and Pali, Biblical Hebrew, Aramaic (Imperial and Biblical), and Greek. The purpose is twofold. On the one hand, to establish which words are cog nates (sharing an Indo-European origin, such as * pre * and *father *), which are loanwords (one language borrowing a word from another), and which are simply similarities. On the other hand, to take advantage of that distinction to assess the thesis that the Greek world received influence from the Achaemenid empire and formed words from it. Four criteria support the comparison. First, a regular phonetic correspondence: two forms are cognates if their sounds correspond according to established rules 655

656 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM (for example, the Indo-European ḱ da š or s in Indo-Iranian and k in Greek). Second, a plausible semantic correspondence. Third, chronology: a word attested in a 10thcentury CE text proves nothing about the 5th century BCE. Fourth, mediation: a borrowing requires a historical channel (the Persian administration, the court of Sardis, Aramean merchants). False friends are also noted — that is, pairs that sound alike but are unrelated. Regarding Pali, its status needs to be clarified. It is a Middle Indo-Aryan language (Praktic), in which the canon of Theravada Buddhism was written down (1st century BCE onward, according to the Sri Lankan tradition); it is not an “older” language than Vedic Sanskrit, and it serves here to show how an Indo-Aryan term evolved outside the Vedic sphere. The Avestan forms of the Gāthās are taken from the Old Avestan Dictionary (Uesugi and Catt, ILCAA, 2024), which also provides the Vedic parallels. 2. Architectural nomenclature allows for the comparison of texts that designate materials, rigging, measuring instruments, porticoes, halls, and spaces of worship. Furthermore, three frameworks are separated: (a) Hebrew and Aramaic from biblical texts, with special attention to Ezra; (b) Classical and Hellenistic Greek, which the Jewish corpus receives through translation and contact; and (c) Iranian, documented epigraphically, without substituting Old Persian for Avestan or transferring Talmudic terms to the 6th–5th centuries BCE.

Hellenic vocabulary and late rabbinic register The Greek terminology ἀρχιτέκτων (arkhitéktōn), στοά (stoá), περίστυλον (perístylon) and βασιλική (basilikḗ) designates offices and buildings from different registries. Achaemenids: the apadāna and the architectural inscription of Susa The Old Persian word apadāna constitutes a distinct case from Hellenisms. Epigraphic research identifies the term in inscriptions of Darius II and Artaxerxes II, including D²Sa and A²Sa / A²Hb, while the monumental type of hypostyle hall already existed under Darius I. This distinction avoids a major anachronism: dating the architectural form to the reign of Darius I does not allow us to assert that the word is preserved in an inscription of that sovereign. Later parallels in Palmyrene Aramaic, Talmudic Aramaic, and other languages of the region prove the late circulation of the name, but they do not constitute contemporary evidence from the 6th century BCE. The foundation inscription DSf of Darius I, transmitted in Old Persian, Babylonian, and Elamite versions, is a document far more directly relevant to the technical circulation of materials and specialists. It lists excavation and mudbrick making, the provenance of timber, stone, and metal, and regional groups of workers. The inscription attributes stonework to Ionians and Lydians, brickwork to Babylo nians, and other labor to Egyptians and Medes. It is a royal representation of imper ial cooperation that can be examined as an ideological and constructive source; it does not, in itself, constitute a complete list of all the workers employed. The chain of proof consists of: (1) the type of monument excavated and dated; (2) the identified ancient inscription and editions of its linguistic versions; (3) the technical noun in the text of that inscription; and (4) possible lexical continuity in

Avestan lexicon of construction Avestan does not preserve a treatise on construction, but it does have a vocabulary of houses, enclosures, and load-bearing elements, almost always in religious or omitic contexts. Mahsa Hashemi and Hossein Najari (2015) compiled some forty words with their loci and etymologies. Their repertoire is used here as a starting list; each cited locus was compared with Peterson’s Avestan text on Geldner (Yt 10; Y 57) or with Darmesteter’s translation (Vd 2, 3, 8, and 15, in SBE 4; Yt 5, in SBE 23). The central locus is Yt. 10.28: Mithra “holds up the columns (stunå) of the high-framed house (berezimitahe nmânahe)” and “makes the posts firm (ãithyå)”; in the same stanza, against those who offend him, he “tears down” (sciñdayeiti) other houses. nmāna-, “house”, is the general word and the first of the series nmāna-, vīs-, zantu-, dahyu-. Y. 57.21 describes the dwelling of Sraoša as hazangrô -stûnem, “of a thousand columns”, self-illuminating within and starry without. Yt. 5.101 gives to the palaces of Anāhitā “a hundred windows” (raocana-) and “a thou-

666 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM sand columns”. In Vd. 2.30 and 2,38, Yima closes the vara- with a door (dvar-) and a window “self-illuminating from within”. Hashemi and Najari’s repertoire also records pairi.daēza-, “enclosed space” (Vd. 3.18: “they will build an enclosure”), the origin of the Greek parádeisos and the Hebrew pardēs; uz.daēza-, “wall” (Vd. 15.36: “who built the wall”); ištiia-, “brick” (Vd. 8.8: “dust of bricks, stones, or dry earth”); and aspō.stāna- and gaō.stāna-, “horse stable” and “ox stable” (Vd. 15.26). The four loci are read thus in Darmesteter’s translation. The article serves as an inventory of loci, not as an etymological authority, and three points are corrected here. First, dəmāna- / nmāna- does not come from a root * men-, “to remain,” but from *dem-, “to build; house” (Vedic dá m-, Greek dómos, Latin domus), and nmāna- is the reduced form. Second, stūnā- designates the “column,” not the “beam,” as shown by Gershevitch’s translation of Yt. 10.28, which the article itself cites. Third, Kaŋhā in Yt. 5.54 is a toponym (according to Darmesteter’s note, a city founded by Siyāvaxš on a mountaintop), not a noun meaning “bronze.” The journal that published the work is not a specialized organ in Iranian studies; its etymologies are contrasted with Bartholomae, Mayrhofer and Cheung, to whom the article refers. For the book’s architectural examination, this lexicon has a twofold value. It shows that Avestan had precise terms for support (stūnā-, ąiθiiā-), enclosure (uz.daēza-, pairi.daēza-), opening (dvar-, raocana-), and material (ištiia-). It also shows that these terms almost always describe Omitic celestial buildings: the abodes of Mithra, Sraošay, and Anāhitā, and the vara- of Yima. The “thousand columns” of these abodes do not describe Persepolis, although they evoke the same type of columned hall built by the Achaemenids. The comparison belongs to the history of architectural imagination and is not useful for dating the texts. 3.1.6. Critical conclusion and correspondences with the work as a whole The inventory allows us to support three conclusions. First, architecture documents contact between specialists in the Persian sphere, independent of any supposed diffusion of dogma: DSf and Achaemenid buildings provide verifiable evidence of material circulation. Second, Hebrew and Aramaic books preserve precise construction terms, especially in Ezra, useful for the history of technical language and for studying its Greek translations, but the sources do not allow us to automat

COMPARATIVE PHILOLOGY 667 ically equate each word with a recovered archaeological technique. Finally, Euclid, Greek building terms, and rabbinic terminology belong to different chronological scales. The absence of a specialized geometric term in a small corpus does not demonstrate a technical incapacity on the part of its speakers. Forms without identifiable locus, edition or transmission tradition do not enter the table of ancient words affirmed as certain. This section, with the Avestan lexicon of 3.1.5, expands on the architectural part of chapter XLVI and relates to chapters VIII (inscriptions of Darius), XXVIII (cult sites and architecture), XLIX (Achaemenid, Parthian, and Sasanian buildings), LIII (comparative lexicon), and the appendix to Ezra. Comparative research gains value if the correlation between term, monument, witness, dating, and edition takes the place often given to mere phonetic similarity. Greek sōtḗr and Avestan saošiiaṇt- are similar in sound and final meaning (“the one who saves”), but they are not cognates: Greek sôs (“healthy”) comes from an Indo-European root *tewh₂- (“to be strong”), and Avestan su- from * ḱewh₁- (“to swell”), whose Greek cognate is kyéō (“to be pregnant”, Beekes and Mayrhofer). There are two distinct roots that converged, independently, on the religious meaning of “the one who saves”. Furthermore, the reading of saošiiaṇt- as “saviour” is secondary: in the Gāthās, according to Uesugi and Catt, the sense is “the one who will strengthen, benefactor” (thriver), and the meaning “saviour” is based on the recent Avestan and the Pahlavi tradition (sōšāns). This coincides with what was said in chapter XXXVII (sec. 8) about the Saošyant. For Hebrew, the verb hôšîaʿ (“to save”) and the noun môšîaʿ are well documented from the Psalms and the Prophets, and in the Persian period the title “saviour” is applied to God (Isaiah 43:3, 11; 45:15, 21). In Pali, the central concept is not salvation by a third party, but liberation (mokkha, vimutti) through one’s own efforts; however, the future Buddha Metteyya (Sanskrit Maitreya, from mitra-, “friend”) offers a debated eschatological parallel to the Saošyant (the derivation of Maitreya from the Iranian Mithra is a minority hypothesis). The parallels are typological: three traditions imagine a future teacher or benefactor, without any demonstrable dependence. 5. The historical discussion is whether the idea came from Iran or Israel (chapter XXXVII), and the lexicon does not resolve that question. 8. Before the Achaemenids, Greeks and Iranians inherited numerous roots (tékhnē, métron, pitér, nómos ...) from a common Indo-European background, and the “Greco-Aryan” hypothesis, which posits a common phase for both branches, is defended by some linguists (W. Three-level evaluation Typological similarity. There are conceptual parallels: the deity as craftsman (Y. 29.6; Prov 8:30; Heb 11:10), a future benefactor or saviour (Saošyant, Metteyya, Messiah), purification with water, and an end that renews existence. Probable mediation. There is mediation in the vocabulary of administration (satrapy, dāt, pitgām, ganza), in that of measures (parasanga, artaba), and in that of the court (paradeisos, mágos); the channel is the empire. Demonstrable dependence. It is not demonstrated for any of the eight terms in this chapter: arkhitéktōn and tašan- are cognates, geōmetría is Greek, sōtḗr and saošiiaṇt- are false cognates, logos has no Iranian equivalent, and for “purity,” “end of the world,” and “resurrection,” the languages express the idea with their own roots. This conclusion, however modest it may seem, is the positive result of the chapter: it separates what is inherited, what is borrowed, and what only resembles it. Chapter XLVII. Mazdaism and Zoroastrianism: The Source of Achaemenid Religion and the Connotations of the Terms Chronological context. Achaemenid religion, 6th–4th centuries BCE, and later Arsacid and Sasanian changes. Mazdaism and Zoroastrianism are used with explicit historical definition, without making modern terminology a uniform ancient self-designation. Continuity and discontinuity of supports The expression “Achaemenid religion” must be constructed from inscriptions, administrative materials, and archaeology of the period, and not defined based on the normative synthesis of much later Pahlavi authors. Long-standing traditions surrounding Ahura Mazdā/Ohrmazd are certainly known, but changes in language, liturgical context, and institution prevent us from treating them as an immutable whole. It will be useful for the apparatus to distinguish four levels of argumentation: contemporary evidence, probable linguistic connection, suggestive structural parallel, and historiographical speculation. The classification does not invalidate a thesis of Iranian contacts, but rather allows us to show precisely where it is strongest and where it must remain provisional. Terminological control: antiquity of a language and antiquity of a doctrine. The Old Avestan Dictionary by Heindio Uesugi and Adam Alvah Catt (ILCAA, Tokyo University of Foreign Studies, 2024) provides a modern tool for analysing the lexicon of Old Avestan and a working edition with translations of the Gāthās. Its usefulness is fundamental to avoiding transferring later doctrinal definitions of Pahlavi Zoroastrianism into a Gathic form. Each etymological proposal must distinguish between attested form, morphological analysis, contextual semantic field, and Spanish equivalence; a similarity of meaning in Hebrew, Aramaic, or Greek does not demonstrate borrowing without phonology, chronology, and contact. The vocabulary of the Persian royal texts also constitutes a distinct corpus, fixed in inscriptions of a political-dynastic purpose. 679

680 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM 1. Approach: two words for a religion The book uses two names, Zoroastrianism and Mazdaism, sometimes as synonyms and sometimes as distinct. This chapter examines the distinction and poses the historical question it contains: Does the religion of the Achaemenid kings, who worshipped Auramazda, derive from the preaching of Zoroaster (and is therefore Zoroastrianism), or is it an older or parallel Iranian-Western religion, only later absorbed and reformulated by the Avestan tradition (and is therefore “Mazdaism” in the strict sense)? The question has no definitive answer. What can be done is to organize the evidence, name the models that scholars have proposed, and point out the connotations each word carries, because in this field the vocabulary itself already contains a thesis. The book’s triad applies. A typological similarity is a resemblance in structure without any claim to contact. A probable mediation requires a plausible historical channel. A demonstrable dependence requires a text that quotes or reproduces another. For the problem of the origin of Achaemenid Mazdaism, almost all the material is at the first two levels; the third is barely reached, and only in shared vocabulary. 2. MAZDAISM AND ZOROASTRIANISM 685 Model Thesis Arguments Difficulties B. Common Iranian Mazdaism There existed a religion of Auramazdā in southwestern Iran, predating or contemporaneous with Zoroaster, which he is said to have reformed in the east. Partial alignment with the recent Avesta; shared vocabulary; the Median magi as a priestly class (Hdt I 101) The language of the inscriptions (Old Persian) and that of the Gāthās (Avestan) are distinct dialects; there is no Persian text that corresponds to the Avesta C. Selective contact The court was familiar with Zoroastrian ideas but incorporated them into its own royal cult. Both the similarities (arta/aša, drauga / druj, daiva) and the differences are explained. It is an intermediate position; it cannot be refuted or proven with current sources. The case of the name Vištāspa warrants caution. Darius’s father, Hystaspes (Hdt I 209; in Old Persian Vištāspa-), bears the same name as Zoroaster’s protector in the Gāthās (Y. 46.14; 51,16). But the name is common throughout the Iranian world, and the two figures do not coincide in place or time, so the onomastic coincidence is an indication, not an identification. Similarly, the presence of a shared vocabulary does not prove that the Persians knew the Avesta: it proves that they shared an Indo-Iranian heritage. The linguistic argument deserves consideration. Old Persian is a dialect of southwestern Iran, and Avestan belongs to the northeast. If the Avesta had been transmitted in the Achaemenid court, we would expect quotations, and there are none. If Achaemenid Mazdaism were Zoroastrianism, we would expect mention of Zarathustra, and there is none either. This is why many scholars prefer to speak of “Achaemenid religion” or “Mazdaism” and reserve “Zoroastrianism” for the tradition that recognizes itself as the heir of Zarathustra. Others maintain that the Avestan tradition is the best available witness to what the court believed. The book adopts the prudent formulation: convergence, not proven affiliation. Documentary Silence and Genres of Evidence Silence about Zarathustra in a royal inscription carries a different weight from silence in a doctrinal treatise. Royal inscriptions legitimate sovereignty, enumerate territories and attribute victories to divine favour; they do not offer exhaustive inventories of belief. Nor does the linguistic difference between Old Persian and Avestan by itself exclude the circulation of prayers in a ritual language distinct from

Consequences for comparison with Yahwism If model A is accepted, Persian-period Yahwism would have come into contact with a religion of prophets, doctrine, and eschatology; if model B is accepted, with the cult of a court whose beliefs differed from those of the Avesta. The con sequences for the four sections of the book are different. In the Achaemenid section (5th – 4th centuries BCE), what is proven is political contact: Cyrus as the anointed one (Isaiah 45:1), the “God of heaven” of Ezra 1:2, the use of the formula in the Aramaic documents from Elephantine, and the Persian administrative vocabulary in late Hebrew and Aramaic. The book does not make these conclusions dependent on either model. In the Seleucid and Parthian courts, and in the time of Jesus, the presence of developed Zoroastrian ideas (resurrection, judgement, ordained angels) is more plausible, and the recent Avesta and Pahlavi books document them, but the dating of their content remains open.

What does condition it is the chosen word: speaking of “Achaemenid Zoroastrianism” implies a connection with the doctrine of Zarathustra that the inscriptions do not authorize, and speaking of “Mazdaism” without further explanation leaves the question open. 7. XV 3.15 and XI 8.4). The Avesta is transmitted in late manuscripts, and the daeuua of Vd. 10.9 and 19.43 (Indra, Sauruua, Naŋhai θiia) are editors ‘ readings. 8. Three-level evaluation Typological similarity. There is a similarity between the Auramazda of the inscriptions and the Ahura Mazdā of the Gāthās: a creator god, guarantor of order (arta-, asha-) and enemy of falsehood (drauga-, druj-). Probable mediation. The Persian court and the communities of Yehud and Elephantine share vocabulary, administration, and, in the case of Cyrus, a religious policy; the mediation is both political and linguistic. Demonstrable dependence. There is no quotation from the Gāthās in the inscriptions, nor a quotation from the Avesta in a biblical text. Dependence is only demonstrable in lexical loans (pitgām, dāt, pardēs) and none of them are theological. Chapter Conclusion Achaemenid Mazdaism and Avestan Zoroastrianism share a core vocabulary (God, order, falsehood, the rejection of the daivas) and differ in what each source omits. The evidence neither confirms nor denies that Darius or Xerxes were disciples of Zoroaster. The words Mazdaism and Zoroastrianism each carry a thesis, and the book uses them with this caveat: Mazdaism for the religion of Auramazda in a broad sense, and Zoroastrianism for the tradition that invokes Zoroaster. 231 Kent, 2nd ed; Schmitt, altpersischen Inschriften der Achaimeniden.

Chapter XLVIII. The Hierarchy of Forces: From Ahura Mazdā to Aŋra Mainyu and Their Indian and Biblical Cognates Chronological context. Hierarchies and vocabulary of Avestan sources and later Pahlavi developments; Vedic and biblical comparisons of independent dates. The list of forces does not constitute an invariable structure from the Persian period. 1. Approach: from the image of the pyramid to the texts The image of a “pyramid of forces” is modern and convenient, and useful if its limitations are remembered. No Avestan or Pahlavi text presents an organizational chart; what we find are lists, pairs of opposites, and narratives that, taken together, order spiritual beings into levels. This chapter reconstructs those levels from Ahura Mazdā to the material world, describes the opposing side headed by Anra Mainyu, and compares the structure with that of the Vedic and Buddhist worlds (as cultural comparativists, whose similarity alone does not prove a common Indo-Iranian heritage) and with the angelology and demonology of Second Temple Judaism. Three layers of sources are separated that should not be mixed: the Gāthās (ancient Avestan), the recent Avesta, and the Pahlavi books (here especially the Bundahišn, in West’s translation, SBE 5, with its numbering). A preliminary note. The correspondence between the Gāthā ethical personifications and the hierarchies of Pahlavi literature requires distinguishing textual phases. The Gāthās offer vocabulary about Ahura Mazdā, opposing spirits, and ethical dispositions, but not necessarily the same systematic organization as the Middle Iranian compilers. THE HIERARCHY OF FORCES 693 The structure also allows for a cosmological reading. According to the Bundahišn (I), Ohrmazd dwells in the boundless light above and Ahriman in the darkness below, with the void (wāy) between them; Ahriman, ignorant of the future, withdraws, defeated by the formula Ahunwar, for three thousand years, and during that time Ohrmazd creates (I 22-23). Their languages, Avestan and Vedic, are very closely related (one can often be switched between them using simple phonetic rules: Indian s for Hiran, ṛ for Ar, etc.), and they share names of gods, ritual terms, and social structures. Pali is a later, Middle Indo-Aryan language and preserves Vedic words with its own distinct evolution. A cultural cognate here refers to a figure or term that derives from a common heritage, even if its function has changed in each region. It does not imply borrowing between the historical Iranian and Indian worlds; it implies an earlier origin. Table 58. THE HIERARCHY OF FORCES 699 7. Three-level evaluation Typological similarity. There is a common structure of a supreme Lord, a group of seven beings surrounding him, intermediaries, guardians, and an adversary with his army. Probable mediation. Contact between Judaism and the Persian world could have transmitted the motif of the group of seven and the formulation of a final con flict between two spirits; mediation is compatible with the calendar and the political setting of the Second Temple. Demonstrable dependence. No Jewish text quotes the Avesta, and no Avestan text quotes the Bible. At the Indian level, cognates are common inheritance, not borrowing, and the relationship between Iran and India is explained by common Indo-Iranian heritage. Chapter Conclusion The Zoroastrian hierarchy (Ahura Mazdā, Spənta Mainyu, Aməša Spəṇtas, Yazatas, Fravašis, humanity) and its mirror image (Aŋra Mainyu, daēuuas, drujes) is not a single pyramid but a system of domains and opposites, which the Pahlavi texts bring to an almost perfect symmetry. Comparison with India reveals a common heritage (Mitra, Yama, Haoma/Soma, ṛta/aša) and a reversal of values in two key terms (ahura / asura, daēuua/deva). Comparison with Judaism shows a strong structural parallel and a probable mediation in later angelology, without demonstrable dependence. Approach and method This chapter explores the architecture associated with Mazdaism and Zoroastrianism in Iran and Iraq, comparing it to two worlds central to the book: the Western (Greek and Roman) and the Hebrew (the Temple of YHW on Elephantine Island and the synagogue). Five building types are examined: the royal tomb (Cyrus’s in Pasargadae, Darius’s in Naqš-e Rostam), the fire altar, the fire temple, the tower of silence (dakhma, studied in Chapter XLV, so only summarized here), and Jewish places of worship. The triad is applied: typological similarity (a similar form without direct contact), probable mediation (a plausible historical channel, such as the Greek artisans in Susa), and demonstrable dependence (a text or find that proves it). Something must be said about the prudence this subject demands. Pasargadae: the tomb of Cyrus and the testimony of Strabo n Pasargadae, Cyrus’s residence in the heart of Persia, preserves a stone tomb: a gabled chamber on a stepped base. Authors from Alexander’s time saw and described it, and Strabo (XV 3,7) transmits their accounts. Alexander saw “the tomb of Cyrus in a paradeisos (park), a small tower, hidden by the foliage of the trees, solid below and with a roof and a very narrow entrance chamber above.” Aristobulus, who entered by order of the king, saw “a golden bed, a table with cups, a golden coffin, many clothes and ornaments with precious stones”; later the tomb was looted, and the bed and coffin were broken, with the corpse moved. The Magi guarded it and received a sheep every day and a horse every month. Strabo also transmits versions of the epitaph. According to Aristobulus: “O man, I am Cyrus, who won the empire for the Persians and was king of Asia; do not envy me, then, for this monument.” According to Onesicritus (who speaks of a tenstory tower): “Here I lie, Cyrus, king of kings,” in a Greek inscription written with Persian letters, and another “Persian-like” one with the same meaning. Aristo of Salamis, later, describes it as having two stories. The discrepancies show that none of the three copied a surviving text: the inscription has not been found, and its authenticity is doubtful. What is certain is the presence of the Magi as guardians, which connects the tomb with the cult of the dead described by Herodotus (I 140): the Persians bury with wax; the Magi expose the corpses to the birds. The kings, therefore, are buried; the exposure, in the Greek testimony, is a custom of the Magi. 3. The tomb of Darius I is identified by the trilingual inscription DNa. Altars and temples of fire: from Cyrus to the Sasani The fire cult is the architectural feature most closely associated with Zoroastrianism, and also the most difficult to date. In the Achaemenid period, there are fire altars depicted in reliefs (the tomb of Darius) and two stone bases at Pasargadae, which have been interpreted as altars; but Herodotus (I 132) states that the Persians did not build altars or kindle fires for sacrifice, and that a covered cult structure is not reliably attested until much later. Towers of Silence: Summary The towers of silence (dakhma, Pahl. dakhmag) are roofless circular structures where corpses are exposed to vultures, according to the Vendīdād (Vd 3, 5, 6, and 8, discussed in chapter XLV). Classical sources attest to the practice of exposing corpses as a custom of the Magi from Herodotus (I 140) onward, and Strabo (XV 3,20; XI 11,3) records Bactrian variants. However, no Achaemenid tower has been found; the oldest surviving towers are late in date, and the elevated circular form visited today at Yazd is later. The Sasanian ossuaries (astōdān), small clay or stone containers for bones, and the Achaemenid royal rock tombs, show that the practice was not uniform and that exposure was not applied to all strata. 6. The Hebrew world: the temple of YHW in Elephantine and the synagogue For a strictly diachronic architectural comparison-from the Yahwist sanctuaries in Elephantine, Jerusalem and Garizim to the synagogues of the 1st century CE, versus the Iranian spaces of fire-see section 2 bis of chapter XXVIII. The distinction between Achaemenid, Seleucid-Parthian, and Sasanian evidence avoids attributing later Iranian architectural forms to the period of Jesus. On Elephantine, an island in the Nile opposite Aswan, there was a garrison of Judeo-Aramaic soldiers in the service of Persia in the 5th century BCE, with a temple dedicated to YHW. It was not a synagogue. The word synagogue (Greek synagōgḗ, “meeting,” from syn- and ágō) designates the assembly and, later, the building; in Hebrew it is bē tha- kĕneset. Elephantine, on the other hand, has a temple with a sacrificial altar, which the documents call in Aramaic ʾgwrʾ (“temple,” a word of Akkadian origin) and, in other passages, mśgdʾ (“place of worship,” from a root meaning “to bow down”; forms according to Porten and Yardeni, TAD). This last term is the origin of the Arabic masjid. The temple is known from a petition addressed in 407 BCE to the governor of Yehud, Bagohi (TAD A4.7), and from the reply (TAD A4.9). The petition states that the temple existed before Cambyses (525 BCE), that he destroyed the Egyptian temples but did not touch the temple of YHWH, and that in the 14th year of Darius II (410 BCE) the commander Vidranga, with the complicity of the priests of the Egyptian god Khnum, had it demolished. It describes the building: five gates of hewn stone, stone columns, doors with bronze hinges, a cedar wood roof, and gold and silver vessels. The temple had an altar of burnt offerings, and offerings of flour, incense, and burnt offerings were made there. The leaders of the community also wrote to the high priest in Jerusalem and to the sons of Sanballat in Samaria. The reply memorandum authorizes the rebuilding of the temple and the offering of flour and incense, but makes no mention of burnt offerings; this is a detail that

Three-level evaluation Typological similarity. The guarded fire (Vesta, Mazdaean fire), the prayer hall (synagogue, fire temple), and the tower-tomb (Cyrus, Lycia) share similar forms without any direct contact. Probable mediation. The Achaemenid palace and its decoration are the result of proven mediation: artisans from various peoples, the use of stone, columns, and staircases. The Persian authorization of the temple at Elephantine and the support for the one in Jerusalem are examples of political mediation. Demonstrable dependence. The Persian fire in Anatolia, with the Magi (Strabo, Pausanias), is a documented case of the establishment of a cult. However, there is no demonstrable dependence between Mazdaean architecture and the temple at Elephantine or the synagogue. Chapter Conclusion Mazdaean architecture is less monumental and later than the image of the “fire temple” suggests. The Achaemenid period is characterized by tombs and palaces; the fire temple as a building is clearly documented from the Parthian and Sasanian periods; the Towers of Silence have not been found from the Achaemenid period. The text on Darius’s tomb is a profession of royal ethics that coincides, in substance, with the epitaph that Strabo (Onesicritus) attributes to the king. In the Hebrew world, the temple at Elephantine is the clearest evidence of a cult of YHWH under Persian administration; the synagogue is a later and distinct develop ment.

Chapter L. Dēnkard, Book V: Ādurfarnbag, Kay Lohrasp and Prophetic History Chronological context. Dēnkard V, a Pahlavi compilation from after the Sasanian Empire, with older traditions. Kay Lohrasp belongs to the narrated religious history; he does not become, without proof, an identifiable historical contemporary of a biblical king. 1. The text: Dēnkard, book V The Dēnkard (“Acts of Religion”) is the largest Pahlavi encyclopedia of Zoroastrianism. Its compilation began in the 9th century and received a final redaction in the 10th century CE, with material that its compilers attribute to Ādurfarnbag ī Farroxzādān (circa 800–830 CE) and Ādurbād ī Ēmēdān (10th century CE). Book V (Dk V) is presented as a collection of Ādurfarnbag’s answers to questions from an interlocutor; the surviving summary of the book states that its remaining five-sixths are a miscellaneous collection of religious topics, “similar to a Rivāyat.” The four chapters discussed here are only the initial summary, not the complete book, and the known extracts from the book come from two translations. The commentary is based on the translation by E.W. West reproduced by avesta.org, whose header mistakenly identifies the fifth part of Pahlavi Texts with the volume number of Sacred Books of the East. The correct printed publication is: West, Pahlavi Texts, Part V, Sacred Books of the East 47 (Clarendon Press, 1897), which includes the beginning of Dēnkard V. Volume 37 of SBE (1892) belongs to a different part of the series and contains material from Dēnkard VIII– IX; its numbering should not be interchanged with that of volume 47. West’s readings are com pared with the version by Peshotan B. Sanjana reproduced by J.H. Peterson on avesta.org (digital edition, 1998; editorial introduction “Sanjana, 1900”). The divergences affect central terms (Table 64), but consulting published versions does not equate to a new reading of the Pahlavi codex; decisions requiring a handwritten witness remain expressly conditioned by that limitation. Kay Lohrasp, Nebuchadnezzar and Jerusalem Chapter 1 states that Kay Lohrasp, a king of the legendary Kayanid dynasty, was sent with Bukht-Narsih from Iran, the “holy house” of the West. The name BukhtNarsih is reminiscent of Bukhtnassar, the Arabic and Pahlavi form of Nebuchadnezzar, whom Tabari presents as a Babylonian governor appointed by Lohrasp and conqueror of Jerusalem (Tabari, trans. Bosworth). Sanjana’s note, however, identifies him with the warrior Reham Godrez. There is an obvious chronological problem here: Nebuchadnezzar II destroyed Jerusalem in 587/586 BCE, before the Persian Empire, and Lohrasp is not a historical figure, but an epic one. The Pahlavi and Islamic tradition integrated the fall of Jerusalem into its own legendary history. The book’s significance is twofold. First, it demonstrates that within the compilation period of the 9th and 10th centuries, a legendary memory of Jerusalem as the locus of their history circulated among Mazdaean communities, along with a narrative of catechesis or conquest in the West. Second, it is a late text (9th century), and therefore does not bear witness to the 5th century BCE: it belongs to the fourth section of the book, the Sasanian-Islamic. It does not prove that the Persians knew the Jews before Cyrus, but rather that medieval Zoroastrians rewrote that relationship. The reliable history of contact remains that of Cyrus and the Second Temple (Ezra 1; 6; Isaiah 45). 3. The prophets before Zoroaster and those to come Dk V 1,7–9 states that the religion was accepted before Zarathustra by “prophets, apostles, and acceptors” (in the West): Gayōmard, from whom come Mašyē and Mašyānē, Sīyāmak, Hōšang, Taxmōruw, Yim, Frēdōn, Manuščihr, Saman, and the Kayánidas. Zarathustra comes after, and there will come “new bearers”: Ušēdar, Ušēdarmā, and Sōšyans (2,15; 3,3). Thus, the series of revelations is a story with three periods: before Zarathustra, Zarathustra, and the three future sons. The struc ture resembles that of Judaism and Christianity (patriarchs, founding prophet, future messiah), and for this reason it is of interest for comparison. But the similarity

718 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM is typological: there is no text that cites the other, and the Pahlavi series is a development of the later Avesta (Yt 13, the Fravašis list). : glory, birth, temptation and resurrection Chapter 2 is a hagiographic summary. Zarathustra was “spiritually formed” in the light of the archangels, born of Pouruspasp and Dogdō with a splendor “like the brightness of fire” that reaches distant lands (2.1–2). Magicians and witches (pairikās), tyrants, Kigs and Karbs try to kill him, and throw him to the wild beasts, “only as a test” (2.3–4). In 2.5 it is said that he “laughed aloud at birth,” because he was received by Vohuman. This tradition of the smiling birth is attributed by Pliny (Natural History VII 72: Zoroaster is the only man of whom it is said that he laughed on the day he was born, and his brain throbbed so much that he rejected the hand that was placed upon him) to Zoroaster, so that Dk V provides a Pahlavi attestation of a motif already recorded by Latin authors. It is a case of cross-confirmation between Rome and Persia, although separated by centuries and a long transmission. In 2.6, Ahriman and many demons come to Zoroaster “with displays of fear, offerings of service, arguments, and supplications,” and leave “disapproved of, defeated, and confused” by the proclamation of the Avesta. This is the account that corresponds to Vd. 19.1–7 (the temptation of Zoroaster, discussed in a previous chapter). The comparison with Matthew 4.1–11 and Luke 4.1–13 remains typological: both are accounts of a teacher tempted by the cosmic adversary, who overcomes him with the revealed word. In the Pahlavi, there are neither the forty days, nor the mountain, nor the quotation from Scripture; only the general motif. In 2.8, Zoroaster declares before Vishtas that a person “possesses life only by destiny, and without his body, but with an equal destiny, the living person is restored” (West’s translation). This is one of the Pahlavi statements concerning the restoration of the body and enters into the discussion of the resurrection: it is the doctrine of the Frašegird in brief. It is a late text; it does not prove that the doctrine was taught in the 5th century BCE (see the chapter on resurrection). In 2.9, “the twelve stars, whose names are those of the twelve zodiacal constellations” and “the ancient sages of Bapel” (Babylon) are mentioned, indicating the connection between Zoroastrianism and Chaldean astronomy, which was known to the Greek authors.

720 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM mention of “the Messiah” and of Mani among those who spread the belief testifies to the Sasanian Zoroastrian view of Christians and Manicheans, who do not find in it a path to salvation but rather a means of disseminating another faith. In 3.4 it is said that Jāmāsp wrote what Zoroaster taught, along with the Avesta and the Zand, “on ox hides, with gold, in the royal treasury,” and that the high priests made copies from there. This is one version of the tradition of the Avesta being written on hides. Other sources give figures: Pliny (Natural History XXX 4) quotes Hermippus as attributing two million verses to Zoroaster with indices of their volumes, and Arab authors give figures for hides (al-Masʿūdī, Murūǧ al- ḏahab). For the book, Dk V attests to a history of transmission that attributes the origin to royal writing; that history is Sassanid and cannot be applied to the 5th century BCE. 6. Chapter 4: The Race of Iran, Glory, and the Kayanids Chapter 4 (in its full text) deals with the “selection and perfection of the race of Iran” and how the “destroyer” introduced defects into creation. The good qualities (good intellect, affection, praise, modesty, hope, liberality, truth, generosity, friend ship) are “particularly included” in Fravak, son of Sīyāmak, and are subsequently altered in the border peoples. Glory (xwarrah, av. xᵛarənah-) passes through the kings: Hōšang, Vaegered, Taxmōruw, Yim, Frēdōn, Airič, Manuščihr, and the Kayanids “were chosen”; the legitimate king is the one who descends from the lineage and in whom glory resides (4,5). Dk V 4,6 adds that Ohrmazd informed Nēryōsang (the yazata messenger) that a similar case is the “supreme Zartoštīh” (the function of Zarathustra) and the glory of the religion, “known only to an Iranian of the best lineage.” This chapter has a clear political and ethnic meaning: the religion belongs to a lineage that is that of the Kayanids and, by inheritance, to the Sasanids. The comparison with Israel has one point of contact, that of a chosen people and lineage (Deuteronomy 7:6; the house of David), and one difference: in Deuteronomy 5 the choice is of an Iranian-Aryan race and of a glory, while in the Bible it is a covenant. In 4:8–9, finally, the “tribe” that West calls Gyemara appears again: it speaks of what it needs, of the recitation of revelation among them, and of a priestly authority that guides the “same tribe.” The impossibility of establishing who they are (Jews,

DĒNKARD, BOOK V 721 according to West; Selamis, according to Sanjana) prevents us from drawing a historical conclusion from this passage. 7. Ecdotic observations Four warnings. First: the bibliographic reference must distinguish the portion of Pahlavi Texts (V) from the volume number of Sacred Books of the East (47), which do not coincide numerically and are easily confused (section 1). Second: the West text circulating on avesta.org is a digital edition with annotations and standardizations by the editor; the book quotes only brief passages, and the licence for an Avestan transcription by Peterson should not automatically extend to all his reproductions of Pahlavi translations and texts: the conditions of each digital resource should be examined separately. Third: the extant Book V of the Dēnkard is, according to the note, an abridged version; the statements are from the abridged version, not the lost original. Fourth: the dating (9th – 10th century) is from the compilation, and the materials may be earlier. 8. Three-level evaluation Typological similarity. The series of prophets, the temptation of the teacher, the resurrection of the body, the ages of metals, and the chosen one by lineage have paral lels in the Jewish, Christian, and Greek worlds. Probable mediation. The coexistence of Zoroastrian, Jewish, Christian, and Manichean communities in Iraq and Persia during the Sasanian and Islamic periods makes contact probable, and Book V of the Dēnkard is one of the pieces of evidence for this coexistence, albeit a controversial one: it lists the Messiah as Mani among those who propagate another belief. Demonstrable dependence. Dependence is not demonstrated; the possible reference to a Talmud (Gyemara) is not supported by Sanjana’s edition, and the story of Lohrasp and Jerusalem is legendary. Chapter Conclusion The Dēnkard V is a late (9th - 10th century) testimony of how Sasanian and postSasanian Zoroastrianism recounted its own history: a series of prophets preceding Zoroaster, a radiant and tempted Zoroaster, a future with destroyers, propagators, and restorers, and a chosen lineage. Its parallels with Judaism and Christianity are

722 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM typological or of late coexistence, not of dependence. The clue of “Jerusalem” and “Gyemara” raises a question that only collation of the original can resolve; it does not constitute proof. Summary Book V of the Dēnkard is presented with its two translations (Table 64) and is read in its themes: Lohrasp, Bukht-Narsih and Jerusalem; the prophets; Zarathustra with his glory, his temptation and the resurrection; the ages of the world (Table 65) and the figures of the end; and the Iranian lineage. Chapter LI. Dēnkard, Book IX: The Gathic Nasks and the Pahlavi Exegesis of the Gāthās Chronological context. Dēnkard IX, Pahlavi exegetical summary transmitted in a compilation prepared between the 9th and 10th centuries CE on earlier Gathic and Nask materials. The date of this exegesis is not that of the composition of the Gāthās nor does it prove its interpretation in the time of Darius. The Dēnkard IX as a testimony of reconstruction, not as a codex of the lost Nasks Book IX of the Dēnkard preserves Pahlavi expositions on materials associated with the Gāthās and the traditional divisions of the Avestan corpus. Its importance is ex ceptional for the history of interpretation, but the summaries and reworkings it transmits are not equivalent to the continuous text of a lost Nask. E.W. West’s English version, published in the Sacred Books of the East and disseminated electronically by Avesta.org, is treated here as a translation of an exegetical tradition with its own criteria for segmentation. In this chapter’s source matrix, the following are kept expressly separate: traditional section title, summary attributed by Dēnkard, any preserved Avestan parallel, proposed philological equivalence, and level of certainty of the identification. When the original Avestan text is missing, no invented back-versions are printed under the label of “old reading”; any conjectural reconstruction is marked as such, with bibliographic discussion. In this way, the positive evidence is preserved without exceeding what is authorized for its transmission. The Dēnkard IX as an index of absent works Book IX of the Dēnkard may preserve data on the organization of lost Nasks and on how their contents were understood within the Pahlavi priestly milieu. However, a summary of a Nask does not allow for the reconstruction of a lost Avestan stanza as a literal quotation. The available documentation requires distinguishing between a preserved Avestan passage, a Pahlavi exegesis referring to that passage, a synopsis of a lost work, and an explanation by the modern editor. The comparative apparatus must retain the identifier of the book, the fargard, and the section, since the pages change between historical printings and digitizations. West’s translation is an access tool and does not replace the Middle Iranian verification. When a relationship with the Gāthās is deduced from thematic similar723

724 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM ity, the note should identify it as an inference, not as an established textual concord ance. Hierarchy of testimonies for the reconstruction of the Nasks. The Dēnkard IX is a Middle Iranian testimony of exegetical reception and memory of the organization of the Avesta. A summary of a lost Nask does not equate to the preservation of its Avestan text, nor does it authorize the retroposition of its Pahlavi formulations into supposed literal quotations. In each correspondence, it must be indicated whether there is a preserved Avestan passage, a Pahlavi explanation, a bibliographical note about a lost work, or a modern reconstruction. The digital edition by E. W. West allows the passages to be located, but to resolve variants of Middle Iranian lexicon, transcription, reading of the scripts, and editing control are necessary. The parallel with the Gāthās will be used in an interpretive sense, not as a guarantee of uninterrupted verbal continuity from the Achaemenid period. 1. The book and its structure Book IX of the Dēnkard is a summary of the Nasks (books) of the Gathic division of the lost Avestan canon. It is a testament to the Pahlavi exegesis gathered in the compilation process of the 9th - 10th centuries CE, but, as West warns, “it is abundantly clear to the experienced translator that there are often Avestan phrases under the Pahlavi passages that appear to be quoted at length from the original Nasks, particularly in Dk 9; but, for some details, there may be no older authority than a Pahlavi commentary.” West’s translation (Pahlavi Texts, Part IV, SBE 37, 1892) is digitized by J.H. Peterson at avesta.org (last revised 2021 according to the title page), with editor’s comments in curly braces and double brackets and standardized spelling according to Kotwal and Boyd (1982). The book covers four Nasks: the Sūdgar (22 fargards, chapters 2–23 of West), the Warštmānsr (23 fargards, chapters 24–46), the Bag (22 fargards, chapters 47–68), and a concluding summary of the Stūd-Yasn (chapter 69), Nask 21 or “original Yasna.” Text-critical note — edition, translation, and recension.
