Each fargard is named after the first words of a hā from the Gāthās: fargard 15 of the Sūdgar is called Kamnamaeza (the first words of Y. 46.1, kam nəmōi zām, according to West’s note), fargard 16, Spenta-mainyu (Y. 47.1), and fargard 10 of the Warštmānsr, Yathaish (Y. 33.1). They are, therefore, successive commentaries on the Gāthās, verse by verse, made on the Pahlavi (Zand) version and not on the Avestan original. West points out that the Bag Nask is “an analytical commentary on the Gāthās”, with a fargard for hā and very short phrases (bagha, “portion”) that are difficult to identify; the first three fargards of the Bag still survive in Y. 19–21, so that the current Yasna preserves a fragment of the summarized text. The authority of Dēnkard IX should be classified as exegetical testimony in Middle Persian, not as a literal restitution of the lost Avestan Nasks. The summaries may preserve earlier material, but their preservation within an Islamic-era compilation precludes retrospectively dating each explanation. In comparison with the Gāthās, three levels will be distinguished: (a) the forms and context of the Avestan stanza; (b) the Pahlavi paraphrase and doctrinal organization; (c) the English version by E.W. West, via its digital edition. When a conclusion depends on a precise word, the English translation will not replace verification of the Iranian original. The millennium of Zarathustra is divided into four periods: the golden one, in which Ohrmazd showed the religion to Zarathustra; the silver one, in which Vishta sp received it; the steel one, in which Adurbadi Mahraspandan, “the organizer of righteousness” (the high priest of Shabuhr II, 4th century CE), was born; and the mixed iron one, “in which there is much propagation of the authority of the apostate and other evildoers, the destruction of the reign of religion, the weakening of all goodness and virtue, and the disappearance of honor and wisdom from the lands of Iran.” The image of mixed iron, and the other elements, coincides with the list in Dk V 3.3 (previous chapter) and with the fourbranched tree of the Zandī Wahman Yasn (ZWY 1.3–5). This is the scheme that has been compared with Daniel 2 and with Hesiod’s ages. What Dk IX adds is an internal dating: the fourth period is the one in which the author lived, beginning in the 4th century, so the theory is Sasanian and cannot be traced back to the 5th century BCE. The comparison with Daniel (2nd century BCE) therefore remains a typological similarity, and the direction cannot be determined. 4. The Ahunwar, first creation: the discussion about the logos Dk IX 47 (Bag, fargard 1) states that Ohrmazd produced the Ahunwar (the formula Yaθā ah ū vairiiō) before all creation, at the request of the archangel, as a “word form” that is the “most intimate and comprehensive sheath” and “the best assembled embodiment of the intelligent omniscience of religion.” He calls it “the germ of germs,” and says that the ahu of Ahu-vairyo is “the first creature” (§3–4). West’s note clarifies that the Ahunwar was recited before the other creations; this is clearly stated in the verses Pahl. Yas. 19.2–5 and 17–20, while the Bundahišn (I 21– 23) places the creation of Vohuman after the recitation of the Ahunwar. This is relevant to the discussion on the logos (chapter on Mantra, Vac, Ahuna Vairya, and logos). A pre-existing divine word, prior to creation and its agent, has

DĒNKARD, BOOK IX 729 parallels in Proverbs 8:22–31 (Wisdom created “at the beginning of her ways”), in Philo’s logos, in the Memra of the Targums,237 and in John 1:1–3. With the Ahunwar, the parallel is typological: there is a pre-existing word that contains the wisdom of the divine plan. But the differences are clear: the Ahunwar is a liturgical formula, a prayer, that is recited and learned; it is neither a person nor a hypostasis of God. And the testimony dates from the 9th century, supported by a Zand text that cannot be precisely dated. There is no evidence that John’s prologue depends on that motif, nor vice versa. The chapter on the logos retains the classification of “typological resemblance”. 5. Eschatology: bridge, middle place, molten metal and renewal The Sūdgar (fargards 15–19) and the Warštmānsr (fargards 9, 10, and 18) bring together important eschatological motifs in the exegetical organization of Dēnkard IX, without thereby establishing a complete system of the Gathic period. At death, the demon Astwihad takes all mortals; the soul “sees only the reward and the bridge to the spiritual state,” and not the body, which it no longer sees; the body is torn apart by dogs and birds, while the “consciousness” (as West translates it) contemplates it with fear “like a sheep before a wolf” (Dk IX 16, § 6). The judgement takes place on the bridge (Dk IX 17: “bridge-judgement of sinners”), and the punishments of hell are described with stark imagery (Dk IX 17 §4–7). West’s note on the intermediate place, which tradition later calls Hamestagān, is close to what other traditions call a waiting place: the motif of an intermediate state of souls is in 1 Hen 22 (four compartments) and in Luke 16:19–31, and whether there is mediation is discussed; for now, the relationship is typological (Nickelsburg 2001, on 1 Hen 22). The passage about molten metal (Dk IX 32 § 25) is the most striking. Ohrmazd says that when renewal occurs, “the molten metal rises upon the earth,” that it does not harm the righteous but harms the wicked, and that “the healthy world that is mine” does not become sick. West’s note specifies that all people are purified in molten metal, and that only the wicked suffer (Bd 30:19–20). It is a final ordeal by fire. It has been compared with Mal 3:2–3 (the refiner’s fire), with Dan 7:9–10 (the river of fire), with 1 Cor 3:13–15 (the fire that tests each person’s work), and with 2 Pet 3:10–12.238 There is a clear typological similarity. Mediation is possible in the 237 Boyarin, “Gospel of the Memra”. 238 Hultgård, “Persian Apocalypticism”.

730 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM apocalyptic literature of the Hellenistic-Parthian period, and the book describes it as probable but not proven: there is no reference to the Avesta in any biblical text. In Dk IX 33, there is also a liturgical scene of great value for architecture and ritual. In the renewal, Zorathustra is the Zot (high priest) of the world, and he is assisted by Vohuvastō (the Hāwanān, who tends the mortar of the haoma), Isvand (Ātarewaxš, the one who feeds the fire), Seno (Frabardār, the one who carries the utensils), and Vištāsp (Srōšāwarz, the one who maintains order). West adds the location of each in the ceremonial space: the Zot to the north; the Hāwanān to the northwest; the Ātarewaxš to the southwest; the Frabardār to the northeast; and the Srōšāwarz to the south, facing the Zot. The plan of the Yasna enclosure is completed with three other priests (Vsp 3,1; Vd. 5.58; 7,17–18), and today the Zōt retains his functions and the Raspī replaces the others. It is the most precise description we have of the order of the ritual space, and it completes the previous chapter on architecture. 6. Mani and the Zand as actualizing exegesis Dk IX 39 (§13–16) characterizes “the heretic Mani” in the commentary on Y. 45.8 ff. A text from the Gāthās, written a thousand years earlier (according to traditional chronology), reads as if it announces Mani, born, according to West’s note, in 215– 216 CE. West infers from this that the Pahlavi version of the Nask must have been made when the Manichean heresy was still fresh in memory, i.e., in the first half of the fourth century, when Adurbadi Mahraspandan was compiling and revising the sacred books. This is a reasonable inference, but not proof. This reveals the nature of the Zand: it is not a neutral translation, but an updat ing commentary that interprets the ancient text in light of present-day problems. The technique resembles that of the Qumran Pesher (for example, 1QpHab), which reads Habakkuk as if he were speaking about the community, and the Chris tian reading of the prophets as prophecies of Jesus (Mt 1–2, for example). This sim ilarity lies in exegetical procedure, not content, and does not imply direct contact: they are parallel responses to the need to update an ancient revelation. For the textual criticism of the book, the consequence is that, when using the Zand to understand the Gāthās, one must separate the Gathic sense (which the book takes from the Uesugi and Catt edition) from the sense that the Pahlavi commentary projects onto it.

DĒNKARD, BOOK IX 731 7. Marriage between close relatives and Herodotus Dk IX 41 mentions xwēdōdah, marriage between close relatives, as part of the arguments for “future existence” and religion. Herodotus (III 31) recounts that Cambyses, in love with one of his sisters, summoned the royal judges to find out if there was a law that allowed a brother to marry his sister; the judges replied that they could find no law that commanded it, but that they had found another that allowed the king of the Persians to do as he pleased; and Herodotus expressly adds that the Persians “did not formerly have the custom of marrying their sisters.” The passage shows that in the 5th century BCE marriage between siblings was not a general Per sian custom, and that the royal exception was justified by a privilege. The religious value of xwēdōdah in the Pahlavi texts is, therefore, later. For the Achaemenid period, Herodotus’s testimony does not allow us to speak of a doctrine. This is one of the points where we must avoid projecting the Dk IX backwards. 8. Edicological and usage observations Four caveats. First: Dk IX essentially preserves a Pahlavi exposition and paraphrase of nasks, not continuous copies of their lost Avestan texts; correspondences with extant Avestan passages, including Y. 19–21, require distinguishing between testimony, interpretation, and West’s editorial gloss. Second: West’s translations are from the late 19th century, with Pahlavi vocabulary that is sometimes read differently today (as seen with the Gyemara of Dk V); Peterson’s edition standardizes the spelling and adds commentary, which facilitates searching but necessitates distinguishing between West’s text and the editor’s notes. Third: Peterson’s edition’s licence restricts the reproduction of passages; the book quotes only brief fragments. Fourth: the chapter and paragraph numbers in this chapter follow West’s numbering, and do not necessarily coincide with the Pahlavi editions of Madan (1911) or Dresden (1966). 9. Three-level evaluation Typological similarity. The preexistence of a divine word (Ahunwar), the final ordeal by fire, the intermediate place, the judgement on the bridge, the updating of the ancient text in a commentary, and the age of metals have parallels in the Jewish, Christian, and Greek worlds. Probable mediation. The coexistence of communities

732 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM in the Sasanian Empire (including the polemic with Mani, the Christians, and the Jews) makes an exchange of motifs in the late period likely; the Dēnkard is evidence that the Mazdaean clergy were familiar with heretics and foreign prophets. Demonstrable dependence. It is not demonstrated in either direction: the Pahlavi material is from the 9th century and the biblical material is earlier; there are no quotations. Chapter Conclusion Dēnkard IX is the best window into the Pahlavi exegesis of the Gāthās and a repository of information on ritual, eschatology, and time theory. It contributes five things to the book: the internal dating of the Metal Ages, the passage of molten metal, the description of the priestly space of the Yasna, the Ahunwar as the first creation, and evidence of how the Zand reworks and interprets ancient materials without automatically fixing the Achaemenid understanding of them. It also reminds us of the limit: everything is later, and where the book compares with the Persian period, it should say “typological” or “possible mediation,” reserving “demonstrable” for cases with text. Summary The chapter sets out the structure of the Gathic Nasks (Table 66) and their passages and uses (Table 67) in four periods. It then examines the relationship between Ahunwar and logos, eschatology (bridge, intermediate place, molten metal, renewal and the space of the Yasna), Mani and the Zand, and the xwēdōdah in relation to Herodotus III 31. Chapter LII. Iranian Poetry and Epic in Zoroastrian Tradition: From the Gāthās to the Šāhnāme Chronological context. From ancient Avestan poetry of disputed date to medieval Persian epic, including the Shahnameh. Medieval literary reception is distinguished from Achaemenid and Sasanian testimonies. 1. Introduction: What is meant by ancient Iranian poetry? The question is whether, besides the Gāthās and the rest of the Avesta, there is any ancient Persian poetry that can be used to study Zoroastrianism. The answer, arranged chronologically, is brief for the Achaemenid centuries and lengthy for later periods. No poetry survives in Old Persian; the royal inscriptions are formulaic prose. However, a set of metrical hymns survives in Avestan; in Middle and Parthian Persian, remnants of oral epic and didactic and debate poetry; and in Modern Persian, a versified epic and biography of Zoroaster. The chapter organizes these works, indicates when they are useful as sources and when they merely illustrate how the past was recounted, and applies the book’s triad. A text with regular measurement or strophic parallelism is considered poetry. The Gāthās certainly are: each line is divided into two hemistichs, separated by a caesura that the Uesugi and Catt edition marks with a slash, and the meter is described by the number of syllables (the Ahunavaitī Gāthā, Y. 28–34, with lines of 7 + 9 syllables). For the other works, the criterion is that given by the editors. 2. Avestan poetry Within the Avesta, distinct sets of genres and linguistic strata must be identified. The Gāthās (Old Avestan; Y. 28–34, 43–51, and 53) are hymns that tradition attributes to Zoroaster (edited here in Texts 7–8, 10–13, and 16–26 based on Uesugi and Catt). The Yasna Haptaŋhāiti (Y. 35–41), also Old Avestan, is liturgical prose; it should not be excluded from the oldest linguistic stratum, nor should this classification be equated with an absolute dating. Y 42 is a supplement of archaic Younger Avestan (H. Humbach, “Gāthās i. Texts”, Encyclopaedia Iranica). The 733

734 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM Yašts (Younger Avestan) are hymns to the Yazatas, and several have metrical sections of short verses (heptasyllabic and octosyllabic, according to studies), especially the more epic ones (Yt 5, 10, 13, 14, 19). They recount the exploits of kings and heroes, including the wars of Vishta and the fall of Zoroaster (Yt. 9.26 and 5,98–112 as reference points). Observation on the chronological ascription of the Gāthās The identification of the Gāthās as a linguistically ancient stratum does not, in itself, authorize a fixed historical date for Zoroaster, nor the automatic attribution of all subsequent ritual elements to its context. Old Avestan is a linguistic category; the textual preservation and the codices that transmitted it correspond to other chronologies. A lexical coincidence with Vedic Sanskrit proves an Indo-Iranian linguistic relationship, not a Persian doctrinal transmission to Judaism. 3. Ancient Persian: no poetry preserved, but reports of songs No corpus of Old Persian poetry comparable to the Gāthās has survived. The inscriptions of Darius, Xerxes, and their successors are solemn prose, with anaphora and parallelism (“Darius the king says ...”), and some scholars have searched for rhythmic structures in them, without reaching a consensus. Information about Persian chants is indirect. Herodotus (I 132) describes how, at each sacrifice, a magus present “sings a theogony” (epae idei theogoníēn), “the kind of incantation they say it is”; without a magus, there is no sacrifice. This is the oldest testimony of a Persian religious chant, and its text has not survived. Xenophon (Cyropaedia I 2) and Strabo (XV 3,18) describe Persian education and mention chants about gods and heroes. To these is added the Greek perspective: Aeschylus’s The Persians (472 BCE), a tragedy in which the shadow of Darius appears, is poetry about the Persians, not Persian, but it shows how Persian religion and monarchy were conceived in Athens. 4. Parthians and Sasanians: minstrels, epic and debate Sasanian centuries (approximately the 3rd century BCE to the 7th century CE), an oral tradition of poet-singers is postulated. The gōsān (“singers, minstrels”), in M. Boyce’s reconstruction (1957), were the Parthian bearers of a heroic and courtly

The Šāhnāme and Zoroastrianism in modern Persian Ferdowsi’s Šāhnāme (“Book of Kings”) (circa 1010 CE) recounts the history of the kings of Iran from Gayōmard to the Arab conquest. The section on Zoroaster and Gushtāsp (Vištāsp) draws on a Zoroastrian tradition and is attributed to an earlier poet, Daqiqi, who was assassinated in the 970s and wrote about a thousand verses on that reign, which Ferdowsi is said to have incorporated (Khaleghi-Motlagh, “Daqiqi,” EIr). It is a source of Islamic memory concerning Zoroastrianism, but not of ancient Zoroastrianism. It shows how the figures of the Avesta (Yim, Frēdōn Zohak, Kay Xusraw) were used to construct a national history, and their relationship with the Dēnkard (V and IX) is a point of contact between two traditions, one poetic and the other priestly. 239 Brunner, “Babylonian Tree”.

738 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM 6. Comparison with Hebrew and Greek poetry The Hebrew world of the Persian period had its own poetry: the Psalms, the poems of Isaiah (Isaiah 44:24–45:7, where Cyrus is the “anointed one” and it says, “I form the light and create darkness”), and the Book of Job. In Aramaic, the Wisdom of Ahiqar, a copy of which exists in Elephantine (5th century BCE), is a collection of sayings that resembles the andarz genre. In the Greek world, the hymn and the epic were the norm. The comparison of genres: hymn (Gāthās, Yašts, Psalms, Orphic hymns), epic (Yašts, Ayādgār, Šāhnāme, Homer), debate (Draxtī Āsūrīg, Sumerian and Akkadian debates, and Ahiqar to some extent), maxims (andarz, Proverbs, Ahiqar). These similarities are typological. Mediation is likely for debate and wisdom (through the Aramaic- Mesopotamian space) and for hymn only within the framework of Near Eastern culture. 7. Ecdotic observations Four warnings. First: the Gāthās are cited with the Uesugi and Catt edition (CC BY 4.0); the other works, with editions whose licence allows brief quotation. Second: Ayādgār ī Zarērān and Draxt ī Āsūrīg are preserved in late Pahlavi manuscripts (from the 13th – 15th centuries), with doubtful readings. Third: the Šāhnāme has a great manuscript tradition and the edition by Khaleghi-Motlagh (1988–2008) is the reference. Fourth: the Zartošt-nāme (1278 CE) and the Qeṣṣe-ye Sanjān (ca. 1600 CE) are medieval and early modern compositions, useful as Parsi community memory, but not as testimony to the Achaemenid period. 8. Three-level evaluation Typological similarity. There are hymns, epics, maxims, and debates in Iran, Israel, and Greece. Probable mediation. Debate and wisdom are transmitted in the Mesopotamian and Aramaic spheres; the Parthian and Sasanian courts preserve an epic that later passes into modern Persian. Demonstrable dependence. There is demonstrable dependence of modern Persian epic only on Avestan and Pahlavi materials (names and episodes). There is no demonstrable dependence between Iranian and Hebrew or Greek poetry.

IRANIAN POETRY AND EPIC AROUND ZOROASTRIANISM 739 Chapter Conclusion The ancient Iranian poetry that serves as a direct source for Zoroastrianism of the Persian period is the Gathica. Everything else is later and should be placed in the fourth section of the book, the Sasanian period and later. Its value is different: it shows how tradition remembered Zoroaster, Vishtasy, and the Kayanids, and how Zoroastrianism became literary memory. Summary After establishing criteria, the chapter describes Avestan poetry, the absence of poetry in Old Persian alongside reports of songs (Herodotus I 132), and the tradition of the gōsān with the Ayādgārī Zarērā and the Draxtī Āsūrīg (Table 68). The Šāhnāme and a comparison of genres conclude the discussion. IRANIAN, MAZDEAN, AND ZOROASTRIAN VOCABULARY 747 Four points of caution should be made regarding this table. First, Old and Younger Avestan are distinct languages, so the same root may not have the same meaning in the Gāthās and the Yašts. Second, Old Persian does not preserve any of the terms in the list provided by Gathic theology, except for Auramazdā, arta-, drauga-, and daiva-; this is one of the reasons why Chapter XLVII questions whether the Achaemenids were Zoroastrians in the strict sense. Third, the Pahlavi tradition interprets the ancient from the perspective of the recent: the glossed trans lations (zand) are evidence of the 9th or 10th century, not of the time of Zoroaster. Fourth, several etymologies (mazdā-, fravaši-, činvat-) are under discussion, and the table indicates the gloss of usage, not a solution. Test criteria for alleged religious loans This concordance adopts an explicit gradation: loanword with compatible phonological correspondences and documentary chronology; possible semantic calque or translation; typological similarity without demonstrated linguistic relation. Mere equivalence in translation—“law”, “truth”, “spirit”, “saviour”—does not constitute a cognate or a loanword. The term in Old Persian, Old Avestan, Younger Avestan, or Middle Persian and its first verifiable attestation in Hebrew, Aramaic, or Greek must be listed separately. The presence of a word in a medieval Pahlavi commentary does not prove that it circulated with the same meaning in Yehud under Darius I. The lexicographical discussion uses the Old Avestan Dictionary (Uesugi–Catt, 2024) for the Gathic lemmas, without automatically extending its results to the Yašts. 3. Ritual and worship Table 70. The supposed identity of Sanskrit hiraṇya- (“gold”) and Avestan zaraṇya-, as well as its use to derive the name Zaraθuštra without further investigation, is not adopted without specialized etymological review. Nor should Vedic and Avestan be described as “almost identical” languages. Methodological and lexicographical references: Christian Bartholomae, Altiranisches Wörterbuch (1904); Manfred Mayrhofer, Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Altindoarischen (1992–2001); Rüdiger Schmitt, Die iranischen Sprachen in Geschichte und Gegenwart (2000); P. O. Skjærvø, The Spirit of Zoroastrianism (2011). Chapter Conclusion The repertoire confirms the division the book maintains from Chapter II onward: the reliable Iranian loanwords in Hebrew, Aramaic, and Greek are almost all technical—administration, law, architecture, clothing—and only pardēs and rāz touch on religious vocabulary, through a shift in meaning in the receiving language. Iranian theological and ritual vocabulary, on the other hand, is compared by functional correspondence, without borrowing. The lexical proximity to Vedic supports a shared Indo-Iranian heritage, not the identity of the rites. Summary This chapter surveys Iranian vocabulary relating to administration, cult, salvation and death; Iranian loanwords in the languages of the eastern Mediterranean; and Greek forms of Iranian names. Its comparative Vedic, Avestan, Greek, Hebrew and Aramaic lexicon distinguishes linguistic form, language, earliest attestation and degree of evidential support.

Chapter Conclusion The repertoire of Parthian and Sasanian buildings serves as an archaeological control for the chapters on fire and worship. Many “fire temples” are so named by analogy with later structures or because of their čahār tāq form, and the hierarchy of fires derives from texts written after the fall of the Sasanian Empire. Archaeology provides fires, altars, and enclosures, but not their classification or theology; therefore, none of these buildings can be used to describe the worship of the Persian period.

Zarathustra, the Magi and the Greek philosophers: testimonies, reception and evidentiary limits The Greek transmission of the name Zoroaster (Zōroástrēs) does not equate to a directly documented history of Zarathustra. A distinction must be made between: a) accounts of observed or collected Persian practices; b) traditions attributing extraordinary antiquity to the Iranian sage; c) retrospective philosophical affiliations; and d) Hellenistic literature attributed to Zoroaster. In this dossier, the existence of a contact route is not to be confused with evidence of doctrinal borrowing. 3.1. Mythical chronologies and attributed authorship Diogenes Laertius, in his Vitae philosophorum I.2, distinguishes two accounts: Hermodorus placed the Magi, beginning with Zoroaster, five thousand years before the fall of Troy; Xanthus of Lydia placed six thousand years between Zoroaster and the expedition of Xerxes. These are literary chronologies transmitted late, not verifiable historical dates. The figure of six thousand years before Plato’s death comes from another account, that of Eudoxus and Aristotle, which Pliny records (NH XXX 3) (Diogenes Laertius, I.2; ed. R.D. Hicks, Loeb Classical Library, 1925). Hermippus of Smyrna composed a work, Perì Mágōn (On the Magi), cited by Diogenes Laertius, I.8. Pliny, in Natural History XXX.4, attributes to Hermippus the cataloging of two million verses under the name of Zoroaster. This figure testifies to a discourse of authority and a tradition of books attributed to the Eastern sage; it does not constitute a verifiable inventory of autograph writings. See Encyclopaedia Iranica, sv. “Hermippus of Smyrna,” and Bidez and Cumont, Les mages hellénisés (1938). 3.2. “Eastern” philosophy and Greek categories Diogenes Laertius, in Books I.1 and I.8–9, attributes dualism, religious knowledge, and an afterlife to the Magi, referring to Aristotle, Dinon, Hermippus, Eudoxus, and Theopompus. The chain of transmission must be maintained: the surviving

MULTILINGUAL CONCORDANCE OF CONCEPTS 773 testimony is that of the later compiler, even when he names a source from the 4th century BCE. The claim that Zoroaster expressly bequeathed a tripartite classification of philosophy into physics, economics, and politics is not proven here. Until its locus is located, the book does not use it as ancient testimony. 3.3. Miletus and cultural exchange: a hypothesis subjected to chronology Thales, Anaximander, and Anaximenes developed the first Milesian philosophy during the 6th century BCE. The Achaemenid conquest of Ionia occurred around the middle of that century: Thales and much of Anaximander’s work predate Persian rule; therefore, it is wrong to present the three as thinkers formed during centuries of subjugation to Persia. The subsequent integration of Ionian cities into the Achaemenid Empire expanded the possibilities for exchange, but it does not prove that Anaximander’s doctrine of the apeiron, Thales’s water, or Anaximenes’s air derive from Zoroastrian principles (Diogenes Laertius II.1–3; Boyce, A History of Zoroastrianism, II [1982], 150 ff.). Mesopotamian and Levantine cosmological models constitutes a competing explanation that must be analysed alongside the Iranian hypothesis. Establishing a causal relationship will require non -generic doctrinal parallels, compatible dating, identifiable mediations, and a reasoned rejection of alternative Greek and Eastern antecedents. 3.4. Pythagoras, Empédocles, Democritus and Plato Later biographies associate Pythagoras and Democritus with the Magi: Diogenes Laertius, VIII.3 and IX.34; Porphyry, Vita Pythagoras, 12; and testimonies summarized in the Encyclopaedia Iranica, “Magi” and “Diogenes Laertius.” Such accounts may document the cultural prestige of Persian wisdom without establishing historically demonstrable encounters with Zoroaster. For Empedocles, broad simil arities regarding purification or transmigration are not sufficient to postulate a specific dependence; an ancient locus that names the Magi or an independent mechanism of transmission is required. In Pseudo-Plato, Alcibiades I, 122a, the “magic of Zoroaster, son of Oromazes” is part of the education of the Persian prince, but the Platonic authenticity of the dialogue remains disputed. 3.5. Renaissance reception: distinct historiographical object Marsilio Ficino and Giovanni Pico della Mirandola reworked genealogies of an ancient wisdom — prisca theologia— that linked Zoroaster, Hermes, and Plato. This phenomenon belongs to the humanist reception of Greek sources and pseudepi-

774 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM graphical texts, not to the direct history of Achaemenid religion. Modern popular accounts of this reception should not be presented as primary authorities for establishing influences on Miletus or early Christianity. 3.6. Documentary hierarchy and conclusions Grade A — historical contact and dated testimony: Persian rule of Ionia and surviving texts describing magical practices. Grade B — mediated ancient reception: Aristotle, Theopompus, Hermippus, or Xanthus as cited by later authors. Grade C — legendary literary tradition: Zoroaster’s personal encounters with Pythagoras, antiquities of five or six millennia, and universal philosophical genealogies. Grade D — conjecture of specific doctrinal influence without documented intermediary. The possibility of contact between Greek and Iranian environments remains, but none of the evidence examined here justifies declaring a general derivation of Greek philosophy from Zoroastrianism. 3.7. Material status of testimonies and control of tradition: The mention of an ancient author does not prove the preservation of their work. The Burning Bush and Fire: Barnea’s Achaemenid–Zoroastrian Hypothesis Burning bush, fire and architecture: a testable set of alternatives The fire of Exodus 3 is a narrative theophany and not, in itself, archaeological evidence for a built fire cult. THE BURNING BUSH AND THE FIRE 785 4. Fire in the Persian religion of the Achaemenid period To test this hypothesis, we must examine the accounts of fire and its chronology. Herodotus (Histories 1.131–132) describes Persians without statues, temples, or altars, and a sacrificial procedure for which no fire was lit; this account does not necessarily summarize all their practices. Strabo does not simply repeat this: Geographica 15.3.13 records an account of fat offerings, and 15.3.14 explicitly describes sacrifices to fire and water, with dry wood, fat, and oil, and with a prohibition against blowing on the flame. In 15.3.15, he places in Cappadocia enclosures where the Magi maintained a fire that did not go out. The differences between these two authors, with their distinct genres, sources, and dates, should be preserved, without harmonizing them into a single description. Quintus Curtius (Historiae 3.3.9–10) recounts that the sacred fire preceded the army of Darius III on silver altars. Achaemenid inscriptions do not describe a complete protocol for fire veneration; the structures at Pasargadae and the reliefs at Naqš-e Rostam require their own functional control. Greek text of Strabo according to the edition by A. Meineke (Teubner, 1877) and historical translation by H.C. Hamilton and W. Falconer, reproduced in Perseus, loci 15.3.13–15. Consulting these digital editions is not presented as reading a codex.250 The result is that the “veneration of fire” in the Achaemenid period is an attested but scarce reality, with an uncertain chronology, and that much of what is known about the Zoroastrian fire cult comes from Sasanian and Pahlavi sources. A study that explains a biblical text by Achaemenid fire practices must show concrete practices from that period, and not just practices attested later. This is the difficulty already pointed out in Chapter LIV: the nomenclature of the fires (Ādur Farnbāg, Ādur Gušnasp, Ādur Burzēn-Mihr; Ātaš Bahrām) is later. 250Quintus Curtius Rufus, Historiae Alexandri Magni 3.3.9–10: “Ignis, quem ipsi sacrum et aeternum vocabant, argenteis altaribus praeferebatur”, digital edition in Packhum, https://latin.packhum.org/loc/860/1/2/2066-2069@1; comparison with The Latin Library, https://www.thelatinlibrary.com/curtius/curtius3.shtml. It is useful to distinguish three objects: (a) the fire that receives offerings; (b) the fire holder or receptacle, designated in Pahlavi as ātašdān; and (c) the ritual bundle of sticks or branches, Avestan barəsman, also known as barsom. THE BURNING BUSH AND THE FIRE 789 Roman testimony and chronological difficulty Strabo, in Geographica 15.3.15, describes in Asia Minor enclosures where Magi kept a fire burning and recited prayers while holding bundles of sticks before the flame. This is a relevant reference because it explicitly associates persistent fire, prayer, and ritual branches. Its date, close to the turn of the era, prevents it from be ing used without mediation as direct proof of how a specific rite was practiced in the 6th century BCE. The continuity of a tradition is a historical hypothesis that re quires intermediate controls, not a property demonstrated by the similarity of its objects. [5] Differential test and alternative hypotheses To assess a possible relationship, four levels must be considered: (i) typological sim ilarity — a fire theophany and Iranian fire rituals; (ii) plausible historical contact between Yahwist communities and the imperial administration; (iii) a possible liter ary reworking in the Achaemenid period, which depends on hypotheses about the composition of Exodus; and (iv) demonstrable textual or ritual dependence, which would require specific features difficult to explain through other traditions. The material examined supports the relevance of the comparison and the general plausibility of the contact, but does not reach the fourth level. Alternative explanations include the Israelite fire theophanies already integrated into the biblical corpus itself (e.g., Exod 19:18; Deut 4:11–12; and Jg 6:21) and the widespread use of fire as a sign of divine manifestation in the ancient Near East. The exceptional nature of a plant that burns but is not consumed is precisely a difference from ritual fire fueled by combustible material. This discrepancy should not be erased to fabricate an iconographic equivalence. Similarly, attributing Ex 3 to the Persian period or identifying a “strict Zoroastrianism” under all the Achaemenid kings would exceed the available evidence. [1–5] Interpretive balance Barnea’s proposal represents a comparative hypothesis worthy of academic discussion and particularly fruitful for a history of Yahwism under Achaemenid rule. Its value lies in suggesting possible mechanisms of cultural transfer, not in demonstrat ing that the bush is literally an ātašdān with burning branches. Chapter LVII. Elephantine: The Documents of the Temple of YHW Chronological context. Elephantine, mainly 5th century BCE; Passover letter of 419, destruction of 410 and petitions of 407, under Darius II. The papyrus of ʾtrwdn is preserved testimony of this environment, not a codex from the reign of Darius I. Critical Clarification on Elephantine. The petition preserved as P. Berlin 13495 constitutes material evidence from the 5th century BCE; therefore, it proves the ex istence of a Yahwist community with its own temple and cultic practices in Achaemenid Egypt. The assertion that the sanctuary predated Cambyses is a fact transmitted by the petitioners, not an independent archaeological dating. In verses 8–9, permission is requested to resume offerings at the altar of YHWH. This documented contact between Persian officials and a Yahwist community does not demonstrate the circulation of specific Avestan eschatological formulations. Critical complement — Provenance dossier and inference chain To avoid confusion between ancient documents and modern equipment, each papyrus in the Elephantine dossier must have a card containing: publisher’s initials; descriptive title; date of the document and dating method; language; material; repository and current shelfmark when verified; text edition; translation used; and reading observations. Mention of a papyrus by another author is literary evidence of the document, not a substitute for the physical medium or a reliable reproduction. The scope of the dossier is twofold. On the one hand, it provides primary evidence of a sanctuary dedicated to YHWH, of communal practices, and of networks of petitions to imperial authorities. On the other, it allows us to study the limits of reconstruction: neither a divine name nor a bureaucratic formula grants direct access to the entirety of the theology of its authors. The chapter differentiates what the text expresses from what can be inferred about imperial policy, and from what can be conjectured about religious exchanges. Only this threefold separation allows us to use Elephantine as a strong case of historical contact without attributing to it doctrines not mentioned. Cowley’s 1923 edition remains usable as a starting point and as evidence of philological decisions; its preface states that the author was unable to carry out all the planned checks on originals. 793

794 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM Extension: archival history and limits of religious inference The Elephantine archive occupies a methodologically distinct position from that of biblical narratives and Pahlavi treatises. Its papyri are documentary materials from a community located in Egypt under Persian rule; the testimonies related to the Temple of YHW provide contemporary data on the practices, interests, and networks of their senders. It is important to distinguish the document’s statement about a sanctuary and a specific request from the general reconstruction of the community’s theology. An archive of letters and financial records is not a systematic confession of beliefs. The documentation concerning the destruction of the temple and the attempts at reconstruction is particularly relevant due to its interlocutors, chronology, and language of political supplication. However, the epistolary account of the events is conditioned by its persuasive purpose. The letters allow us to study how the group represented itself before the authorities, but a petition does not offer a neutral inventory of all the island’s cults. The existence of additional divine names in the records requires analysis of genre and documentary formulae before asserting uniform polytheism, Iranian syncretism, or the replacement of the worship of YHWH. Each document can be described in a five-level entry: I, preserved object and provenance; II, paleographic or internal date; III, diplomatic transcription with noted restitutions; IV, translation distinct from the editorial restitution; V, sociohistorical interpretation. This entry would allow for a grading of certainties: a fully visible reading of the papyrus does not have the same status as a reconstruction of lost letters or a modern historiographical attribution. The Cowley edition (1923) should be cited as an edition, not as a manuscript, and its identifiers should be consistent with those of the Porten-Yardeni TAD corpus when consulted directly. The strength of the argument for this thesis lies in the fact that these documents reveal institutional plurality and religious negotiation within the Achaemenid framework. However, coexistence under the same empire does not demonstrate the spread of Zoroastrian eschatology or a doctrinal reform of Jerusalem. This second hypothesis requires an independent chain of textual, chronological, and social evid ence. The comparison with Ezra should relate scribal practices, imperial mediation, correspondence, and cultic authority, but it should not automatically identify all its actors or equate its ritual norms.

THE DOCUMENTS OF THE TEMPLE OF YHW 795 Elephantine: cult, documents and social reconstruction The documented existence of a YHWH sanctuary at Elephantine proves the reality of provincial worship in Persian Egypt; however, it does not establish, without further argument, what priestly practices were followed in Jerusalem during the same decades. The letters dealing with the destruction and restoration of the temple are testimonies to political strategies, networks of interlocutors, and institutional memory. Inferences about beliefs must be limited to the practices and denominations actually attested. Cowley’s edition (1923) retains high historical value, but the transcription of damaged consonants and the restoration of names require comparison with Porten and Yardeni and, if possible, current photographs of the papyrus. Inventory of document types of Elephantine The Temple of YHW on Elephantine Island (near Syene, modern-day Aswan) is one of the principal contemporary documentary testimonies of a Yahwist sanctuary outside Judea during the Persian period, and thus occupies a central place in the book. The sources that mention it are primarily Aramaic papyri from the Jewish military community (ḥyl yhwdyʾ, “Jewish garrison”), not ostraca. The Elephantine ostraca (section D of TAD) are brief notes, lists, and short letters, and their contribution to this topic is limited to names containing the theophoric element YHW; the information about the Temple itself is found in the papyri. This chapter organizes these documents, indicates what each one says, and outlines the precautions required for their use. It does not reproduce the complete Aramaic texts: those of the petition to Bagohi and the Passover letter appear in the translations and dossiers of Part XI. The list of contributions includes three recipients—YHW, Eshbetel, and Anatbetel —which demonstrates a broader Yahwism in the Diaspora than that of Jerusalem during the same period. This fact proves neither systematic polytheism nor syncretism with Mazdaism, but it does preclude describing the community as exclusively Yahwist. The Archive as a Selection of Voices The Elephantine papyri do not provide a neutral, continuous account of communal life. Contracts, contribution lists, letters and petitions select people and events for different purposes. In a petition, claims about the sanctuary’s antiquity and the petitioners’ loyalty serve a persuasive function; in a contract, provisions concerning property establish obligations between parties. Historical comparison becomes more precise when it asks who speaks, to whom, with what purpose and through which formula. An ancient writing surface establishes the antiquity of the document, but does not automatically corroborate every claim it contains or make it representative of all Yahwist communities. Clarification on the use of the name YHW and dedications The divine name YHW reflects a contemporary local cultic usage and should not be simply standardized with a different Hebrew form when reproducing the documentary text. The lists of contributions and the names of deities must be interpreted within their administrative context and in the context of a military community in Egypt. Their coexistence in the document alone does not allow for the reconstruction of the theological program of all Jews in the Diaspora, nor does it identify a specific Zoroastrian influence. The analysis must consider the medium, the edition used, the letters preserved versus those restored, and the type of document before drawing conclusions for the thesis of religious contacts.

802 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM 4. What correspondence adds to the book’s question The episode reveals three features useful for comparison with the Iranian world. First, the intervention of Persian power: the temple is destroyed with the complicity of the local governor of Syene (Vidranga, the Iranian name) and rebuilt with the permission of the governor of Yehud; Persian authorities decide on matters of worship. Second, the formula of the petition, which recognizes Bagohi and Delaia as political authorities, shows a community seeking legitimacy from two centres, Jerusalem and Samaria. Third, the response limited to the offering of plant food and incense, which contrasts with the practices of the Temple in Jerusalem and raises the question of whether the blood sacrifice of Jews was tolerated in Persian Egypt next to a temple of the ram-god Khnum, where the sacrifice of sheep was acceptable. For the hypothesis studied in the previous chapter, that of cultic fire in the priestly tradition, the papyri offer indirect evidence: the altar of the temple of YHW received incense offerings, and therefore a fire must have burned there, although no document describes its tending or calls it “perpetual.” Silence is not proof of absence. The book maintains the rule of not attributing to the community a Zoroastrian -type fire cult that the papyri do not attest to. 5. THE DOCUMENTS OF THE TEMPLE OF YHW 807 II. The testimony of destruction (410 BCE) The decisive document is the petition from Jedaniah and other priests to Bagohi/ Bagoas, governor of Yehud: TAD A4.7 = Cowley 30, P. Berlin 13495. The document is dated 20 Marḥešván of the 17th year of Darius II (407 BCE) and refers to the demolition at Tammuz in the 14th year (410 BCE), when the satrap Arsames was absent. The petition blames priests of Khnum (Ḫnum /Khnum) who acted in collusion with Vidranga, the local Persian authority, who transmitted the order to his son Nafayna, commander of the garrison at Syene. According to the petitioners, Egyptian troops and other soldiers stormed the sanctuary, destroyed columns and five stone gateways, burned cedar coverings and fittings, and seized metal objects. This account is a partisan contemporary testimony and does not, in itself, constitute an independent judicial investigation. The petitioners themselves maintain that the temple predated Cambyses (conquest of Egypt, 525 BCE) and was not damaged at that time. This argument seeks to legitimize the reestablishment of the cult by appealing to a previous situation en dorsed by imperial authority; it does not authorize the deduction of an exact found ing date nor that the Persian court expressly approved each ritual practice.

THE DOCUMENTS OF THE TEMPLE OF YHW 811 V. Open historiographical problems Motivation for destruction The record indicates the involvement of priests from Khnum, but does not offer a complete and impartial explanation of their motives. It is plausible to analyse cultic competition, animal sacrifice, sacred topography, and military administration, without turning any of these interpretations into documented fact. Imperial authority The episode does not establish a policy of persecution ordered by Darius II. The narrative presents a local action during Arsames’ absence. The intervention of Bagohi and Delaías demonstrates the search for provincial mediation; it requires distinguishing between governmental competence, religious authorization, and diplomatic rhetoric. Architecture Pillars, five carved stone portals, bronze pieces, a cedar structure, and metal vessels are textual data from the report. Without archaeological remains unequivocally identified with the temple, there is no basis for reproducing an exact plan or for formally equating it with the Temple in Jerusalem. Polytheism and Yahwist diversity The existence of a sanctuary outside Jerusalem and the coexistence of divine names in local documentation prevent treating Achaemenid Yahwism as a homogeneous system. Value for the Iranian thesis Elephantine demonstrates institutional coexistence and cultural negotiation within a Persian imperial framework. It does not, in itself, prove that the doctrine of YHW derives from Ahura Mazdā or that an Iranian eschatology circulated among its
812 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM priests. The conclusion should be graded as first-rate political -administrative evidence and insufficient doctrinal evidence.

THE DOCUMENTS OF THE TEMPLE OF YHW 813 VI. Articulation with the testimonies of the monograph The Elephantine documentation links chapters XI, XL, and LVII in three ways that must be kept distinct. First, the chronology of the community is reconstructed from written documents, not from a continuous, retrospective narrative. Second, the petitions concerning the sanctuary of YHW are self-serving statements from those seeking political authorization, not impartial records corroborating every detail of the episode. Third, the TAD A4.7–A4.9 series is presented as comparative documentation: a properly critical facing edition requires line segmentation, recto and verso, condition of the physical object, records of restitutions and variants, and verification of the Cowley and Porten – Yardeni editions. The comparison is particularly useful for studying the scope of Persian provincial mediations, but it does not, on its own, allow us to derive a doctrinal identity between the worship of YHWH and that of Ahura Mazdā. The texts already reproduced in Chapter XL should be preserved, and a distinction should be made between the reading of the papyrus, editorial restitution, translation, and historical commentary.

Approach Dura-Europos, on the Syrian Euphrates, is an exceptional archaeological site that offers, within the same city and half a century, a synagogue, a Mithraeum, and a Christian house-church, in addition to temples of Semitic and Palmyrene deities. Founded as a Hellenistic city around 300 BCE, it came under Parthian rule in the 2nd century BCE, was captured by Rome in 165 CE, and fell to the Sasanian army of Shabuhr I around 256 CE. It thus presents a case study of the frontier world between Rome, Parthia, and the Sasanian Empire, especially for the 2nd and 3rd centuries CE; the preserved religious buildings are not contemporary testimonies of Jesus. The Sasanian siege The city fell around 256, after a siege in which the Sasanian lords dug mines under the walls and the Romans countermined, as revealed by excavations that uncovered the remains of soldiers from both sides in the tunnels. To fortify the wall against attack, the defenders filled the buildings attached to it with earth, thus preserving the paintings of the synagogue and the Mithraeum, which remained buried until the 20th century. This circumstance explains their exceptional preservation and should not be interpreted as a feature of religious worship. The fall of Dura is both an episode of Sasanian military expansion on the Euphrates, and the confrontation between the kings of Iran and Rome over this border forms the political backdrop for the chapters on the Sasanian period. Dura-Europos contributes three things to the book’s central theme. It shows that Jewish, Christian, and pagan communities coexisted in a border city with comparable material resources. It testifies to Mithraism in an Iranian context of origin and a Roman context of practice. And it offers a scenario in which the exchange of religious ideas was possible, but it doesn’t prove it: physical proximity is not evidence of dependence. The book, therefore, uses it at the level of probable mediation. Dura-Europos provides evidence of religious coexistence during the Roman and Sasanian periods, not a direct window into the 5th century BCE. The roughly contemporaneous nature of the decorated synagogue, the Christian meeting house and the Mithraeum allows for a comparison of community architectures and borderland visual cultures; however, it does not demonstrate doctrinal affiliation between their cults. Roman Mithraism must be distinguished from the mentions of Mithra in the Avesta and from the Achaemenid royal invocations. A correspond

Archaeological reception warning What we see of Dura-Europos today is largely a reconstruction. The site was excavated between 1928 and 1937 by Yale University and the Académie des Inscriptions et Belles-Lettres; the synagogue paintings were moved to the National Museum of Damascus, and the mithraeum and baptistery of the house-church were reassembled in the Yale University Art Gallery. The seminal publications (the Prelimin ary and Final Reports, especially C.H. Kraeling’s volumes on the synagogue, 1956, and on the Christian building, 1967) document the excavations, but their interpretations depend on the state of research at the time. Since 2011, the site has suffered extensive looting, documented by satellite imagery, which now prevents the re-examination of many contexts on-site. Therefore, in this chapter a distinction is made between what was excavated, what was moved and what was reconstructed, and what is a modern museographic solution is not attributed to the old building. Chapter Conclusion Dura-Europos documents, for the 3rd century CE, a synagogue with narrative paintings, a Roman soldiers’ mithraeum, and a Christian meeting house in the same border city between Rome and Sasanian Iran. This coexistence proves religious plurality and shared material culture, not doctrinal affiliation; nor does it directly illuminate the Achaemenid period. Its place in the book is that of a possible mediation in later times, and as such it is used. Chapter LIX. Mani and Manichaeism in the Sasanian Empire Chronological context. Mani and the birth of Manichaeism in the 3rd century CE, under the Sasanids; expansion and later testimonies. This religious synthesis is several centuries later than 1st-century Christianity. Manicheanism: internal sources and adversarial accounts The evidence comprises internal Manichaean texts, polemical accounts from Christian or Zoroastrian adversaries, and modern reconstructions. These testimonies may agree on the existence of certain institutions or controversies and diverge radically in their interpretations of its doctrines. No single hostile compendium can, on its own, take the place of a self-description. The Sasanian setting of the emergence, spread and persecution of Manichaeism belongs to a historical phase much later than Darius I. Its inclusion illuminates religious exchange and conflict in Late Antiquity; it does not provide retrospective evidence for the origins of Persian-period Jewish eschatology. Source criticism of religious controversy. The emergence of Manichaeism belongs to the 3rd century CE, several centuries after Darius I and the Achaemenid Aramaic texts. Its dualistic cosmologies and its connections with Christian, Iranian, and Mesopotamian traditions allow us to study contacts in Late Antiquity, but they cannot be used as direct evidence of the Achaemenid court religion. The apparatus must distinguish between the work attributed to Mani, the fragment actually preserved in a vernacular language, the account of an adversary, and the historian’s reconstruction. The proposed biographical date, the dating of the testimony used, and the chronology of a specific doctrine must also be separated. This distinction prevents a resemblance to Judaism or early Christianity from being automatically interpreted as a 5th -century BCE Persian borrowing. 1. Approach Mani (Middle Persian: Mānī; 216–274 or 277 CE; the date of his death is debated) founded a universal dualistic religion in the Sasanian Empire that incorporated Jewish, Christian, Iranian, and Indian elements and spread from the Mediterranean to China. He is relevant to this book for three reasons: he emerged within the con827

828 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM text of Judeo-Christian Baptist communities in Babylon; he reworked material of Jewish origin (the Book of Giants); and he was persecuted during the reign of Bahram I, in a climate where the priest Kerdir enumerated his religious enemies, among whom were the Jews. The dates and titles in this section are those of the standard bibliography, with the caveats indicated. 2. Life and Environment According to Manichean tradition, Mani was born in southern Babylonia, near Seleucia-Ctesiphon, in 216 (still under the Parthian Empire), and his father took him to a Baptist community. The main source for this period is the Cologne Codex of Mani, a minuscule Greek scroll describing his upbringing in a community traditionally identified with the Elkasites. The first revelation (around age twelve) and the second (around age twenty-four, in 240) led him to leave the community and preach. He won the favour of Shabuhr I, to whom he dedicated the only book he wrote in Middle Persian, the Shabuhragan. He died, according to tradition, in prison under Bahrām I. The Dēnkard V cites Mani (Manih) among the heretics that the text combats, as seen in chapter L. 3. Works and doctrine Table 88. He uses Jewish material related to the Aramaic Book of Giants from Qumran (fragments such as 1Q23, 4Q203 and 4Q530– 532). He links Mani to the Enochic tradition. Letters, Psalms and prayers Syriac and Central Asian languages Epistles and devotional literature. Manichean hymns in Parthian and Middle Persian (see chapter LII). The doctrine distinguishes two principles, light and darkness, and three “moments”: the past of separation, the present of mixture, and the future of renewed separation. The scheme resembles Zoroastrian dualism but differs from it on one essential point: for Mazdaism, matter is good and created by Ohrmazd, while for Mani it is the product of darkness. This is why the Pahlavi manuscripts of the Orthodox tradition treat him as the most dangerous of heretics. 4. The persecution and Kerdir’s list The priest Kerdir (Kartīr), a dominant figure during the reign of Bahram II and likely the instigator of Mani’s persecution, left inscriptions at Naqš-e Rostam, Naqsh-e Rajab, and the Kaʿba-ye Zardošt (KKZ). In the Kaʿba inscription, he boasts of having secured the dominance of the Zoroastrian religion over other faiths. The list of communities he claims to have attacked, according to standard interpretations, includes Jews (Yahūdān), Buddhists (Šamanān), Brahmins (Brāmanān), “Nazarenes” (Nāzarāyē), Christians (Kristyān), Baptists (Makdagē), and Manicheans (Zandīgān). For the book, the list matters because it provides Iranian testimony that by the end of the third century there were Jewish communities in the Sasanian Empire that the Mazdaean priests viewed as religious rivals, and that this rivalry could have consequences. The relationship between Manichaeism and the sources of the book can be summarized on three levels. There is a typological resemblance to Qumran dualism

830 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM (1QS III–IV) and to Zoroastrianism; there is probable mediation through the Baptist environment of Babylon, the Enochic traditions, and the Sasanian court; and there is no demonstrable dependence on a specific source, but rather a deliberate synthesis that Mani presents as the culmination of previous religions. To reconstruct Mani, one must separate internal Manichean testimonies from the hostile accounts transmitted by Zoroastrian, Christian, and Muslim authors. The tradition concerning his upbringing in a Mesopotamian Baptist community and the subsequent development of a missionary religion cannot be reduced to a simple variant of Mazdaean dualism. The opposition between light and darkness also belongs to other religious vocabularies; the mechanisms of creation, cosmic mixing, anthropology, and liberation differ according to the corpus. The Kirdir inscriptions possess a material and chronological status distinct from the Denkard and other later Pahlavi compilations. Therefore, their comparison with Qumran, not with Christianity, must be framed as a problem of historical contexts and transmission, not as a proven doctrinal genealogy. Distinction between Manichaean and Sasanian polemic sources The Manichean sources themselves are late compared to Mani and are scattered: the Cologne Codex of Mani (Greek, in a small-format parchment codex), the Coptic texts found at Medinet Madi around 1930 (Kephalaia, Psalter, Homilies), the fragments in Middle Persian, Parthian, Sogdian, and Uyghur from Turfan, and the Chinese texts from Dunhuang. Hostile accounts form another set: the Acta Archelai and the Christian authors who followed them, Augustine, Ephrem, and Alexander of Lycopolis; the Fihrist of Ibn al-Nadīm, from the 10th century; and, on the Mazdean side, the controversy of Dēnkard III and chapter 16 of the Škandgumānīg wizār, both from the 9th century. The Kerdir inscription, from the 3rd century, is the only contemporary Sasanian testimony, and it only names the Zandiks among the persecuted. Every statement about Mani’s doctrine must cite the body of texts to which its source belongs. Chapter Conclusion Mani belongs to the 3rd century CE and the Sasanian court, not the Persian period. His relevance to the book is threefold: he originated in a Baptist community in Babylon, he reworked the Book of Giants of Enochic tradition, and he appears, along with the Jews, on the list of those persecuted at Kerdir. Manichaeism is a de-

MANI AND MANICHAEISM IN THE SASANIAN EMPIRE 831 liberate synthesis, not a link between Achaemenid Iran and Judaism, and its dualism cannot be used as retroactive evidence of ancient Zoroastrianism. Summary The chapter presents the life and works of Mani (216–274 or 277 CE), his doctrine of the two principles and the three moments, and the persecution under Bahram I and Bahram II with the Kerdir list. It distinguishes Manichean sources from Christian, Islamic, and Mazdaean polemics, and situates the relationship with Judaism within the framework of late mediation. Chapter LX. Parsi Liturgical Manuals: The Ritual of the Vendīdād and the Nīrangs Chronological context. Modern Parsis liturgical manuals and their transmission of Avestan texts and nīrangs from earlier strata. The date of publication and the history of each ritual instruction must be distinguished from the antiquity of the recited prayer. Linguistic strata and usage rights in contemporary manuals The manuals of the priest Jal Noshirvan Panthaky — Vandīdād Saade (2016), Vandīdād-bā-Nirang (2016), and Pazand and Avesta Nīrangs (2023) — are testimonies of contemporary liturgical practice and transmission. The third explicitly acknowledges a transliteration from the Gujarati printed tradition linked to Phiroze Shapoorji Masani and is presented as a resource for recitation. Its ritual organization does not necessarily coincide with the sequence of the philological editions of the Avesta and, therefore, requires precise equivalences by formula and sec tion. Pāzand designates the writing of Middle Iranian materials in Avestan script, not a linguistic variety simply interchangeable with Old Avestan. In each ritual example, the Avestan segments, Middle Iranian passages, and modern English glosses must be identified to prevent a pedagogical transliteration from being treated as diplomatic testimony. The use of these materials will be selective and critical; the copyright notices of modern editions require obtaining permission for any extensive reproductions. The ritual manual and the historical edition are not the same source Vandīdād Saade (2016) presents the twenty-two fargards in Latin liturgical transliteration and offers a pronunciation guide. Its value is high as a document of transmission and contemporary Parsi practice, but the orthography adapted for recitation should not uncheckedly replace the philological transliterations used for the Avestan variants. Pazand and Avesta Nīrangs (Panthaky, 2023) is a modern presentation, stemming from a Gujarati publishing tradition, that brings together prayers and instructions with elements from various periods. The work also describes formulations geared toward contemporary religious needs; these should be studied as received, not transposed to the Achaemenid period. For a historical comparison of purification rituals and prayers, it is advisable to distinguish between preserved Avestan 833

The edition of the Nīrangs, Pazand and Avesta Nīrangs with their Meaning in English (Jal Noshirvan Panthaky, 2023), states that it is transliterated from a Gujar ati book by Phiroze Shapoorji Masani; its index organizes formulae subsequent to the nyāyeš and yašts, instructions for observance, and other ritual uses. This modern testimony describes a transmitted practice but does not, in itself, provide a critical edition in Avestan or Pahlavi characters. The concepts of water, fire, and purity will only be compared with passages from Ezra, Daniel, and other biblical texts when the context, ritual function, and a plausible historical horizon coincide. Variant readings that depend solely on contemporary devotional instructions will not be incorporated as ancient readings. 1. Approach: three modern Parsis liturgical manuals Avestan and Pahlavi texts studied in academic editions differ from modern reception evidence. This chapter examines three liturgical manuals from the contemporary Parsi tradition, prepared by the priest (ervad) Jal Noshirvan Panthaky (Mississauga, Ontario): the Vandīdād Saade (2016), with the twenty-two fargards in Latin transliteration and a pronunciation guide; The Vandīdād-bā-Nirang (2016, 445 pages), which brings together the Avestan text of the Vendīdād with the officiant’s ritual instructions, and Pāzand and Avesta Nīrangs (2023, 333 pages), an English translation and transliteration of Ervad Phiroze Shapoorji Masani’s Gujarati book on ritual formulae (nīrang) in pāzand and Avestan. All three are copyrighted by the compiler, and therefore the book does not reproduce them: it describes their structure, cites technical names, and gives the order of the rites, which is a matter of tradition and not of the author’s writing. The methodological caveat is the same as always in this work: these are testimonies of a living liturgy, printed in Latin transliteration from 19th- and 20th-century Gujarati books, and not testimonies of the Persian period. They serve to show how ancient texts are used today and to raise questions, not to reconstruct the Achaemenid or Sasanian cult. pāzand is Middle Persian written in the Avestan

The third group resembles, in both function and subject matter, the apotropaic texts of Sasanian Mesopotamia. Between the 5th and 7th centuries CE, incantations in Aramaic, Babylonian, Jewish, Mandaean, and Syriac were written in the re gion on clay bowls that were buried upside down in houses. These incantations targeted demons, diseases, witchcraft, and the evil eye. Classic editions, such as Montgomery’s (Aramaic Incantation Texts from Nippur, 1913), are in the public domain. The fact that the two corpora share some themes does not demonstrate any connection: the bowl incantations come from Jewish, Mandaean, and Christian communities, while the Masani nirangs belong to the Parsi tradition, with a compositional chronology that cannot be established. What can be stated is that the religious world of Sasanian Mesopotamia, where these communities coexisted with Mazdaism, produced on both shores a parallel repertoire of ritual defence of the house, and that its comparative study, with the critical editions, is a task that this book does not address. 5. General conclusion 1. The question and the method The research compares Yahwism under Achaemenid rule with evidence from Iranian religion. The period 539–332 BCE primarily encompasses the Levant; Gaugamela corresponds to 331 BCE and the death of Darius III to 330 BCE. The comparison distinguishes documented borrowing, probable mediation, and typological similarity; it also considers local development in contact with other cultures and regional inheritances. Contemporary evidence does not align with the uncertain date of composition of an Avestan passage or with a later Pahlavi compilation. This method was applied to four successive sets of documents, without omitting their Neo-Assyrian and Neo-Babylonian antecedents: first, the transformations under Achaemenid rule from 539 BCE; second, the Hellenistic and early Parthian environments; third, Judaism and Christianity of the 1st century CE, in territories subject to various powers; fourth, the Sasanian elaborations and the medieval Pahlavi compilations. Each set retains its chronology, its documentary genre, and its evidentiary density. The 6th century BCE cannot be explained solely from the later religious testimonies nor from a sequence of transmission from Persia to Judaism without intermediaries. A caution about material comparisons is necessary. Magical gems, anguipede figures and related iconographic repertoires from Egypt and the Roman Mediterranean belong to settings of religious exchange distinct from the Persian court of the sixth century BCE. Any connection with Iranian names or symbols must be supported by evidence of date, provenance, inscriptional context and intervening traditions. An uninterrupted Achaemenid → Gnostic → Christian genealogy cannot be inferred from visual resemblance alone. Nor does the name “Abraxas” identify every anguipede image or establish an Iranian etymology. 2. What the book allows us to affirm Iranian loanwords can be identified in Hebrew and Aramaic, particularly in the vocabulary of office, communication, law and court life. Each proposed etymology retains its degree of certainty and its attested variants. The history of dāt, pitgām and pardēs attests to linguistic contact; rāz acquires a revelatory function in Daniel. These semantic developments do not show that an entire religious doctrine came 843

844 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM from the source language. Greek terms must be examined along their own routes of transmission. Second, there is documented contact at Elephantine. Aramaic papyri allow us to reconstruct a Jewish military community that maintained a temple of YHWH, appealed to the Persian governor (as in the case of the petition to Bagohi), and whose names and vocabulary show Iranian influences. But the hypothesis that the worship of this community reflects Mazdaean practices, as has been recently proposed, remains under debate; the book treats it as a proposal worthy of examination, not as a definitive conclusion. The conceptual comparisons involve texts with different dates and functions. Y. 30 and 1QS do not necessarily articulate the same form of dualism; the biblical “anointed one” and the developing figure of the Saošyant likewise require independent histories. Yt. 19 describes the raising of the dead and the renewal of existence, and deserves consideration alongside later Pahlavi witnesses. Yet neither the date of the relevant Avestan formulation nor a channel by which it reached the authors of Daniel has been demonstrated. Theopompus adds an important external testimony, not proof of transmission. Achaemenid inscriptions express devotion to Auramazda and opposition to falsehood, but they do not offer a comprehensive description of the kings’ religion. XPh alone does not prove a uniform imperial monotheism. The silence regarding Zoroaster is a fact that must be considered in conjunction with the function of the epigraphic genre. Greek descriptions and archaeology can complement this testimony, while preserving their differences in date, location, and perspective. 3. What the book does not allow us to state It is not possible to assert that Jesus was originally interpreted as the Saošyant: the hypothesis presupposes the development of an idea of a universal saviour that the ancient Avestan sources do not have and which, in the Pahlavi sources, is presented in a framework very different from the Gospel one. It is not possible to maintain that the temptation of Jesus depends on Vendīdād 19; the two accounts share a motif (the messenger tested by the spirit of evil, with an offer of dominion), but the number forty and the structure of the Gospel account have a sufficient biblical basis. An etymology that links the word logos with an Iranian root cannot be accepted without further ado; The book showed that logos has no cognate, and that the

GENERAL CONCLUSION 845 parallel with matra must be formulated as a functional correspondence. Nor is there proof that Christmas, Christian baptism, or the calendar of festivals originated from Mithraism or Zoroastrianism; what exists are coincidences of dates and symbols that require a case-by-case examination. Historical Results and the Strength of Hypotheses The general thesis accommodates findings of different strengths without forcing a choice between total influence and complete isolation. Administrative loanwords establish linguistic contact where etymology and transmission are documented. An eschatological resemblance also requires an account of the motif’s history and the direction of its reception. Where those links are absent, the parallel retains heuristic value: it defines a problem and identifies corpora for comparison, but cannot be presented as demonstrated dependence. Each chapter’s conclusions must therefore be read in relation to its unit of evidence—word, formula, practice, representation or doctrine—and cannot automatically be transferred from one category to another. One limitation lies in the distance between composition, transmission, and pre served testimony. The extensive Pahlavi texts, compiled in the 9th and 10th centur ies, may incorporate earlier material without each motif being dated. Avestan transmission also requires linguistic, ritual, and manuscript criticism. Quotations from indirect transmission remain marked; a prose revision does not eliminate this need for verification. 4. Influence and convergence: balance of the thesis The balance of the inquiry supports a graduated, rather than a universal, thesis of Iranian influence. Linguistic and administrative contacts are demonstrable. Royal imagery and certain institutional or cultic correspondences are plausible fields of mediation, though each requires its own evidence. The more ambitious comparisons—dualism, judgement, resurrection and the final saviour—remain hypotheses graded individually in Appendix D. Darius I provides an important historical centre of gravity for contact through imperial administration, royal representation and temple policy; this does not date the later doctrinal systems to his reign. A lex-

846 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM ical borrowing cannot give an unverified theological parallel the certainty that the borrowing itself possesses. The model that best respects the documents allows for communities in contact that preserve, reinterpret, and occasionally adopt external elements. It should be compared with specific Iranian transmission, Mesopotamian antecedents, and Hellenistic circulation. The existence of contact does not compel the selection of a general dependency; nor does similarity necessitate isolation. The matrix records this distinction and leaves open the questions that the evidence does not resolve. Alternative evidence of mediation. The Iranian explanation gains strength when there is priority given to a specific formulation, a plausible channel, and shared diagnostic features; it loses strength when it depends solely on a late Pahlavi synthesis or a universal motif. This matrix does not require choosing an exclusive cause: it distinguishes overlapping influences and degrees of certainty. Mesopotamia, Babylon, and Egypt provide documented scenarios of contact at different times. Dura-Europos shows urban coexistence of cults in the 3rd century CE, and Babylonian Talmudic literature belongs to later contexts of reception. These testimonies do not retrospectively complete an Achaemenid channel. It must be proven in each case who transmitted which practice, through which language, and in which period. 5. Perspectives In archaeology, records of artifacts and contexts with authorized publication of images are required. Rabbinic, Syriac, and Armenian sources must be treated according to their own processes of composition and transmission. The book’s proposed criterion for this task is simple: each parallel should be presented with its source, date, and possible channel, allowing the reader to decide, with the tables in hand, the extent of the evidence. If the book has helped to move a similarity from intuition to a testable hypothesis, or to abandon one that cannot withstand scrutiny, it will have fulfilled its purpose. Evidentiary balance (summary of the argument). The firm documentary contribution concerns imperial contact and the circulation of legal, administrative, and courtly vocabulary: in these areas, there are Iranian, Aramaic, and Hebrew testimonies comparable in form, function, and context. A general conclusion of religious dependence cannot be drawn from them. Doctrinal comparison retains heur-

GENERAL CONCLUSION 847 istic value when contrasting Y 30, Yt 19, Dan 12:1–3, 1QS III–IV with Christian receptions, provided that the dates of composition, manuscript transmission, literary genre, and available historical channels are taken into account. The proof of transmission requires a cumulative argument: (a) chronological precedence of a relevant formulation, not merely antiquity of the language; (b) specific correspondence of form and function, not a generic religious theme; (c) documentable agents and spaces of exchange; and (d) reasoned exclusion of shared inher itances or independent developments. In the absence of one or more links, the comparison remains a hypothesis and does not stand as evidence. Royal inscriptions, the Elephantine documents, and the Persepolis record show actual contacts; they do not, in themselves, prove the transfer of resurrection, angelology, or messianism. The interpretive framework thus distinguishes four levels: documented contact; lexical transfer in specific words; plausible institutional mediations subject to local control; and religious parallels of priority or dependence still debated. This gradation does not invalidate the dialogue between Judaism and Iranian traditions: it specifies what can be concluded from each testimony without projecting Sasanian or medieval Pahlavi formulations onto Darius I. Multiple Transmissions. Possible parallels in angels, demonology, judgement, and world renewal will be evaluated alongside biblical, Mesopotamian, and Levantine antecedents, and with attention to Greek and Hellenistic reinterpretations. Chronological order alone does not demonstrate the direction of borrowing. For the main hypothesis, the result is “proven contact, probable ideological and cultic influence, doctrinal transfer sustained by convergence”; the distance between these degrees is not a deficiency of the analysis, but rather the form a thesis takes when measured against the preserved dossier.
