OG differentiates three destinations in its transmitted syntax (life; reproach; dispersion and everlasting shame); Θ has a twofold contrast. Do not reduce OG to two destinations without noting its additional clause. Daniel 12:3: wise and righteous OG: οἱ κατισχύοντες τοὺς λόγους μου (‘those who uphold / make my words prevail’); Θ: ἀπὸ τῶν δικαίων τῶν πολλῶν (‘from among the many righteous’; syntax debated). The Old Greek shifts the reference toward fidelity to the speaker’s words; Θ remains closer to the Hebrew field of righteousness, but neither expression should be flattened into a verbatim translation of the MT. Daniel 12:4: the end of the age OG: πλησθῇ ἡ γῆ ἀδικίας (‘the earth be filled with injustice’); Θ: πληθυνθῇ ἡ γνῶσις (‘knowledge be increased’). Substantial interpretive divergence. It may reflect translation technique, exegesis or a variant Vorlage; none of these explanations is established by the contrast alone. Editorial control. The readings cited here are the published OG and Θ textual forms, not diplomatic transcriptions newly collated from P. 967. The OG of Daniel 12:2 distinguishes life, reproach, and dispersion with lasting shame; Θ sets life against lasting reproach and shame. At 12:3, the OG clause about upholding “my words” and Θ’s difficult construction about the righteous must each be interpreted within its own Greek syntax. At 12:4, “the earth be filled with injustice” (OG) and “knowledge be increased” (Θ) are distinct readings, but the claim that OG translated a different Hebrew consonantal Vorlage remains a hypothesis rather than an established palaeographic finding. Vendīdād: English Study Translation (Mediated) Preliminary note on this translation The Vendīdād (Vīdēvdād, “law against demons”) is the only one of the books of the Avestan Sasanian canon that is preserved complete; It consists of twenty-two fargards (“chapters”) of very uneven content: mythical geography (1), the myth of Yima (2), agriculture and the purity of the land (3), contracts and crimes (4), laws of purity (5–8), the nine-night purification (9), formulae of exorcism (10–11), mourning (12), the dog (13–15), menstrual impurity (16), hair and nails (17), priestly duties (18), the temptation of Zarathustra and death and the fate of the soul (19), the first physician (20), healing spells (21), and the diseases of Aŋra Mainyu (22). Its final redaction is late, and its written fixation dates from the Sasanian period. No data allows it to be projected directly to the Achaemenid period, and therefore its use in this book is comparative and it is dated in each case. Source and textual scope. The twenty-two fargards are presented in an English study rendering mediated by the Spanish translation of James Darmesteter, The Zend-Avesta I: The Vendîdâd, SBE 4 (1880; revised 1895; North American reproduction 1898), consulted at avesta.org/vendidad/. Darmesteter predates Geldner (1886–1896) and cannot derive from a text subsequently established by him. The translated text, Darmesteter’s historical notes and the author’s explicitly identified comments remain distinct. Modern rubrics and intercalated Yasna or Visperad sequences are not incorporated as text of the nask. Digital glosses signed -JHP are excluded; notes 433–462 in Vd 8 identify their source numbers. Modern liturgical reception is examined in Chapter LX. Scope. Darmesteter’s version relies heavily on the Zand and must be compared with subsequent philology. The references are to the notes following each fargard. 904 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM The Avesta and the Zand The historical title “Zend-Avesta” does not designate a separate work with the status of a second canonical book: it derives from the association of the Avesta (the text, in the Avestan language) with the Zand (the translation and exegetical commentary, primarily in Middle Persian or Pahlavi), which the Sasanian tradition transmitted along with it. This is why the 19th-century editions (Anquetil-Duperron, Westergaard, Darmesteter) include “Zend-Avesta” in their titles. There is no canonical book called “Sedavesta”: what should be studied, and what this book does in chapters L, LI, and LX and in the fargards that follow, is the relationship between the Avestan text, its Pahlavi translation, and the subsequent commentaries. The relationship between text, translation, and exegesis is studied as a problem of transmission. Sixteen perfect lands created by Ahura Mazdā, and as many plagues created by Aŋra Mainyu Introduction and synopsis of Darmesteter This chapter is an enumeration of sixteen perfect lands created by Ahura Mazdā, and of as many plagues created in opposition by Aŋra Mainyu. Many attempts have been made not only to identify these sixteen lands, but also to draw historical conclusions from their order of succession, as if it represented the actual order of migrations and settlements of the ancient Iranian tribes. But there is nothing in the text to support such broad inferences. We have here only a geographical description of Iran, viewed from a religious perspective. Of those sixteen lands, nine can be identified with certainty, namely:

The various plagues created by Aŋra Mainyu to mar the native perfection of Ahura’s creations provide instructive information about the religious condition of several Iranian countries at the time this Fargard was written. Harat appears to have been the seat of puritanical sects that took rigorism to extremes in the law of purific ation. Sorcery was prevalent in the Helmend River basin, and the Pairikas were powerful in Kabul, which is a Zoroastrian way of saying that Hindu civilization prevailed in those regions, which in fact in the two centuries before and after Christ were known as White India, and remained more Indian than Iranian until the Muslim conquest. Airyanem Vaeja, Iran-Vej, is the holy land of Zoroastrianism: Zoroaster was born there and founded his religion there (Bd 20.32; 32.3); there the first animal couple appeared (Bd 14.4; Zadspram, 9.8). From its name, “the Iranian seed,” it seems to have been considered the original seat of the Iranian race. It has generally been supposed to belong to eastern Iran, like the provinces listed after it, mainly because of the name of its river, the Vanguhi Daitya, which in Sasanian times (as Veh) was the name of the Oxo. But Bd. clearly states that Iran-Vej is “bordering Adarbajan” (29.12); Now, Adarbaijan is bordered by the Caspian Sea to the east, by the Rangha provinces to the west, by Media proper to the south, and by Arran to the north. The Rangha provinces are irrelevant, since they are mentioned at the end of the Fargard (verse 20), and the climatic conditions of Iran-Vej, with its long winter, likewise exclude Media and suit Arran, where summer lasts only two months (cf. § 4, note 6). The name itself agrees, for the country known as Arran seems to have been known to the Greeks as ‘Arania (Stephen of Byzantium), which brings it closer to our Airyanem. On the Vanguhi Daitya, see the following note. 14. The Vanguhi Daitya, belonging to Arran, must be the present Aras (the classical Araxes). The Aras was called Vanguhi, like the Oxo, but was distinguished from him by the addition Daitya, which made him “the Vanguhi of the Law” (the Vanguhi next to whom Zarathustra received the Law). 15. “There are many khrafstras in the Daitik, as they say: the Daitik is full of khrafstras” (Bd 20.13). Snakes abound on the banks of the Araxes (Morier, A Second Journey, p. 250) today as much as in the time of Pompey, whose road from Albania to Hyrcania was blocked (Plut.) 16. Arran (Karabakh) is famous for its cold winters as much as for its beauty. On Naoroz (the first day of spring), the fields are still covered in snow. The temperature does not soften before the second half of April; no flowers appear before May. Summer, marked by the migration of nomads from the plains to the mountains, begins around June 20 and ends in mid-August.

Mythos of Yima [Jamshed] Introduction and synopsis of Darmesteter This Fargard can be divided into two parts. Part One (1-20). Ahura Mazdā proposes to Yima, son of Vivanghat, that he receive the law from him and bring it to humankind. Upon his refusal, he orders him to protect his creatures and make them prosper. Yima, consequently, makes them thrive and multiply, banishes death and disease from them, and expands the earth threefold, which had become too small for its inhabitants. Part Two (21 to the end). Faced with the approach of a terrible winter, which will destroy all living creatures, Yima, advised by Ahura, builds a Vara to keep there the best representatives of each species of animals and plants, and there they live a life of perfect happiness. It is difficult not to recognize in this latter legend a Zoroastrian adaptation of the flood, whether taken from the Bible or from Chaldean mythology. The resemblance is so striking that it did not escape the Muslims, and Macoudi states that certain authors place the date of the flood in the time of Jamshed. There are essential and necessary differences between the two legends, the main one being that in the monotheistic narrative the flood is sent as punishment from God, while in the dualistic version it is a plague from the daēvas; but the core of both legends is the same: the hero in both is a righteous man who, warned beforehand by God, builds a refuge to receive chosen specimens of humanity, destined to one day replace an imperfect humanity, destroyed by a universal calamity. Fargard 4. Contracts and Outrages Introduction and synopsis of Darmesteter This Fargard is the only one in the Vendīdād that deals strictly with legal objects. I a. Classification of contracts according to the value of their object (§ 2). — A contract is cancelled by paying the amount of the contract one degree higher (§§ 3–4). Religious responsibility of the family for the violation of a contract by one of its members (§§ 5–10). Punishment of the Mihr-Druj (one who breaks a contract) (§§ 11–16). II a. Definition of the insults known as agerepta (threatening attitude), avaoirishta (aggression) and aredush (blows) (§ 17). Penalties for threats (§§ 18–21); for assaults (§§ 22–25); for blows (§§ 26–29); for wounds (§§ 30–33); for wounds that cause bleeding (§§ 34–36); for broken bones (§§ 37–39); for homicide (§§ 40–43).

1012 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM Fargard 9. The Barashnum of the Nine Nights Introduction and synopsis of Darmesteter Regarding the name Barashnom, see Vd 8.40, note 50. Synopsis. I a (1–11). Description of the place for the purification of the impure (the Barashnom-gah). I b (12–36). Description of the purification. II (37–44). Fees of the purifier. III (47–57). The false purifier; his punishment. Sections 45 and 46 belong rather to the following fargard. The ceremony described in this fargard is known among the Parsis as barashnom no shaba, or “Barashnom of the Nine Nights,” because it lasts nine nights (see § 35). It is the great purification, the most efficacious of all; it not only cleanses the defiled person but also opens the heavens for them (see Vd 19.33). Thus, although it was originally intended only for a person defiled by a dead person, it became, during the Parsi period, a pious practice that could be performed without having touched a corpse; moreover, its performance was prescribed at least once during the Nuzudi period (at fifteen years of age, when a young Parsi becomes a member of the community), in order to wash away the natural impurity contracted in the womb (Saddar 36). The priest who wishes to appear before the Warharan fire or to celebrate the Yasna or Vendīdād service must also submit to it. Text Ia. 1. Fargard 10. formulae recited during the purification process Introduction and synopsis of Darmesteter Today, before placing the deceased in the coffin, two priests recite the Gāthā Ahunavaitī (Yasna 28–34): this is called the Gāh sārnā (chant of the Gāthās: gāthāo srāvayēiti). From the following fargard, it appears that in ancient times the five Gāthās and the Yasna Haptaŋhāiti were recited. Certain stanzas were recited several times and with a certain emphasis (framrava), and were followed by certain formulae. The purpose of this fargard is to show what these stanzas are, how many times each was recited, and to give the corresponding formulae. Text 1. Zarathustra asked Ahura Mazdā: “O Ahura Mazdā! The upaman: how long it lasts for different relatives Introduction and synopsis of Darmesteter This chapter is found only in the Vendīdād Sādah; it is missing from the Vendīdād zand-pahlavi. This is apparently due solely to the accidental loss of some folios in the only manuscript from which all the copies known so far are derived; and, in fact, even in the oldest manuscripts the following fargard is numbered as thirteenth (Westergaard, Zend-Avesta, preface, p. 5). The prescriptions in the preceding chapter are general and do not depend on the relationship of the faithful to the deceased; those in this fargard, however, are of a special nature and apply only to the close relatives of the deceased. Their purpose

1034 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM is to determine how long the period of “absence” (upaman) should last for the different relatives. It is not explained what is meant by this word; but, since the word upaman is commonly used to indicate the abode of the impure in the Armest-gāh, separated from the faithful and from all clean objects, this word upaman seems to indicate a certain period of mourning, marked by abstention from usual occupations. The duration of the upaman varies according to the degrees of kinship; and in each degree it is doubled for relatives who have died in a state of sin (i.e., with a sin not redeemed by the Patet: see Vd. 9.49, note 30). The relative duration of the upaman is as follows: For the head of the family (§ 7): 6 months (or one year). First degree. For the father or mother (§ 1), for the son or daughter (§ 3), for the brother or sister (§ 5): 30 days (or 60). Second degree. For the grandfather or grandmother (§ 9), for the grandson or granddaughter (§ 11): 25 days (or 50). Third degree. For the t io oo la t ía (§ 13): 20 days (or 40). Fourth degree. For the first cousin (§ 15): 15 days (or 30). Fifth degree. For the son or daughter of a cousin (§ 17): 10 days (or 20). Sixth degree. Atonement for the death of a water dog Introduction and synopsis of Darmesteter This fargard is merely an appendix to the final clauses of the preceding fargard (§ 50 ff.). It describes in detail how the killing of a water dog (an otter) can be expiated. The extravagance of the prescribed penalties may well cast doubt on whether the le gislation of the Vendīdād ever had any substantial practical existence. These exorbitant prescriptions seem intended only to impress upon the minds of the faithful the enormity of the offence to be avoided.

APPENDICES D–E: CRITICAL MATRIX AND STUDY TRANSLATION 1083 Fargard 19. The Temptation of Zarathustra Introduction and synopsis of Darmesteter I (§§ 1–3). Aŋra Mainyu sent the demon Buiti to kill Zarathustra; Zarathustra loudly sang the Ahunwar, and the demon fled, confused by the sacred words and by Zarathustra’s glory. Ia (§§ 4–10). Anra Mainyu himself attacks him and poses riddles that he must solve under penalty of death. The Prophet repels him with celestial stones, given by Ahura, and announces that he will destroy his creation. The demon promises him dominion over the world if he worships him, as his ancestors have done, and renounces the religion of Mazda. Zoroaster disdainfully rejects his offers. He announces that he will destroy him with the weapons given by Ahura, namely, the implements of sacrifice and the sacred words. Then he recites the Tatthwa Peresa, that is, the Gatha, in which he asks Ahura for instruction on all the mysteries of the material and spiritual world. The remainder of the Fargard contains samples of the various questions posed by Zarathustra and the answers given by Ahura. It is a compendium of Revelation (cf. HN). II (11–17). How to destroy the impurity born from contact with the dead? — By invoking the Mazdean Religion. A series of invocations taught by Ahura and de veloped by Zarathustra (15–16). III (18–19). How to promote the prosperity of creation? — Through the rites of the baresman [barsom]. IV (20–25). How to purify the man and the clothes contaminated by the dead? — With gomez, water and perfume. V (26–34). On the retribution of deeds after death; on the fate of the wicked and the righteous; the Chinwad bridge. II a (34–42). Another series of invocations. VI (43–47). The demons, dismayed by the birth of the Prophet, rush back to hell. As can be seen from the preceding analysis, the essential part of this Fargard consists of sections I and VI, the remainder being an indefinite development. APPENDICES D–E: CRITICAL MATRIX AND STUDY TRANSLATION 1099 Fargard 20. Thrita, the first healer Introduction and synopsis of Darmesteter It has already been seen (Farg. VII, 44) that there are three kinds of medicine: that which heals with the knife, that which heals with herbs, and that which heals with sacred incantations. The present Fargard deals with the origin of medicine, in particular herbal medicine. Its inventor was Thrita, of the family of the Sāma, to whom Ahura Mazdā caused ten thousand medicinal plants to descend from heaven, which grew around the tree of eternal life, the white Hom or Gaokerena (§ 4). This Thrita is mentioned only once more in the Avesta, in Yasna 9.7, where he appears as one of the first priests of Haoma. This explains his medical expertise: since Haoma is the plant of eternal life, it is natural that one of its first priests was the first healer. This Fargard contains only one allusion to the origin of knife medicine [surgery], which, it seems, was revealed by Khshathra Vairya (§ 3). The last paragraphs (§§ 5–12) deal with the medicine of spells. The functions attributed here to Thrita were sometimes conferred on his almost namesake Thraētaona [Faridū] (see Westergaard, Fragments, II). Hamza makes Thraētaona the inventor of medicine (ed. Gottwaldt, p. 23; cf. Mirkhond, Early Kings of Persia, trans. Shea, p. 152); the Tavīds (exorcism formulae) against disease bear his name, and we find in the Avesta itself his Fravaši invoked “against scabies, burning fever, humors, cold fever (Vd 7.58), incontinence, against plagues created by the serpent (Yt13.131).” From the last words of this passage we see that the disease was understood as coming from the snake; in other words, it was considered a kind of poisoning [n. 850], and for this reason the snake slayer (Aži Dahāka) [Zohāk] was invoked to act against it. Text 1. Zarathustra asked Ahura Mazdā: “Ahura Mazdā, Benevolent Spirit, Maker of the material world, you Holy One! Who was the first of the healers [n. 851], of the wise, the happy, the wealthy, the glorious, the strong, the Paradhatas [n. 852], to turn back disease from disease, to turn back death from death [n. 853], and first to turn away the point of the sword and the fire of fever from the bodies of mortals?”

Exodus 3:1–15: The Burning Bush This passage is the central focus of chapter LVI. It is worth reading with three philological observations. First: the text does not speak of an altar or a vessel of fire, but of a “flame of fire” (labbat ʾēš) “in the midst of the bush” (mittôk hassĕneh), in which the “angel of YHWH” appears (v. 2) and which is later identified with God himself (vv. 4–6); the bush “was burning” and “was not consumed” (v. 2). Second: the command to remove one’s sandals (v. 5) has a direct parallel in Joshua 5:15 and is based on the holiness of the place (ʾadmat-qōdeš), not on that of the fire. Third: the place is “the mountain of God, Horeb” (v. 1), whose theophanic tradition is attested in texts that critics consider to predate the Persian period (for example, Judges 5:4–5 and Deuteronomy 33:2), and the priest of Midian, Jethro, links the scene to a non-Mazdaean context; therefore, a demonstrable dependence on the Iranian fire cult cannot be affirmed (see Table 81). It is possible, however, as a working hypothesis regarding the later priestly redaction, to ask whether the vocabulary of fire and purity in the passage was enriched through contact with the Persian cult; this question is discussed in chapter LVI. Ezra 1:1: Cyrus’s “first year” in Babylon is understood within the post-539 BCE horizon; the date of the narrated event does not automatically date the preserved literary version. 1130 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM Philological and Historical Notes. (1) Ezra 2:59–63: the demonstration of ancestry defines regulated access to priestly service. The exclusion in 2:62 refers to genealogical record-keeping, not to bodily contamination inferred without proof. (2) The term tiršātāʾ (2:63), the governor’s title, must be analysed separately before proposing an Iranian loanword with an unequivocal etymology. (3) The total of 42,360 (2:64) is attested in both Ezra and Nehemiah, but it does not agree with the simple sum of all the preserved subtotals; the discrepancy is a critical problem, not a fact to be quietly altered. Exegetical, philological and witness control notes 1. 3.1: The formula “as one man” expresses the unity of the assembly and does not allude to an Iranian institution. The seventh month of the ritual calendar and the exact historical date, which the passage does not specify, must be kept distinct. 2. 3,2–3: the centrality of the altar precedes the construction of the temple. In 3.3 the elec tronic witness transcribes ketiv ‫ ויעל‬and qere ‫ ;ַוַּיֲעלּו‬The plural is translated according to the qere and the difference is preserved in the apparatus. 3. 3,4–6: ‫ ֻּס ּכ ֹו ת‬designates the Feast of Tabernacles. The perpetual burnt offering, the calendar, and the Mosaic law belong to the Yahwist representation of the passage; an Avestan ritual parallel does not yet constitute borrowing evidence. 4. 3,7: ‫ ְּכ ִר ְׁש יֹו ן‬refers to the authorization attributed to Cyrus. 5. 3,8–9: Levitical organization, supervision of works, and the twenty-year threshold are statements of the narrative; they should not be transferred to the exact reconstruction of a sixth-century BCE work without external documentation.

(4) The expression “king of Assyria” in 6:22 is the transmitted reading, even though the immediate context deals with the reconstruction in the Persian period; it should not be replaced in the translation with “king of Persia.” It can be understood as a retrospective imperial reference or an inherited designation, but such an explanation is an interpretation, not a variant. 1140 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM Critical Notes on Ezra 7:1–11 and 7:27–28. (1) The genealogy in 7:1–5 is a literary sequence of priestly lineage; its continuity does not prove that all intermediate generations are enumerated. (2) sōfērmāhîr (7:6): “skillful scribe” indicates competence and does not require a translation of “write quickly.” (3) The “seventh year” in 7:7–9 belongs to the narrative framework of Artaxerxes; its identification with an absolute calendar date must be justified separately. (4) 7:9, yəsud: “began” interprets a form of disputed meaning; the initial narrative value is preserved without asserting a closed etymology. (5) 7:11, paršegen: “copy” identifies the declared status of the letter, without guaranteeing diplomatic authenticity. The letter itself is in Aramaic (7:12–26); 7:27 returns to Hebrew. (6) 7:27–28 also changes register, from royal decree to autobiographical praise; the “hand of YHWH” is the narrator’s theological language and not a proven Iranian formula. (7) For the Greek apparatus, the Ezra-Nehemiah tradition and 1 Ezra must be examined separately; they have not been merged in the Hebrew text. This presentation includes material presence and numbering, not an exhaustive philological verification of each lexical decision. (7) The ancient Greek of Daniel and the tradition of Theodotion exhibit relevant differences in 9:24–27; they are described by their independent textual systems, without introducing invented variants or attributing readings to specific manuscripts. These images of final campaigns and death near the holy mountain do not correspond linearly with ancient information regarding the end of Antiochus IV in the eastern part of the empire in 164 BCE. The majority historical-critical explanation considers this divergence an indication that the author narrates earlier events in considerable detail and projects an outcome that did not occur as predicted. There are different recapitulative and theological readings; these should be recorded as interpretations, not as facts. Daniel 10-12: Historical, Philological and Comparative Commentary on the Final Vision Literary Unity and Method. Daniel 10:1–12:13 forms a narrative whole: 10 introduces the seer and the messenger; 11 develops a history of empires expressed as revelation; 12 articulates the deliverance, the awakening of the dead, and the timing of the crisis. The narrative places Daniel in the third year of Cyrus (10:1), but this literary setting does not allow us to date the composition of the vision to the sixth century BCE. The reconstructed timeframe

1194 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM for much of 11:21–12:13 is the Antiochene persecution of 167–164 BCE. It is important to systematically distinguish between the time of the narrative, the presupposed history, the composition, and the manuscript transmission. The translation of the Hebrew text appears in Appendix F and is not repeated here; an exegesis of individual passages with precise references is provided. 7 bis.1. Daniel 10: Cyrus, the man clothed in linen, and the princes of Persia and Greece Daniel 10:1–3 places the revelation in the third year of Cyrus, the ruler associated with the Persian conquest of Babylon (539 BCE). The text presents three weeks of mourning or abstinence; it does not necessarily describe an absolute fast, specifying that Daniel abstained from choice foods, meat, wine, and anointings. The period of twenty- one days corresponds narratively to the resistance of the prince of Persia for the same number of days (10:13). This is a significant literary construction; to transform the numerical symmetry into a verifiable chronology of heavenly events would exceed the scope of the text. The figure who appears by the river, or Ḥiddeqel —usually identified with the Tigris —is dressed in linen and wears a gold belt; his body shines and his voice has a superhuman intensity (10:4–6). The formal comparison with Ezekiel 1 and 9:2–3 and with the visions in Daniel 7–8 is pertinent. However, the character is not given an unequivocal personal name in 10:5–6: identifying him without question with Gabriel or Michael is an exegetical decision, not a translation. It is also necessary not to automatically identify all the figures who speak to or touch Daniel throughout the chapter as if the narrative always specified a single agent. In 10:13, 20–21, the Hebrew term śar designates a prince, chief, or leader. The traditional interpretation understands the prince of Persia and the prince of Greece as celestial powers linked to peoples and kingdoms, in contrast to Michael, “your prince.” The alternative reading proposed by Tim Meadowcroft allows for the examination of political referents and maintains that the narrative leaves the celestial and historical planes permeable. None of these hypotheses allows for a direct equation of the prince of Persia with Ahura Mazdā, Aŋra Mainyu, a specific yazata, or a supposed Zoroastrian hierarchy documented under Cyrus. The historical, linguistic, and textual link must be demonstrated before asserting any affiliation. The “book of truth” (sefer emet, 10,21) functions as the literary authority for the coming revelation. It is important to distinguish its function — a celestial record of events —from that of the “book” in which those destined for salvation are recorded (12,1): the association is possible, but the material identity of both books is not explicitly stated.

Daniel 11: A History of Persia, Macedonia, the Seleucids, and the Ptolemies The first verse (11:1) refers to the “first year of Darius the Mede,” while the prologue of 10:1 is set in the third year of Cyrus. This distinction must be preserved: it is a retrospective articulation internal to the messenger’s discourse, not a continuous royal chronology nor a basis for equating this literary Darius with Darius I, son of Hystaspes. In 11:2, the succession of three Persian kings and a fourth, especially wealthy one, is a selective enumeration: the Achaemenid Empire had more than four rulers. The frequent association of the last with Xerxes I (Greek campaign of 480 BCE; Herodotus, Histories 7) depends on how Cyrus and the short-lived ruler Bardiya/Gaumata are counted. This difficulty should be noted without imposing a single list as a literal reading of the Hebrew. The “powerful king” of 11:3–4 is identified in the dominant historical analysis with Alexander III of Macedon; the partition of his kingdom represents the disintegration after 323 BCE. The contrast does not establish an immediate sequence of successions between Xerxes and Alexander: other Persian kings intervene between their reigns. In 11:5–20, “south” and “north” are understood geographically in relation to Judea: Ptolemaic Egypt and the Seleucid monarchy centred in Syria. The dynastic marriages (11:6 and 11:17), expeditions, and alternations between the two kingdoms must be contextualized within Hellenistic history, without projecting them onto the period of Darius I or turning the descriptions into literal diplomatic records. In 11:21–39, the identification of the royal figure with Antiochus IV Epiphanes (175– 164 BCE) is historically sound in its general outlines, although the details require separate examination. The Egyptian campaigns, the Roman resistance in 168 BCE (11:30; Polybius, Histories 29.27), and the suppression of regular sacrifice with the “abomination of devastation” (11:31) make the temple crisis of 167 intelligible. The ancient Jewish sources are not homogeneous: 1 Maccabees 1:54–59; 4:52–59 and 2 Maccabees 6–7; 10:1–8 have different emphases, chronologies, and objectives. The rededication of 164 BCE... CE constitutes a point of documentary comparison, not an automatic equivalence with each apocalyptic term of Daniel. In 11:40–45, the king of the north meets his end near the holy mountain. This account differs from the narrative of Antiochus IV’s death during his eastern campaign in 164 BCE (1 Maccabees 6:1–16; 2 Maccabees 9; Polybius 31:9, according to the fragmentary tradition; J.D. Bing and Joseph Sievers, “Antiochus,” Encyclopaedia Iranica). For historical -critical analysis, this divergence serves as a clue to understanding the final outcome before the historical conclusion is known; there are distinct theological and recapitulative interpretations, which should be noted as such. The translation preserves the discrepancy without emending the text.

Daniel 12: Michael, judgement, resurrection and timeframes for liberation Michael reappears as the “great prince” who protects the people (12:1), in continuity with 10:13, 21. The period of distress is presented as an exceptional crisis and culminates in the salvation of those whose names appear in the book. This expression relates to the biblical imagery of the register of the living (Exodus 32:32–33; Malachi 3:16), without demonstrating dependence on a specific Persian celestial book. The contrast between the book of 10:21 and that of 12:1 must be kept clear in the translation and commentary. Daniel 12:2 describes how “many” (rabbîm) of those who sleep in the dust will awake; some to everlasting life and others to lasting disgrace. It is a cardinal testimony of resurrection and retribution in Second Temple Jewish literature. The philological discussion revolves in part around the scope of “many”: it is not permissible to substitute the term with “all” without note, nor to deduce from the word that the text conclusively denies any broader projection. In 12:3, the maskîlîm, the “learned” or “wise,” shine like the firmament: the passage links suffering, teaching, and vindication. Their identification with a unique historical organization during the Maccabean Revolt remains a hypothesis. Ecdotic remission — Daniel 12:2–3. For the OG/ Θ differences in the images of awakening, the additional expression concerning dispersion, and the formulation concerning those who “make my words prevail” (OG 12:3), see the apparatus in Chapter XVI. In this commentary on Daniel, the value of the Masoretic Hebrew as the base text for the translation is maintained; the presence of Greek variants does not, by itself, allow us to determine which would be the original form or to date an Iranian eschatological borrowing. The relationship with Isaiah 26:19, Ezekiel 37, and other Jewish testimonies compels us to consider internal developments within the tradition before attributing the doctrine of resurrection to an Iranian source. The Avestan materials on final renewal and the Pahlavi texts on resurrection are legitimate comparisons, but they do not constitute the same chronological testimony: the date of the religious stratum, the composition of the preserved text, manuscript transmission, and modern translation must be distinguished. Terminological equivalences such as “resurrection” and “renewal of the world” are insufficient to support a historical influence. In 12:4, 9, the revelation is commanded to remain sealed until the time of the end; this literary device explains its retrospective authority. In 12:7, “a time, times, and half a time” appear (cf. 7:25). The numbers 1,290 days (12:11) and 1,335 days (12:12) must be preserved as two distinct figures, without harmonizing them with the “2,300 evenings and mornings” of 8:14. Their interpretation may be related to successive horizons of expectation during the crisis, but the exact correspondence with a verifiable calendar is not derived

HEBREW AND ARAMAIC TEXT OF THE CITED BIBLICAL PASSAGES 1199 8. Historical dossier. Antiochus IV Epiphanes and the desecration of the Jerusalem temple (175–164 BCE) Documentary status. The file brings together Jewish literature from the crisis, Greco-Roman historians, and later testimonies. It is essential to distinguish the dating of the events (175–164 BCE), the composition of each work, and the date of their manuscripts. None of the Maccabean narratives should be used as a literal transcription of a Seleucid decree preserved in the royal archives. 8.1. Government, priesthood and Hellenization before 167 Antiochus IV, of the Seleucid dynasty, occupied the throne from 175 to 164 BCE. The dispute between Onias III, Jason, and Menelaus for the high priesthood constitutes an essential political condition of the crisis. According to 2 Maccabees 4:7–26, Jason negotiated his investiture and promoted a gymnasium and a Hellenizing civic organization in Jerusalem; Menelaus then obtained the priestly dignity through a higher offer. 1 Maccabees 1:11–15 refers to Jewish groups favourable to the adoption of Greek customs. The sources diverge on personal details and responsibilities: it is not methodologically legitimate to describe “the Jews” as a uniform bloc or to equate Hellenization with the abandonment of Judaism. policy and the dynastic legitimation of the sovereign belong to the Hellenistic horizon, not to the reign of Darius I. The epithet Epiphanḗs (“divine manifestation”) has the value of royal ideology; its appearance does not determine the precise meaning of all the initiatives concerning the temple. 8.2. Egypt, Rome and the unleashing of violence (169–168) Antiochus intervened militarily in Egypt; the withdrawal from the 168 campaign occurred in the face of a Roman mission, recounted with particular clarity by Polybius, Histories 29.27, an episode of the circle drawn by Popillius Laenas. The Greek testimony here offers a historical control external to Daniel and the Maccabees. The sequence of the raids on Jerusalem and the plundering of the sanctuary is narrated from different perspectives in 1 Maccabees 1:20–28 and 2 Maccabees 5:1–27. The casualty figures in 2 Maccabees 5:13– 14 are quantitative elements of the narrative and not audited demographic records. Daniel 11:29–30 reflects the king’s return from Egypt and the humiliation inflicted by the “ships of Kittim.” 1 Maccabees 1:29–40 and 2 Maccabees 5 describe the militarization of Jerusalem and the establishment of a garrison. The location and development of the Acra must be analysed using archaeology and topographical analysis; an exact plan cannot be deduced from the literary narrative alone.

1200 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM 8.3. Cultic measures, prohibitions and desecrated sanctuary (167) 1 Maccabees 1:41–64 attributes to the king decrees against traditional sacrifices, Sabbath observance, festivals, circumcision, and the preservation of the Law scrolls. In 1:54, the establishment of the “abomination of devastation” is placed on the 15th of Kislev in the year 145 of the Seleucid era (167 BCE); 1:59 describes sacrifices on the transformed altar on the 25th. 2 Maccabees 6:1–7 adds the dedication of the Temple of Olympian Zeus in Jerusalem and the sanctuary of Gerizim to Zeus the Hospitaller, along with forced ceremonies. A distinction must be drawn between what each work recounts and modern reconstructions of the institutional process. The religious coercion described in the narratives includes episodes of martyrdom for dietary practices and legal fidelity (2 Maccabees 6:18–31, Eleazar; 7:1–42, mother and seven sons). The representation is confessional, and its exemplary function is constitutive of the text. Current historiographical discussion questions the idea of a single universal order applied homogeneously from the capital and examines the interaction of priestly elites, taxation, revolt, and imperial administration (Honigman, 2014; Kratz, 2024). 8.4. Resistance, cultic restoration and death of the king (166–164) 1 Maccabees 2–4 describes Mattathias and Judas Maccabeus and constructs a heroic narrative of resistance. 1 Maccabees 4:36–59 recounts the purification of the sanctuary, the dismantling of the desecrated altar, the construction of a new altar, and its rededication on the 25th of Kislev in the year 148 CE, equivalent to December 164 BCE. The eight-day celebration constitutes the fundamental literary antecedent of Hanukkah. 2 Maccabees 10:1–8 offers a parallel narrative and non- identical liturgical explanations; the two versions should not be conflated. The accounts of Antiochus’s death preserved in 1 Maccabees 6:1–16 and 2 Maccabees 9:1–29 exhibit differences in location, causality, and moralizing rhetoric. The relationship of Daniel 11:40–45 to the historical outcome is especially important: the final campaign described does not clearly coincide with the king’s death in the eastern part of the empire. This divergence reinforces the literary analysis of apocalyptic expectation rather than a mechanical reading of all its imagery as a chronicle. 8.5. Chronological and documentary matrix, 175–164 BCE 175 BCE — Rise of Antiochus IV; dispute over the Jerusalem priesthood. Source: 2 Mac 4,7–26. Type: retrospective literary narrative with interest in civic conflicts. 169–168 BCE — Narrated Egyptian campaigns and plunder of Jerusalem. Sources: 1 Maccabees 1:16–28; 2 Maccabees 5; Daniel 11:25–30. External political control: Polybius, Histories 29.27 (168).

HEBREW AND ARAMAIC TEXT OF THE CITED BIBLICAL PASSAGES 1201 167 BCE — Suppression of regular sacrifice and new cult imposed at the sanctuary. Sources: 1 Maccabees 1:41–64; 2 Maccabees 6:1–7; Daniel 11:31 and 12:11. Kislev dates from 1 Maccabees 1:54 and 1:59. 166–164 BCE — Maccabean resistance and restoration. Sources: 1 Macc 2–4; 2 Macc 8– 10. Military figures are not extrapolated as administrative data. 164 BCE — 25 Kislev: rededication of the temple. Sources: 1 Maccabees 4:52–59; 2 Maccabees 10:1–8. Death of Antiochus in the eastern campaign: 1 Maccabees 6 and 2 Maccabees 9 (non-identical accounts). 8.6. Ancient books and authors for studying this crisis: dating, language and transmission Daniel, especially chapters 7–12. Hebrew and Aramaic; final redaction of the visions generally placed during the crisis of 167–164 BCE, although it incorporates earlier traditions and accounts. Jewish testimony close to the crisis, not a contemporary Persian court chronicle. 1 Maccabees, especially chapters 1–6. Original Hebrew not preserved as a complete work; transmitted mainly in Greek. Composed after the events, probably at the end of the 2nd century BCE. Historiographical source favourable to the Hasmonean dynasty. 2 Maccabees, especially chapters 3–10. A Greek work presented as an abridged account of a five-book history of Jason of Cyrene (2 Macc 2:19–32); Jason’s extensive work is lost. The abridged account was composed after the crisis, with its terminus provided by the letters in 2 Macc 1. It offers a theological perspective on the temple and martyrdom. Polybius, Histories, Book 29.27 (2nd century BCE; Greek). A testimony of Mediterranean politics and Roman intervention in Egypt; not a direct history of the Temple in Jerusalem. Ecclesiasticus or Ben Sira (Wisdom of Jesus ben Sira), Hebrew original from the beginning of the 2nd century BCE, Greek translation by the grandson after 132 BCE. Relevant as an antecedent of priestly structures, not as an account of the measures of 167. Enochite literature, especially the “Apocalypse of the Animals” (1 Enoch 85– 90). Tradition preserved entirely in Ge’ez, with Greek antecedents and Aramaic fragments from Qumran; its context is related to the Maccabean environment, although composition and material evidence have different dates. Book of Jubilees. Hebrew work from the 2nd century BCE, preserved mainly in Ge’ez and in Hebrew fragments from Qumran. Document of debates on calendar, law and identity; not a direct account of the reign of Antiochus. Diodorus Siculus, Historical Library (1st century BCE; Greek), and Livy, History of Rome from its Foundation 45.12 (Augustan period; Latin). They provide information on

1202 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM Greco-Roman diplomacy and politics; they require comparing what is preserved of each episode. Flavius Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 12.237–264 and 12.316–325, and Jewish War 1.31–40 (1st century CE; Greek). Late accounts that rework Maccabean sources; they should be studied for their dependence and divergences, not as independent testimony of 167. Porphyry, Against the Christians, Book 12 (3rd century CE; lost), transmitted in fragments and polemic by Jerome, Commentary on Daniel (early 5th century CE; Latin). It is indirect testimony for the history of the interpretation of Daniel and its references to Antiochus. 8.7. Comparative apparatus and fundamental philological decisions Dan 11:30 · ṣiyyîm kittîm The expression is historically linked to the Roman intervention in Egypt in 168 (Polybius 29.27). A historical identification does not authorize translating the consonantal Hebrew directly as “Romans” without a footnote. Dan 11:31; 12.11 · hattāmîd / šiqqûṣ məšōmēm It is translated as “regular sacrifice” and “devastating abomination.” 1 Maccabees 1:54 and 2 Maccabees 6:2–5 provide context for the vocabulary, without confirming the exact physical form of the object. The passage about Zeus belongs to the testimony of 2 Maccabees and not to the words of the text of Daniel. Dan 11:33–35 and 12,3 · maskîlîm The translation “wise men” or “learned men” refers to their pedagogical function; their correspondence with Maccabean fighters is a matter of debate, not an unequivocal identification. Dan 11:40–45 · last campaign The predicted outcome diverges from accounts of the king’s final campaigns. Maintaining the visible discontinuity between apocalyptic sources and historical reconstructions is a condition for source criticism. Dan 12:2 · rabbîm / ḥayyê ʿôlām “Many” and “everlasting life” retain their original meaning without implying a universal scope for the resurrection. The comparison with Iranian developments is thematic and historical, not a proven affiliation.

(1) Daniel 8:9: The antecedent of “one of them” should be examined in light of the four horns and the four winds of the preceding verse; the translation retains the pronoun without resolving this dispute. (2) Daniel 8:11: The reproduced original shows the visible juxtaposition of ‫ הּוַר ם‬/ ‫ הרים‬in the electronic edition; a problematic textual form should not be conflated with a secure historical reconstruction. (3) Daniel 8:12: The syntactic relations of ṣābāʾ, hattāmîd, and bəpāšaʿ allow for alternatives; a translation is offered and the difficulty noted. (4) Daniel 8:14: “Two thousand three hundred evenings and mornings” avoids unexplained conversion of this expression into a number of days. The calendrical interpretation needs separate discussion. Notes on context and intertextuality. (5) Daniel 8:20–22 expressly interprets ram = Media and Persia and male goat = Greece; no Iranian comparison can omit this internal exegesis. (6) The visions of Daniel 8 are situated literarily in the time of Belshazzar, but their main historical problem belongs to the horizon of the Seleucid persecutions of the 2nd century BCE, so their redaction cannot simply be attributed to Darius I. (7) Daniel 8:23–25 allows us to discuss the figure of Antiochus IV, without turning the symbolism of the horn into direct evidence of Zoroastrian borrowing. 1224 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM 4. Daniel 2:4–7,28: Literary Aramaic The appendix preserves the Aramaic transcription of Daniel 2:4b– 7:28. Chapter XLII already offers continuous English study translations mediated by the Spanish working edition of that section, including chapters 4–7, with Hebrew numbering. It is distinguished from the Book of Ezra by its narrative and apocalyptic character and by its debated chronology of composition (2nd century BCE for the book as a whole in its final form, with earlier traditions). The clearest Iranian passages are the terms rāz (“mystery”, 2,18–19.27–30.47; 4,6), ʾazdāʾ (“firmly decreed”, 2,5.8), dāt (“law”, 6,6.9.13.16) and pitgām (“word”, 3,16; 4,14). Sources and linguistic strata. The Yasna Haptaŋhāiti (Y. 35–41) belongs to Old Avestan; Younger Avestan passages are identified separately and cannot indiscriminately be analysed through an Old Avestan lexicon. PHILOLOGICAL AND COMPARATIVE NOTES 1. Edition Limit. The table above transcribed only Y. 1.1a – e. The added segment completes the rest of the invocation Y. 1.1, but the alphabetical division f – j is an auxiliary segmentation of this monograph, not a universal numbering of the Avestan editions. 2. huδāmanō and vouru.rafnaŋhō (Y. 1.1). The syntactic interpretation of the series requires checking the epithets according to the case and their agreement with Ahura Mazdā; “good mental disposition” and “ample help” are provisional equivalents, not lemmas established by a comprehensive critical dictionary. 3. yō nō daδa / yō tataṣ̌ a / yō tuθruiie (Y. 1.1). The triple relative construction refers to the creation, configuration and maintenance of the community; it does not in itself allow us to postulate dependence on biblical creation narratives. 4. vaŋhu manah, aša vahišta, xšaθra vairiia and spənta ārmaiti (Y. 1.2). Semantic translation is privileged and Avestan terminology is preserved in a glossary. The ritual association of these entities does not constitute proof that Achaemenid Yahwism knew them under this same configuration. 5. haurvatā ty amərətāt. “Fullness” and “Immortality” express cultic pairs here and should not be equated without mediation with the resurrection of the dead in Daniel 12 or Christian eschatology. 6. gə̄uš tašan / gə̄uš urvan. “Former of the bovine” and “soul of the bovine” remain distinct: the fusion of both expressions would conceal the organization proper to the Iranian cosmology and cult. 7. ātar. The fire invoked in Y. 1.2 is an Avestan cultic figure. The analogies with the burning bush (Ex 3) require demonstrating historical circulation and functional coincidence, not only the presence of fire as a religious symbol. 8. Comparative critical apparatus of Y. 1.3–1.5 (notes linked to the loci) 1 [Y. 1.3, niuuaēδaiiemi / haṇkāraiiemi]. They are consistently translated as “I invoke and celebrate [this rite].” The verbal duplication expresses the liturgical action; Mills opts for “I announce (and) carry out.” The term “rite” is an explanatory supplement, not an autonomous word from the original. 2 [Y. 1.3–1.5, aṣ̌ ahe ratu-]. Ratu- (rector, regulator, ritual authority or regulated period) is distinguished from aša (true order/righteousness). The formula “rector of order” does not imply semantic identity with the biblical judges or angels.

YASNA: Y. 35–41 AND LATER SELECTIONS 1269 3 [Y. 1.3, Hāvan; Y. 1.4, Rapithwin; Y. 1.5, Uzayēirina]. The invocations articulate periods of the day. They do not in themselves constitute proof of the adoption of prayer times by the Achaemenid Yahwist communities. 4 [Y. 1.3, miθrahe]. The description of Mithra through multiplied listening and vigilance has a laudatory function; it does not allow the Avestan Mithra to be equated without historical medi ation with the Roman mystery Mithras. 5 [Y. 1.4, ātar]. The reference to the fire of Ahura Mazdā is cultic. A comparison with Ex 3 should distinguish the biblical narrative function of fire from its Avestan liturgical invocation; see the discussion of Gad Barnea’s hypothesis in chapter LVI. 6 [Y. 1.5, apąm napāt]. The theonym is retained in the translation and an etymological gloss is proposed; it should not be automatically equated with an angel, a messiah or a baptismal being in Jewish or Christian traditions. 7 [Textual Status]. Philological and comparative apparatus (Y. 1.6) 1. [niuuaēδaiiemi / haṇkāraiiemi] The double introductory verb is retained as “I invoke and celebrate” for consistency with Y. 1.3–5. It should not be interpreted as two separate ceremonies. 2. [aiβisrūθrimāi / aibigaiiāi] Liturgical designations associated with the evening-night period; technical names are retained. The exact time equivalence must be justified by studies of the ritual calendar, not inferred from a modern clock. 3. [aṣ̌ aone, aṣ̌ ahe raθβe] The formula is translated “worthy of aša and rulers of the ritual order”; ratu- does not necessarily mean “king” or “messiah.” The decision is terminological, not a textual variant. 4. [zaraθuštrōtəmāi] Title of a priestly character linked to Zarathustra; it is preserved transliterated, avoiding translating it without explanation as “the prophet Zarathustra”. Its institutional value and dating require specific study. 5. [frauuaṣ̌ inąm] Fravaši is left in the translation, without assimilating it to “angel”, “soul” or “saint” of the biblical vocabulary. Mills uses a functional solution in English; the religious equivalence between traditions is not demonstrated by that translation. 6. [vərəθraγnahe / vanaiṇtiiā̊ uparatātō] The terminology of victory and superiority belongs to a liturgical invocation. It does not by itself allow us to derive Jewish notions of final judgement, resurrection or messianic triumph.

Yasna I.7–I.10 is presented in a study translation mediated by the Spanish text, with an electronic Avestan transcription in the dossier following I.12. Its boundaries follow K. F. Geldner, Avesta: The Sacred Books of the Parsis (1886–1896), through the digital transcription of Geldner’s text, Avesta/Yasna, §§1.7–1.10, with reference to TITUS. Y. 1.7 — Study English translation. “I announce and celebrate this liturgy for Ušahin, consecrated according to the aš ay ruler of aša; for Bərəjya and Nmanya, rulers consecrated according to the aša; for Sraoša, companion of Aši, who possesses reward, victorious and promoter of the world; and for the most righteous Rašnu and Arštā, who promote and make the world prosper”. Y. 1.8 — English study rendering of the Spanish study translation. “I announce and celebrate this liturgy for the monthly periods, governing asha; for the interval of the new moon, consecrated according to asha; and for the full moon and the waning phase, likewise consecrated according to asha.” The segmentation of aṇtarəmā̊ ŋhāi and vīṣ̌ aptaθāica requires further lexical control; this ritual series should not be confused with a documented adoption of the Hebrew calendar. Y. 1.9 — English study rendering of the Spanish study translation. “I announce and celebrate this liturgy for the ritual rulers of the annual cycles: Maidyozarem, Maidyoshahem, Paitishahem, Ayathrem [with the epithets relating to the increase of fertility and generative power], Maidyarem and Hamaspathmaidyem, and for the seasons as regulators of the rite.” The epithets in brackets are made explicit as an interpretation, not as an additional festival name. Y. 1.10 — Study English translation. “I announce and celebrate this liturgy for the thirty-three rulers of Asha who gather around Havan, established by Ahura Mazdā and proclaimed by Zarathustra as rulers of Asha Vahišta”. Comparative explanatory apparatus 1 [Y. 1.7]. Ušahin designates a liturgical interval; Bərəjya and Nmanya are ritual designations. Avoid confusing this verse with the confessional formula of Y. 1.23, re-

1272 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM lated to Y. 0.7 and Y. 27.12. The Spanish reading translates by function and retains the proper names. 2 [Y. 1.7]. Sraoša, Rašnu, and Arštāt are not automatically equivalent to angels in Judaism. Their comparison requires distinguishing cultic personification, semantic field, and datable evidence from each tradition. 3 [Y. 1.8]. The opposition between lunar phases corresponds to the transmitted Mazdaean ritual calendar; neither this sequence nor its translation alone demonstrate a borrowing from the Hebrew calendar during the period of Darius I. 4 [Y. 1.9]. Yasna 1.11–1.12: astral invocation, fire and waters — English rendering of the Spanish study translation Editorial note. The following translations have been prepared from the historic English version by L.H. Mills (SBE 31, 1887). Therefore, their status is that of an indirect study translation. Yasna 1.11 — Indirect English translation for study. “I invoke and celebrate this liturgy for both Ahura and Mithra, exalted, enduring, and in accordance with the true order; for all the stars, creations of Spənta Mainyu; for the star Tištrya, bright and glorious; for the Moon, which contains the seed of cattle; for the radiant Sun, of swift steeds, eye of Ahura Mazdā; and for Mithra, lord of the region. YASNA: Y. 35–41 AND LATER SELECTIONS 1273 Yasna 1.12 — Indirect English translation for study. “I invoke and celebrate this liturgy for you, Fire, son of Ahura Mazdā, together with all fires; for the good waters, all waters created by Mazda; and for all plants that Mazda created.” Comparative apparatus and justification of translation (Y. 1.11–1.12) 1. [Y. 1.11, Ahura and Mithra]. The nominal association of both figures is preserved without transforming it into a doctrine of two equal gods. The function of the invocation is liturgical. It does not in itself demonstrate ontological dualism or religious influence on Judaism. 2. [Y. 1.11, Tištrya]. The Iranian theonym is retained and glossed as a star; its traditional astronomical identification with Sirius requires differentiated treatment from its religious personification. 3. [Y. 1.11, Moon and “seed of cattle”]. The cosmological image is preserved without paraphrasing it as a Hebrew doctrine of creation. The comparison must consider its own function within the Avestan imaginary. 4. [Y. 1.11, Sun “eye of Ahura Mazdā”]. 5. [Y. 1.12, Fire]. “Son of Ahura Mazdā” reproduces the liturgical personification noted by Mills; it is not an equivalence of theological kinship with Jewish or Christian messianic figures. Compare the differentiated examination of Ex 3 and the bibliography of Gad Barnea in chapter LVI. 6. [Y. 1.12, Waters and plants]. The catalogue integrates elements of the world created in the ritual action. The thematic coincidence with cosmogonic narratives does not constitute proof of borrowing. 7. [Source actually used]. Explanatory and comparative apparatus — Yasna III.5–8 1. III.5: “approach” provisionally translates the verb interpreted by Mills as a formula of invocation and ritual approach; it does not imply physical displacement towards all the entities listed. This choice must be confirmed against the concrete Avestan form. 2. III.5: ratu is preserved as a technical term of authority or ritual regulation. “Lord”, “judge” and “norm” capture possible nuances, but a universal equivalence would be misleading; the context determines the translation. 3. III.5–6: yazata designates that or that which is worthy of worship. It should not be automatically equated with “angel” or “god” in the biblical sense: functions and contexts will be compared, not labels. 4. III.6–8: Hāvanī, Rapithwina and Uzayēirina refer to temporary ritual presidencies or bands; other names function as epithets and liturgical authorities. Maintaining their transliteration avoids fabricating biblical calendrical equivalents. 5. III.6: The expression “a thousand ears and myriad eyes” is a hyperbole applied to Mithra. The similarity to images of divine vigilance in other corpora does not authorize inferring textual borrowing. 6. III.7–8: Aša Vahišta and Apąm Napāt are left in transliteration. Especially in this latter case, the similarity to water and fire traditions requires an Indo-Iranian study and chronological stratification before formulating hypotheses about Yehud. 7. III.8: fravaši is not translated as “soul” or “angel.” The sequence of names and blessings is a ritual enumeration; it cannot be dated entirely to the 6th–5th century BCE simply because it preserves traditional material. Explanatory device — Yasna III.9–13 1. And III.9. Ušahina designates a nocturnal ritual period; Sraoša, Rašnu and Arštāt are cited by their traditional names. Their functions should not be directly equated with those of angels or judges in Jewish texts. 2. And III.10. The lunar sequence documents the ritual calendar of the received text. It does not prove the adoption of a specific calendar by Yehud; that hypothesis would require independent chronological and administrative evidence. 3. And III.11. And III.12. “Thirty-three” is an internal count of the ritual text. It does not in itself constitute a historical correspondence with other sets of beings or religious authorities. 5. And III.13. Tištriia is an Iranian astral figure. The presence of references to the moon, sun, and stars suggests comparing liturgical and cosmological genres first before inferring the circulation of doctrines. 6. Control of the translation. “I wish to approach” follows Mills’ English resolution for the recurring ritual formula; it is contrasted with the Avestan forms and with the syntactic regime.

Agreement with that reproduction does not constitute an independent collation of the Avestan manuscripts. 2. House, offspring, and flocks (IV.5). The text asks for protection for a domestic and productive community. It can be functionally compared with house blessings in biblical texts, but the parallel does not demonstrate an Iranian borrowing, nor does it provide an Achaemenid dating of the formula. 3. Fravašis (IV.6, 11). The Iranian term is retained instead of being automatically translated as “angels” or “souls of the dead.” The precise identification of their

The formulae bring together liturgical periods and venerated entities. The epithet of “a thousand ears” and “innumerable eyes” should not be used indiscriminately as proof of the Iranian origin of the attributes of the biblical divinity. 5. Apąm Napāt (IV.10). The traditional name is preserved — with the gloss “Descendant of the Waters” —and it is avoided to identify it with YHWH or with an angelic figure. Their names relate to obedience/listening, justice and righteousness; the specific religious functions do not authorize a one-toone correspondence with celestial agents of Daniel or Qumran. 7. Philological, textual and comparative commentary 1. The forms Yazamaide and aCahe ratUm are repeated as a formulaic structure: “we venerate” and “lord of order/rectity.” Not all invoked entities should be interpreted as sovereign gods equivalent to Ahura Mazdā.

1316 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM 2. Apąm Napāt is a figure related to the waters and has Indo-Iranian parallels, including the Vedic Apām Napāt. The etymological parallel between the names does not allow us to derive from it a specific historical relationship with the theophany of Exodus 3. 3. Fravaši designates an Iranian concept with its own functions and should not be mechanically translated as “angel”. The equivalence with biblical angels or guardians is a functional analogy conditioned by different chronological contexts. 4. Rašnu and Arštāt are associated with righteousness and order. Their comparison with the Hebrew ‫( ִמ ְׁש ָּפ ט‬mišpāṭ, justice/judgement) and ‫( ֶצֶד ק‬ṣedeq, righteousness) is semantic; they are not cognates. 5. No manuscript variant of J2, K4, P1 or B2 is assigned here to a witness without direct inspection. 6. The repetition of liturgical formulae reflects a stratified composition. The practices described in the transmitted Yasna should not be automatically dated to the 6th century BCE; the Achaemenid contact thesis requires independent contemporary evidence. Critical apparatus and explanatory notes for Y VI.11–21 1. VI.11. Ātar (“Fire”) appears personified and linked to Ahura Mazdā. The ritual formula does not demonstrate that all historical forms of fire veneration were uniform in Achaemenid and Sasanian times. See also Y 36. 2. VI.12. Mąθra spənta designates the sacred word or formula, not an etymological equivalent of the Hebrew ‫( ָּד ָב ר‬dābār) nor of the Greek λόγος (lógos). Comparisons are semantic and must be justified by context. 3. VI.13. The adjective translated by Mills as “unconsumed” refers here to glory (xᵛarənah), not to a burning bush. Its figurative coincidence with Exod 3:2 does not, in itself, constitute literary dependence. 4. VI.14. 5. VI.17–19. Haurvatāt, Amərətāt, Sraoša, and fravaši are retained as specific denominations. They are not directly equated with angels, individual immortality, or biblical categories without regard to textual genre, chronology, and function.

Y. 8.1. “Asha Vahisha” is proclaimed as a blessing and well-being. I ritually present the food offering myazda, along with Haurvatāt, Amərətāt, the consecrated portion of the cattle, the haoma and its juice, firewood, and perfumes. These gifts accompany the praise of Ahura Mazdā, the formula Ahuna Vairya, the words of blessing, and the ritual expressions associated with Zoroaster. May our offering be fully received. Y. 8.2. (The rattu responds.) Partake of this offering, you who, by your righteousness and conduct in accordance with order, are worthy to receive it. Y. 8.3. To the Ameša Spəntas, to the Mazdayan religion, to the righteous men and women, and to the libations is addressed: whoever professes this religion and wishes to live according to the liberality of the right order must be instructed in it. Whoever invokes fervently, but refuses to adhere to the prescribed words, approaches — according to the text’s warning — a condemned ritual formula. Zarathustra said: “Praise be to Haoma. Who was the first mortal who squeezed you into the physical world? What reward did he receive and what benefit did he gain?” Y. 9.4. Haoma, righteous and “death-remover,” replied: “Vīvaŋhvant was the first mortal who prepared me in the physical world.” As a reward, he received the birth of Yima, called “shining,” renowned for his numerous flocks and likened to the sun. In the narrative, Yima ensured that under his authority, cattle and men were free from death; that plants and waters did not suffer drought; and that men’s food did not run out. Y. 9.5. “In the reign of Yima, swift in movement, there was neither cold nor heat, neither old age nor death, nor envy caused by the daēvas. Father and son walked with the appearance and vigor of fifteen-year-olds while Yima, son of Vīvaŋhvant, possessor of numerous flocks, ruled.” The ages and conditions belong to the mythical time of the story, not to a demographic record. Y. 9.6. Zarathustra asked: “Who was, Haoma, the second mortal who prepared you in the corporeal world? What blessing was bestowed upon him, and what benefit did he gain?” The question deliberately repeats the formula of IX.3. Y. 9.7. Haoma answered: “Āθβiia was the second mortal who prepared me in the corporeal world. He received this blessing: that a son, Θraētaona, of the lineage of heroes, be born to him.” The answer connects the ritual act with the birth of a character from the legendary genealogy.

1326 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM Y. 9.8. “The dragon of three jaws, three heads, and six eyes, endowed with a thousand powers and immense strength, an adversary associated with the druj and hostile to settlements. The passage presents it as a creation of Aŋra Mainyu to harm the corporeal world and destroy the communities linked with aša.” “Dragon” and “demon” are equivalent readings, not zoological classifications nor evidence of a systematized dualism in the time of Dari or I. Y. 9.9. Zarathustra asked: “Who was the third mortal who prepared you in the corporeal world? What blessing did he receive and what benefit did he gain?” The verbal parallelism with IX.3 and IX.6 organizes the genealogical series. Y. 9.10. Haoma answered: “The rita was the third to prepare me; he obtained the birth of two sons, Urvāxšaya and Kərəsāspa. The first is described as a judge who confirms the order; the second, as a powerful young man, with curly hair and carry ing a mace.” The legal characterization of the first here follows Mills’s interpretive choice and needs direct lexical control. Y. 9.11. “Kərəsāspa slew a horned dragon that devoured men and horses; the creature, green and poisonous, dripped venom from its body. In another scene, the hero cooked meat in an iron cauldron on the monster’s back at midday. Burned, the animal rose up and spilled the boiling water; Kərəsāspa fled in fear.” The sequence belongs to the heroic narrative and does not describe a documented material cultic practice. Y. 9.12. Zarathustra asked: “Who was the fourth mortal who prepared you for the physical world, Haoma? What blessing did he receive and what benefit did he gain?” The questioning pattern of the three previous scenes is maintained. Y. 9.13. Haoma answered: “Pourusha was the fourth to prepare me; the blessing he obtained was that you, Zarathustra, were born in his house: righteous, adversary of the daevas and friend of the wisdom of Mazda.” The discourse continues in IX.14 with the celebrity of Zarathustra in Airyanəm Vaējah; it is not appropriate to anticipate that clause in IX.13 nor to confuse this traditional space with an Achaemenid province. documentary control — Yasna IX.4–13. Supplementary notes and comparative apparatus — Yasna XI.4–18 1. XI.4–5. The “tongue and the left eye” appear as a ritual part reserved for Haoma. XI.9. Comparative Interpretation. Gippert proposes understanding the passage not as a series of independent numbers nor as a coded message referring to Judaism, but as a concatenation of Gathic echoes and incipits that allow for a sequential reading. The explanation requires morphological and textual comparison with the Avestan edition; it does not, in itself, demonstrate transmission to Judaism. The recitation is attributed to the rāspi within the context of the haoma liturgy. 5. XI.10. The “better world of the righteous” belongs to the eschatologicalritual lexicon of prayer. As a comparison with Jewish expectations, it is evidence of thematic similarity, not independent proof of doctrinal borrowing. 6. XI.11–16. 1352 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM Y. 12.4. Renunciation of hostile powers. I renounce the protection and author ity of the daēvas, considered evil and deceitful, separated from good and associated with falsehood; I also renounce their supporters, the practitioners of harmful arts, and conduct that damages beings. I reject them in thought, word, and deed. Y. 12.5. Model of revelation. From the way in which Ahura Mazdā instructed Zarathustra in their encounters and questions, the renunciation of the daevas is presented as authoritative religious teaching. [In Mills, XII.5 includes part of an enumeration whose editorial separation affects the distribution between sections 4–6.] Y. 12.6. Personal Profession. As Zarathustra rejected the authority of the daēvas, so too I, a worshipper of Mazda and a supporter of his teaching, renounce that dominion in whatever circumstances I may find myself. Y. 12.7. Community of faith. I subscribe to the religion to which the waters, plants, and well-created cattle belong; the religion of Ahura Mazdā, creator of cattle and righteous beings; the one professed by Zarathustra, Kavi Vițta, Frațaōțtra, and Jamața, and by the righteous saoțyants who perform acts of salvation. [The enumeration expresses religious affiliation; it does not constitute a contemporary chronology of all the figures.] Y. 12.8. Triple commitment. [The enumeration of epithets is more extensive in Mills and contains terms of disputed interpretation, among them the one he translates as “marriage between relatives”; the formulation is abbreviated here so as not to feign a fixed meaning.] Critical and comparative apparatus of Yasna XII 1. Religious identity (XII.1, 8). The phrase fravarānē is a declaration formula, not an occupation, and is not proof of the existence of an identical creed throughout the Achaemenid period. It is important to distinguish between the date of composi tion, ritual fixation, and preserved manuscript tradition.

YASNA: Y. 35–41 AND LATER SELECTIONS 1353 2. daēva (XII.1, 4–6). The negative connotation of the term in the Avesta does not, in itself, authorize equating each daēva with the Hebrew šē do with “demon” in all textual phases. The comparison requires chronology and lexical analysis. 3. Spəntā Ārmaiti (XII.2). The ritual personification of devotion and its relationship with the earth must be analysed together with the Gāthās, avoiding reducing it without nuance to a “goddess of the earth”. 4. Difficulty of XII.3. Mills, SBE 31, pp. 248–249, admits in a footnote an alternative that reverses his initial interpretation of free movement. Peterson offers a reading favourable to freedom of residence. The passage should not be used to reconstruct a state policy against nomadism without discussing the alternative. 5. Saošyant (XII.7). The plurality of “benefactors/saviours” and the traditional names do not automatically identify the late eschatological saviour nor prove influence on Jewish messianisms. The transmission hypothesis is evaluated by strata. 6. Matrimonial term (XII.9). Mills linked a religious epithet to marriages between relatives, but the semantics of xᵛaētuuadaθa- and its historical interpretations require specialized bibliography and chronological stratification. It should not be normalized as unquestioned social instruction. 7. Comparative repertoire. The triads of thought, word, and deed appear in XII.8 and in other Mazdaean texts. Any comparison with biblical formulations on heart, lips, and works must specify texts, dating, and mechanism of contact; analogy does not prove dependence. 8. 1354 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM XII.1 — nāismī daēuuō; fravarānē. The initial formula functions as a cultic declaration of rejection of the daēvas and adherence to the teaching of Ahura Mazdā. “Demons”, when used for daēva-, requires a historical note. XII.2 — spəntąm ārmaitīm. The explicit choice of Ārmaiti is formulated as religious acceptance and protection of communities with livestock. It is not appropriate to derive Achaemenid legislation on nomadism or property from the liturgical phrase alone. XII.3 — mobility and settlement. A study translation is maintained in the text and a double semantic possibility is maintained in the apparatus. XII.4-6 — repetitive formulation of renunciation. The negative anaphora and the repetition of the renunciation in the first person are part of the text, not redundancies that should be removed. The version without optics does not reproduce its exact distribution. XII.7 — saoš́ iiaṇtąm appears in the plural. Its translation requires identifying the plural function of the word in the chain of venerated figures. It is not permissible to silently convert it into a single eschatological saviour nor to conclude dependence on Jewish messianism. XII.8 — āstuiiē and the triad humatəm manō / hūxtəm vacō / huuarštəm š́iiaoθanəm. The repetition of “professed” sustains a ritual formula of affirmation; thought, word, and deed form three distinguishable members, not a loose slogan. The similarities to biblical exhortations demand dating of both sets and independent channel testing. XII.9 — xvaētuuadaθąm: controversial social and ritual term, not susceptible to an approving or condemnatory paraphrase without exposing alternative analyses. The current text points out the problem, but lacks specific apparatus per lemma and specialized bibliography that distinguishes Sasanian interpretation and meaning in the transmitted Avestan context. Documentary and hermeneutic apparatus — Yasna XI.1–3 1. The tripartite structure (cow, horse, Haoma) is a sequence of personifications and ritual imprecations. It is not proposed that the animals delivered historical speeches, nor is the scene attributed to a practice demonstrated in the Persian province of Yehud. 2. The curse against the loss of offspring and dishonor appears in XI.1 and XI.3; its repetition should be retained, not removed as stylistic redundancy. No identity with biblical formulae is inferred from the mere similarity of the sanctions. 3. XI.1: Mills specifically interprets the improper use of the fed animal. 4. XI.2: The terms Mills translates as “spanner of the racers,” “stretch no coursers,” and “circuit” do not automatically authorize the reconstruction of an institutional Achaemenid hippodrome. This monograph retains the equestrian references without imposing a specific material typology.

This chapter comments on the prayer Yaθā ah ū vairiiō (Ahuna Vairiia) and is not a separate composition. Together with Y. 20–21, it preserves part of the Avestan exegesis related to the Bag Nask, also known from the accounts in Dēnkard VIII –IX. The antiquity of the commented-on formula must be distinguished from the composition and transmission of the commentary; its preservation in the Yasna does not allow the whole to be dated to the Achaemenid period. YASNA: Y. 35–41 AND LATER SELECTIONS 1391 Explanatory Apparatus — Y 21. The chapter elaborates on Yeŋhē hātąm; the prayer itself appears in Y. 27.15 and also functions as a liturgical transitional formula. Its position after the commentaries on Y 19 and Y 20 does not demonstrate that the three prayers were composed simultaneously; moreover, Yeŋhē hātąm (Y. 27.15) presents archaizing Younger Avestan, unlike the other two formulae in Old Avestan. References: C. J. Brunner, “Yeŋhē Hātąm,” Encyclopaedia Iranica (2015); Skjærvø, “Bag Nask,” Encyclopaedia Iranica III/4 (1988), pp. 400–401. The transcribed Avestan text is preserved without fabricating alternative readings. Historical -textual note — Bag Nask and Yasna 19–21. Chapters Y. 19.20, and 21 preserve the surviving Avestan portion of the commentary on three prayers: Yaθā ah ū vairiiō (Y. 27.13), Aṣ̌ əm vohū (Y. 27.14), and Yeŋhē hātąm (Y. 27.15). The description of the Bag Nask in Dēnkard VIII – IX is evidence of later reception and organization, not the material preservation of its remaining Avestan chapters. It is important not to confuse the Bag Nask with the collection of Yašts due to the similarity of designations transmitted as Bagān/Bayān. 1492 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM critical apparatus of translations — Series I (selective control) This supplement comments on readings and translation decisions for passages identified in the main body of the work. In each case, it distinguishes the source text, the alternative interpretation, and the historical consequence. The examination is selective: it includes only the loci identified and does not replace a complete critical apparatus for each verse or papyrus. No contemporary scholarly translation protected by copyright is reproduced extensively. Ezra 4:8–6:18 and 7:12–26 (Aramaic) — The translation must preserve the distinction between narrative discourse and incorporated chancery formulae. The Aramaic titles and commands can be compared with imperial papyri, but the fact that a biblical document employs plausible chancery features does not in itself prove the diplomatic authenticity of a decree from the time of Darius. The apparatus records loanwords and administrative designations by verse, separating etymology from function in context. Scholarly basis: D. Marcus, Biblia Hebraica Quinta, Ezra and Nehemiah (2006); TAD I: Letters, Porten-Yardeni (1986); Masoretic edition printed in the book. Ezra 7:12 (title) — The expression presenting Artaxerxes as “king of kings” can be translated literally and commented on as a formula of sovereignty in the imperial register. It is not equivalent to a Mazdaean confession nor does it, in itself, de termine the date of composition of the whole. The English translation should preserve the title without turning it into a theological interpretation. Academic basis: Aramaic text of Ezra 7:12 in the Masoretic tradition; Marcus, BHQ (2006) as a contrast edition. Daniel 2:4b and 7:28 (linguistic boundaries) — The Aramaic portion of Daniel begins at 2:4b and ends at 7:28; continuous translation should not obscure the shift to Hebrew at 8:1. The labels “Hebrew” and “Aramaic” pertain to the examination of the transmitted form and do not, on their own, provide a date for each narrative. Scholarly basis: Masoretic Text; Biblia Hebraica Stuttgartensia, ed. K. Elliger and W. Rudolph; with the Qumran witnesses to Daniel (1Q71–72, 4Q112– 116, 6Q7) as a point of comparison.
