Scope of the series: Seventeen comparative notes. They offer selective arguments and references, not a validation of the thousands of loci in the volume. The complete ancient translations form an integral part of the book. critical apparatus for translations — Series II (Gāthās, Y. 32–34) Scope and method. This series examines eight key loci of Y. 32–34 without disrupting the continuity of the sixteenth, fourteenth, and fifteenth stanzas of these three hymns. The Avestan text and the corresponding English study translation remain in chapter XLIII. Published interpretations by Insler (1975), Humbach and Faiss (2010), M.L. West (2010), the lexicographical edition and translation by Uesugi and Catt (2024), and available scholarly repertories are compared. Y. 32.1 — θβōi dūtåŋhō åŋhāmā. The English translation uses “that we may be your houses.” This turn of phrase requires a gloss: the translation tradition of Bartholomae/Moulton, Insler, and West understands dūtåŋhō as “messengers” or “envoys,” while Humbach and Faiss proposed an analysis related to “home” or “domestic unit.” This is not a simple variant between manuscripts, but a difference in lexical and pragmatic analysis. The domestic option, preserved as a study reading, is related to the alternative “that we may be your messengers”; the last clause (“to those who are hostile to you”) changes nuance depending on the subject adopted. One should avoid constructing from the term an Achaemenid missionary institution or a genealogy of the biblical “messenger”. Y. 32.3 — daēuua-, akāt̰ manaŋhō yb ū mii ā̊ haptaiθē. The plural of daēuua- intervenes in an invective against powers and their worshipers; It is not automatically equivalent to the Christian concept of “demon.” The expression of the “seventh” region not part of the earth appears in traditional versions, but its contextualization in later Iranian cosmological geography does not certify that the poet describes an administrative jurisdiction of Darius I. The reference must be presented as a poeticcosmographic resource, without identifying the “seven” with satrap ies or territories of Persian dominion. Y. 32.7 — xᵛaēnā aiiaŋhā. “With glowing metal” or “by means of incandescent metal” preserves the instrumental construction adopted here. The adjective “mol-

DOCUMENTARY CONSISTENCY AND EDITING CRITERIA 1497 ten” is not required by this phrase alone. The internal comparison with Y. 51.9, where a distinct adjective supports “molten metal”, and with later ordeal literature concerns the development of a motif rather than verbal identity. Scholarly translations may reflect different reconstructions of the scene; the commentary should therefore preserve the distinction between incandescent and molten metal. Y. 32.8 — Yima and his transgression. The Gathic text mentions Yima in a passage of controversial interpretation. One traditional exegetical line, which draws on the Pahlavi reading, links the verse to the provision or consumption of beef; other reconstructions differ in the attribution of the transgression and in the reading of its predicate. The Pahlavi explanation should not be taken as direct proof of the meaning of the ancient verse. Y. 33.1–2 — retribution and ethical antithesis. The contrast between aša and druj and the mention of acts or words directed at the deceiver demands preserving the semantic values of the context: neither a form of retribution stated in ritual poetry nor the translation “do harm to the deceiver” authorizes deriving a general norm of religious violence. The apparatus must distinguish the possible meaning of the verb, its subject, and the scope of the judgement; it must not retroject, without mediation, the developed eschatology of the Pahlavi texts. Y. 33.14 — tanuuascīt̰ xᵛax́ iiā̊ uštanəm. The verse presents Zarathustra’s offering of the vitality or life force of his own body along with thought, word, and deed. A recent discussion of possessive morphology in the Bulletin of the School of Oriental and African Studies reproduces and comments on this locus. The expression is a dedication of the person in a liturgical context; it does not in itself constitute an announcement of bodily resurrection nor should it be directly linked with the Christian language of the sacrifice of Jesus. Y. 34.4–5 — fire and controversial designations. Fire can act as a sign of help or harm depending on the context of verse 34.4; it should not be taken without other evidence to be a description of Achaemenid court ritual. In 34.5, the following appears: daēuuāišcā xrafstrāiš maṣ̌ iiāišcā. The form and meaning of xrafstra- are debated; a gloss such as “body-eaters” does not constitute separate documentary evidence. It is advisable to preserve the original, to make explicit that the translation of the categories depends on syntactic analysis, and to distinguish the uses of the later Avesta, which are more related to beings considered harmful.

1498 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM Y. 34.13 — saošyant-. The term corresponds to a plural of beneficial agents in this context and does not require identifying a single personal redeemer. The Encyclopaedia Iranica (“Saošyant”, William W. Malandra) documents the semantic shift from “benefactor” or “helper” in references that can also designate contemporaries, toward more specific eschatological functions in later traditions. For comparison with Christianity, distinguish the usage in the Gāthās, the more recent Avestan testimonies, and the Pahlavi systematization: similarity of function does not equate to proven historical transfer. 1500 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM Philological dependency scale by locus Contemporary material evidence, with a verifiable repository, inventory number or shelfmark, and line (e.g., Achaemenid inscriptions or papyri from the 5th century BCE). Level 2: Ancient text transmitted in later copies and reconstructed through an identifiable edition; original and variants must be distinguished from the date of composition. Level 3: Modern scholarly translation whose textual basis and semantic choices are documented. Level 4: Indirect English translation, produced from a bridge language, which requires controlling for the losses and reinterpretations resulting from that mediation. Level 5: Historical analogy or hypothesis about contacts, which requires, in addition to the initial readings, chronology, agents, and transmission route. These levels describe the type of access to the source, not an automatic numerical score on the author’s quality. Operational protocol: For each decisive quotation, the following are recorded: abbreviation and locus, language, edition used, medium and date (when known), English translation already present in the volume, one or two contrasting academic translations, lexical or syntactic difference, exegetical effect, and degree of historical proof. If two translations differ, the apparatus indicates whether the difference arises from a textual witness, a grammatical segmentation, a restitution, or a hermeneutic choice. An unproven divergence between translators will not be presented as a manuscript variant. Five chronological strata that should not be confused I. The Gāthās and the core of the Yasna Haptaŋhāiti (Y. 35–41) belong to Old Avestan; some prayers linked to this core share this stratum, but Yeŋhē Hātąm (Y. 27.15) and the addition Y 42 are written in archaic Younger Avestan. Their linguistic antiquity alone does not provide an exact date or a demonstration of circulation in Yehud. II. The Late Avesta — including the Yašts and the Vidēvdād — brings together compositions and developments of uneven chronology; its liturgical transmission does not amount to a uniform redaction under Darius I. III. Achaemenid inscriptions and archives constitute the contemporary material horizon for the study of the empire (6th – 4th centuries BCE); they allow us to document practices, languages, and institutions, but they do not replace the reconstruction of doctrines absent from these testimonies. IV. Daniel, Qumran, and early Christianity belong to successive Second Temple and Roman periods, whose con-

Glossary Additional comparative glossary: documentary definitions aša — Avestan term for truth, right order or normativity, whose semantic scope changes with genre and context; not an automatic equivalent of a legal statute. druj — Avestan term for deception or the Lie, sometimes personified; compare Old Persian drauga- without assuming identical contexts. ahura — Avestan title or noun designating a lord/divine being; distinct from the full name Ahura Mazdā. Ahura Mazdā — “Wise Lord”, the chief deity in Mazdaean religious traditions; distinct from automatically identifying any Jewish or Greek deity by translation. Auramazdā — Old Persian form associated with Achaemenid royal inscriptions; contextual relation to Ahura Mazdā requires distinction of language and witness. daēva — Avestan designation with contested religious valuation and historical development; do not routinely equate with Christian “demon”. Aməša Spəṇta — “beneficent immortal”, a category of Iranian religious entities whose grouping varies between textual strata. saošiiaṇt- — a benefactor or saviour-related form in Avestan traditions; distinguish grammatical number and later eschatological elaborations. frašō.kərəti — eschatological renovation or making-wonderful in later Iranian tradition; chronology of its formulations requires source-specific control. Yasna — a Zoroastrian liturgical corpus and, in lexical use, worship or ritual performance; capitalization depends on whether the corpus or the common noun is intended. Vendīdād / Vidēvdād — transmitted designation of a ritual and legalpurity corpus; separate modern scholarly spelling from historical book titles. 1503

1504 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM Yašt — Avestan hymn or praise-text within a conventionally designated literary corpus. mąθra — Avestan ritual utterance or sacred formula; its semantic field is not identical to Greek logos. barəsman — ritual bundle of twigs or related liturgical implement; identify context before proposing a symbolic equivalent. haoma — plant, pressed ritual substance and personified being according to context; do not conflate all three. fravaši — protective or pre-existing spiritual aspect in Zoroastrian textual traditions, varying by period and usage. činvat- — associated with the bridge of judgement in Iranian eschatological traditions; reconstruct historical stages separately. ātar — Avestan word for fire, also personified in religious contexts; not every reference describes a physical temple altar. daxma — Avestan and later Iranian funerary terminology; distinguish textual use and archaeological structures. Pāzand — Middle Iranian language materials written in Avestan script; a writing practice, not a synonym for Old Avestan. ketiv — the consonantal form transmitted as written in the Masoretic text; distinct from the reading tradition. qere — the reading tradition associated with a Masoretic form; record it explicitly rather than silently replacing ketiv. YHW — divine-name form attested in Elephantine documentation; do not mechanically equate its vocalization with later Hebrew traditions. Yehud — Persian-period province and documentary designation in a particular administrative horizon. TAD — Textbook of Aramaic Documents from Ancient Egypt, the Porten–Yardeni editorial corpus; cite subdivision and locus. Mibtahiah — woman documented by Elephantine Aramaic legal instruments, especially property and marriage records; prosopographical claims require specific documents.

The repertory is comparative and indicative, not a critical etymological dictionary based on the systematic consultation of Bartholomae, Mayrhofer, Chantraine, Beekes, and de Vaan. Term Greek and Latin Iranian Relationship and assessment Geometry Greek geometry: gê (“earth”) + métron (“measure”) av. zam- (“earth”); av. mā- (“measure”); Middle Persian handāzag (“measure”) Av. zam- is cognate with the Greek chthṓn, not with gê, which is of obscure etymology; métron and Av. mā- are cognates. There is no Zoroastrian loanword in the Greek word. There is, however, an Iranian loanword in Arabic: handasa (“geometry, engineering”) comes from Middle Persian handāzag. Architecture gr. architéktōn: archi+ téktōn (“carpenter, builder”); Lat. architectūra av. tašan- (“craftsman, creator”) from the root taš- (“to carve, to form”) Indo-European cognate of téktōn (also Sanskrit takṣan-), not a loanword. The root belongs to the common vocabulary of the craft of shaping wood or stone. Angle Latin angulus; Greek gōnía (“angle, corner”) from gónu (“knee”) av. žnu- (“knee”) Gōnía and av. žnu- are cognates (Sanskrit jānu). Angulus has another root (reconstructed root h₂enk-, “to bend”). Phonetic coincidence with ángaros (Persian messenger), no relation. Philosophy gr. philosophy: phílos + sophia av. mazdā- (“wise”); xratu- There is no formal relationship. The hypothesis “love of Mazda” lacks phonetic and documentary basis. There is a semantic parallel (divine wisdom). Ahura gr. Ὡρομάζης, ant. Persian Auramazdā; Greek transcription of an

GLOSSARY 1515 Term Greek and Latin Iranian Relationship and assessment Mazdā Ὠρομάσδης av. ahura- mazdā- Iranian name; mazdā- is explained as “the one who puts in the mind”. Aeon gr. aiṓn; lat. aevum, aetas av. āyu- (“life, duration”) Indo-European cognate; the Greek concept of “eternity” is its own development. It is unrelated to zruuan- (“time”). Logos gr. logos (légō); Lat. legō without established cognate; related concept: av. mąθra- (“word of power”) No lexical relation; analogy of function in Pahlavi. Sky (of stone) gr. ákmōn (“anvil”); lat. caelum (another root) av. asman- (“stone, sky”) Cognate of ákmōn. The stone sky of Bundahišn is an IranianVedic image. Caelum is not cognate of asman-. Maitreya Sanskrit maitreya- < maitrī < mitra- av. e θ ra-; ant. Persian Miça- Certain lexical relationship within Sanskrit; relationship with the Iranian god, disputed. Paradise gr. paradeisos av. pairidaēza- Demonstrable loan from Iranian to Greek and Hebrew (pardēs). Magician gr. mágos; lat. magus ancient Persian maguš Demonstrable loan; origin of “magic”. Result. Among the proposed terms (geometry, architecture, angle), none is a Zoroastrian loanword in Spanish or Greek. The two actual points of contact are others: Indo-European cognates (tašan- /tektōn, žnu- / gonu) and a loanword in the opposite direction, from Persian to Arabic (handāzag > handasa), which is the Arabic word for “geometry” and “engineering.” The demonstrable Iranian loanwords in the Greek language belong to other fields: paradeisos, magos, ángaros, satrapēs.

Chronological guide to the sixty chapters Historical horizon of analysis, not date of composition of all sources nor dating of the manuscripts. It complements the synchronized chronology of Appendix A (539–332 BCE) and shows the chronological shifts of the comparison. Chapter Dominant chronological horizon I Linguistic contact in the Achaemenid Empire, 6th–4th centuries BCE; the date of each borrowing depends on its first attestation and the stratum of the biblical book that preserves it. II Persian loanwords transmitted through Imperial Aramaic, 6th–4th centuries BCE, and their preservation in biblical works of diverse composition. A word of Achaemenid origin may remain in a Hellenistic text. III Greek translations and reception from the Hellenistic and Roman periods; New Testament of the 1st century CE. The Persian antecedents are earlier: Septuagint, ancient Greek of Daniel and Theodotion do not constitute a single moment of translation. IV The Avesta is an ancient and young composition of disputed chronology; its organisation and transmission were Sasanian, and copies are medieval. The entire Avesta is not dated to the reign of Darius I. V The ancient Avestan linguistic stratum of the Gāthās, without a definitively agreed-upon date; later liturgical transmission and modern edition. Comparison with biblical texts requires dating these independently. VI Young Avestan of the Yašts and Vendīdād: 1560

CHRONOLOGICAL GUIDE TO THE SIXTY CHAPTERS Chapter 1561 Dominant chronological horizon liturgical strata and formation of disputed dates; later written evidence. They are not automatically identified with the documented practice of the 5th century BCE. VII Achaemenid Empire, c. 550–330 BCE; distinguish Darius I (522–486 BCE) from his successors. The documented royal religion and the transmitted Avestan corpus are different sets of evidence. VIII Achaemenid inscriptions from the 6th–4th centuries BCE, with special attention to Darius I (522–486 BCE) and Xerxes I (486– 465 BCE). Each inscription should be placed within its specific reign and on its corresponding substrate, without applying a single formula to all kings. IX Administration of Persepolis under Darius I and Xerxes I. The Fortification and Treasury tablets belong to different sets and dates; their cultic payments do not describe the entirety of later Zoroastrianism. X Achaemenid imperial policy, 6th–4th centuries BCE; local Egyptian, Mesopotamian, and Levantine evidence. The policy of one sovereign does not become a general decree of toler ance for the entire empire. XI Yahwist community of Elephantine, primarily 5th century BCE; destruction of the temple in 410 and petitions in 407, under Darius II (423–404). Not to be confused with Darius I. XII Aramaic chancery formulae and documents

1562 Chapter PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM Dominant chronological horizon from Elephantine of the 5th century BCE; ʾtrwdn belongs to the dossier of Darius II. Modern interpretations of the term should be distinguished from its ancient attestation. XIII Yehud, Samaria, and Idumea during the Achaemenid period and its subsequent transitions. The documentation of each territory requires its own dating; a Hellenistic situation cannot be retroactively projected to the 5th century BCE. XIV Cyrus II and the Persian horizon of Isaiah 44– 45, 6th century BCE; later Jewish expectation and Avestan traditions of disputed dating. Saošyant and messiah are compared by strata, not as simultaneous and already equivalent titles. XV Renewal in Avestan texts from different strata; Hellenistic Jewish apocalyptic literature and Sasanian and later Pahlavi developments. The exposition distinguishes between possible antecedents and later formulations of the doctrine. XVI Iranian resurrection traditions and their testimonies of various dates; Daniel 12 in the critical horizon of the 2nd century BCE; later Jewish and Christian reception. The date of the physical witness does not fix the origin of a belief. XVII Two spirits in Y 30, from the ancient Avestan stratum; Jewish, Persian, and Hellenistic texts; Qumran from a later period. A theology reconstructed from the Bundahišn is not attributed to Darius I.

CHRONOLOGICAL GUIDE TO THE SIXTY CHAPTERS 1563 Chapter Dominant chronological horizon XVIII Vendīdād 19, a young Avestan of disputed composition, and Gospel narratives transmitted in the 1st century CE. The interval between traditions and the dating of their sup ports prevent treating the narratives as contemporary testimonies. XIX Ancient and later Avestan traditions, Second Temple Jewish literature, and Christian reception. The first century CE corresponds to Arsacid Iran and the Roman sphere of early Christianity, not to the empire of Darius I. XX Second Temple, conventionally 515 BCE–70 CE; Qumran in the centuries before 70 CE; Daniel’s final visions in the 2nd century BCE. Not all of this development is concentrated in the Persian period. XXI From Achaemenid antecedents to Hellenistic Judaism and to Christianity of the 1st century CE; Arsacid Iran contemporary with the latter. Successive mediations must be documented at each stage. XXII A long-term comparison: Achaemenid monarchy, Second Temple period, Arsacid and Sasanian Iran, and subsequent transmission. The word Zoroastrianism does not designate a static religious form throughout its history. XXIII Saošyant in Avestan sources from different strata and in later Pahlavi developments; Jesus and Christian reception from the 1st century CE. A late Pahlavi testimony does not establish priority over the gospels. XXIV Iranian Mithras and Roman Mithras: Avestan

1564 Chapter PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM Dominant chronological horizon and Achaemenid traditions versus Roman documentation from the first centuries CE; Early Church from the 1st century. Shared name, cultic organisation and historical transmission are distinguished. XXV Avestan cosmogony and Middle Iranian reworkings; Bundahišn preserved in recensions and manuscripts after the Sasanian period. The discussion does not make a Pahlavi compilation a contemporary document of Cyrus. XXVI Traditions concerning time and Zurvan are attested by sources from various periods, including Late Antiquity and Pahlavi literature. Any priority over a Jewish or Christian text depends on an identifiable early testimony. XXVII Greek logos from ancient philosophy to Hellenistic Judaism and early Christianity; Vedic and Avestan comparativists of their own chro nology. Semantic similarity does not synchronize the compositions. XXVIII Achaemenid, Parthian, Sasanian, and Roman architecture; Mithraea, synagogues, and temples with specific construction dates. The 1st century CE and later buildings should be distinguished from contemporary representations of Darius I. XXIX Greco-Iranian contacts since the Achaemenid period, Hellenistic developments, and Roman reception; Maitreya belongs to an independent Buddhist history. A comparison of the saviour requires specific paths and dates. XXX Mitra and Agni in the Vedic world, Mithra in

CHRONOLOGICAL GUIDE TO THE SIXTY CHAPTERS Chapter 1565 Dominant chronological horizon Iran, and Mithras in Roman times. These are three distinct historical contexts; the Indo-Iranian affinity does not equate to ritual identity with Roman imperial Mithraism. XXXI Four comparative periods: Achaemenid, Hellenistic and Arsacid, Roman, and Sasanian. The first century CE belongs to the contemporary Arsacid and Roman worlds; the Sasanian phase begins in 224 CE XXXII A long-term religious history, from Avestan sources of disputed dating and the Achaemenid religion to Arsacid and Sasanian Iran. The evolution of a term or doctrine must be supported by its successive testimonies. XXXIII Plutarch wrote during the Roman imperial period, 1st–2nd centuries CE; the fires of Lycia and the accounts of Iran have their own local contexts. His testimony may preserve earlier traditions without becoming a contemporary source for Darius I. XXXIV Vedic and Avestan traditions, transmitted liturgical formulae, and the reception of the logos in Hellenistic and Roman periods are discussed. The relative linguistic dating and the dating of the manuscript are recorded separately. XXXV Achaemenid calendars and later evidence from Zoroastrian, Cappadocian, and Jewish systems. Name or month correspondences must be dated before reconstructing a borrowing or a reform. XXXVI Iranian purifications transmitted in Avestan

1566 Chapter PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM Dominant chronological horizon and later sources; Arsacid sphere and Jewish and Christian practices of the Roman period. Modern Parsi manuals are not direct descriptions from the 1st century CE XXXVII A linguistic and historical comparison between Indo-Iranian traditions, Jewish and Christian texts, and Roman and later reception. Christmas, baptism, and resurrection require independent chronologies; no single etymology demonstrates doctrinal borrowing. XXXVIII Royal inscription of Darius I at Behistun, c. 520 BCE, and Aramaic transmission preserved on a later support from Elephantine. The date of the original inscription and that of the Aramaic copy do not coincide. XXXIX Letter of the Elephantine Passover, 419 BCE according to the usual correlation, fifth year of Darius II. The document does not belong to the reign of Darius I nor does it prove without argument a direct order from the king. XL Destruction of the temple in 410 and requests for reconstruction from 407 BCE, under Darius II; distinguish the episodes of the drafting of each letter and its copies. XLI Arsames’ administration in Egypt under Achaemenid rule, mainly the second half of the 5th century BCE. The attribution and dating of each letter must be kept linked to its support. XLII Ezra narrates the Persian period, but the composition of its surviving form and that of its

CHRONOLOGICAL GUIDE TO THE SIXTY CHAPTERS Chapter 1567 Dominant chronological horizon literary documents require independent criticism. Daniel situates narratives in ancient courts and its final visions within the critical horizon of the second century BCE; the Masoretic text used is transmitted by a medieval codex. XLIII Gāthās and Young Avestan of disputed dating; Achaemenid inscriptions datable by reign; liturgical reuse and later copies. The verses of Y 27 or Vd 19 are not automatically dated by the accompanying inscriptions. XLIV Plutarch, 1st–2nd centuries CE, and earlier sources that he quotes or reworks. His account of Magi and dualism belongs to a Roman-era Greek reception, not to an Achaemenid inscription. XLV Iranian funerary practices, classical testimonies, and late Zoroastrian and Parsi documentation. The preserved dakhmas and modern manuals do not, on their own, provide the architectural form of the Achaemenid rite. XLVI Vocabulary from various languages and periods: Old and Young Avestan, Old and Middle Persian, Biblical Hebrew and Aramaic, and Greek. Each cognate, loanword, or semantic comparison should be placed by its earliest attested occurrence. XLVII Achaemenid religion, 6th–4th centuries BCE, and later Arsacid and Sasanian changes. Mazdaism and Zoroastrianism are used with explicit historical definition, without making modern terminology a uniform ancient selfdesignation.

1568 PERSIA AND ANCIENT JUDAISM Chapter Dominant chronological horizon XLVIII Hierarchies and vocabulary of Avestan sources and later Pahlavi developments; Vedic and biblical comparisons of independent dates. The list of forces does not constitute an invariable structure from the Persian period. XLIX Iranian Achaemenid, Parthian, and Sasanian architecture, and later funerary and cultic evidence; Jewish and Western parallels dated by building. Formal similarities require context of construction and circulation. L Dēnkard V, a Pahlavi compilation from after the Sasanian Empire, contains older traditions. Kay Lohrasp belongs to the narrative religious history; he does not become, without evidence, an identifiable historical contemporary of a biblical king. LI Dēnkard IX, a 9th-century CE Pahlavi exegetical summary of earlier Gathic and Nask materials. The date of this exegesis is neither that of the composition of the Gaths nor does it prove their interpretation in the time of Darius. LII From ancient Avestan poetry of disputed date to medieval Persian epic, including the Shahnameh. Medieval literary reception is distinct from the Achaemenid and Sasanian testi monies. LIII Loanwords and equivalents documented at different stages: Old Persian and Imperial Aramaic, Biblical Hebrew, Greek, and Middle Persian. The origin of the word, the date of the text that preserves it, and its local meaning are recorded separately.

CHRONOLOGICAL GUIDE TO THE SIXTY CHAPTERS 1569 Chapter Dominant chronological horizon LIV Buildings from the Arsacid and Sasanian periods, with archaeological dating by complex; political transition of 224 CE. Attribution to a cult requires its own evidence, in addition to the form of the building. LV Greek authors from the Classical to the Imperial and Late periods; multilingual vocabulary of uneven transmission. A late quotation from an ancient author must identify both dates and the chain of preservation. LVI Ex 3, a narrative time prior to the Persian period and a debated literary composition; hypotheses of Achaemenid contextualization and Barnea’s modern reading. The proposed influence should not be confused with an established documentary date for the episode. LVII Elephantine, mainly 5th century BCE; Passover letter of 419, destruction of 410 and petitions of 407, under Darius II. The ʾtrwdn pa pyrus is a preserved testimony of this environment, not a codex from the reign of Darius I. LVIII Dura-Europos in the 2nd–3rd centuries CE, especially its 3rd-century religious buildings. The material coexistence is located on the Roman-Iranian frontier and not within the Achaemenid framework. LIX Mani and the birth of Manichaeism in the 3rd century CE, under the Sasanian dynasty; its expansion and subsequent testimonies. This religious synthesis is several centuries later than 1st-century Christianity. LX Modern Parsi liturgical manuals and their

Addendum. Supplementary Sources This addendum brings together six groups of sources that extend the existing chapters: Avestan tradition, the Babylonian Talmud, Pahlavi purity law, Jewish apocalyptic literature, Elephantine documents and the correspondence of Arsames. Ancient sources, their transmission and modern editions are distinguished. Its references can also be located through the volume’s term concordances and indexes. 1. The Avestan text according to the manuscripts: the Corpus Avesticum Berolinense The Corpus Avesticum Berolinense (CAB), directed by Alberto Cantera at the Institute of Iranian Studies of the Freie Universität Berlin with funding from the German Research Foundation (Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft), is the first attempt to edit the entire Avestan corpus within its ritual context. Unlike the editions by Spiegel, Westergaard, and Geldner, which separated the texts from the ceremon ies, the CAB presents them in the sequence of the liturgy and preserves the ritual in dications from the manuscripts and meta-ritual literature. It is accompanied by the Avestan Digital Archive (ADA), with images of the manuscripts, and a concordance between Geldner’s numbering and that of the CAB. Appendix G reproduces Y. 54–72 from Peterson’s transcription of Geldner; Chapter LX examines modern Parsi reception of Vd 19. The CAB edits texts in their ritual context with its own numbering and correspondences to Geldner. Its critical text is not an individual witness’s reading: attribution to a codex requires identification and consultation of the apparatus or facsimile. See https://cab.geschkult.fu-berlin.de/. 2. The Babylonian Talmud and the Zoroastrian priests The Babylonian Talmud, formed in Sasanian Mesopotamia, is the Jewish corpus that most directly documents coexistence with state Zoroastrianism. Zoroastrian priests appear in it as ḥabbar (plural ḥabbarê) and amgušā, “magician,” and some passages name the Zoroastrian gods. The following three loci are quoted 1581

from the vocalized text of the William Davidson edition (Koren-Steinsaltz) published in Sefaria. a) Sanhedrin 39a: Hormiz and Ahormiz. ‫ ִמ ַּפ ְל ָג ְך‬,‫ ִמ ַּפ ְל ָג ְך ְל ִע יַּלאי ְּד הֹו ְר ִמ יז‬:‫ֲא ַמ ר ֵליּה ָה הּוא ַא ְמ ּגּוָׁש א ְל ַא ֵּמ יָמ ר‬ .‫ְל ַת ַּת אי ְּד ַא הֹו ְר ִמ יז‬ “A certain magician told Ameimar: ‘From your upper half you belong to Hormiz; from your lower half, to Ahormiz.’” Ameimar replied that, if that were so, Ahormiz would not allow Hormiz to urinate in his territory. Hormiz and Ahormiz transcribe the Middle Persian names of Ohrmazd and Ahrimen (Ahura Mazdā and Aŋra Mainyu). For Zoroastrian doctrine, the entire body is a creation of Ohrmazd: the division of the body between two gods conveys, or caricatures, a popular version of dualism, and Ameimar, a Babylonian sage of the late 4th and early 5th centuries, refutes it by reduction to absurdity. b) Shabbat 11a: the ḥabbar in the scale of the dominions. .‫ ַּת ַח ת ׇנְכ ִר י ְו ֹלא ַּת ַח ת ַח ָּב ר‬.‫ַּת ַח ת ִיְׁש ָמ ֵע אל ְו ֹלא ַּת ַח ת ׇנְכ ִר י‬ “Better under Ishmael than under a foreigner; better under a foreigner than under a ḥabbar.” The saying, attributed to Rav (3rd century), continues with the same gradation: better under a ḥabbar than under a Torah scholar, and bet ter under this than under an orphan or a widow. The gradation places the Zoroastrian priest below any foreigner: for the rabbis of Babylon, the authority of the Mazdaean clergy was among the most burdensome. c) Yevamot 63b: the arrival of the ḥabbarê. .‫ ְׁש ָג א ְנַפ ל‬,‫ ֲא תֹו ַח ָּב ֵר י ְל ָב ֶב ל‬:‫ֲא ַמ רּו ֵליּה ְל ַר ִּב י יֹו ָח ָנן‬ .‫ָּג ְזרּו ַע ל ְׁש ֹלָׁש ה ִמ ְּפ ֵני ְׁש ֹלָׁש ה‬ “They told Rabbi Johanan, ‘ The rabbarei have come to Babylon.’ He staggered and fell.” When they told him they accepted bribes, he sat down again. The passage adds: “They decreed three things because of three things”: meat, because the priestly portions were not being given; bathing, because ritual immersion was being neglected; and the exhumation of the dead, because the festivals of the Gentiles were being celebrated. The three decrees touch upon areas regulated by Zoroastrian law: meat, water, and, above all, burial. The Vidēvdād condemns the burial of corpses because they

contaminate the earth (Fargard III), and the exhumation of Jewish dead is the most direct application of this rule. The passage is often associated with the rise of the Sasanian dynasty (224 CE) and the increased power of its clergy. For the overall study: Shai Secunda (The Iranian Talmud, 2014, in the General Bibliography) sets out the method for reading Bavli in its Sasanian context; Yaakov Elman (2007) studies the accommodation and resistance of the Babylonian sages to Middle Persian legal culture; and Yishai Kiel (2016) compares the sexual ethics of Bavli with the Pahlavi doctrine of marriage between relatives (xwēdōdah). 3. The law of purity in Pahlavi: the Šāyast nē šāyast and the Pahlavi Vīdēvdād The Šāyast nē šāyast, “The Permitted and the Forbidden,” is a Pahlavi treatise on ritual law from the late Sasanian period, probably after 623 CE (Vahman, Encyclopaedia Iranica). Its first chapters deal with the degrees of sin and its expiation (I), defilement by a corpse and the rite of the sag-dīd, the gaze of the dog (II), the menstruating woman (III), and the sacred cord and shirt (IV). It was edited by J.C. Tavadia (1930); F.M. Kotwal edited the supplementary texts (1969), and E.W. West translated it into English in volume 5 of the Sacred Books of the East (1880). Chapter III begins thus in West’s translation: “The clothing of a menstruating woman that she takes for her use is defiled.” The rules that follow regulate the room, the tapestries and cushions, the water, and the food that the woman touches. It is the same area regulated by Leviticus and Numbers (Masoretic text, Leningrad Codex): ‫ְו ִא ָּׁש ה ִּכ י־ִת ְה ֶיה ָזָב ה ָּד ם ִיְה ֶיה ֹזָב ּה ִּב ְב ָׂש ָר ּה ִׁש ְב ַע ת ָיִמ ים ִּת ְה ֶיה ְב ִנָּד ָת ּה‬ ‫ְו ָכ ל־ַה ֹּנֵגַע ָּב ּה ִיְט ָמ א ַע ד־ָה ָע ֶר ב‬ “When a woman has a discharge, and the discharge from her flesh is blood, she shall be in her uncleanness for seven days, and whoever touches her shall be un clean until evening” (Lev 15:19). ‫ַה ֹּנֵג ַע ְּב ֵמ ת ְל ָכ ל־ֶנֶפ ׁש ָא ָד ם ְו ָט ֵמ א ִׁש ְב ַע ת ָיִמ ים‬ “Whoever touches a dead body of any person will be unclean for seven days” (Numbers 19:11). The overlap in subject matter is striking: the corpse, menstrual blood, contagion by contact, time limits, and purification. The texts, however, belong to very

different periods. The final redactions of Leviticus and Numbers are usually placed in the Persian period; the Mishnah (treatises Nidda and Ohalot) dates from around 200 CE, and the Shayast ne Shayast is late Sasanian. The comparison documents parallel systems of purity and their legal development, not a direct dependence. Mahnaz Moazami (2014) edited and translated the Vidēvdād Pahlavi with commentary; her edition shows how Sasanian jurists interpreted the Avestan purity laws translated in Appendix E. 4. Jewish Apocalypticism: The Fate of the Dead Chapter XLVI (§ 7) compares the Jewish resurrection with the final Mazdaean renewal. Three Jewish texts from different dates give the complete sequence: an intermediate place for souls, the restitution of bodies by the earth, and the judgement. “These cavities have been created for this purpose: that the spirits of the souls of the dead may gather in them, yea, that all the souls of the children of men may gather here [...] until the day of their judgement” (1 Hen 22,3; Book of the Watchers, 3rd century BCE; English translation by R. H. Charles). “The earth will give up those who sleep in it, and the dust those who dwell in it in silence, and the secret chambers will give up the souls that were entrusted to them. And the Most High will appear on the throne of judgment” (4 Ezra 7:32–33, c. 100 CE; King James Version, 2 Esdras). “For the earth will then surely give back the dead that it now receives to preserve them” (2 Bar 50:2, c. 100 CE; English version by R. H. Charles). The sequence has a close parallel in Bundahišn 34 (Agostini and Thrope, 177– 182), where the bodies are restored before the molten metal test. Chronology weighs against a simple derivation: the Bundahišn dates from the 9th – 10th centuries CE, and the Book of the Watchers from the 3rd century BCE. Jason M. Silverman (Persepolis and Jerusalem, 2012) proposes studying Iranian influence on apocalyptic literature not as a borrowing of isolated motifs, but through the means of transmission, both oral and written, and through a hermeneutics of revelation shared in the Persian Empire.

historiographical debate: Winston and Barr Two articles establish the terms of the debate that runs through this book. David Winston (“The Iranian Component in the Bible, Apocrypha, and Qumran: A Review of the Evidence,” 1966) reviewed the coincidences between Iranian and Jewish texts and argued that this component existed and should be taken seriously. James Barr (“The Question of Religious Influence: The Case of Zoroastrianism, Judaism, and Christianity,” 1985) discussed what it means to speak of religious influence and what evidence it requires. The two positions correspond to the two poles of the Critical Matrix of Hypotheses (Appendix D). Achaemenid Aramaic documents: Bactria and the letters of Arsames The Bactrian Aramaic documents from the Khalili collection, published by Joseph Naveh and Shaul Shaked (2012), comprise thirty leather documents and eighteen notched wooden accounting tablets, written in official Aramaic in the fourth century BCE. The tablets are dated to the third year of Darius III; a leather supply list to the seventh year of Alexander; and another document mentions Bessus, the usurper of the Persian throne. They are the easternmost evidence of the Achaemenid Aramaic chancery, the same administrative tradition as the letters of Arsames (chapter XLI) and the Aramaic letters of Ezra (4:8–6:18; 7:12–26). For Arsames’ letters, the current reference edition is that of Christopher J. Tuplin and John Ma (2020), in three volumes.
